case_summary.text: Sum paid to eliminate competition entailing advantage for specified time was capital in nature, says ITAT

IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure

IT: Where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietary concern, and in terms of agreement, company did not acquire copyright, but only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, license fee paid would be a revenue expenditure

IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Non-compete fee paid to director on his retirement to restrict him from sharing his experience was revenue exp.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made payment to 'S' and said payment had not been made for acquiring a brand name, but for facilitating acquisition of brand name, which in turn, made substantial improvement in earning capacity of assessee's business, expenditure incurred by assessee company for payment made to 'S' was a revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX: Where assessee paid a non-compete fee to restrain another party from operating in same business segment, such payment merely protected or enhanced assessee’s business profitability and facilitated more efficient conduct of business, and though it could confer an enduring advantage, same was not in capital field and did not result in creation of any new asset or accretion to profit-earning apparatus; therefore, non-compete fee was allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1)

INCOME TAX : Where assessee entered into an agreement with Pfizer to terminate licensing, distribution and supply rights granted earlier to it in exchange of an agreed consideration and claimed termination charges paid to Pfizer as revenue expenditure, since termination of agreement with Pfizer was an agreement for purchase of assets and amount paid under this agreement was on account of purchase price of said assets, charges paid by assessee to Pfizer were in nature of capital expenditure and not in nature of revenue expenditure

IT : Where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietory concern, in view of fact that in terms of agreement only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, however, it had not acquired copyright itself, license fee paid by assessee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where in view of non-compete agreement entered into by assessee with a company from which it acquired business, non-compete fee paid by assessee would form part of initial outlay on acquisition of business, Assessing Officer was justified in treating said non-compete fee as capital expenditure and disallowing same under section 37(1)

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect against High Court ruling that where assessee made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Non-compete fee paid to holding co. to do chit fund business in northern Telangana was a revenue exp.

IT: Where assessee claimed onetime consolidated fees paid to its holding company, GRM, for use of trademark as revenue expenditure, since same had an enduring benefit and was applicable till assessee ceased to be subsidiary of GRM, Assessing Officer was justified treating same as capital expenditure

TRANSFER PRICING : Where enduring benefit is not only criteria to decide nature and character of an expenditure and necessary test is whether it is for acquisition of any capital asset or for purpose of carrying on business, deriving revenue from it and marketing support services cannot however be considered as acquisition of a capital asset since support services are for purpose of sale of products manufactured by assessee and, therefore, it is clearly established that it is for efficient running of business and deriving revenues therefrom thus, in such circumstances, fees paid by assessee for marketing support services rendered by IBM, is clearly revenue in nature and is allowable as deduction under section 37.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, ITES provider, had made payment to its Indian counterpart for acquiring part of its business relating to debt collection service since assessee was not in debt collection service business before acquiring said business, expenditure incurred for acquiring completely new business set up was income generation tool and, hence, capital in nature

INCOME TAX : Where non-compete fees was paid to individuals who had experience in business of consultancy for not to engage themselves in similar kind of business activities for a period of 3 years and such consideration was independent and not part of cost of acquisition of business paid to shareholders, payment of such fee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Sum paid by bank for installation of application software which enhanced efficiency of operations was revenue exp.

III INCOME TAX : Expenditure such as professional fees, legal charges, due diligence fees etc. which resulted in acquisitions should form part of cost of investment i.e., capital expenditure while expenditure incurred in respect of failed acquisitions would be revenue expenditure as no capital asset came into existence

IT : Where compensation received by assessee on loss of agency business was not from person to whom payment was made for securing said agency business, expenses incurred for securing agency business was capital expenditure while compensation received was revenue in nature
Dual treatment: Exp. on expansion of business was a revenue exp. even if it was capitalized in books
IT : Where assessee made payment as non-compete fee for purpose of business of assessee, expenditure was on revenue count
Legal exp. incurred on feasibility report preparation for acquisition of a new brand was revenue exp.
Fees for due diligence of target entities to assist in their main stream businesses is allowable as revenue exp.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee entered into an agreement with Pfizer to terminate licensing, distribution and supply rights granted earlier to it in exchange of an agreed consideration and claimed termination charges paid to Pfizer as revenue expenditure, since termination of agreement with Pfizer was an agreement for purchase of assets and amount paid under this agreement was on account of purchase price of said assets,
Exp. incurred by assessee on tenancy rights during acquisition of running business was in nature of revenue exp.

IT : Where non-compete fee paid by assessee was for purpose of its business and it did not entail any enduring benefit to assessee in its business, payment of such fee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Expenditure incurred by assessee company on travelling related with mergers and acquisitions of entities engaged in similar business, was to be treated as capital expenditure and as part of cost of improvement
IT : Expenditure on training of employees would be revenue expense
Brokerage, commission or service charges paid to facilitate brand name acquisition allowable as revenue exp.: HC
Sum paid to clear title of hotel building for new business wasn't revenue exp; ITAT upheld penalty

IT : Where legal expenses incurred by assessee was to ensure proper acquisition of brand which was in existing line of assessee's business and same was in nature of consultancy, therefore said expenditure was to be treated as revenue in nature
IT: It is only if non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature, can be said to be a capital expenditure; payment of restrictive covenant is revenue expenditure

IT: In case of assessee, an event management company, expenditure incurred on purchase of fire detection alarm and traffic barrier would be treated as revenue expenditure but purchase of motor car would be capital expenditure
Sum paid in settlement for acquiring possession of business premises was to be treated as capital exp.
Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under sec. 37(1): SC
Sum incurred by Audio Co. to acquire copyrights of sound tracks is revenue in nature
Sum incurred by coaching institute on scholarship to attract more students allowed as revenue exp.
Payment made for taking legal advice for purchase of business division is a capital exp.
Exp. incurred for identifying potential healthcare technology cos. for acquisition is revenue in nature: ITAT
Sum incurred to run business smoothly, and not to bring new asset into existence, is a revenue exp.: HC

IT : Where payment was made to tenants to vacate hotel premises to convert it in a shopping complex, since expenditure incurred by assessee was in respect of making asset fit for utilization for new business, such expenditure would be capital expenditure; where assessee claimed said expenditure as revenue expenditure, penalty under section 271(1)(C) was to be imposed
Payment of consultancy fees to carry on business more efficiently and profitably is a revenue exp.
INCOME TAX : Where tenor of non compete agreement was only for 18 months, assessee did not derive any enduring benefit; payment effected by assessee was to be treated as a revenue expenditure
Royalty paid for technical know-how to set-up new business held as capital expenditure

IT : Where assessee transferred its manufacturing unit to SDPL which converted it into a profit making unit, higher compensation paid by assessee to SDPL subsequently to regain ownership and control of said profit making unit amounted to capital expenditure not eligible for deduction under section 37(1)
IT : Amount of fee paid to Ex-Managing Director on his retirement as non-compete fee is a revenue expenditure
IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where assessee paid non-compete fees to a company on termination of agreement, since by paying said fees, assessee acquired rights which not only gave it enduring benefit but also protected assessee's business against competition, impugned non-compete fees paid by assessee would be capital in nature, however, it would be an intangible asset on which assessee was entitled to claim depreciation
Non-compete fee allowable as revenue exp. as it didn’t result in any enduring benefit to assessee in business

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company offering training courses in field of financial services took over business of ‘W’, who was also carrying on similar activities, for a consideration which was claimed by assessee-company as revenue expenditure - Revenue, however, treated it as of capital nature - Whether essence of agreement being taking over of business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, said expenditure fell in category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

HEADNOTE: section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-capital or revenue expenditure-assessee, carrying on business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in licensed public cinema theatres, paid rs. 1,50,000 to a rival to induce the latter not to compete with it for nine years-whether payment was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1)-held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

On reference, the assessee-company contended that since the expenditure was incurred for acquiring the film shorts, it should be taken to have been expended for acquiring stock-in-trade of the assessee's business :

HELD: The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11] Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

HELD: It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

and the net revenue that will be collected by the State will be an attempt on public interest. It is of utmost importance that there should be as many bidders as possible in such an auction, so that maximum revenue could be obtained by the State. Purchasing of rival bidders, therefore, on the face of it, will be harmful to public interest and the very object of conducting the auction gets defeated or diluted when intending bidders are sought to be kept away by one of the bidders. In the instant case, the assessee had purchased a rival bidder so that he could not come forward to participate in the auction. This was contrary to public interest as well as public welfare and, therefore, opposed to public policy. The payment made which, on the face of it was contrary to public policy could not be recognized as a valid payment for the purpose of the Act. Whatever is expended to obtain an asset used in a trade or business is a capital expenditure; however, if the expenditure is incurred in the course of the business to earn the current income, prima facie it may be a revenue expenditure.

The test for determining whether an expenditure is capital or revenue, varies depending upon the nature of the business acquired. When the period of the business and the duration during which the right to carry on the trade is itself limited, the elimination of a rival from competing, while obtaining the right to trade has nothing to do with the expenditure incurred in the course of carrying on the trade. The expenditure here is incurred at the threshold to obtain the right to vend liquor. It was in the nature of investment made to set up the business and, therefore, should be treated as a capital investment. The expenditure incurred in the instant case was incurred once and for all with a view to bring into existence the asset or the advantage of obtaining the privilege to vend liquor for one year. The entire business itself was of one year's duration. The expenditure incurred to obtain this right or privilege cannot be just treated as expenditure incurred only for one year because the very business asset had a life of one year only. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure could not be accepted.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the Revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1951 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 1999-2000 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns, engaged in similar business as going concern, for certain consideration - In addition, assessee undertook to pay certain amount per month to said concerns for a period of 15 years in consideration of non-compete obligation undertaken by them and claimed said payments as revenue expenditure - Whether said payments, having been made for eliminating competition in same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years, were of capital nature and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961 - capital or revenue expenditure-assessee-company hpg and two other companies ngp and wg engaged in the same line of business were running in loss as total installed capacity of product manufactured by them was far in excess of demand-under tripartite agreement among them to save their industry from possible annihilation, ngp agreed to withdraw from business for five years in consideration of rs. 25 lakhs to be paid to it by hpg and wg in prescribed instalments-whether rs. 2,50,000 paid by hpg to ngp as first instalment was capital expenditure-held, on facts, yes

FACT: HPG, the assessee-company and two other companies, viz., WG and NGP, were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling wired and figured glass products. They entered into a tripartite agreement in which it was noticed that the installed capacity in the country for making such products being far in excess of the demand, all these companies were incurring losses and that in order to save this industry from further heavy losses and possible annihilation, it would be in the common interest of these three companies if one of them, viz., NGP, did not make or sell these products for a period of five years. In the interest of commercial expediency, it was agreed that in return, HPG and WG would pay Rs. 12,50,000 each to NGP in instalments as set out in the agreement. The agreement was to remain in force for five years, unless terminated earlier by consent of all the three parties in writing. In pursuance of this agreement, HPG paid a sum of Rs. 2,50,000 to NGP in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1970-71 and claimed it as a revenue deduction. The ITO, however, treated the amount as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal eventually accepted the assessee's claim.

On reference:

HELD: If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

FACT: The assessee-company was in the business of finance. During the relevant assessment year, it purchased the business of computer software along with certain assets and liabilities belonging to LSI.

During the short period of its existence, LSI did some preliminary work in developing some technical knowledge basis of software in banking sector. Before formal takeover of LSI, four directors of LSI entered into agreement, called restrictive covenant with the assessee agreeing not to carry on the business of computer software development and marketing and other related business for a period of five years in consideration of cash paid by the assessee. For the relevant assessment year, the assessee claimed the amount paid to the directors as deduction from its income. The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure and added it to the income returned by the assessee for the reason that the payment was made to avail exclusive rights of the services of professionals for a period of five years and to ward off the competition and, therefore, the payment was distinctly in nature of capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the payment was not capital in nature, but revenue in nature.

On appeal by the revenue :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had drawn an inference that the master mind of the company was its managing director who paid the amount to the four persons so that the assessee-company could achieve benefit by taking over LSI and enlisting the services of the professionals to the assessee-company after pre-empting the availability of their services to any rivals in the field. The Commissioner (Appeals) further drew an inference from the written note filed on behalf of the assessee that the restrictive covenants were only negative agreements in the sense that the four experts were prevented from working for others in the field of software for a period of five years. Such negative agreement did not bring into existence any assets for the assessee, not to speak of any asset of enduring advantage that justified treatment of expenditure-in-question as capital expenditure. The four recipients were under no obligation to work for the assessee-company as per the terms of restrictive covenant agreements, and, hence, the question of any advantage of enduring benefit accruing to the assessee as a result of those agreements, did not arise. The purpose of the restrictive agreements was to prevent others, including recipients, from gaining any advantage from their expertise in the field of software. The inference neither had been controverted by the department nor any other material was brought on record from which the observations of the Commissioner (Appeals) could be established otherwise. [Para 12]

Any advantage derived by the assessee from the services of the four persons was unrelated to the restrictive covenant agreements. Their recruitment into the company was like any other recruitment effort of the company and they were at liberty not to work for the company and work elsewhere in other lines of vocation. Apart from these four, the assessee recruited scores of other software professionals and there was no difference between the recruitment of the four from the others. Thus, when once the covenant agreements and subsequent recruitment of these four persons were considered to be unconnected events, any advantage derived by the assessee out of their services could not be linked up with restrictive covenant agreements. Hence, the amounts paid by the assessee as a result of the agreements could not be treated as capital expenditure on the ground that the company derived any enduring advantage out of such services. [Para 13]

Further, it was clarified before the Commissioner (Appeals) that in LSI they could not develop any concrete product but, only did some preliminary work in developing technical knowledge basis for Banking Sector and that company earned some income from providing consultancy services and customized software to clients. The Principal Promoter of the assessee-company, managing director’s expertise in the field of finance as a contributory factor to the development of these products was as crucial as the contribution of the four persons and other software specialists recruited by the assessee-company. Therefore, in view of all these facts and circumstances, it was clear that organizational, financial, managerial and intellectual resources were provided by the assessee-company that largely contributed to development of the software products which sustained the assessee-company in spite of dismal performance of the finance wing. The success of the software division of the company, therefore, could not be attributed to the four persons only, much less to the negative character of the restrictive covenant agreements. Therefore, it was clearly established that the amount paid by the assessee was not in the nature of capital expenditure but in the nature of revenue expenditure. The Com- missioner (Appeals) had discussed the decisions relied upon by the Assessing Officer as well as the assessee and then only came to the conclusion that the expenditures incurred by the assessee were revenue in nature. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2009-10 - Assessee purchased one division of 'N' chemicals by way of slump sale - Assessee paid certain amount as non-compete fee which represented difference in value of tangible and intangible assets and lump sum amount paid for taking over business - It was found that on account of payment of non-compete fee, seller was restrained from carrying on similar type of business for three years - Whether since payment of non-compete fee resulted in enduring benefit to assessee, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure; it was capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure  IT : Payment made for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division, was to be treated as capital expenditure  IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where assessee paid commission on export sales at same rate at which it had been paid by seller of business earlier, disallowance made by Assessing Officer taking a view that a part of commission payment was excessive, was to be deleted  IT : Foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by assessee in respect of outstanding foreign currency term loan was to be allowed as business loss  IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business  IT : Where Assessing Officer made disallowance in respect of dividend income by relying upon Rule 8D of Income-tax Rules, 1962, since said rule was applicable for assessment year 2008-09 while assessment year under consideration was 2007-08, impugned disallowance was to be deleted

FACT: The assessee purchased one division of 'N' Chemicals which was transferred to the assessee by way of slump sales. The assessee treated the same as capital expenditure in the books of account and claimed depreciation on said amount. For the purpose of computing total income under the Act, the assessee treated Rs. 6.80 crores as non-compete fee on the basis of the value of the intangibles determined by the valuers.

The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure by holding that the amount claimed as fee for non-compete was nothing but goodwill of the business.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, took a view that by entering into a restrictive covenant the assessee had warded off a potential competition from the transferor. He thus held that amount paid as non-compete fee was to be regarded as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: In the instant case the non-compete fee although identified separately by the valuer but it was inbuilt in the lump sum consideration. The assessee split the lump sum consideration in various tangible and intangible assets on the basis of report of the valuers which was not doubted either by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the present case, the only dispute was relating to the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores, the said amount was difference in the value of tangible/intangible assets of the going concern which was purchased by the assessee and the lump sum amount paid for taking over the business, so it was in the nature of the goodwill and since the assessee was having the enduring benefit particularly when there was a covenant on the seller for not to run the similar type of business for three years. Therefore, the said amount cannot be considered as revenue in nature as has been held by the Commissioner (Appeals). Since the amount under consideration was in excess of the value of tangible and intangible asset and was a part of the lump sum consideration for acquiring the business, so it was a goodwill. [Para 30]

Therefore, by considering the totality of the facts, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside on this issue and the view taken by the Assessing Officer that the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores was nothing but goodwill of the business and a capital expenditure is upheld.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether an expenditure incurred on warding off competition in business from a rival dealer will constitute a capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure, it is not necessary that non-compete fee is paid to create monopoly rights - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

On second appeal :

on stand alone basis could not be accepted. [Para 97]

Coming to the nature of expenditure in question, it can be seen from the various tests laid down in the earlier decided cases that broadly the basic tests to determine the nature of an expenditure remain the same even in the context of a modern situation and those tests include the test of initial outlay of the business, the aim and object of the expenditure, enduring benefit test and the test of fixed and circulating capital. [Para 122] Applying the aforementioned tests to the facts of the instant case, it may be stated that the so-called 'non-compete agreement' was part & parcel of the entire transaction. The assessee had acquired a business concern in India with its outlay (more particularly described elsewhere in this order) and the entire transaction was outlined in the MoU dated 4-11-1996. The aggregate amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was determined as the total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets referred to in article 1 and the Ballabgarh land and building referred to in article 2. The purchase price itself stated that the amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was to be paid as total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets and Ballabgarh land and building. [Para 123]

It can be seen that non-compete agreement was made Appendix 'M' to the agreement dated 2-11-1997 and was, thus, part and parcel of the main agreement, the signing and execution whereof was a condition precedent. [Para 124.1]

It could be mentioned here that the total purchase price of Rs. 52.5 crores envisaged in MoU vide clause 3 included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores which was to be paid for non-compete agreement. The other sum of Rs. 49.85 crores was to be paid in respect of various assets. If these two sums were aggregated, then the total amount would come to Rs. 52.5 crores which was the agreed purchase price. The assessee-company was incorporated for the purpose of effectuating the transactions agreed in the MoU. The purpose of the assessee-company for which it was incorporated was that 'Tecumseh USA', being a leading global compressor manufacturer, was interested in purchasing compressor related operations of Whirlpool India for the Indian compressor market. Thus, the very intention and purpose was to establish business in India by taking over the compressor and related operations of Whirlpool India in India. The non-compete agreement was part and parcel of the whole transaction and could not be treated to be a separate transaction. [Para 125]

The case of the assessee would fall under the test which describes that if the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for the expansion of the business or a substantial replacement of the equipment, then it would fall under the capital expenditure. It was not an expenditure incurred while the business was being carried on. Though it had been the contention of the assessee that non-compete agreement was executed subsequent to the date of main agreement, yet such contention of the assessee could not be accepted as in the main agreement itself the non-compete agreement was appended as 'M' without which the transaction was not complete, as by including the amount paid for non-compete agreement the purchase price as stated in MoU could be arrived at. [Para 126]

The incurring of expenditure also brought an enduring benefit to the assessee if the same was examined from the proposition of law laid down in the case of Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC) wherein their Lordships have considered the period of five years as providing an enduring advantage to the assessee irrespective of the fact that the payment was to be made annually. [Para 127]

It is well-settled that expenditure incurred on warding off competition in the business even to a rival dealer will constitute capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure it is not necessary that non-compete fee be paid to create monopoly rights. [Para 129]

In view of aforesaid, it was to be held that the expenditure of Rs. 2.65 crores claimed by the assessee in pursuance of non-compete agreement dated 10-7-1997 was capital expenditure, the deduction of which could not be granted to the assessee as revenue expenditure. [Para 131]

EDITOR'S NOTE

Following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Punjab State Industrial Development Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT[1997] 225 ITR 792 / 93 Taxman 5, it was to be held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee on increasing its authorized share capital was a capital expenditure and could not be allowed as deduction.

Further R being MD of the assessee must have been getting salaries for the services rendered by him in the past and question of any amount being assigned for such past services did not arise. There was no scope for recognising the past services of R and to allocate any amount out of the impugned amount given to R. The assessee-company had not brought anything on record to show that R acquired special expertise or experience in the bus-body building activities. It was not the case of the assessee that R had got any special training in India or abroad in the bus-body building operation or he himself had made any research or was personally involved in such activities. If these were the facts, then this was not a ground for giving the amount to R. The assessee was running in losses and even if some salary was being given to R, a sum of Rs. 1.29 crores shall not be in any manner near to the amounts R would have earned as profit from company or would have got emoluments to that extent. What was the criterion of assessee-company to arrive at this figure of Rs. 1.29 crores was not explained.

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

In the facts of that case, this Court held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for the better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should therefore be treated as revenue expenditure. Consequently, the appeal by the assessee was allowed and the question of law answered in the affirmative and against the revenue. [Para 23.2]

■ The next case that is adverted to is the case of CIT v. Madras Auto Service (P.) Ltd. [1998] 99 Taxman 575 (SC)/[1998] 233 ITR 468 (SC). In this case, the respondent assessee, a tenant, had incurred expenditure on demolition and construction of a new building which was to vest in the landlord. Assessee in lieu of incurring the actual cost of construction was entitled to use the premises for a period of 39 years at a reduced rent. The entire capital cost of construction was claimed by the assessee as revenue expenditure on the ground that the assessee had not acquired any new asset or such expenditure did not result in any enduring advantage to the assessee in the capital field. The above stand of the assessee was accepted by the ITAT and the High Court. When revenue came up in appeal before this Court, it was held that right from inception, the building was of the ownership of the lessor. Therefore, by spending this money, the assessee did not acquire any capital asset. The only advantage which the assessee derived by spending the money was that it got the lease of a new building at a low rent. From the business point of view, therefore, the assessee got the benefit of reduced rent. The High Court has, therefore, rightly considered this as obtaining a business advantage. The expenditure is, therefore, to be treated as revenue expenditure. [Para 24]

■

Having adverted to the relevant case laws, one may now examine the nature and character of non-compete fee; whether payment of non-compete fee is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure. Non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. It may be by way of a written agreement or by an oral understanding. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. Purpose of non-compete payment is to give a head start to the business of the payer. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the business of the payer or for enhancing the profitability of the business of the payer by insulating the payer from competition. [Para 25]

■

Thus non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance the profitability of the business, thereby facilitating the carrying on of the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, by restricting a competitor in business, is not in the capital field. [Para 26]

■

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates in carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring of such expenditure. [Para 27]

■

The non-compete compensation from the stand point of the payer of such compensation is so paid in anticipation that absence of a competition from the other party may secure a benefit to the party paying the compensation. However, there is no certainty that such benefit would accrue. Notwithstanding such an arrangement, the payer (assesee) may still not achieve the desired result. In so far the present case is concerned, on account of payment of non-compete fee, the assessee had not acquired any new business and there is no addition to the profit making apparatus of the assessee. The assets remained the same. The expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of the same business. Further, there is no complete elimination of competition. Such payment made by the appellant to L&T did not create a monopoly of the appellant over the business of electronic products/ equipments. Payment was made to L&T only to ensure that the appellant operated the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment made to L&T cannot, therefore, be considered to be for acquisition of any capital asset or towards bringing into existence a new profit earning apparatus. [Para 28]

■

That being the position, it is opined that payment made by the appellant to L&T as non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1). [Para 29]

■

Consequently, the impugned judgment and order of the Delhi High Court dated 5-11-2012 passed in Income Tax Appeal No. 492/2012 is hereby set aside. The question framed is thus answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 30]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Non-compete fee - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one on revenue account - Held, yes - Assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with one 'U' for a period of 5 years - It paid a certain sum as non-compete fee to 'U' and claimed same as revenue expenditure - 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to clientele and pricing of products; as a business proposition, assessee entered into non-compete agreement - Whether payment was in respect of performing of business of assessee and, thus, expenditure was on revenue account and not on capital account - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee made payment as non-compete fee for purpose of business of assessee, expenditure was on revenue count

FACT: Facts

•

The Court granted a scheme of amalgamation of some companies with the assessee-company.

•

The assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with 'U' former chairman and managing director of the amalgamating companies and paid a certain sum to 'U' by way of non-compete fee.

•

It claimed said amount as a revenue expenditure but did not write off same in its books of account.

•

The Assessing Officer found that non-compete agreement had increased the assessee's market presence and improved its potential to have better results in the market; the payment made over a period of more than five years once was for procuring an enduring benefit to the business. Consequently, he held that the expenditure was in the capital field and disallowed said claim.

•

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the decision of the assessing authority.

•

The Tribunal, by a cryptic order, rejected the assessee's claim.

Argument of assessee

•

The agreement entered into between the assessee with 'U' would clearly show that the expenditure was only on the revenue account.

Argument of revenue

•

When the assessee had not written off the said expenditure in its accounts and the amount paid was to ward off any competition in the business of the assessee, the expenditure made was only a capital expenditure.

Issue involved

•

Whether non-compete fee paid to the ex-managing director was a revenue or a capital expenditure?

HELD: •

As far as the question as to whether an expenditure could be a capital expenditure or revenue expenditure is concerned, the concept that the expenditure yielding an advantage of enduring nature would be only a capital expenditure, has been fine-tuned, that even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one of revenue account. [Para 14]

•

It is not denied by the revenue that 'U' was the chairman and managing director of some of the companies which got merged with the assessee-company. 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to the clientele and the products, including the pricing of the products. By a process of amalgamation, the assessee had acquired the business of the amalgamating companies. However, for the fruitful exercise of its business as a business proposition, the assessee thought it fit to enter into a non-compete agreement with a person who had the knowledge of the entire operations, so as to get the full yield of the amalgamated company's business. In that context, rightly, the assessee took a commercial decision to pay non-compete fee to 'U' and going by the decision of the Apex Court, that the payment was in respect of the performing of the business of the assessee, it was to be held that the expenditure is only on revenue account and not on capital account. In the circumstances, the order of the Tribunal was set aside. [Para 19]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1972-73 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of manufacture of ink - One A was managing director of assessee-company for about 18 years and left it on 31-10-1971 - To exploit his experience A decided to manufacture and sell ink - A partnership firm consisting of his wife and two daughters, was formed - All preparations such as Government's approval, opening of and operation of bank account, advertisement, etc. were made - On 14-2-1972 assessee entered into an agreement with said firm whereby it agreed to close down its business and assessee in consideration thereof agreed to pay a sum of Rs. 1 lakh to it - As agreed payment was made, A's firm was dissolved and A also left India - Whether on facts payment made by assessee brought into existence an enduring benefit and, thus, it was an expenditure of capital in nature - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture of ink. One A was the managing director of the assessee for about 18 years and left it on 31-10-1971. Thereafter he entertained the idea of utilising his experience with the assessee in the manufacture and sale of ink. A partnership firm was formed consisting of his wife and two daughters of A for the purpose of manufacture and sale of writing ink. All the preparations such as industrial licence, an industrial site, opening of bank account, advertisements, etc., were made. Thereafter, an agreement was entered into on 14-2-1972 between the assessee and the partnership whereby the assessee agreed to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 to the firm by way of compensation and firm agreed to discontinue the aforesaid business forthwith and also agreed to not to commence said business at any time within a period of five years. As per agreement the aforesaid amount was paid to the firm and the firm was closed down. For the assessment year 1972-73 the assessee claimed that the aforesaid payment was revenue expenditure, deductible in computing its income. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim and held that the expenditure was incurred by the assessee once and for all to ward off competition in the business and also with a view to bring into existence an enduring benefit or advantage to the assessee with no competition whatsoever. Thus, the expenditure was an item of capital expenditure. On second appeal, the Tribunal also held it as an expenditure of capital nature.

On reference:

HELD: It is now well settled that the character of expenditure will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case not by the application of rigid tests, but by deriving support from many aspects of the whole lot of circumstances and the ultimate answer would depend upon a commonsense appreciation of the guiding features.

In the instant case, the assessee had established a good reputation and market for writing inks by the manufacture and sale of ink, under the brand name 'quink'. In the agreement, there was a recognition of the formation and establishment of the partnership by A for the manufacture and sale of writing inks, similar to those made and sold by the assessee and it being a powerful potential competitor.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 - Whether payment which frees an assessee from liability to make recurring revenue payments is revenue expenditure; though such benefit may be of an enduring nature but if it does not create any asset, then it cannot be treated as capital expenditure - Held, yes - During relevant year, promoters of a company Tata-IBM bifurcated its business activities and framed a separate entity (assessee-company) - Various assets of erstwhile Tata-IBM were agreed to be transferred to assessee for certain consideration - Assessee made payments on account of transfer of certain employees to it and on account of transfer of data base of domestic business and claimed same as revenue expenditure - However, Assessing Officer held that transfer of employees and database to assessee was to be considered as transfer of valuable asset giving an enduring advantage to it over a long period of time and, therefore, expenditure incurred for said transfer could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Admittedly, by making payment for getting domestic customer database, assessee had only got right to use that database; company which had provided such database was not precluded from using such database and, hence, expenditure incurred was for use of database and not for its acquisition - As regards payment made for transfer of human skill, that expenditure had been incurred to save expenses on training and on recruitment of employees which were under revenue field and, thus, it freed assessee from liability to make recurring revenue payments - Whether in view of above, payment on both counts was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: Tata-IBM company was jointly promoted by Tata and IBM. During the financial year 1997-98, the two promoters agreed to bifurcate the business activities of the company into separate entities, viz., the assessee-company and Tata-IBM company. As per the agreement, various assets of the erstwhile Tata-IBM were transferred to the assessee for a certain consideration. As mutually agreed upon, the assessee made payments on account of transfer of certain employees to the assessee and on account of transfer of the database of the domestic business, and claimed deduction of same as revenue expenditure. In respect of the value of data base, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee itself had amortized the above expenditure over a period of 5 years in its books of account. According to him, the benefit that accrued to the assessee was of an enduring nature. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that the payment had been made towards acquisition of a capital asset and, therefore, such expenditure was not allowable as a revenue expenditure. In respect of the value of personnel transferred, the Assessing Officer concluded that the employees transferred to the assessee were to be considered as valuable assets, which would give an enduring advantage to it over a long period of time, and in case such employees were not viewed as valuable assets, there could not have been any necessity to pay such huge compensation towards an arrangement of their transfer to the assessee. Thus, the Assessing Officer treated the compensation paid by the assessee to Tata-IBM towards the so called transfer of human skills and the so called customer data base as part and parcel of overall consideration mutually agreed upon for the taking over of the software segment of the business of the erstwhile Tata-IBM. The Assessing Officer, therefore, disallowed the expenditure claimed as revenue expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: If the revenue wanted to hold that the consideration paid by the assessee as per the agreement was for the transfer of the business being undertaken by Tata-IBM Ltd., then such receipts should have been held as capital in the hands of the recipient. However, in the case of the recipient, the revenue had treated the receipts as revenue receipts and included those in the income. The matter had travelled up to the Tribunal and the Tribunal had held that the receipts were revenue in nature. The revenue could not blow hot and cold at the same time. Once it had taken the stand that the receipts in the hands of the recipient were revenue in nature, then such payments could not be held as capital in the hands of the payer representing the consideration paid for the transfer of business. In the instant case, the recipient had not been taxed under the head 'Capital gain' on the transfer of the business. Hence, the action of the Assessing Officer in holding that the receipts represented the receipts on account of transfer of business could not be upheld. [Para 7.1]

-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes FACT: The assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate. The assessee had acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores. The industry/plant so purchased was to include entire business undertaking situated at Ponada including movable and immovable properties and all other tangible and intangible assets relating to the business of manufacturing of aforesaid chemicals. The assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them. The said agreement provided forrestriction on ‘V’ and ‘M’ to engage in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate directly or indirectly for a period of 5 years for a cash consideration of Rs. 6 crores to be paid upfront. In the books of account, the assessee wrote off one-fifth of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores because the period during which agreement was to remain in force was 5 years but in the computation of income furnished along with return, the assessee claimed whole of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that the expenditure was not incurred for improving the profitability, as there was no existing business and the assessee had acquired the business of chemicals for the first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to the company and disallowed the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores claimed as revenue expenditure and treated it as capital expenditure.
