The Assessing Officer also disallowed the alternative claim made by the assessee that if the expenditure in question was not considered as revenue expenditure, then the assessee by having entered into non-compete agreement as per which ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ were not to carry on either manufacturing or trading business in the two chemicals for a period of five years, the assessee had acquired commercial/business rights for a period of 5 years to carry on manufacturing and trading activities in both the chemicals undisturbed and freely for a period of five years, which were of intangible nature entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the assessee might be allowed depreciation. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not acquired any specific intellectual right by making payment of Rs. 6 crores, which was eligible for depreciation under section 32.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. He held that no doubt the assessee earlier was doing only some trading business in the chemicals but it was not much; another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India; by making a payment of Rs. 6 crores to ‘V’ the advantage had accrued to the assessee and that too of enduring nature and, accordingly, the expenditure was capital in nature and; the impugned expenditure could not be considered as deferred revenue expenditure and, accordingly, could not be allowed proportionately in five years as contended by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the non-compete fees of Rs. 6 crores paid by the assessee to ‘V’ did not bring in any asset as mentioned in section 32(1)(ii) so as to qualify for depreciation.

On second appeal :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had specifically admitted that the assessee was carrying on trading business in the chemicals, though he further observed that it was not much. Further, the Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted that another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India, but in the central eastern part of India ‘D’ did not have any hold worth the name.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessee-company was manufacturer of front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles - To expand its business, assessee entered into an agreement with a company, named (SML) to purchase one of its units - Payment was made by assessee to SML towards non-compete fee and for other obligation and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about agreement as also all intellectual property and other data and information - Whether payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards non-compete obligation and, thus, capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee entered into an agreement for purchase of assets and liabilities of a newly set up factory of a company (SML), and paid a certain sum for obtaining requisite permission and approvals in smooth transfer of factory to assessee, said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards non-compete obligation

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles. It entered into an agreement for purchase of assets and liabilities of a newly set up factory, established by a company, named, SML in Madras. According to the assessee, the consideration in the said agreement was in two parts - First Rs. 1.30 crores towards the net asset value and secondly Rs. 70 lakhs paid on account of non-compete clause for a period of five years.

The Assessing Officer held that the intention of the assessee was to keep competitors out of the market thereby increasing sales, and, thus, the said amount could not be held to be revenue expenditure as it derived long term benefit and, thus, it was capital expenditure.

The assessee approached the Commissioner (Appeals) who held that since the non-competition period was for a short term of five years, the expenditure was revenue in nature.

The Tribunal reversed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and restored the finding of the Assessing Officer on the ground that the assessee was the only manufacturer in India for front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles and being the sole manufacturer, it acquired an enduring benefit. Thus, the expenditure was capital in nature as the assessee eliminated its only competitor after acquiring the factory, thereby perpetuating its exclusivity in the market.

On appeal:

HELD: A perusal of the agreement clearly points to the fact that while the consideration of Rs.1.30 crores was towards the net value of assets, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is "for obligations and covenants". [Para 13]

The clauses of the agreement go to show that the amount of Rs.70 lakhs is not merely payment towards the non-compete clause but also towards various other obligations which were imposed upon SML and had a direct bearing on the final execution and implementation of the agreement. To argue that the entire consideration was towards the non-compete fee would, therefore, be an incorrect statement, inasmuch as the clauses of the agreement do not reflect so. The emphasis in the agreement is towards the takeover of the assets of SML, and it was to ensure that the agreement bears fruition that the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs has been apportioned for various obligations and covenants imposed on SML. [Para 14]

Under these circumstances, the question that is to be decided is whether the expenditure of Rs.70 lakhs incurred is of capital or revenue nature. The consideration of Rs.70 lakhs was clearly towards ensuring that there will be no impediment in the smooth transfer of SML's factory to the assessee. It should be complete and final. From the facts placed before the Court, there really did not appear to be any serious threat whatsoever in order for the assessee to pay the non-compete fee to SML which had not even commenced its manufacturing. From the nature of the transaction, it is clear that the acquisition of SML's unit was, for expansion purposes. It was to expand and increase production by acquiring a new undertaking. The entire business with capital assets was acquired. The payment was bifurcated into two parts, Rs. 130 lakhs towards net assets and Rs.70 lakhs for other obligations and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about the agreement as also all the intellectual property and other data and information. The said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards the non-compete obligation. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961—Capital or revenue expenditure—Assessee-company was engaged in business of developing minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc.—It had mining lease of survey no. 40 at a certain place—Another company, mmc, having prospective licence for extracting fluorspar in respect of adjacent survey no. 30, had preferential right for obtaining a lease thereon, but government rejected mmc's application for lease—MMC took legal proceeding and obtained interim orders restraining government from giving lease on survey no. 30 to any other party pending final outcome of litigation—Assessee-company also needed survey no. 30 to run its beneficiation plant for desired number of years—To expand business and ward off competition, assessee paid Rs. 3 lakhs to mmc on the latter agreeing to withdraw aforesaid legal proceedings, thus facilitating way for assessee to obtain long-term lease on survey no. 30—Whether said expenditure was capital or revenue in nature—Held, on facts, it was capital expenditure

Section  28(i) of the income-tax act, 1961—Business deduction/loss—Assessee constructed bridge over a river to facilitate laying of water pipes leading to its beneficiation plant—Said bridge was washed away in heavy floods and assessee wrote off expenditure incurred thereon—Whether said expenditure admissible as business deduction—Held, on facts, no

Section 45, read with sections 2(47) and 48, of the income-tax act, 1961—Capital gains/loss – Allowability—Whether expenditure referred to under the caption 'business deduction/loss' deductible as short-term loss—Held, on facts, no

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of development of minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc., including extraction of fluorspar. It held a mining lease on Survey No. 40 in a certain village. Another company MMC held a prospecting licence for extracting fluorspar from the adjacent Survey No. 30 and applied for a mining lease thereon and prepared a prospecting report also. Under section 11(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, MMC had a preferential right for obtaining such a lease, but the Government rejected its application whereupon it went to Court for redress and obtained interim orders restraining the Government from giving the said Survey No. 30 on lease to any other party. Meanwhile the assessee-corporation had also applied for a mining lease on the said Survey No. 30. It had spent considerable amount on erecting its beneficiation plant for fluorspar which could run for the desired number of years only if it could get raw material from Survey No. 40 as well as Survey No. 30. The assessee-corporation, therefore, with a view to expanding its business, avoiding competition on the adjacent land and getting the required raw material for the desired number of years, entered into an agreement with MMC whereby it paid a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs to MMC on latter agreeing to withdraw the pending legal proceedings and give up its claim to Survey No. 30 to clear the assessee's path for obtaining a lease thereon. The assessee claimed, the aforesaid payment of Rs. 3 lakhs as revenue expenditure in the assessment year 1970-71. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim, holding the expenditure to be of capital nature. The AAC upheld the ITO's order on the ground that the benefit derived from the payment was of an enduring nature. The Tribunal confirmed the AAC's order.

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2002-03 - Whether it is only if non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature, can it be said to be a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether where non-competition agreement entered into by assessee engaged in setting up power projects was to prevent rival company from establishing power plant in State for a period of three years and such, restrictive covenant eliminated competition in business only for a while and it was neither permanent nor advantage derived by assessee was enduring in nature, such expenditure could not be held to be capital expenditure and same had to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]IT: It is only if non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature, can be said to be a capital expenditure; payment of restrictive covenant is revenue expenditure

FACT: The assessee was a company involved in setting up of power projects. The assessee was initially promoted by three companies including KHPL represented by one R. Raju. Due to certain disputes, an agreement was signed according to which said R. Raju would exit from assessee-company and would stay away of all contacts, suppliers, funding agencies and other business associates of the assessee. The non-competition agreement was only for a limited period of three years to ward off competition in territory of Andhra Pradesh. The assessee paid Rs. 3.25 crores to KHPL and claimed deduction as revenue expenditure.

The Assessing Officer held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee was capital expenditure in nature, without bringing about any depreciable asset into existence. He, therefore, disallowed the expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred did not relate to acquisition of an asset or a right of permanent character or an advantage of enduring nature and, thus, such expenditure could not be held to be capital expenditure. However, the same had to be allowed as revenue expenditure as it was paid for the business.

On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On the revenue's appeal before the High Court:

HELD: The non-competition fee of Rs. 3.25 crores paid by the assessee was allowable as revenue expenditure of the business of the assessee. The non-competition agreement entered into by the assessee with KHPL was to prevent R. Raju from establishing a power plant in Andhra Pradesh for a period of three years. The amount was paid, and a non-competition agreement was entered into, is not in dispute. The law declared by the judgment of the Supreme Court, and the Delhi High Court, is that it is only if the non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature can it be said to be a capital expenditure. The agreement prevented R. Raju from establishing a power plant only for a period of three years from the date of the agreement. The restrictive covenant was neither permanent nor was the advantage derived by the assessee therefrom of an enduring nature. The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in holding that the assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making payment of a non-competition fee; and it merely eliminated competition in its business for a while. [Para 10]

The appeal fails and is, accordingly, dismissed. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922) - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1953-54 to 1955-56 - Assessee-company took over routes of various private operators and paid compensation to get rid of competition from said operators - Whether compensation so paid was an expenditure of capital nature and, thus, it could not be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: During the three assessment years 1953-54 to 1955-56, the assessee-company whose 98 per cent shares were held by the State of Orissa and the Central Govt. took over the routes of various private operators and paid compensation. Its claim for deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act in respect of compensation amount was disallowed by the department upto the stage of the Tribunal.

On reference :

HELD: If the expenditure relates to the domain of running the business concern, then, ordinarily, it would be revenue expenditure. If, on the other hand, the expenditure is made to acquire a certain business to free the business of the assessee from competition, then the expenditure is one of a capital nature. The ultimate conclusion would depend on the character of the expenditure.

In instant case, the assessee-company acquired the unexpired permits and thereby got rid of competition from private operators who were on the field prior to the acquisition. The investment was clearly one of a capital nature.

That being the conclusion, the amount was rightly not allowed as a deduction.

Note : The case was decided against assessee.

year of payment or in the alternative the same should be spread over a period of 5 years as non-competition covenant was only for 5 years. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee holding that the purchase price paid for non-competition covenant was in the nature of goodwill and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order holding that the expenditure was in the nature of capital expenditure.

On second appeal : HELD: In order to determine the nature of expenditure, one has to examine the facts of the each case independently. No hard and fast rule can be laid down to determine the nature of expenditure. If an assessee acquires any capital asset or enduring benefit for a longer period, the expenditure may be called to be a ‘capital expenditure’. In the instant case, the assessee had purchased the shipping business from the vendor against a lumpsum consideration of Rs. 43,47,000 comprising of cost of goodwill of Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 38,47,000 for non-competition covenant fees for a period of 5 years. From a perusal of the non-competition clause contained in the agreement, it was clear that in lieu of receipt of a non-competition fees, the vendor was restrained from doing similar type of business in any capacity for a period of 5 years within India. This condition would not apply to a business carried on by the vendor outside the India. Period of condition was fixed up to 5 years and, thereafter, the vendor was at liberty to enter into similar type of business activity. Further from the other provisions of the agreement, it was not borne out that the vendor was permanently restrained from doing the shipping business in future. Meaning thereby, it was a temporary arrangement made with the vendor in order to settle down its new business of shipping. It has been repeatedly held by the Apex Court and various High Courts that an expenditure incurred to avoid competition, if dictated by business necessity and commercial exigencies, would be allowable as a revenue expenditure as the benefit derived out of it is directly related to the enhancement of profitability of business. In the instant case, by avoiding a main competition from the vendor, the assessee had derived the benefits out of it to enhance its profitability only and it was not a case that the competition was eliminated permanently or for a longer period. Moreover, it was not a case of the revenue that the vendor was only competitor in this line of business. There were other business constituents who were engaged in the similar type of business and a threat of competition was also there to be faced by the assessee from those business constituents. This covenant was executed only for a period of 5 years and that too only for Indian territory. If the assessee intended to do its business outside Indian territory, it had to face the competition from the vendor also. Meaning thereby, this covenant was not executed for a permanent elimination of the competition from the seller. Therefore, the benefit was derived by the assessee for a limited period of 5 years and that too only in Indian territory. Therefore, the non-competition covenant fees paid by the assessee to the vendor could not be treated as capital expenditure. The covenant was executed on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down the assessee in a new acquired business of shipping and the benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability. As such, the expenditure incurred by the assessee was a revenue expenditure and the same was to be allowed as a business expenditure. [Para 23]

Further, since the assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, this expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and the corresponding expenditure be allowed in every year. Therefore, the impugned order was to be set aside and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to allow the total expenditure over a period of 5 years in which the non-competition covenant fees remained in force. [Para 24]

EDITOR’S NOTE

Where the assessee had not furnished any details in respect of sundry expenses either before the lower authorities or before the Tribunal, the lower authorities were justified in disallowing 10 per cent of sundry expenses.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of Assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63 - Assessee, a union of truck operators provided facilities to its member operators in matter of booking their trucks and charged commission at rate of 5 per cent on gross booking - Out of commission so received, one-half was paid to members of union whose trucks could not be booked - Whether since payment was made to eliminate competitors and to carry on business unfettered by competition, payment was of capital nature and was not permissible deduction as revenue expenditure in computing assessee's total income - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a union of truck operators in the Subzi Mandi area. It wrong found provided facilities to truck operators in the matter of booking of their trucks and charged commission at 5 per cent of gross booking. After keeping one-half of such commission the assessee used to return the balance to those members of the union whose trucks were not booked. The payment was not allowed as deduction by the ITO. On appeal the AAC decided in favour of the assessee. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the payment was in the nature of capital expenditure.

On reference :

HELD: The amount in question was paid only to those members whose trucks were not booked. But for this payment, they would have otherwise competed in the business with the assessee. The object of the payment was to eliminate those competitors and to carry on the business unfettered by competition. The assessee made the payment to acquire this right of these persons. This led to enhance the value of its existing assets to make them more profit-yielding. The expense, therefore, could not be a revenue expense but was of a capital nature. The Tribunal was therefore right, in holding that amount so paid was not a permissible deduction for the purpose of income-tax.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital or revenue expenditure - Assessee purchased its present business during assessment year 1974-75 from vendor with all assets and liabilities including liability to pay bonus to workers for period prior to date of takeover - After bonus amount was quantified, assessee paid a part of bonus in year 1974-75 and balance amount during year 1975-76 and claimed it as a revenue expenditure - Whether balance bonus paid in accounting year relevant to assessment year 1975-76 was revenue expenditure - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, a private limited company, purchased its present business on 1-12-1973 from vendor during the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1974-75, with the stipulation that it would settle with the labour all their claims in respect of bonus for the period preceding 1-12-1973. The dispute with the Union of workers as to the actual rate of payment of the bonus was finally settled on 8-11-1974, as a result of which the assessee agreed to pay bonus at 19 per cent. The assessee then claimed the entire amount of bonus as its revenue expenditure for the years in which it was paid. A part of the amount had been paid in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1974-75 and the balance amount in the following accounting year which was in question. The Tribunal had disallowed the assessee's claim for the assessment year 1974-75, on the ground that it was a capital expenditure. However, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim in respect of the balance bonus paid in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1975-76 towards the liability of the previous accounting year treating that amount as a revenue expenditure.

On reference :

HELD: It could not be gainsaid that in agreeing on the price at which the business was taken over by the assessee from the vendor all the liabilities as well as the assets of the firm had been taken into account. One of the liabilities obviously was the liability towards bonus for the period preceding the date of the takeover. It was known to the assessee that as consideration for the takeover, it would have to incur a liability to the full extent finally determined as the amount payable as bonus for the period preceding the takeover. The amount, thus, spent in payment of bonus for that period was not an amount expended by the assessee to carry on, and earn the profits or gains of the business which it took over, but an amount expended to obtain the business which it purchased. That was not an expenditure, which partook the character of revenue, but it was clearly a capital expenditure. Therefore, the balance bonus paid during the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1975-76 was not a revenue expenditure.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-Assesses took over as sole proprietor, business of firm in which he was partner, consequent on its dissolution due to death of one partner-Later, he converted business into partnership firm by admitting his son as partner-Still later, sons of deceased partner filed suit against assessee for reopening of earlier dissolution and for restraining assessee from carrying on business-Suit settled by compromise decree under which assessee paid lump sum to plaintiffs as final settlement-Whether sum so paid was allowable as revenue expenditure-Held, on facts, yes
Rule of practice-Stare decisis-Applicability as between decisions of larger bench of supreme court and smaller bench.

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a partnership concern. When the firm dissolved due to death of one partner, the assessee took over the business as a going concern after paying certain money to the deceased's heirs towards purchase of their interests in the partnership assets. He carried on the business for some time as a sole proprietor and, thereafter, converted it into a partnership by taking his son as partner. Later on, the assessee was faced with a suit instituted by some of the minor sons of the deceased-partner of the erstwhile partnership, demanding reopening of earlier dissolution and restraining the assessee from carrying on business. The suit was eventually compromised, when the assessee agreed to pay them Rs. 40,000 in full settlement. He claimed the payment as an admissible deduction, but the ITO disallowed the claim since it did not relate to the partnership business then carried on by the assessee. While the AAC allowed the impugned claim, the Tribunal negatived the same, holding that the expenditure was incurred by the assessee to protect his business and, hence, was capital in nature.

On reference :

HELD: It is well settled that expenditure laid out for the acquisition or improvement of a fixed capital asset or for perfecting title or for getting rid of a defect in the title, would be capital expenditure. However, if it is incurred to protect the trade or business of the assessee or to protect his assets from attack, then it would be revenue expenditure.

In considering the nature of the expenditure, it would not be proper to proceed on the basis of the correctness of the pleadings in the suit, as the matter was not adjudicated upon by the Court. The pleadings represent mere allegations and unless the statements were proved they would merely remain as allegations. So long as there was no adjudication on the conduct of the assessee, the allegations made should not colour the determination of the issue.

In the instant case both parties to the litigation had given the go-by to their respective pleadings when they entered into a mutual compromise. There was nothing express or implied in the terms of the compromise to suggest that the impugned payment was towards payment of the balance of the purchase price of the deceased partner's share in the business. The assessee had already become the owner of the assets long ago and he had to defend the attack on the assets. This was, thus, clearly a case where the expenditure had not brought into existence any capital asset or enduring benefit. It would, therefore, be safe and reasonable to hold that qua the assessee the suit was an attack }on the title to his business and the impugned payment warded off that attack. The Tribunal was not justified in assuming that the payment under the compromise decree was the means by which the assessee had acquired full title to the business.

In this view of the matter, the impugned amount was a revenue expenditure.

The doctrine that a larger Bench of the Supreme Court has more authoritative force than a smaller Bench is relevant only as between cases which yield different ratio decidendi, and not where the one hands down a decision and the other merely lays down a dictum.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee firm was ferry contractor plying launches across river - Right to ferry was auctioned for a year and during relevant year assessee was highest bidder - Whether money paid by assessee to prospective bidders at auction in order to prevent them from competing with petitioners at auction, was in nature of revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was carrying on business as ferry contractors plying launches across the river. The right to ferry was auctioned for a year and the petitioners were the highest bidders. The assessee paid certain amount to sixteen individuals who were prospective bidders at the auction in order to prevent them from competing with the petitioners at the auction. In their return for the assessment year 1964-65, the assessee claimed said amount as a deduction on the ground that the amount was paid for shutting out the other bidders. The ITO held that this deduction was not admissible. This view was confirmed by the AAC on appeal.

On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the said sum could be deducted in computing the assessee's income as it was a revenue expenditure.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case the most important circumstance that had to be borne in mind was that the ferry contract was only for a period of one year. The amounts paid by the assessee to buy off competition were paid only for the purpose of securing that advantage during that year. It could not, therefore, be said that these amounts were paid for securing an enduring advantage. They were paid in order to enable the assessee to derive more profits in the business by reducing the lease amount payable to the Government for operating the ferry. It was thus an amount paid for the purpose of the business. It could not be said that it was paid for the purpose of acquiring the business and not for the purpose of running it.

It was not contended that the lease amount paid for obtaining the right to operate the ferry was not in the nature of a revenue expenditure and was not deductible. There was no difference in the instant case between the lease amount and the amount paid to the other intended bidders in order to prevent them from competing and thus reduce the lease amount so that ultimately the assessee could derive more profits.

The question whether a particular expenditure is revenue expenditure incurred for the purposes of business must be determined on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances, and by the application of principles of commercial trading. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

Viewing the expenditure incurred in the instant case in such a context that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

FACT: On incorporation the assessee-company became one of the partners of the firm 'NS', with effect from 1-8-1976. That firm was dissolved on 31-12-1976 and as a consequence the assets and liabilities of the erstwhile firm along with the business vested with the assessee-company. The dissolution deed that was drawn up, specified about the royalty that would be payable to the retiring partners for not doing such business for fifteen years arising out of the business of firm. The assessee by virtue of the dissolution deed, which was agreed to by it, provided royalty in its books by crediting to the two retired partners. The amount of royalty which was so shown as payable to the two retired partners for various assessment years, was claimed as revenue expenditure; but that was not accepted by the ITO. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

-competition agreement was to enhance the assessee’s sales of relevant two chemicals in central and eastern parts of India without any competition. Even otherwise, the benefit to be procured by the assessee for a period of five years could not be said to be of ‘enduring nature’, and since the revenue authorities had rejected the assessee’s claim solely on the ground that the benefit procured by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’, the orders of the revenue authorities could not be upheld. Even if the benefits derived by the assessee in the instant case were of enduring nature, then also the assessee was to succeed because of the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 /3 Taxman 69 and the findings to the effect that the effect of the agreement in question being directly related to the sale and production capacity of two chemicals, which in turn had effect of carrying on the assessee’s business efficiently and profitably in central and eastern parts of India and the test of enduring nature would fail and the expenditure had to be held as revenue expenditure.

Therefore, the expenditure incurred by the assessee by entering into a non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ was of revenue nature and, hence, an allowable deduction.

The another observation of the Assessing Officer for holding the expenditure in question to be capital expenditure was that there was no fear of competition from ‘V’ or that ‘V’ would not have been able to compete within a period of 5 years and that the assessee was to continue to get the benefit, even after 5 years, which was of ‘enduring nature’. However, the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) had considered the threat of competition only with reference to ‘V’ and not with reference to its founder ‘M’ in his individual capacity and, therefore, the conclusion arrived at by them could not be sustained in law. Further, the chemicals produced by ‘V’ before sale of the manufacturing plant to the assessee were being sold in a particular area, i.e., in the central and eastern parts of India and probably without any brand which would mean that whatever market ‘V’ and its founder had captured was only because of their personal rapport with the consumers of these two chemicals and, therefore, in the presence of other manufacturers of these two chemicals situated in that area ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ could enter into market for selling the chemicals produced by those manufacturers and were definitely a potential threat at least in central and eastern parts of India. Consequently, the revenue authorities’ observation that the benefit to be derived by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’ because ‘V’ was not in a position to compete during the period of 5 years because it could not start manufacturing these chemicals within 5 years and by that the assessee would get established itself so well in the market that it would be difficult to dislodge was misplaced, without any basis or reasoning and devoid of any merit. The expenditure had to be seen from the angle of the business or the businessman and not from the revenue’s attitude and it is so because had the assessee any mala fide intention to reduce its tax burden, it could have easily included the payment of Rs. 6 crores in purchase price of the manufacturing plant itself and could have purchased the plant for Rs. 35 crores instead of Rs. 29 crores. In that case, the assessee would have got depreciation on whole of the amount, i.e., including payment of Rs. 6 crores and in that situation nobody was going to question the assessee’s bona fide and, therefore, to term the expenditure as of capital nature, only because the assessee had claimed the payments separately, was not justified.

res received by assessee from same company - Assessing Officer held that question of paying any service charge to very person/concern giving such loan did not arise as there was no service rendered so as to merit any separate payment - According to Assessing Officer real impact of transaction was reduction of loan liability of assessee - Whether, since expenditure had effect for period of loan which was stated to be seven years, 1/7th of service charges could be allowed in year under consideration - Held, yes FACT: The assessee purchased two distilleries. As per the agreement, an amount of Rs. 10 crores was given to their promoters for the restrictive covenant not to compete with the assessee for 10 years with a view to facilitate its profits by eliminating competition from the promoters. The Assessing Officer observed that there were limits to the price of shares of a company determined by market forces and in the instant case it was difficult to imagine that such limits would not have been operative and the assessee was left with no option but to pay the cost of acquisition over and above the price paid for the acquisition of the shares of these companies to their promoters; that, in order to claim the payments as allowable deduction, the transaction was given the colour of payments as non-competition fees, but, in fact, the real purpose of those payments was to compensate the promoters of the companies owning the two distilleries for the cost of the distilleries; that it was not the case of the assessee that the payments were made to any distillery owner or business rival and it was also not the case of the assessee that the persons who were paid the said amounts possessed special expertise and skill so as to threaten the business of the assessee; and that the circumstance that these persons’ companies/ distilleries did not produce any brand of liquor with national market presence, did not support the case of the assessee as to the real purpose or motive of the said payments. He, therefore, held that the claim of the assessee for allowability of Rs. 10 crores as business expenditure was nothing but part of the cost of distilleries and added it to the income of the assessee. On appeal, it was submitted that agreement for non-competition fees was for 5 years and based on certain decisions, it was claimed that where the benefit was not of enduring nature but was to exhaust in a short period, the expenditure was of revenue nature. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the payment could not be taken as the revenue expenditure because the agreements were to run for a long duration of 10 years unfettered by any stipulation of termination; that payment of non-competition fees could have some rationale if the competition was between equals producing the same commodity and that the promoters of the two distilleries taken over were no match for the assessee who had monopoly of manufacturing and marketing its own brand names. He, therefore, held that there was no business necessity for making the non-competition fees of Rs. 10 crores and upheld the disallowance.

On further appeal :

HELD: The expenditure incurred in violation of a provision of the Act would not be an allowable deduction, as held by the Supreme Court in Maddi Venkataraman & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1998] 229 ITR 534 / 96 Taxman 643 and as held by the Karnataka High Court in CIT v. Bangalore Arrack Co. [1993] 201 ITR 25 payment to ward off competition being against a public policy will not be an allowable deduction. [Para 5.5]

In view of the above, the payment made by the assessee to ward off competition for the period of 10 years would be a payment for acquiring an enduring benefit which could not be allowed as deduction in view of the later decision of the Madras High Court in the case of Chelpark Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1991] 191 ITR 249 / 56 Taxman 29 and those of Calcutta and Madhya Pradesh High Courts. The disallowance was, accordingly, to be upheld. [Para 6]

to be proportionately reduced and if the firm 'R' Brothers ceased to carry on business in Calcutta, the annuities would forthwith cease.

In view of aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held that the payment in question constituted revenue expenditure which, having admittedly been laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business, was properly allowable as an admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xii) of the 1922 Act.

On reference : HELD: In determining whether a particular item of expenditure comes under the category of "capital" or "revenue" it is necessary to consider carefully the nature of the concern, the ordinary course of business, usually adopted by such firms, the object with which an expense is incurred and the actual effect thereof. It is only then that it can be decided under what category a particular expenditure falls. In instant case, the goodwill of the firm in which M was interested had for a separate consideration been transferred to the assessee entitling the latter to the benefit of the connections of M with 'R' Brothers. The annuity, which was made payable to M and to his wife, was in consideration of M not entering into competition during his lifetime with assessee. There was no question that under this latter provision a benefit accrued in favour of assessee, but was it of an enduring nature ? One very important provision was introduced in the agreement which must not be overlooked. The payments were made contingent upon the receipt by assessee of a certain amount from R Brothers with the further proviso that under certain circumstances the entire annuity might be stopped, irrespective of the fact whether or not assessee, continue to receive brokerage from R Brothers or whether annuities continued to be paid till the end of the two lives. M was restrained from entering into competition with the assessee-firm till the end of his natural life. There could be no question that M was definitely and permanently kept out of the filed of competition.

On the special facts arising in instant case and on the interpretation of the terms of contract as evidenced by the agreements, it must be held that the amount in question was not an item of capital expenditure but was a revenue expenditure allowable as an admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xii) of 1922 Act as it stood before its amendment in 1946.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1955-56 to 1958-59 - Whether in deciding question whether expenditure was in nature of capital expenditure or business expenditure laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for purpose of assessee’s business, one must not confine one selves only to agreement between parties and said question must be decided in light of facts and circumstances of each case - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-company took over business carried on by a firm and made payment of pension amount to employees of firm in consideration of their past services rendered by them to firm and to abstain them from being engaged or employed in business of kind carried on by assessee-company, it could be said that payment made was for purposes of business and has in nature of business expenditure and would not partake of nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: Whether the expenditure was in the nature of a capital expenditure or a business expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee’s business, one must not confine oneselves only to the agreements between the parties. The question must be determined in the light of all the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no rule that if there is a written agreement between the parties the authorities and the High Court must look only to that written agreement and nothing else.

It is now settled law that the question whether the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each case.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 - Assessee-company acquired brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement - Under a separate non-compete agreement, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company as consideration for restraining it from competing in business of products similar to Lacto Calamine for a period of ten years - Amount paid as non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure by assessee - Whether in cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and benefit of restrain acquired by assessee for period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit - Held, yes - Whether therefore, by paying non-compete fee, it could be said that assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by assessee was in nature of capital expenditure and not revenue in character as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of manufacture of medicines and Lacto Calamine, purchased the brand name ‘Lacto Calamine’ from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement. Subsequently, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company under a non-compete agreement for restraining it from competing directly or indirectly in the business activities carried on by the assessee. The payment so made for the purchase of brand name was accounted for by the assessee as an item of capital expenditure but the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs paid as non-compete fee was claimed as a deduction being revenue in nature under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer, however, rejected the assessee’s said claim by holding that non-compete fee paid by it to ‘D’ was a capital expenditure inasmuch as by making said payment the assessee had acquired an advantage of an enduring nature by way of freedom from competition that would have been induced by ‘D’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1990-91 - Assessee was a representative agent of HP products in India - In order to ensure its monopoly status and eliminate any competition in its business for two years assessee entered into an agreement under which it agreed to pay consideration to BSL - BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products - Whether expenditure in question was of capital nature inasmuch as assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of selling, marketing and distribution of various products of Hewlett Packard (HP). It was a representative agent of HP products in India. In order to ensure its monopoly status and eliminate any competition in its business for two years the assessee entered into an agreement with BSL under which the assessee paid a consideration of Rs. 1.68 crore immediately and an equal amount was payable after one year. It was debited to profit and loss account as a proportionate amount for five months treating it as business expenditure in the year ended 31-3-1990. The Assessing Officer disallowed by holding that the said expenditure was capital in nature as it resulted in benefit of enduring nature. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) endorsed the finding of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: One of the tests to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure is whether the expenditure in question was for bringing into existence an asset or an advantage of an ‘enduring nature’ and was made once and for all meaning thereby an expenditure made once for all for procuring an enduring benefit. The expressions ‘enduring benefit’ and ‘rights of a permanent nature’ are only descriptive and not definitive and are related in meaning not synonymous with perpetual or everlasting. [Para 7]

In the instant case, BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products. Even though the period of two years was mentioned in the agreement, the predominant intention and purpose, as discernible from the stipulations in the agreement, clearly indicated that the assessee-company had obtained the monopoly rights on a permanent basis and BSL went out of its business of dealing in test and measurement products, of HP, inasmuch as it released its entire workforce connected with the line of business started by the assessee. Expenditure in question was clearly of a capital nature inasmuch as the assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years. The disallowance of expenditure was, therefore, justified. [Paras 8 and 12]

For the aforesaid reason finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 13]

FACT: • The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

HELD: Nature of expenditure incurred by assessee

• In the present case, the assessee is a joint venture between 'S' corporation and L&T. Apparently, the agreement entered into with the L&T in view of the changed relationship ensures that the latter does not enter into the same business. Although it is contended that the advantage is only by way of facilitation of the assessee's business and ensuring greater efficiency as well as profitability, on the other side, what can be seen is that the arrangement was to endure for a substantial period, i.e. 7 years coupled with the fact that the L&T had its own presence in consumer goods sector and would be able to put up an effective competition for business engaged in by the assessee, there is no doubt that the amount is to ensure a certain position in the market by keeping-out L&T. In such circumstances, it is opined that the deduction cannot be claimed as a revenue expenditure, it clearly falls within the capital field. [Para 10]

Depreciation in case of intangible asset

• The question arises as to whether a non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for seven years amounts to a depreciable intangible asset. Each of the species of rights spelt-out in section 32(1)(ii), i.e. know-how, patent, copyright, trademark, license or franchise as or any other right of a similar kind which confers a business or commercial or any other business or commercial right of similar nature has to be 'intangible asset'. The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the ownership. In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance 'in rem'.

• However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity. The right can be asserted in the present instance only against L&T and in a sense, the right 'in personam'.

The nature and character of the payment in the hands of the assessee would depend upon the purpose of the payment and the nature of the benefit enured to the assessee by such payment. What is to be seen in this case is whether the assessee has gained anything by virtue of this agreement. Perhaps not. Because, by the agreement the period of non-competing was 5 years only. It was further extended by a further period of 5 years and the payment is payable every year. The second agreement also contains the same terms & conditions as in the first agreement. Without going into the second agreement, which is additional evidence filed. It is found that various clauses in the first agreement itself demonstrate that the agreement was initially for a period of 5 years and even the consideration is an annual payment based on the annual turnover. Therefore, it appears to be a payment for loss of revenue to the holding company and is dependent upon the business carried on by the assessee. The agreement is also liable to be terminated with prior notice of 10 months. The agreement also includes various other services to be provided by the holding company to the assessee company and the payment was not just for non-competition. In this view of the matter also, the payment made by the assessee to the holding company is revenue expenditure as without the said payment, the assessee could not have carried on its business more efficiently and profitably. Therefore, the payment is in the nature of revenue expenditure and is an allowable deduction under section 37(1). [Para 9]

In the result, assessee's appeal is allowed. [Para 10]

Further, the departure of A from the assessee-company and the prospect of his making available his experience and expertise in the manufacture and marketing of ink to his wife and daughters, who were the partners of the firm, would have rendered the goodwill of the assessee vulnerable, as the assessee, when it commanded the benefit of the services of A, was in an advantageous position. That resulted in the assessee buying of potential competition, which was a positive detriment owing to such competition, and had also enabled the assessee not only to safeguard its goodwill, but also to enhance it. The payment of Rs. 1,00,000 by the assessee to the partnership was to secure advantages resulting in the removal from the arena of a possible competition and securing the elimination of a risk or detriment to the assessee due to competition. Though under the terms of the agreement, the benefit of the restrictive covenant was to enure only for a period of five years, from the facts stated in the order of the Tribunal and also the terms of the dissolution deed, it was seen that the partnership, which was a potential competitor, had also vanished and A had also left the shores of India. That would clearly establish that what the assessee had paid for was of permanent or enduring quality, in the sense that the competition had been totally eliminated and a protection had been acquired for the business of the assessee as a whole. In other words, the amount paid by the assessee was no part of the working or operational expenses of the assessee, but its aim and object was acquisition of an advantage of enduring nature, viz., freedom from competition from the partnership for the rest of the period of the business activities of the assessee.

Therefore, the consideration paid in terms of agreement was an expenditure of capital nature.

FACT: The assessee-company was doing financing business and its main source of income was dividend and interest. The board of directors of the assessee-company decided to enter into the new business of entertainment. Therefore, the assessee-company amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’, which was owned by the film star Amitabh Bachchan, and this was approved by the jurisdictional High Court. The assessee paid certain lump sum amount to the two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for the next ten years. The assessee claimed deduction of the same as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and treated the expenditure in question as a capital expenditure. He held that the payment in question was made for acquiring a new asset, i.e., the brand/copyright, that is to say, a source of earning profit itself. The Assessing Officer also rejected the contention of the assessee that the artists were not prevented totally in carrying on their profession as artists, holding that, in fact, by virtue of the aforesaid agreements the assessee had an exclusive control over the services of the artists. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the artists had agreed to perform the diverse acts for the assessee, whereby the assessee could generate revenues from them and also copyrights on the products. for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure. (3) If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operation, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]
