FACT: HAL was a government company. The rail coach division which was functioning as a unit of HAL was transferred on 1-1-1965 as a going concern to BEML, another government company, which was the present assessee HAL had incurred development expenditure towards designs and models of integral coaches which it had amortised and had been claiming and was allowed deduction on amortisation principle. At the time of transfer of the division, there was unabsorbed expenditure of a certain amount in the books of HAL, which, according to the terms of the transfer was also taken over by BEML and reimbursed to HAL. Originally, the assessee (BEML) claimed only a part of the amount as deduction in the relevant assessment year on the amortization principle. Subsequently it claimed the entire amount as revenue expenditure in its assessment for the assessment year 1965-66. The ITO dissallowed the first claim and did not consider the second. On appeal, the AAC allowed part of the expenditure on amortisation basis, but the Tribunal accepted the revenue's appeal and restored the ITO's order.

HAL had also executed preliminary works relating to manufacture of heavy earth moving equipment unit and had incurred expenditure of a certain amount, a major portion of which represented technical assistance fee paid to the collaborator. On transfer of this unit to BEML, the latter reimbursed this expenditure to HAL and claimed it as deduction in its assessment. The claim was not allowed by the ITO and the assessee's appeals to the AAC and the Tribunal were also rejected. For its conclusion that the expenditure was of capital nature and, therefore, not allowable, the Tribunal followed the Karnataka High Court's decision in Mysore Kirloskar v. CIT [1968] 67 ITR 23 . The other reason for the Tribunal upholding the disallowance was that at the time the collaboration agreement was entered into, the HAL was not manufacturing any article of the type of earth moving equipment, and the expenditure on drawings, etc., was initial outlay of the business. The remaining expenditure was on training of officers and, according to the Tribunal, the experience gained by them was an intangible asset of the assessee-company and, hence the expenditure was of capital nature.

On reference:

HELD: So far as the unabsorbed revenue expenditure on development of designs and models of integral coaches, was concerned, HAL had not claimed it earlier because it was following the amortisation principle of accounting. But that was no bar for the assessee (BEML) to claim the amount in toto in the assessment year in question as business expenditure, since the amount was admittedly paid in the relevant year for the purpose of its business.

The main reason given by the Tribunal for disallowing the claim of the assessee, viz., that the assets taken over by the assessee in consideration for the payment representing this expenditure were mainly of an intangible nature, was inaccurate. The assessee paid that amount towards unabsorbed expenditure incurred by HAL on development of designs and development of various models of rail coaches, etc., taken over by the assessee. In the case of HAL, similar claim had been allowed by the revenue accepting the amortisation basis. There was, therefore, no justification for denying the claim of the assessee, in the instant case.

Regarding the payment made for technical know-how, the decision relied upon by the Tribunal had since been overruled and in Mysore Kirloskar Ltd. v . CIT [1978] 114 ITR 443 (Kar.) , the Full Bench had taken the view that payments made under agreement for acquisition of technical know- how should be considered as business expenditure. Therefore, the payment made in the instant case towards technical assistance fee must be regarded as revenue expenditure. The distinction made by the Tribunal between initial outlay of expenditure and current needs of the business of the assessee was equally untenable. In fact, no distinction can be made between initial investment to commence busi- ness and current expenses for continuing production. The nature of the expenditure for obtaining technical know-how cannot ordinarily depend upon the time at which the collaboration agreement came into existence. It may depend upon the purposes for which it was entered into and the benefits derived therefrom.

So far as the nature of the amount paid by the assesses to HAL towards the expenditure incurred by the latter on training the officers was concerned, the reasoning of the Tribunal was right, so that the relevant amount had been rightly disallowed.

the penalty holding that the genuineness of expenditure was not doubted and there was a difference of opinion between the assessee’s stand and that of the Assessing Officer; that merely because the assessee accepted the allowance of one-fourteenth of the amount under section 35A as against the entire claim, that should not go against it; and that the difference of opinion could not lead to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed its income by furnishing inaccurate particulars.

On appeal by the department : HELD: The auditors of the assessee-company had treated the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores as deferred revenue expenditure to be amortised over a period of 3 years and it was, accordingly, debited to ‘Deferred revenue expenditure account’. Accordingly, in the balance-sheet and profit and loss account as at 31-3-1998 an amount of Rs. 71,66,667 was written off and balance of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was shown as balance under the head ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. It showed that in the profit and loss account only a claim of Rs. 71,66,667 was made as per auditor’s note. However, in computation of income, the assessee added Rs. 71,66,667 to the declared loss and claimed the entire sum as deduction. The balance sum of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was taken in the balance-sheet under the head ‘Miscellaneous expenditure’ stating that sum as ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. Thus, after adding the said sum, the assessee claimed, in the computation of income, the entire sum of Rs. 2.15 crores as revenue expenditure in the relevant assessment year. [Paras 10, 11 and 12]

The facts in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were entirely different from those of the instant case. Thus, the assessee’s reliance on the said decisions and then claiming the entire amount paid in purchasing new business as revenue expenditure was misplaced and incorrect. [Para 16]

In the instant case, the assessee purchased (i) a running business, (ii) right to publish two titles and (iii) complete and exclusive ownership basis along with all the rights and benefits attached thereto. As an ancillary to the purchase of titles and running business, the assessee also got detailed list of subscribers, advertisers and employees, who wanted to continue with the assessee after takeover. Thus, in addition to titles, the assessee also purchased something akin to goodwill. Same customers and advertisers would remain attached to the titles. [Para 18]

The tests to come to the conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature are that the expenditure is incurred to :

(i )set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in the same line.

(ii )commence a business.

(iii )acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity.

(iv )acquire an asset.

(v )acquire a source of generating income.

All the tests led to one inescapable conclusion that what the assessee had spent was for acquiring a new business/new assets/an enduring benefit and a source of income. From all the tests, the expenditure incurred could not have been considered under section 37(1) under which claim was made.

Hence, the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores was a capital expenditure. [Para 20]

The decisions in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were not even remotely connected with the assessee’s case. An issue on which the Tribunal has expressed an opinion in favour of the assessee or which has been regarded as debatable by any court would certainly be debatable on which there can be another opinion. There could not be second opinion, and had not been, on the facts of the assessee’s case, that the expenditure incurred on acquiring a new business, a source of income, an asset and benefit of enduring nature could not be revenue in nature. Hence, there was no debatable issue in the instant case. [Para 21]

In the instant case, the facts missing from the return filed were : (i) to whom the payment of Rs. 2.15 crores was made, when and how. (ii ) copy of agreement with the seller [which was given at the time of scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) only]. (iii) that the assessee was purchasing a new business. (iv) the names of the journals and the fact that the titles were purchased on an exclusive ownership for all the time to come along with all the paraphernalia of employees and space on rent. Thus, the claim of the assessee that the expenditure in question was a revenue expenditure was not bona fide. [Paras 24 and 25]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee was engaged in business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products - Assessee-company acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by assessee with latter - Consideration for such transfer included certain non-compete fee which was limited for a period of five years - For assessment year 2005-06, assessee filed its return of income wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, however, disallowed same on ground that payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay - Commissioner (Appeals) held that expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years - On second appeal, Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by assessee was capital in nature, as such disallowed claim - It was noted that assessee itself treated expenditure as capital in books of account - Likewise, in schedule 2 to balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets' - This also showed that assessee treated this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature - Whether in view of above, Tribunal rightly held expenditure as capital in nature - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

Section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/Rate of - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether in view of facts stated under heading 'Business expenditure - Allowability of', matter was to be remanded back to Assessing Officer to determine as to whether depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) was to be allowed on non-compete fee paid by assessee - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products. During the year under consideration, the assessee company had acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by the assessee with the latter. The consideration for such transfer was stated as Rs. 18.92 crores which included a sum of Rs. 5.94 crores by way of non-compete fee which was limited for a period of 5 years. For the assessment year 2005-06, the assessee filed its return of income, wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay, non-allowable under section 37. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by the assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as the period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years. The Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by the assessee was capital in nature, as such it disallowed the claim. Further, while dealing with the cross-objection filed by the assessee, the Tribunal restored the alternate plea in respect of allowance of depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) to the file of the Assessing Officer for deciding it.

On appeal:

HELD: Re: non-compete fee, whether capital or revenue:

The assessee itself treated the expenditure as capital in the books of account. However, at the same time, it was maintained that since it was paid for loss of business that 'KOAL' would suffer, the same was treated as revenue in nature. Likewise, in schedule 2 to the balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets'. This also showed that the assessee treats this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature. [Para 12]

In view of above, the Tribunal rightly held that the expenditure was capital in nature. [Para 14]

Re: applicability of section 32(1)(ii):

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether once expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred restraining recipient for a short or limited period, expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase profitability of assessee and is not a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Assessee purchased running business of a firm along with its goodwill and paid certain amount to partners of that firm for not carrying on same line of business for five years - Whether expenditure incurred by assessee was revenue in nature and, hence, allowable - Held, yes - Whether, however, since expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in relevant assessment year as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: During the relevant assessment year, the assessee purchased goodwill along with the running business from a firm for Rs. 10 lakhs. The assessee further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of said firm for not carrying on same line of business and other related fields for 5 years. In the computation of income, the assessee claimed the expenditure of Rs. 5 lakhs as revenue expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer treated the said expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee had purchased the goodwill and other rights for Rs. 10 lakhs which was treated to be capital expenditure. The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance - Before final acquisition, assessee was appointed as an administrator of company and was put in charge of establishment - Assessee paid certain amount to 'M' being deprivation charges and claimed said amount as revenue expenditure - Whether since amount had been paid as compensation for deprivation of income which 'M' would have earned, had it not been deprived of possession and no part of said amount was paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of undertaking of 'M', amount paid by assessee was in nature of revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance. During the period of litigation before final acquisition, the assessee was appointed as administrator of 'M' and it was put in charge of the establishment. The assessee paid a total consideration of Rs. 320.79 lakhs to 'M' out of which Rs. 122.79 lakhs (at the rate of Rs.11.39 lakhs per annum) was for deprivation of management and Rs. 198 lakhs was for acquisition of the undertaking. The assessee claimed that amount of Rs. 122.79 lakhs paid by it was a revenue expenditure. The Commissioner disallowed the assessee's claim and treated the entire amount as a capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal found that out of the amount of Rs. 320.79 lakhs, the amount of Rs. 198 lakhs was a capital expenditure, but the another sum of Rs. 122.79 lakhs, being deprivation charges, was in the nature of revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: From the calculation of the compensation, as broken up, it was clear that Rs. 198 lakhs was paid for acquisition of the undertaking of 'M'. Obviously, that was a capital expenditure, which was no more in dispute, and so far as that amount was concerned, admittedly, the title passed on from 'M' to the assessee, only by virtue of section 7 of the Metal Corporation (Nationalization and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 meaning thereby that till then the entire undertaking continued to be the property of 'M'. Notwithstanding that, since 'M' was deprived of the management and possession, as an administrator was appointed, who had run the industry during the intervening period, and who might have earned profit or might have incurred losses, but then the fact did remain, that 'M' could not run the undertaking, and earn any income therefrom. It appeared that said factor which had been taken into consideration, and it appeared to be agreed upon that 'M' would have earned the profits at the rate of Rs. 11.39 lakhs per annum, had it not been deprived of the possession and, therefore, it was directed to be compensated for the period during which it stood deprived of the possession and management. [Para 5]

If the acquisition would not have gone through, or would have ultimately failed, even then, 'M' would have been entitled to compensation for the deprivation, obviously, in which event the amount would not have been capable of being described as capital expenditure. Obviously, therefore, if the things went through, then too, that part of the amount could not be said to be the capital expenditure. Yet, another aspect of the matter was that no part of the amount of Rs. 122.79 lakhs was shown to have been intended, or have been contended by the parties, as paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of the undertaking of 'M'. [Para 6]

In that view of the matter, considering from any stand point, said amount could not be said to be a capital expenditure, and the Tribunal had rightly found so. The appeal, thus, having no force, was to be dismissed. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Holding company was doing business of chit fund in undivided State of Andhra Pradesh - Assessee-company was floated by holding company to do chit fund business exclusively in northern Telangana Districts - Holding company and assessee entered into a business agreement by which holding company rendered various services - In this agreement, both assessee and its holding company demarcated areas in which they shall carry out business operations - Assessee had to pay 1 per cent of its annual turnover to its holding company - Initially agreement was for a period of five years - Assessing Officer held that this agreement was for giving non-compete fee by assessee to its holding company which was capital in nature and hence, he disallowed same - Whether since agreement in question also included various other services to be provided by holding company to assessee company and payment was not just for non-competition agreement, payment made by assessee to its holding company was revenue expenditure as without payment of such non-compete fee, assessee could not carry on its business more efficiently and profitably - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure

FACT: The holding company was doing chit fund business in the undivided state of Andhra Pradesh. The assessee-company was floated by the holding company to do the chit fund business exclusively in northern Telangana Districts. Both the holding company and the subsidiary company entered into an agreement, according to which the assessee had to pay 1 per cent of its annual turnover for a period of five years as non-compete fee to the holding company for not carrying out its business in northern Telangana Districts. The agreement was also liable to be terminated at any time with a notice of 10 months by either parties. The payment made by the assessee was claimed to be revenue in nature on the ground that the payment was not only for non-competing, but was also for several other services rendered by the holding company to the assessee. It was also submitted that the assessee did not derive any benefit of enduring nature and, therefore, it could not be termed as capital expenditure.

The Assessing Officer was not convinced with the assessee's contentions. He held that the non-compete fee was capital in nature and, hence, disallowed the same and brought it to tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: As per various clauses of the agreement the holding company and the assessee herein have demarcated the areas and territory in which they shall operate and each of the two shall not carry out the operations in the areas allocated to each of them. The consideration to be paid by the assessee to its holding company for such restriction on its activities is at 1 per cent of the annual turnover. It is the case of the assessee that though the resolutions passed by the Board of Directors of the holding company was that the non-compete fee agreement is valid till 31-12-2060. The agreement was for a fixed period of 5 years only and the agreement was also liable to be terminated at any time with a notice of 10 months by either parties. [Para 4]

The first argument of the assessee was that, the holding company has offered the receipt to tax in its hands and therefore, it should be treated as revenue expenditure in the hands of the assessee as well. But, whether such treatment in the hands of the recipient would clinch the issue? It would not, because the nature of the payment could be capital in the hands of the payer, while it could be revenue receipt in the hands of the payee. For example, in the hands of the purchaser of a machinery, the payment would be capital in nature, while in the hands of the seller, it could be revenue receipt. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that because the receipt in the hands of the recipient i.e. the holding company has been accepted as a revenue receipt, it should be treated as revenue expenditure in the hands of the assessee is not acceptable. [Para 5]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where assessee purchased merchant banking division of other company and paid non-compete fee for restricting transferor from carrying out similar business for 36 months, same would be capital in nature [In favour of revenue]   As per transfer of business agreement, the assessee had purchased the merchant banking division from IGFL. The assessee in terms of agreement had also paid non-compete fee of Rs. one crore to the transferor and Rs. 70 lakhs to one S who was the managing director as well as shareholder of the transferor company for restricting the above persons from carrying out similar business and for preventing them from doing certain other actions. The assessee claimed said expenditure as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed expenditure as capital expenditure. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the expenditure had only facilitated higher efficiency and profitability of the assessee there being no changes in the fixed assets of the assessee. He, therefore, allowed expenditure as revenue expenditure.  Held that non-compete expenditure had been incurred in connection with setting up of the new business. Therefore, the expenditure had to be considered as capital in nature. Further, the non-compete agreement was valid for a period of three years which has to be considered as sufficient length of time to treat the expenditure as capital in nature. The protection acquired by the assessee from competition was not part of the working of the business and went on to appreciate the whole of the capital amount. Accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961—Capital or revenue expenditure—Assessee-company was engaged in business of developing minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc.—It had mining lease of survey no. 40 at a certain place—Another company, mmc, having prospective licence for extracting fluorspar in respect of adjacent survey no. 30, had preferential right for obtaining a lease thereon, but government rejected mmc's application for lease—MMC took legal proceeding and obtained interim orders restraining government from giving lease on survey no. 30 to any other party pending final outcome of litigation—Assessee-company also needed survey no. 30 to run its beneficiation plant for desired number of years—To expand business and ward off competition, assessee paid Rs. 3 lakhs to mmc on the latter agreeing to withdraw aforesaid legal proceedings, thus facilitating way for assessee to obtain long-term lease on survey no. 30—Whether said expenditure was capital or revenue in nature—Held, on facts, it was capital expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee was engaged in business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products - Assessee-company acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by assessee with latter - Consideration for such transfer included certain non-compete fee which was limited for a period of five years - For assessment year 2005-06, assessee filed its return of income wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, however, disallowed same on ground that payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay - Commissioner (Appeals) held that expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years - On second appeal, Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by assessee was capital in nature, as such disallowed claim - It was noted that assessee itself treated expenditure as capital in books of account - Likewise, in schedule 2 to balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets' - This also showed that assessee treated this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature - Whether in view of above, Tribunal rightly held expenditure as capital in nature - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2009-10 - Assessee purchased one division of 'N' chemicals by way of slump sale - Assessee paid certain amount as non-compete fee which represented difference in value of tangible and intangible assets and lump sum amount paid for taking over business - It was found that on account of payment of non-compete fee, seller was restrained from carrying on similar type of business for three years - Whether since payment of non-compete fee resulted in enduring benefit to assessee, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure; it was capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure  IT : Payment made for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division, was to be treated as capital expenditure  IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where assessee paid commission on export sales at same rate at which it had been paid by seller of business earlier, disallowance made by Assessing Officer taking a view that a part of commission payment was excessive, was to be deleted  IT : Foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by assessee in respect of outstanding foreign currency term loan was to be allowed as business loss  IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business  IT : Where Assessing Officer made disallowance in respect of dividend income by relying upon Rule 8D of Income-tax Rules, 1962, since said rule was applicable for assessment year 2008-09 while assessment year under consideration was 2007-08, impugned disallowance was to be deleted

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 - Assessee-company acquired brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement - Under a separate non-compete agreement, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company as consideration for restraining it from competing in business of products similar to Lacto Calamine for a period of ten years - Amount paid as non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure by assessee - Whether in cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and benefit of restrain acquired by assessee for period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit - Held, yes - Whether therefore, by paying non-compete fee, it could be said that assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by assessee was in nature of capital expenditure and not revenue in character as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 - Whether payment which frees an assessee from liability to make recurring revenue payments is revenue expenditure; though such benefit may be of an enduring nature but if it does not create any asset, then it cannot be treated as capital expenditure - Held, yes - During relevant year, promoters of a company Tata-IBM bifurcated its business activities and framed a separate entity (assessee-company) - Various assets of erstwhile Tata-IBM were agreed to be transferred to assessee for certain consideration - Assessee made payments on account of transfer of certain employees to it and on account of transfer of data base of domestic business and claimed same as revenue expenditure - However, Assessing Officer held that transfer of employees and database to assessee was to be considered as transfer of valuable asset giving an enduring advantage to it over a long period of time and, therefore, expenditure incurred for said transfer could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Admittedly, by making payment for getting domestic customer database, assessee had only got right to use that database; company which had provided such database was not precluded from using such database and, hence, expenditure incurred was for use of database and not for its acquisition - As regards payment made for transfer of human skill, that expenditure had been incurred to save expenses on training and on recruitment of employees which were under revenue field and, thus, it freed assessee from liability to make recurring revenue payments - Whether in view of above, payment on both counts was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Where assessee-firm took over running business of a trust and transfer was irrevocable, recurring payment made by assessee to trust for use of goodwill and other assets of trust could only be treated as capital expenditure
The assessee-firm had taken over a hotel and restaurant under the name ‘Vishala’ which was acquired in pursuance of an agreement between the assessee-firm and S. Family Trust. Earlier to the agreement, the aforesaid trust was carrying on business under the name and style of ‘Vishala’. Even in the assessee-firm, the trust was one of the partners. It was claimed by the assessee that the assessee had to pay a recurring expense of Rs. 1 lakh or 5 per cent of its sale, whichever was more, per year, for the use of goodwill and other assets of the trust under agreement, dated 2-6-1983. This payment was claimed to be of revenue nature and, therefore, to be deducted while computing appellant’s income.
Held that, in the instant case, there was transfer of a running business with all assets and liabilities including goodwill. There was absolutely no clause in the agreement which would indicate that transferor on the happening of a particular event was entitled to get back the running business or any part thereof. The party of the first part had no right at all to terminate the agreement. Therefore, there was complete transfer of running business from party of first part to party of second part for a consideration as provided in clause (8) of the agreement. The consideration as provided in the above clause was the total consideration for all assets including building, furniture and other assets and goodwill. The right vested in the party of first part in no way affected the passing of the property from the said party to party of second part. The mere fact that consideration was to be paid annually or through instalment would not affect the transfer of asset and the running business which was clearly of capital nature.
The conduct on the part of the assessee clearly clinched the issue that a capital asset in the shape of running business of restaurant and hotel was transferred to the assessee under the agreement. On building and other assets the assessee claimed depreciation as owner for the consideration paid as per clause (8) of the agreement. Having regard to the fact that amount in question was paid for acquiring an asset of enduring nature, the payment was rightly held to be of capital nature and not deductible.

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-During 1960 assessee-company entered into a 20-year agreement with foreign company for obtaining technical consultation and training facilities-Assesses paid Rs. 12 lakhs in lump sum initially and was to reimburse actual expenses incurred by foreign company from time to time in rendering stipulated services-Tribunal allowed assessee to spread said expenditure of Rs. 12 lakhs over 20-year period of agreement, treating it as revenue expenditure and thereby rejecting revenue's stand that it was capital expenditure which could not be spread over above-said period-Whether tribunal's view legally correct-Held, on facts, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance - Before final acquisition, assessee was appointed as an administrator of company and was put in charge of establishment - Assessee paid certain amount to 'M' being deprivation charges and claimed said amount as revenue expenditure - Whether since amount had been paid as compensation for deprivation of income which 'M' would have earned, had it not been deprived of possession and no part of said amount was paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of undertaking of 'M', amount paid by assessee was in nature of revenue expenditure - Held, yes

SECTION 37(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CAPITAL OR REVENUE EXPENDI
TURE-ASSESSEE-FIRM TOOK OVER NEW LINE OF BUSINESS IN GAS DISTRIBUTION AGENCY FROM COMPANY AND PAID FEES FOR TECHNICAL SERVICES RENDERED 
BY THAT COMPANY FOR CARRYING ON SAID BUSINESS-ITO DISALLOWED 
ASSESSEE’S CLAIM FOR DEDUCTIONS OF FEES SO PAID AS CAPITAL EXPENDITURE 
ON THE GROUNDS THAT BUSINESS HAD MERELY CHANGED HANDS AND THAT NO TECHNICAL SERVICES WERE REQUIRED FOR CARRYING ON ESTABLISHED AND RUNNING BUSINESS-WHETHER AAC WAS RIGHT IN ALLOWING ASSESSEE’S 
CLAIM-HELD, YES

IV. Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income (Revenue or capital receipt) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2008-09 - Assessee paid an amount of Rs. 1.30 crores for purpose of taking liner business of a German company from their existing agent and same was transferred to assessee's name - Later on, assessee lost business to Agent of German Company - On termination of agency, assessee received compensation of Rs. 59.96 lakhs from parent company - Assessee set off compensation received out of payment made for purpose of securing agency business and claimed balance amount as revenue expenditure - It was observed that compensation received by assessee was not from person to whom payment of Rs. 1.30 crores was made for securing agency business and, thus, had nothing to do with acquiring of agency - Whether treatment given by Assessing Officer of expenses incurred for securing agency business as capital expenditure and receipt of compensation on termination of agency business as revenue in nature was justified - Held, yes [Para 29] [In favour of revenue]

I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee company was incorporated in pursuance of joint venture agreement by and between LT Ltd. and 'S' Corporation, Japan - Prior to joint venture agreement, LT was engaged in business of developing, manufacturing, marketing, distributing and selling various electric equipments and products in India and it had a well established country-wide sales network in India - LT and 'S' Corporation, Japan established assessee company with limited liability for purpose of importing, marketing and selling in India certain electric and electronic office products - During relevant assessment year assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to LT in lieu of latter, not setting up undertaking/assisting in setting up any undertaking carrying on business of selling, marketing and trading of electronic office product for a period of 7 years in India - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee paid to LT under section 37(1) - Assessing Officer took a view that expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, therefore, amount so paid was to be treated as capital in nature - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since payment had been made to ward off competition for a period of 7 years during which assessee company could have set up its products and reputation in market, expenditure in question could not be treated to have been incurred in revenue field - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, authorities below were justified in rejecting assessee's claim - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2002-03 - Whether it is only if non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature, can it be said to be a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether where non-competition agreement entered into by assessee engaged in setting up power projects was to prevent rival company from establishing power plant in State for a period of three years and such, restrictive covenant eliminated competition in business only for a while and it was neither permanent nor advantage derived by assessee was enduring in nature, such expenditure could not be held to be capital expenditure and same had to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]IT: It is only if non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature, can be said to be a capital expenditure; payment of restrictive covenant is revenue expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1995-96 - Whether payment made to avail possibility of 
 an advantage should be considered as a payment made to remove a possible disadvantage and it is not a payment to acquire an enduring advantage - Held, yes - Assessee-company which was doing only financing business amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’ carrying on business of entertainment and paid certain amount to two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan, by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for next ten years - Assessee-company claimed deduction of amount paid as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Assessing Officer disallowed assessee’s claim and treated expenditure as capital expenditure for a new distinct business - Whether since Memorandum of Association authorized transferee-company to carry on business of transferor-company, it could not be said that payment was made by assessee for new and distinct business - Held, yes - Whether services of artists were obtained for ten years, but for facilitating their continued co-operation, which would go to increase assessee’s profitability, it was for 120 days in a year and artists were free to work anywhere else and, therefore, payment made to artists was for user of brand equity or talents and not for acquisition of capital asset as such - Held, yes - Whether assessee made payment to avail performance of artists when it was expedient to get artists in interest of trade and, therefore, same was allowable as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since expenditure was incurred in year under consideration, same was to be allowed in year of payment itself - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-Compete fee) - Assessee-company, engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors - Assessee's claim for deduction of said expenditure was rejected by Assessing Officer on ground that it was in nature of capital expenditure - Tribunal upheld order passed by Assessing Officer - Whether since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 15] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether once expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred restraining recipient for a short or limited period, expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase profitability of assessee and is not a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Assessee purchased running business of a firm along with its goodwill and paid certain amount to partners of that firm for not carrying on same line of business for five years - Whether expenditure incurred by assessee was revenue in nature and, hence, allowable - Held, yes - Whether, however, since expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in relevant assessment year as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1990-91 - Assessee was a representative agent of HP products in India - In order to ensure its monopoly status and eliminate any competition in its business for two years assessee entered into an agreement under which it agreed to pay consideration to BSL - BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products - Whether expenditure in question was of capital nature inasmuch as assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowable as - Assessment years 1973-74 and 1974-75 - Company M, which was sole distributor of assessee-company's product, was amalgamated with assessee - Amalgamation was done with a view to take advantage of services of experienced staff and existing distribution organisation of company M which was expected to ultimately result in increased profitability - Tribunal recorded a finding that as a result of amalgamation there was a radical alteration in framework of business of assessee-company - Whether legal expenditure incurred by assessee on aforesaid amalgamation was capital in nature - Held, yes - Whether fact that aforesaid acquisition of M by assessee was intended to increase profitability of assessee could convert capital expenditure into revenue expenditure - Held, no - Whether to hold a particular expenditure as revenue expenditure, nexus between expenditure and profitability should be proximate - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether to come to conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature, tests to be applied are where expenditure is incurred to set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in same line, to commence a business, to acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity, to acquire an asset and to acquire a source of generating income - Held, yes - Assessee purchased right, titles and ownership of two magazines/periodicals and agreement entered into between assessee and seller of two titles provided, inter alia, that seller was owner and publisher of titles, which were free from all charges, liens and encumbrances and assessee could, after purchase, use title and information in course of its
 business - Assessee claimed sum of Rs. 2.15 crores paid for acquiring titles of two magazines as revenue expenditure - Whether all tests led to one inescapable conclusion that what assessee had spent was for acquiring a new business/new assets/an enduring benefit and a source of income - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores was a capital expenditure not allowable under section 37(1) - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1978-79 - Whether compensation paid for acquiring assets, goodwill and to avoid competition in trade by vendor, being expenditure to acquire right of enduring benefit, would be capital expenditure in nature - Held, yes

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether payment made to ward off competition in business would constitute capital expenditure if object of making that payment is to derive an advantage by eliminating competition over some length of time; however, same result would not follow if there is no certainty of duration of advantage and same can be put on an end any time - Held, yes - Whether payment made by assessee-company to purchaser of its insecticides plant for restricting from selling and distribution of fast selling major products i.e. Thimet, Malathion and Abate, and for parting with specialized knowledge and expertise in relation to those products for a specific period of time, was required to be considered as capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 3.3] [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 2000-01 - Assessee-company had purchased shipping agency business from a vendor/seller 
through certain agreement - It had purchased said business for 
a consideration of Rs. 43,47,000, comprising of cost of goodwill at 
Rs. 5 lakhs and non-competition covenant fees of Rs. 38,47,000 - Assessee claimed that it had paid non-competition covenant fees to vendor for 
a period of 5 years and same was to be allowed as revenue expenditure 
in year of payment or in alternative same should be spread over 
 a period of 5 years - Lower authorities treated said expenditure as capital expenditure and, accordingly, disallowed assessee’s claim - Whether since assessee had made payment of non-competition fees on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down itself in a new acquired business of shipping and benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability, and was for a limited period of 5 years; and that too only in Indian territory, in such circumstances, payment of non-competition fees was allowable as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - Whether further since assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, said expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and corresponding expenditure was to be allowed in every year - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether an expenditure incurred on warding off competition in business from a rival dealer will constitute a capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure, it is not necessary that non-compete fee is paid to create monopoly rights - Held, yes

I. Section 37(1), read with section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Director, payments to) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietory concern, in view of fact that in terms of agreement, company did not acquire copyright, but only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, licence fee paid would be a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - [Paras 21 and 22] [In favour of assessee]IT: Where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietary concern, and in terms of agreement, company did not acquire copyright, but only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, license fee paid would be a revenue expenditure  IT: Where there were no findings of fact recorded that provisions of section 47 were invoked for claiming exemption from capital gains while making transfers from sole proprietary concern to assessee-company, deeming provision of sub-section(3) of section 47A could not have been invoked

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-Whether payments made for obtaining technical knowledge, advice and information, and for providing training facilities for assessee's employees, to bring assessee-company into effective and efficient operation are of revenue nature-Held, yes

SECTION 37(1)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CAPITAL OR REVENUE EXPEN-
DITURE-UNDER SCHEME OF AMALGAMATION APPROVED BY HIGH COURT, A BANKING COMPANY MERGED WITH ASSESSEE-COMPANY, RESULTING IN IN-
CREASED CAPITAL BASE AS WELL AS LARGER AVAILABILITY OF FUNDS TO ASSESSEE-WHETHER LEGAL EXPENSES INCURRED BY ASSESSEE FOR EFFECTING 
SAID MERGER WERE ALLOWABLE AS REVENUE EXPENDITURE-HELD, NO

Section 37(1), read with section 147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether where during original assessment, Assessing Officer had accepted non-compete fee paid by assessee-company to NPPL under a business purchase agreement as a revenue expenditure and passed an order under section 143(3) allowing same, re-opening of assessment by issue of impugned notice under section 148 treating said fees as capital expenditure was a mere change of opinion and did not constitute of any reasons to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where during original assessment, Assessing Officer had accepted non-compete fee paid by assessee-company to NPPL under a business purchase agreement as a revenue expenditure, re-opening of assessment by issue of impugned notice under section 148 treating said payment as capital expenditure was merely a change of opinion and thus was liable to be set-aside

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Non-compete fee - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one on revenue account - Held, yes - Assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with one 'U' for a period of 5 years - It paid a certain sum as non-compete fee to 'U' and claimed same as revenue expenditure - 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to clientele and pricing of products; as a business proposition, assessee entered into non-compete agreement - Whether payment was in respect of performing of business of assessee and, thus, expenditure was on revenue account and not on capital account - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee made payment as non-compete fee for purpose of business of assessee, expenditure was on revenue count

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Business expenditure-Assessee took over business with certain assets and liabilities of predecessor-firm along with right to act as sole selling agent of company manufacturing liquor-Assessee agreed to pay some fully paid up shares to partners in consideration of sale and royalty of RE. 1 per case of liquor sold for assignment of right to carry on sole selling agency-Whether payment of royalty was allowable as revenue expenditure-Held, no, as it was capital expenditure

Section 37(1), read with section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Capital asset) - Assessment year 2010-11 - During relevant year, assessee, a foreign company, had acquired third party debt collection services as well as part of analytical business of its Indian counterpart as going concern on "as is where is basis" - Out of total consideration, assessee paid certain amount towards acquisition of tangible assets, and remaining amount as payment towards customer contracts, which it claimed as revenue expenditure - Being of view that such expenditure had given enduring benefits to assessee, Assessing Officer treated said expenditure as capital in nature - It was found that assessee had made payment for acquiring customer contracts and assembled workforce, which were nothing but capital assets and would give enduring benefits to assessee, and assessee was not in said business - Whether expenditure incurred for acquiring completely new business set up was income generation tool and, hence, capital in nature - Held, yes - Whether, however, when payment made by assessee was not disputed and was in terms of an agreement between two parties, Commissioner (Appeals) could not arbitrarily and unitarily reduce a part of payment made for computing depreciation - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [Partly in favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, ITES provider, had made payment to its Indian counterpart for acquiring part of its business relating to debt collection service since assessee was not in debt collection service business before acquiring said business, expenditure incurred for acquiring completely new business set up was income generation tool and, hence, capital in nature

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Whether to test whether benefit derived by assessee by making a payment is of enduring nature, only point to be considered is whether threat which is perceived at time of agreement/incurring of expenditure will cease to exist after expiry of period or will re-occur - Held, yes - Whether where threat has potential of re-occurring after expiry of period, then benefit derived cannot be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate - It acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores - Assessee had also entered into another ‘non-compete agreement’ with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them - Under said agreement ‘V’ and ‘M’ were restricted to engage themselves in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with abovesaid chemicals for period of 5 years - In return assessee claimed whole of expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that expenditure was not incurred for improving profitability as there was no existing business and assessee had acquired business of chemicals for first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to company and disallowed claimed expenditure - Whether since ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with assessee even after a period of five years, it could be said that threat which was perceived at time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at expiry of period of five years and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Whether carrying on of same business prior to entering into non-compete agreement is not necessary to appreciate as to whether non-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1), read with section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Capital asset) - Assessment year 2010-11 - During relevant year, assessee, a foreign company, had acquired third party debt collection services as well as part of analytical business of its Indian counterpart as going concern on "as is where is basis" - Out of total consideration, assessee paid certain amount towards acquisition of tangible assets, and remaining amount as payment towards customer contracts, which it claimed as revenue expenditure - Being of view that such expenditure had given enduring benefits to assessee, Assessing Officer treated said expenditure as capital in nature - It was found that assessee had made payment for acquiring customer contracts and assembled workforce, which were nothing but capital assets and would give enduring benefits to assessee, and assessee was not in said business - Whether expenditure incurred for acquiring completely new business set up was income generation tool and, hence, capital in nature - Held, yes - Whether, however, when payment made by assessee was not disputed and was in terms of an agreement between two parties, Commissioner (Appeals) could not arbitrarily and unitarily reduce a part of payment made for computing depreciation - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [Partly in favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1962-63 - During relevant accounting year, assessee company took over business carried on by a firm including its employees - Aforesaid firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at age of 57½ years and paying them gratuity at time of retirement - Assessee-company also had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees on retirement, but there was no fixed age of retirement for employees - As per terms of agreement of taking over business, assessee-company was to retire all its employees who had exceeded age of 57½ years and to pay them gratuity - Assessee-company did so and claimed amount paid as revenue expenditure - ITO taking a view that amount so paid was nothing but part of business consideration held that expenditure in question was capital in nature and not allowable as deduction - AAC as well as Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - On instant reference, it was seen that Tribunal had recorded finding that there was an existing scheme for employees of assessee-company who were paid this amount by way of gratuity - It was also recorded that payment was made under circumstances as would ensure retention of remaining staff and contentment amongst them - Whether in aforesaid findings, order passed by Tribunal allowing assessee's claim was to be upheld - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-Compete fee) - Assessee-company, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors - Assessee's claim for deduction of said expenditure was rejected by Assessing Officer on ground that it was in nature of capital expenditure - Tribunal upheld order passed by Assessing Officer - High Court by impugned order held that since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Whether special leave petition filed against impugned order was to be dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect against High Court ruling that where assessee made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922) - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1953-54 to 1955-56 - Assessee-company took over routes of various private operators and paid compensation to get rid of competition from said operators - Whether compensation so paid was an expenditure of capital nature and, thus, it could not be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee company paid certain amount to English company under agreement between them for certain information provided by English company - Under agreement assessee company was not entitled to use information after termination of agreement and was prohibited from disclosing said information, process etc. during currency of agreement and also after determination of agreement - Whether amount paid by assessee company to English company was not for purpose of bringing into existence any asset or advantage of enduring nature and, therefore, said expenditure was not capital expenditure but revenue expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or-Revenue expenditure-Whether legal charges paid in connection with amalgamation of a race club with the assessee-race club was revenue expenditure-Held, yes

section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - One GD started certain transport services under partnership firms on certain routes, 
 and subsequently admitted his son GG also in said partnerships - In relevant financial year there were certain changes in constitution of said partnerships, net effect of which was that all old partners, including GD and GG retired from said firms step by step and new partners entered in their places - GG and GD were paid certain amounts by said firms supposedly on account of giving assurance by them that they would not carry on competing transport services on those routes for a period of five years - Whether said compensation was in fact paid for three purposes, i.e., (i) for share in assets of said partnerships, (ii) for share of goodwill in same, and (iii) for restrictive covenant in terms of section 36(2) of the Partnership Act, and not only for restrictive covenant as claimed by assessees - Held, yes - Whether that part of compensation amount which was referable to items (i) and (ii) was to be treated as on capital amount and was, therefore, not allowable in assessee-firm's hands - Held, yes - Whether that part of compensation which related to item (iii) as aforesaid, was to be allowed as revenue expenditure in assessee-firm's hands as no asset of enduring advantage was brought in thereby - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee-company claimed legal expenses incurred on its amalgamation with another company as revenue expenditure - ITO disallowed assessee’s claim holding that said expenditure was capital expenditure - Tribunal, however, allowed assessee’s claim - Whether since amalgamation of two companies is resorted to for smooth and efficient conduct of business of company, whether it is transferee-company or transferor-company, merely because assessee-company was transferor-company, it could not be held that expenditure on legal fees was not incurred wholly and exclusively for purpose of business of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in allowing assessee’s claim - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of Assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63 - Assessee, a union of truck operators provided facilities to its member operators in matter of booking their trucks and charged commission at rate of 5 per cent on gross booking - Out of commission so received, one-half was paid to members of union whose trucks could not be booked - Whether since payment was made to eliminate competitors and to carry on business unfettered by competition, payment was of capital nature and was not permissible deduction as revenue expenditure in computing assessee's total income - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non - Compete fees) - Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee-company entered into a non-compete agreement with one, 'RM' for a period of five years - It paid a certain sum as non-compete fee and claimed same as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer disallowed same stating that payment was of capital nature and was not allowable under section 37(1) - It was not disputed that expenditure was laid out and expended for purpose of business - Further, on account of payment of non-compete fee, assessee had not acquired any new business or any new source of income and that profit making apparatus and assets used to run business remained same - Whether since payment made as non-compete fee did not entail any enduring benefits to assessee in its business, same was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Para 48] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where non-compete fee paid by assessee was for purpose of its business and it did not entail any enduring benefit to assessee in its business, payment of such fee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital or revenue expenditure - Assessee purchased its present business during assessment year 1974-75 from vendor with all assets and liabilities including liability to pay bonus to workers for period prior to date of takeover - After bonus amount was quantified, assessee paid a part of bonus in year 1974-75 and balance amount during year 1975-76 and claimed it as a revenue expenditure - Whether balance bonus paid in accounting year relevant to assessment year 1975-76 was revenue expenditure - Held, no

The Assessing Officer found during the course of assessment proceedings that a sum of Rs. 2.5 crores was reflected as a cost of office building purchased as on 31-3-2000. But in a subsequent year the company classified the amount as 'loans and advances' and added back the depreciation claimed on the office building. On the change of the stand, the assessee explained that a sum of Rs. 2.5 crores was given by an earlier company, namely, JI Ltd. for acquiring the use of premises for business purposes. This advance was given by JI Ltd. when it was not amalgamated with the assessee-company. After amalgamation, the claim of depreciation which continued to be passed on to the assessee-company was claimed but the error was rectified by filing the revised return. Thus, an error had crept in classifying the sum of Rs. 2.5 crores as an asset which was thereafter reclassified as 'loans and advances'. The Assessing Officer, however, did not agree with this explanation and held that the assessee-company had made advances to one of the directors of the company by camouflaging it as a security deposit. The company had paid huge interest on its borrowings to the extent of Rs. 83,42,846. He also held that reclassification of fixed assets into 'advances' was done with a mala fide intent to evade payment of tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim on the ground that expenditure of Rs. 2.5 crores was incurred out of share capital raised by JI Ltd. and it had no element of cost.  Held that investment in the property was done by JI Ltd. prior to its amalgamation with assessee-company and was out of funds raised in public issue by that company. Later on, this company merged with the assessee resulting in transfer of asset to the present company. Even though reclassification from 'asset' to 'loans and advances' may not be free from doubt but the fact that the investment in the property was clearly out of interest-free funds being the share capital raised by earlier company. Therefore, the question of disallowing interest paid by the assessee-company did not arise. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where assessee, engaged in business of development of software and portal sites, incurred expenditure on lease rental, travelling, stationery, professional charges, advertisements, etc., for developing portal/website, right over which was transferred to another company and in lieu thereof 70 per cent of revenue would come to coffers of assessee, expenditure so incurred by assessee was allowable as revenue expenditure [In favour of assessee]   The assessee was in the business of development of software and portal sites and earning revenue therefrom. It had incurred expenditure on lease rental, travelling, stationery, professional charges, advertisements, etc., for developing portal/website right over which was transferred to one VGS as per agreement with them and in lieu thereof 70 per cent of revenue would come to the coffers of the assessee. The Assessing Officer held that the expenditure in question was capital expenditure.  Held that once the assessee was in the business of developing software and portals then the development of the portal for VGS would only be an extension or a part of the existing business of the assessee. Therefore, expenditure incurred thereon would only be of revenue nature.

facts.text:
