The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

(3) If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operation, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature. (5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]

Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

On reference, the assessee-company contended that since the expenditure was incurred for acquiring the film shorts, it should be taken to have been expended for acquiring stock-in-trade of the assessee's business :

The assessee-company was in the business of finance. During the relevant assessment year, it purchased the business of computer software along with certain assets and liabilities belonging to LSI.

During the short period of its existence, LSI did some preliminary work in developing some technical knowledge basis of software in banking sector. Before formal takeover of LSI, four directors of LSI entered into agreement, called restrictive covenant with the assessee agreeing not to carry on the business of computer software development and marketing and other related business for a period of five years in consideration of cash paid by the assessee. For the relevant assessment year, the assessee claimed the amount paid to the directors as deduction from its income. The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure and added it to the income returned by the assessee for the reason that the payment was made to avail exclusive rights of the services of professionals for a period of five years and to ward off the competition and, therefore, the payment was distinctly in nature of capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the payment was not capital in nature, but revenue in nature.

On appeal by the revenue :

The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles. It entered into an agreement for purchase of assets and liabilities of a newly set up factory, established by a company, named, SML in Madras. According to the assessee, the consideration in the said agreement was in two parts - First Rs. 1.30 crores towards the net asset value and secondly Rs. 70 lakhs paid on account of non-compete clause for a period of five years.

The Assessing Officer held that the intention of the assessee was to keep competitors out of the market thereby increasing sales, and, thus, the said amount could not be held to be revenue expenditure as it derived long term benefit and, thus, it was capital expenditure.

The assessee approached the Commissioner (Appeals) who held that since the non-competition period was for a short term of five years, the expenditure was revenue in nature.

The Tribunal reversed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and restored the finding of the Assessing Officer on the ground that the assessee was the only manufacturer in India for front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles and being the sole manufacturer, it acquired an enduring benefit. Thus, the expenditure was capital in nature as the assessee eliminated its only competitor after acquiring the factory, thereby perpetuating its exclusivity in the market.

On appeal:

Assessee, a manufacturer and exporter of bulk drugs and other pharmaceuticals, had, during relevant previous year, through an agreement dated 2-1-2003 acquired from 'M' Ltd. 'S' Ltd. and 'V', their pharmaceuticals business comprising of therapeutic segments of neuropsychiatry, cardio-vascular and anti-diabetes as well as nutraceuticals and dietary supplements including the intellectual property rights and goodwill for a total price of Rs. 24 crores, excluding fixed assets and value of outstanding inventory. The assessee claimed a sum of Rs. 2 crores paid towards non-compete fee as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer noted that assessee had paid Rs. 2 crores up-front and the period of non-compete agreement was long enough to be considered as resulting in an advantage of enduring nature. Thus, the Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's claim treating the expenditure in question as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture of ink. One A was the managing director of the assessee for about 18 years and left it on 31-10-1971. Thereafter he entertained the idea of utilising his experience with the assessee in the manufacture and sale of ink. A partnership firm was formed consisting of his wife and two daughters of A for the purpose of manufacture and sale of writing ink. All the preparations such as industrial licence, an industrial site, opening of bank account, advertisements, etc., were made. Thereafter, an agreement was entered into on 14-2-1972 between the assessee and the partnership whereby the assessee agreed to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 to the firm by way of compensation and firm agreed to discontinue the aforesaid business forthwith and also agreed to not to commence said business at any time within a period of five years. As per agreement the aforesaid amount was paid to the firm and the firm was closed down. For the assessment year 1972-73 the assessee claimed that the aforesaid payment was revenue expenditure, deductible in computing its income. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim and held that the expenditure was incurred by the assessee once and for all to ward off competition in the business and also with a view to bring into existence an enduring benefit or advantage to the assessee with no competition whatsoever. Thus, the expenditure was an item of capital expenditure. On second appeal, the Tribunal also held it as an expenditure of capital nature.

On reference:

During the relevant assessment year, the assessee purchased goodwill along with the running business from a firm for Rs. 10 lakhs. The assessee further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of said firm for not carrying on same line of business and other related fields for 5 years. In the computation of income, the assessee claimed the expenditure of Rs. 5 lakhs as revenue expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer treated the said expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee purchased one division of 'N' Chemicals which was transferred to the assessee by way of slump sales. The assessee treated the same as capital expenditure in the books of account and claimed depreciation on said amount. For the purpose of computing total income under the Act, the assessee treated Rs. 6.80 crores as non-compete fee on the basis of the value of the intangibles determined by the valuers.

The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure by holding that the amount claimed as fee for non-compete was nothing but goodwill of the business.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, took a view that by entering into a restrictive covenant the assessee had warded off a potential competition from the transferor. He thus held that amount paid as non-compete fee was to be regarded as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee-company, engaged in the business of manufacture of medicines and Lacto Calamine, purchased the brand name ‘Lacto Calamine’ from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement. Subsequently, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company under a non-compete agreement for restraining it from competing directly or indirectly in the business activities carried on by the assessee. The payment so made for the purchase of brand name was accounted for by the assessee as an item of capital expenditure but the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs paid as non-compete fee was claimed as a deduction being revenue in nature under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer, however, rejected the assessee’s said claim by holding that non-compete fee paid by it to ‘D’ was a capital expenditure inasmuch as by making said payment the assessee had acquired an advantage of an enduring nature by way of freedom from competition that would have been induced by ‘D’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance. During the period of litigation before final acquisition, the assessee was appointed as administrator of 'M' and it was put in charge of the establishment. The assessee paid a total consideration of Rs. 320.79 lakhs to 'M' out of which Rs. 122.79 lakhs (at the rate of Rs.11.39 lakhs per annum) was for deprivation of management and Rs. 198 lakhs was for acquisition of the undertaking. The assessee claimed that amount of Rs. 122.79 lakhs paid by it was a revenue expenditure. The Commissioner disallowed the assessee's claim and treated the entire amount as a capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal found that out of the amount of Rs. 320.79 lakhs, the amount of Rs. 198 lakhs was a capital expenditure, but the another sum of Rs. 122.79 lakhs, being deprivation charges, was in the nature of revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal :

The assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate. The assessee had acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores. The industry/plant so purchased was to include entire business undertaking situated at Ponada including movable and immovable properties and all other tangible and intangible assets relating to the business of manufacturing of aforesaid chemicals. The assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them. The said agreement provided forrestriction on ‘V’ and ‘M’ to engage in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate directly or indirectly for a period of 5 years for a cash consideration of Rs. 6 crores to be paid upfront. In the books of account, the assessee wrote off one-fifth of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores because the period during which agreement was to remain in force was 5 years but in the computation of income furnished along with return, the assessee claimed whole of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that the expenditure was not incurred for improving the profitability, as there was no existing business and the assessee had acquired the business of chemicals for the first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to the company and disallowed the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores claimed as revenue expenditure and treated it as capital expenditure. The Assessing Officer also disallowed the alternative claim made by the assessee that if the expenditure in question was not considered as revenue expenditure, then the assessee by having entered into non-compete agreement as per which ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ were not to carry on either manufacturing or trading business in the two chemicals for a period of five years, the assessee had acquired commercial/business rights for a period of 5 years to carry on manufacturing and trading activities in both the chemicals undisturbed and freely for a period of five years, which were of intangible nature entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the assessee might be allowed depreciation. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not acquired any specific intellectual right by making payment of Rs. 6 crores, which was eligible for depreciation under section 32.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. He held that no doubt the assessee earlier was doing only some trading business in the chemicals but it was not much; another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India; by making a payment of Rs. 6 crores to ‘V’ the advantage had accrued to the assessee and that too of enduring nature and, accordingly, the expenditure was capital in nature and; the impugned expenditure could not be considered as deferred revenue expenditure and, accordingly, could not be allowed proportionately in five years as contended by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the non-compete fees of Rs. 6 crores paid by the assessee to ‘V’ did not bring in any asset as mentioned in section 32(1)(ii) so as to qualify for depreciation.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company had purchased the shipping agency business from a vendor/seller through certain agreement. It had purchased the said shipping business for a consideration of Rs. 43,47,000, comprising of cost of goodwill at Rs. 5 lakhs and non-competition covenant fees of Rs. 38,47,000. The assessee claimed that it had paid the non-competition covenant fees to the vendor for a period of 5 years and the same was to be allowed as revenue expenditure in the year of payment or in the alternative the same should be spread over a period of 5 years as non-competition covenant was only for 5 years. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee holding that the purchase price paid for non-competition covenant was in the nature of goodwill and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order holding that the expenditure was in the nature of capital expenditure.

On second appeal :

Tata-IBM company was jointly promoted by Tata and IBM. During the financial year 1997-98, the two promoters agreed to bifurcate the business activities of the company into separate entities, viz., the assessee-company and Tata-IBM company. As per the agreement, various assets of the erstwhile Tata-IBM were transferred to the assessee for a certain consideration. As mutually agreed upon, the assessee made payments on account of transfer of certain employees to the assessee and on account of transfer of the database of the domestic business, and claimed deduction of same as revenue expenditure. In respect of the value of data base, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee itself had amortized the above expenditure over a period of 5 years in its books of account. According to him, the benefit that accrued to the assessee was of an enduring nature. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that the payment had been made towards acquisition of a capital asset and, therefore, such expenditure was not allowable as a revenue expenditure. In respect of the value of personnel transferred, the Assessing Officer concluded that the employees transferred to the assessee were to be considered as valuable assets, which would give an enduring advantage to it over a long period of time, and in case such employees were not viewed as valuable assets, there could not have been any necessity to pay such huge compensation towards an arrangement of their transfer to the assessee. Thus, the Assessing Officer treated the compensation paid by the assessee to Tata-IBM towards the so called transfer of human skills and the so called customer data base as part and parcel of overall consideration mutually agreed upon for the taking over of the software segment of the business of the erstwhile Tata-IBM. The Assessing Officer, therefore, disallowed the expenditure claimed as revenue expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of security and access control system integration. The assessee entered into a Business Purchase Agreement (BPA) with DETPL. As per the BPA, the assessee-company purchased the business of DETPL for a consideration of Rs. 11.71 crores. Some of the employees of DETPL were terminated, while others were retained. The purchase consideration included a sum of Rs. 54.43 lakhs as non-compete fees paid to 'S' and a sum of Rs. 43.55 lakhs paid to him for the purchase of patents.

The payment of non-compete fees was treated as revenue expenditure in the computation of total income as per the Income-tax Act, while in the books of account it was treated as an asset by the assessee.

The Assessing Authority held that non-compete fees is capital in nature and, therefore, he disallowed it as a revenue expenditure.

In appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), the assessee contended that, if the non-compete fee is paid for warding off the competition for a short period, the expenditure would be of a revenue in nature deductible under section 37 and if the non-compete fees is treated as capital in nature, then it would be expenditure incurred for the purpose of other intangible assets and hence depreciation at the rate of 25 per cent should be allowed for the relevant assessment years. However, the Appellate Authority held that the non-compete fee is in the nature of capital expenditure. However, it held that no depreciation was allowable.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee is in the nature of capital expenditure. It is in the nature of a business or commercial right and depreciation is allowable on such an asset and, thus, allowed the appeal.

The assessee-milk co-operative society, paid compensation to another milk co-operative society for acquiring their assets, goodwill as well as to avoid competition in trade. The Tribunal held the expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the same.

On reference :

During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

The assessee, a registered accountant, was doing some business. Subsequently, he was employed by one 'S' who was also doing similar business at 'K'. After some time, the assessee was taken as a working partner of the 'K' branch. Subsequently, under an agreement, evidenced by a letter addressed by the assessee to 'S', the assessee became the owner of the 'K' branch. The letter which evidenced the agreement between 'S' and the assessee stated that the goodwill was to be valued at half the net profits (book profits) of the 'K' office for the three years ending with 31-3-1949 and that no case of the 'K' office was to be taken by 'S' without the consent of the assessee and without an office being opened by 'S' and without repayment of half fee collected for such case during the period the goodwill had been paid by the assessee to 'S'. 'S' in pursuance of this agreement, received a sum from the assessee. The assessee claimed that that sum should be deducted as a revenue expenditure. However, the department and the Tribunal held that the aforesaid sum was a capital expenditure.

On reference :

Facts

•

The Court granted a scheme of amalgamation of some companies with the assessee-company.

•

The assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with 'U' former chairman and managing director of the amalgamating companies and paid a certain sum to 'U' by way of non-compete fee.

•

It claimed said amount as a revenue expenditure but did not write off same in its books of account.

•

The Assessing Officer found that non-compete agreement had increased the assessee's market presence and improved its potential to have better results in the market; the payment made over a period of more than five years once was for procuring an enduring benefit to the business. Consequently, he held that the expenditure was in the capital field and disallowed said claim.

•

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the decision of the assessing authority.

•

The Tribunal, by a cryptic order, rejected the assessee's claim.

Argument of assessee

•

The agreement entered into between the assessee with 'U' would clearly show that the expenditure was only on the revenue account.

Argument of revenue

•

When the assessee had not written off the said expenditure in its accounts and the amount paid was to ward off any competition in the business of the assessee, the expenditure made was only a capital expenditure.

Issue involved

•

Whether non-compete fee paid to the ex-managing director was a revenue or a capital expenditure?

The assessee was a company involved in setting up of power projects. The assessee was initially promoted by three companies including KHPL represented by one R. Raju. Due to certain disputes, an agreement was signed according to which said R. Raju would exit from assessee-company and would stay away of all contacts, suppliers, funding agencies and other business associates of the assessee. The non-competition agreement was only for a limited period of three years to ward off competition in territory of Andhra Pradesh. The assessee paid Rs. 3.25 crores to KHPL and claimed deduction as revenue expenditure.

The Assessing Officer held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee was capital expenditure in nature, without bringing about any depreciable asset into existence. He, therefore, disallowed the expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred did not relate to acquisition of an asset or a right of permanent character or an advantage of enduring nature and, thus, such expenditure could not be held to be capital expenditure. However, the same had to be allowed as revenue expenditure as it was paid for the business.

On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On the revenue's appeal before the High Court:

The assessee's sources of business income were exports and commission received from Indian and foreign authorities. He claimed deduction on account of commission paid by him to GFC as against his receipt of commission. The Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) held the expenditure as capital in nature and disallowed the same. On further appeal, the Tribunal accepted the assessee's pleas that GFC had helped him in obtaining better price and there was a regular MOU between them specifying the terms of the understanding and the commission was paid accordingly. The Tribunal opined that if the expenditure eliminated for good a competitor then it was a capital expenditure but if the expenditure related to ward off competition in individual transaction leaving the competitor surviving in the field, then it was merely a revenue expenditure. According to the Tribunal the test which divides an expenditure between the capital and revenue was one of enduring benefit.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee purchased two distilleries. The Assessing Officer observed that there were limits to the price of shares of a company determined by market forces and in the instant case it was difficult to imagine that such limits would not have been operative and the assessee was left with no option but to pay the cost of acquisition over and above the price paid for the acquisition of the shares of these companies to their promoters; that, in order to claim the payments as allowable deduction, the transaction was given the colour of payments as non-competition fees, but, in fact, the real purpose of those payments was to compensate the promoters of the companies owning the two distilleries for the cost of the distilleries; that it was not the case of the assessee that the payments were made to any distillery owner or business rival and it was also not the case of the assessee that the persons who were paid the said amounts possessed special expertise and skill so as to threaten the business of the assessee; and that the circumstance that these persons’ companies/ distilleries did not produce any brand of liquor with national market presence, did not support the case of the assessee as to the real purpose or motive of the said payments. He, therefore, held that the claim of the assessee for allowability of Rs. 10 crores as business expenditure was nothing but part of the cost of distilleries and added it to the income of the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the payment could not be taken as the revenue expenditure because the agreements were to run for a long duration of 10 years unfettered by any stipulation of termination; that payment of non-competition fees could have some rationale if the competition was between equals producing the same commodity and that the promoters of the two distilleries taken over were no match for the assessee who had monopoly of manufacturing and marketing its own brand names. He, therefore, held that there was no business necessity for making the non-competition fees of Rs. 10 crores and upheld the disallowance.

On further appeal :

The assessee was a manufacturer of tractors, jeeps and motorvehicles. It incurred expenses to the tune of Rs. 7.97 crores, towards acquiring various companies and entities, Indian and overseas. The assessee claimed such expenditure to be revenue in nature, incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee. The Assessing Officer, however, denied the claim and held the expenditure to be capital in nature.

• The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

The ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that the compensation paid was not to get rid of any onerous agreements, but to acquire a profit-making apparatus and, therefore, the payment was a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the Assessing Officers order.

On second appeal, Tribunal upheld the Commissioner (Appeal)’s order.

On reference, assessee’s case was that the distributors were dealing with the products of the assessee and, after termination of the agreements, the taking over of the business of distributors would not amount to acquisition of business or capital asset.

The assessee-company, a manufacturer of certain types of gears, had entered into an agreement with a foreign company which was to provide technical knowledge, information and advice required to bring the assessee into effective and efficient operation for the manufacture of these gears. The foreign company was also to provide complete drawings, designs, data information and advice and to give facilities for training the assessee's employees at the company's works in the foreign country. On reference :

■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal of the assessee as being devoid of any merit. The High Court opined that expenditure incurred by the assessee by way of non-compete fee paid to L&T could not be claimed as a revenue expenditure as it was clearly a capital expenditure. Despite holding the expenditure to be capital in nature, the High Court was of the further view that the non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for 7 years did not result in depreciable intangible asset. It was held that the right acquired by the assessee by payment of non-compete fee was a right in personam only against L&T for a period of 7 years. It was not a right in rem.

■

Adverting to the expression 'similar business or commercial rights' appearing in section 32(1)(ii), the High Court opined that it has to necessarily result in an intangible asset against the entire world to qualify for depreciation under the said provision. The High Court therefore dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

However, the Assessing Officer held that such payment of non-compete fee would result into enduring benefits to the assessee. Accordingly, the same was treated as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such a payment was paid for a restriction of three years and therefore, there is no question of any enduring benefit coming to the assessee. Moreover, the said Ex-Managing Director expired before the said period of three years, thus, such a payment was nothing but revenue expenditure.

On appeal by the Revenue:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of development of minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc., including extraction of fluorspar. It held a mining lease on Survey No. 40 in a certain village. Another company MMC held a prospecting licence for extracting fluorspar from the adjacent Survey No. 30 and applied for a mining lease thereon and prepared a prospecting report also. Under section 11(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, MMC had a preferential right for obtaining such a lease, but the Government rejected its application whereupon it went to Court for redress and obtained interim orders restraining the Government from giving the said Survey No. 30 on lease to any other party. Meanwhile the assessee-corporation had also applied for a mining lease on the said Survey No. 30. It had spent considerable amount on erecting its beneficiation plant for fluorspar which could run for the desired number of years only if it could get raw material from Survey No. 40 as well as Survey No. 30. The assessee-corporation, therefore, with a view to expanding its business, avoiding competition on the adjacent land and getting the required raw material for the desired number of years, entered into an agreement with MMC whereby it paid a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs to MMC on latter agreeing to withdraw the pending legal proceedings and give up its claim to Survey No. 30 to clear the assessee's path for obtaining a lease thereon. The assessee claimed, the aforesaid payment of Rs. 3 lakhs as revenue expenditure in the assessment year 1970-71. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim, holding the expenditure to be of capital nature. The AAC upheld the ITO's order on the ground that the benefit derived from the payment was of an enduring nature. The Tribunal confirmed the AAC's order.

On reference:

The assessee-firm purchased the business of export of hides and skins carried on by one G as a sole proprietary concern. Under the terms of the purchase, the take over by the assessee-firm was of the business as a whole including goodwill, trade mark, import and export quota rights as well as trade outstandings and trade debts. Subsequent to the take over of the business, the assessee-firm had to settle claims of certain foreign buyers in respect of short supply of goods sold by the assessee's predecessor and made payments to them, which it claimed as a business outgoing. On appeal, the ITO and the AAC rejected the assessee's claim for deduction. On further appeal the Tribunal, however, held that the amount paid was an item of business expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred by the assessee for the purpose of its business, and that the expenditure was not of a capital nature.

On reference, the revenue argued that the payment was not admissible as expenditure as it was not a legal or commercial obligation of the assessee and that, in any case, it was of a capital nature.

The assessee paid certain amount for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division of 'N' Chemicals.

The Assessing Officer opined that the expenses were incurred to bring new assets into existence, resulting in the benefit of enduring nature. He, therefore, treated those expenses as capital in nature.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that payment in question was allowable as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee purchased a hotel which had remained closed due to labour problems. At the time of purchase, the assessee had to pay Rs. 6.31 lakhs as compensation to the employees who were retrenched by the earlier management, as per agreement with the representatives of the workmen. The assessee contended that as the liability had to be incurred in order to run the business, it should be allowed as revenue expenditure. Alternatively, it was contended that it should be allowed as a capital expenditure and depreciation should be allowed on it. The Assessing Officer treated it as a capital expenditure but did not allow depreciation in respect thereof. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the Assessing Officer's order holding that the expenditure was not part of the purchase consideration and the payment was not as per agreement between the transferor and the assessee. The Tribunal, however, was of the view that since the assessee could not have conducted the business unless the compensation was paid, it was capital expenditure incurred in connection with or incidental to the acquisition cost of the asset and allowed assessee's claim for depreciation.

On reference :

The assessee had set up two new two star hotels during the relevant assessment year. Certain expenses in the form of salaries, training and development of general managers, service engineers, etc,. were incurred by the assessee after the setting up of its business but before the date of commencement of business to enable smooth functioning of the activities post commencement of business to provide uninterrupted and better services to the guests in the hotel without any obstruction.

These expenses though treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the books of account, but for the purpose of income tax, the same were claimed as revenue expenditure in full in the year of incurrence.

The Assessing Officer disallowed said expenditure by treating the same as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition.

On revenue's appeal:

held.text:
•

As far as the question as to whether an expenditure could be a capital expenditure or revenue expenditure is concerned, the concept that the expenditure yielding an advantage of enduring nature would be only a capital expenditure, has been fine-tuned, that even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one of revenue account. [Para 14]

•

It is not denied by the revenue that 'U' was the chairman and managing director of some of the companies which got merged with the assessee-company. 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to the clientele and the products, including the pricing of the products. By a process of amalgamation, the assessee had acquired the business of the amalgamating companies. However, for the fruitful exercise of its business as a business proposition, the assessee thought it fit to enter into a non-compete agreement with a person who had the knowledge of the entire operations, so as to get the full yield of the amalgamated company's business. In that context, rightly, the assessee took a commercial decision to pay non-compete fee to 'U' and going by the decision of the Apex Court, that the payment was in respect of the performing of the business of the assessee, it was to be held that the expenditure is only on revenue account and not on capital account. In the circumstances, the order of the Tribunal was set aside. [Para 19]

The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

If the expenditure relates to the domain of running the business concern, then, ordinarily, it would be revenue expenditure. If, on the other hand, the expenditure is made to acquire a certain business to free the business of the assessee from competition, then the expenditure is one of a capital nature. The ultimate conclusion would depend on the character of the expenditure.

In instant case, the assessee-company acquired the unexpired permits and thereby got rid of competition from private operators who were on the field prior to the acquisition. The investment was clearly one of a capital nature.

That being the conclusion, the amount was rightly not allowed as a deduction.

Note : The case was decided against assessee.

The amount in question was paid only to those members whose trucks were not booked. But for this payment, they would have otherwise competed in the business with the assessee. The object of the payment was to eliminate those competitors and to carry on the business unfettered by competition. The assessee made the payment to acquire this right of these persons. This led to enhance the value of its existing assets to make them more profit-yielding. The expense, therefore, could not be a revenue expense but was of a capital nature. The Tribunal was therefore right, in holding that amount so paid was not a permissible deduction for the purpose of income-tax.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

It could not be gainsaid that in agreeing on the price at which the business was taken over by the assessee from the vendor all the liabilities as well as the assets of the firm had been taken into account. One of the liabilities obviously was the liability towards bonus for the period preceding the date of the takeover. It was known to the assessee that as consideration for the takeover, it would have to incur a liability to the full extent finally determined as the amount payable as bonus for the period preceding the takeover. The amount, thus, spent in payment of bonus for that period was not an amount expended by the assessee to carry on, and earn the profits or gains of the business which it took over, but an amount expended to obtain the business which it purchased. That was not an expenditure, which partook the character of revenue, but it was clearly a capital expenditure. Therefore, the balance bonus paid during the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1975-76 was not a revenue expenditure.

It was not possible for G’s group to recognise the past services of R as already both the groups were having serious disputes and the matter was pending before the High Court. G’s group had removed R from his position in the assessee-company and Board of Directors and restrained R from operating bank accounts of four companies of this group and from attending day-to-day work. No specific amount had been earmarked for alleged past services. Further R being MD of the assessee must have been getting salaries for the services rendered by him in the past and question of any amount being assigned for such past services did not arise. There was no scope for recognising the past services of R and to allocate any amount out of the impugned amount given to R.

The assessee-company had not brought anything on record to show that R acquired special expertise or experience in the bus-body building activities. It was not the case of the assessee that R had got any special training in India or abroad in the bus-body building operation or he himself had made any research or was personally involved in such activities. If these were the facts, then this was not a ground for giving the amount to R. The assessee was running in losses and even if some salary was being given to R, a sum of Rs. 1.29 crores shall not be in any manner near to the amounts R would have earned as profit from company or would have got emoluments to that extent. What was the criterion of assessee-company to arrive at this figure of Rs. 1.29 crores was not explained.

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Admittedly, the assessee was participating in an auction to obtain the privilege of vending liquor. The question was whether elimination of a rival from competing with the auction will be opposed to public policy. This question cannot be considered in isolation de hors the nature of the trade, privilege or the right with respect to which the auction is held. If the subject-matter involved is a trade which could be normally considered as a lawful trade and the individual has a fundamental right to carry on such a trade, eliminating a rival trader from operating in the same field will be incidental to the exercise of that fundamental right. On the other hand, if the subject-matter is loosely referred to as trade or business but actually is not recognised as trade or business in respect of which no fundamental right exists and only the State has the exclusive privilege to indulging in such a trade or business, different considerations should prevail. In the latter case, the State may engage in this trade of a pernicious character only because it is inevitable to do so having regard to the public interest such as the absolute need to raise revenue for the State which in turn is utilised for the public welfare. It may also be a case where the State engages itself in such a business or trade to minimise the public harm, which otherwise would result to the public, if the trade or business is carried on by the citizens at large.

It is now quite firmly established that none has a fundamental right to carry on the trade in vending liquor. The right given to trade in this regard is actually a privilege conferred by the State and normally these privileges are conferred by auctioning the right to vend, in the case of arrack.

What the bidder pays to the State is not only towards the liquor to be obtained but it would include normally the price for the privilege which he obtains by being the successful bidder in the auction.

It is clear, therefore, that there should be a fair auction of the right to vend liquor and the fairness should be decided not only with reference to the competing bidders but also with reference to public interest. The public revenue is affected either way as a result of the auction. Any attempt made which has a bearing on the ultimate result of the auction and the net revenue that will be collected by the State will be an attempt on public interest. It is of utmost importance that there should be as many bidders as possible in such an auction, so that maximum revenue could be obtained by the State. Purchasing of rival bidders, therefore, on the face of it, will be harmful to public interest and the very object of conducting the auction gets defeated or diluted when intending bidders are sought to be kept away by one of the bidders.

In the instant case, the assessee had purchased a rival bidder so that he could not come forward to participate in the auction. This was contrary to public interest as well as public welfare and, therefore, opposed to public policy. The payment made which, on the face of it was contrary to public policy could not be recognized as a valid payment for the purpose of the Act. Whatever is expended to obtain an asset used in a trade or business is a capital expenditure; however, if the expenditure is incurred in the course of the business to earn the current income, prima facie it may be a revenue expenditure.

The test for determining whether an expenditure is capital or revenue, varies depending upon the nature of the business acquired. When the period of the business and the duration during which the right to carry on the trade is itself limited, the elimination of a rival from competing, while obtaining the right to trade has nothing to do with the expenditure incurred in the course of carrying on the trade. The expenditure here is incurred at the threshold to obtain the right to vend liquor. It was in the nature of investment made to set up the business and, therefore, should be treated as a capital investment. The expenditure incurred in the instant case was incurred once and for all with a view to bring into existence the asset or the advantage of obtaining the privilege to vend liquor for one year. The entire business itself was of one year's duration. The expenditure incurred to obtain this right or privilege cannot be just treated as expenditure incurred only for one year because the very business asset had a life of one year only. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure could not be accepted.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the Revenue.

on stand alone basis could not be accepted. [Para 97]

Coming to the nature of expenditure in question, it can be seen from the various tests laid down in the earlier decided cases that broadly the basic tests to determine the nature of an expenditure remain the same even in the context of a modern situation and those tests include the test of initial outlay of the business, the aim and object of the expenditure, enduring benefit test and the test of fixed and circulating capital. [Para 122] Applying the aforementioned tests to the facts of the instant case, it may be stated that the so-called 'non-compete agreement' was part & parcel of the entire transaction. The assessee had acquired a business concern in India with its outlay (more particularly described elsewhere in this order) and the entire transaction was outlined in the MoU dated 4-11-1996. The aggregate amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was determined as the total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets referred to in article 1 and the Ballabgarh land and building referred to in article 2. The purchase price itself stated that the amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was to be paid as total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets and Ballabgarh land and building. [Para 123]

It can be seen that non-compete agreement was made Appendix 'M' to the agreement dated 2-11-1997 and was, thus, part and parcel of the main agreement, the signing and execution whereof was a condition precedent. [Para 124.1]

It could be mentioned here that the total purchase price of Rs. 52.5 crores envisaged in MoU vide clause 3 included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores which was to be paid for non-compete agreement. The other sum of Rs. 49.85 crores was to be paid in respect of various assets. If these two sums were aggregated, then the total amount would come to Rs. 52.5 crores which was the agreed purchase price. The assessee-company was incorporated for the purpose of effectuating the transactions agreed in the MoU. The purpose of the assessee-company for which it was incorporated was that 'Tecumseh USA', being a leading global compressor manufacturer, was interested in purchasing compressor related operations of Whirlpool India for the Indian compressor market. Thus, the very intention and purpose was to establish business in India by taking over the compressor and related operations of Whirlpool India in India. The non-compete agreement was part and parcel of the whole transaction and could not be treated to be a separate transaction. [Para 125]

The case of the assessee would fall under the test which describes that if the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for the expansion of the business or a substantial replacement of the equipment, then it would fall under the capital expenditure. It was not an expenditure incurred while the business was being carried on. Though it had been the contention of the assessee that non-compete agreement was executed subsequent to the date of main agreement, yet such contention of the assessee could not be accepted as in the main agreement itself the non-compete agreement was appended as 'M' without which the transaction was not complete, as by including the amount paid for non-compete agreement the purchase price as stated in MoU could be arrived at. [Para 126]

The incurring of expenditure also brought an enduring benefit to the assessee if the same was examined from the proposition of law laid down in the case of Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC) wherein their Lordships have considered the period of five years as providing an enduring advantage to the assessee irrespective of the fact that the payment was to be made annually. [Para 127]

It is well-settled that expenditure incurred on warding off competition in the business even to a rival dealer will constitute capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure it is not necessary that non-compete fee be paid to create monopoly rights. [Para 129]

In view of aforesaid, it was to be held that the expenditure of Rs. 2.65 crores claimed by the assessee in pursuance of non-compete agreement dated 10-7-1997 was capital expenditure, the deduction of which could not be granted to the assessee as revenue expenditure. [Para 131]

EDITOR'S NOTE

Following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Punjab State Industrial Development Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT[1997] 225 ITR 792 / 93 Taxman 5, it was to be held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee on increasing its authorized share capital was a capital expenditure and could not be allowed as deduction.

Under section 37(1) any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession is allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", provided it is not in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee. The line that divides revenue expenditure from capital expenditure is often very thin and hazy. None of the tests evolved from time to time determine what is attributable to capital and what to revenue is either exhaustive or of universal application. Each case depends on its own facts. To decide, therefore, on which side of the line the expenditure falls, it is necessary to look at the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure and the nature of the right acquired. If it is incurred by the assessee for the purpose of creating, curing or competing his title to capital, it must be regarded as capital expenditure. But, if it is for the purpose of protecting his business, it would be considered as revenue expenditure. Moreover, it is the true nature of the expenditure that is relevant and not the description given to it by the assessee in his books of account or other documents.

In the instant case, the said payment was required to be made by the assessee for acquisition of the interest of his brother. In the partnership to enable him to become the sole owner of the business hitherto run in partnership with him. It was not a payment made for the purpose of protecting the business, as contended by the assessee and described in the cash book of the assessee. Such payment could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of running the business. In truth and substance, it was in the nature of capital expenditure, because the real purpose of this payment was to acquire the interest of his brother in the business of the said firm, which was a profit-yielding asset and was, therefore, in the nature of capital expenditure which was not allowable as deduction under section 37(1).

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.
