It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature. This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

The problem of deciding whether any given item of business expenditure is capital or revenue would depend for its solution on a consideration of and depends upon a multitude of factual and other circumstances. As an elementary proposition it may be said that where a business is acquired or where there is a substantial addition to the capital equipment of a business or where there is an increase in the capital structure of an existing business, then the outgoing in all these cases, must be regarded as capital outlay and not as revenue expenditure. On the other side, again as an elementary proposition, it may be said that all current or day to day or running expenses in a business must be regarded as items of revenue expenditure.

In the instant case there was not a direct item of expenditure connected with any such capital item such as acquisition of a capital asset or its expansion. The item of expenditure in question was no doubt connected with the amalgamation of the two business concerns, but was directly incurred in meeting legal charges and court expenses.

In such a situation, the expenses incurred by the assessee in connection with amalgamation of another company with it, should be allowed as revenue expenditure.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

The non-competition fee of Rs. 3.25 crores paid by the assessee was allowable as revenue expenditure of the business of the assessee. The non-competition agreement entered into by the assessee with KHPL was to prevent R. Raju from establishing a power plant in Andhra Pradesh for a period of three years. The amount was paid, and a non-competition agreement was entered into, is not in dispute. The law declared by the judgment of the Supreme Court, and the Delhi High Court, is that it is only if the non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature can it be said to be a capital expenditure. The agreement prevented R. Raju from establishing a power plant only for a period of three years from the date of the agreement. The restrictive covenant was neither permanent nor was the advantage derived by the assessee therefrom of an enduring nature. The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in holding that the assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making payment of a non-competition fee; and it merely eliminated competition in its business for a while. [Para 10]

The appeal fails and is, accordingly, dismissed. [Para 12]

The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

But, it could not be said that the expenditure should be treated as capital expenditure only for the reason that the assessee had not obtained an enduring benefit. Both the agreements and payments were made contemporaneously, as the assessee had acquired the brand right of the new product in its entirety and the non-compete clause was separately deduced in another agreement. Therefore, the non-compete agreement was, in fact, a part and parcel of the main contract of acquiring the brand right. The agreement whereby the assessee acquired the brand right for Rs. 85 lakhs and the non-compete agreement executed after paying Rs. 40 lakhs, both were to be considered and understood in unison. The two agreements were not representing two different events. The subject-matter of both the agreements was one and the same and for the purpose of declaring that the assessee had acquired the brand right of the product known as Lacto Calamine. When both the agreements were taken together, it was clear that payment of Rs. 40 lakhs was nothing but a part of the consideration for acquiring the brand right of the product. Instead of executing a single agreement for the entire amount of Rs. 125 lakhs, the assessee had executed two agreements for Rs. 85 lakhs and Rs. 40 lakhs, qualifying the latter amount as paid for non-compete agreement. The reason for splitting up the agreement was best known to the assessee. As matter of fact, it was clear that by executing both the agreements the assessee had transacted only one business, i.e., the business of acquiring exclusive brand name of the product ‘Lacto Calamine’. [Para 24]

A perusal of the agreement clearly points to the fact that while the consideration of Rs.1.30 crores was towards the net value of assets, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is "for obligations and covenants". [Para 13]

The clauses of the agreement go to show that the amount of Rs.70 lakhs is not merely payment towards the non-compete clause but also towards various other obligations which were imposed upon SML and had a direct bearing on the final execution and implementation of the agreement. To argue that the entire consideration was towards the non-compete fee would, therefore, be an incorrect statement, inasmuch as the clauses of the agreement do not reflect so. The emphasis in the agreement is towards the takeover of the assets of SML, and it was to ensure that the agreement bears fruition that the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs has been apportioned for various obligations and covenants imposed on SML. [Para 14]

Under these circumstances, the question that is to be decided is whether the expenditure of Rs.70 lakhs incurred is of capital or revenue nature. The consideration of Rs.70 lakhs was clearly towards ensuring that there will be no impediment in the smooth transfer of SML's factory to the assessee. It should be complete and final. From the facts placed before the Court, there really did not appear to be any serious threat whatsoever in order for the assessee to pay the non-compete fee to SML which had not even commenced its manufacturing. From the nature of the transaction, it is clear that the acquisition of SML's unit was, for expansion purposes. It was to expand and increase production by acquiring a new undertaking. The entire business with capital assets was acquired. The payment was bifurcated into two parts, Rs. 130 lakhs towards net assets and Rs.70 lakhs for other obligations and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about the agreement as also all the intellectual property and other data and information. The said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards the non-compete obligation. [Para 15]

Even the non-compete obligations in clause 11 appear to be illusory in nature and restricted to 'constant velocity joints or any other competitive products'. Clearly, the same is of limited nature and there was also no obligation of non-compete imposed upon the promoter directors of SML. In fact, as stated during the course of arguments, the managing director of SML became the corporate director of the assessee. Thus, the non-compete clause and the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs are not completely and exclusively inter-linked. The payment of Rs.70 lakhs, which is a substantial sum, i.e., more than half of the consideration paid for the net assets of the unit itself, was for a multitude of obligations and covenants which were fastened upon SML and not only towards the non-compete obligations. [Para 16]

It is clear that the consideration of Rs. 70 lakhs was not expressly towards the non-compete obligation, but towards smoothening the process of acquisition of the asset, i.e., the unit of SML in Madras as approvals that were required from the financial institutions, income tax authorities and other governmental authorities were towards the finalisation and closure of the acquisition process. Other covenants and obligations imposed upon SML, i.e., warranties, confidentiality, etc., added value to the asset being acquired. There is no doubt that in the facts of the present case, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is a capital expenditure and hence the question of law is answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 18]

It is now well settled that the character of expenditure will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case not by the application of rigid tests, but by deriving support from many aspects of the whole lot of circumstances and the ultimate answer would depend upon a commonsense appreciation of the guiding features.

In the instant case, the assessee had established a good reputation and market for writing inks by the manufacture and sale of ink, under the brand name 'quink'. In the agreement, there was a recognition of the formation and establishment of the partnership by A for the manufacture and sale of writing inks, similar to those made and sold by the assessee and it being a powerful potential competitor.

The desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership was also clearly spelt out from the terms of the agreement. The negotiated settlement under the terms and conditions set out in the agreement, was clearly relatable to the desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership backed by the experience and expertise of the ex-managing director, whose wife and daughters were the partners in the same line of business activity as that of the assessee. Undoubtedly, the activity of the partnership in setting up a competitive business was harmful to the assessee and the agreement was the outcome of the prospect of power competition from the partnership and a desire on the part of the assessee to protect itself against that disadvantage. Further, the departure of A from the assessee-company and the prospect of his making available his experience and expertise in the manufacture and marketing of ink to his wife and daughters, who were the partners of the firm, would have rendered the goodwill of the assessee vulnerable, as the assessee, when it commanded the benefit of the services of A, was in an advantageous position. There was, thus, a positive detriment to the assessee due to the competition from the partnership and against such damaging competition, the assessee obtained the benefit of a restrictive covenant against such powerful competition. That resulted in the assessee buying of potential competition, which was a positive detriment owing to such competition, and had also enabled the assessee not only to safeguard its goodwill, but also to enhance it. The payment of Rs. 1,00,000 by the assessee to the partnership was to secure advantages resulting in the removal from the arena of a possible competition and securing the elimination of a risk or detriment to the assessee due to competition. Though under the terms of the agreement, the benefit of the restrictive covenant was to enure only for a period of five years, from the facts stated in the order of the Tribunal and also the terms of the dissolution deed, it was seen that the partnership, which was a potential competitor, had also vanished and A had also left the shores of India. That would clearly establish that what the assessee had paid for was of permanent or enduring quality, in the sense that the competition had been totally eliminated and a protection had been acquired for the business of the assessee as a whole. In other words, the amount paid by the assessee was no part of the working or operational expenses of the assessee, but its aim and object was acquisition of an advantage of enduring nature, viz., freedom from competition from the partnership for the rest of the period of the business activities of the assessee.

Therefore, the consideration paid in terms of agreement was an expenditure of capital nature.

In order to determine the nature of expenditure, one has to examine the facts of the each case independently. No hard and fast rule can be laid down to determine the nature of expenditure. If an assessee acquires any capital asset or enduring benefit for a longer period, the expenditure may be called to be a ‘capital expenditure’. In the instant case, the assessee had purchased the shipping business from the vendor against a lumpsum consideration of Rs. 43,47,000 comprising of cost of goodwill of Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 38,47,000 for non-competition covenant fees for a period of 5 years. From a perusal of the non-competition clause contained in the agreement, it was clear that in lieu of receipt of a non-competition fees, the vendor was restrained from doing similar type of business in any capacity for a period of 5 years within India. This condition would not apply to a business carried on by the vendor outside the India. Period of condition was fixed up to 5 years and, thereafter, the vendor was at liberty to enter into similar type of business activity. Further from the other provisions of the agreement, it was not borne out that the vendor was permanently restrained from doing the shipping business in future. Meaning thereby, it was a temporary arrangement made with the vendor in order to settle down its new business of shipping. It has been repeatedly held by the Apex Court and various High Courts that an expenditure incurred to avoid competition, if dictated by business necessity and commercial exigencies, would be allowable as a revenue expenditure as the benefit derived out of it is directly related to the enhancement of profitability of business. In the instant case, by avoiding a main competition from the vendor, the assessee had derived the benefits out of it to enhance its profitability only and it was not a case that the competition was eliminated permanently or for a longer period. Moreover, it was not a case of the revenue that the vendor was only competitor in this line of business. There were other business constituents who were engaged in the similar type of business and a threat of competition was also there to be faced by the assessee from those business constituents. This covenant was executed only for a period of 5 years and that too only for Indian territory. If the assessee intended to do its business outside Indian territory, it had to face the competition from the vendor also. Meaning thereby, this covenant was not executed for a permanent elimination of the competition from the seller. Therefore, the benefit was derived by the assessee for a limited period of 5 years and that too only in Indian territory. Therefore, the non-competition covenant fees paid by the assessee to the vendor could not be treated as capital expenditure. The covenant was executed on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down the assessee in a new acquired business of shipping and the benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability. As such, the expenditure incurred by the assessee was a revenue expenditure and the same was to be allowed as a business expenditure. [Para 23]

Further, since the assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, this expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and the corresponding expenditure be allowed in every year. Therefore, the impugned order was to be set aside and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to allow the total expenditure over a period of 5 years in which the non-competition covenant fees remained in force. [Para 24]

■ In another case, the assessee was the manufacture of the antibiotic penicillin. In its initial years, it could produce only about 5000 units of penicillin per milli-liter of the culture-medium. With a view to increase the yield of penicillin, assessee negotiated with Meiji Seika Kaisha Ltd. of Japan. The negotiations ended in an agreement whereby and whereunder, Meiji agreed to supply the technical know-how to increase production of penicillin to more than 10000 units for a consideration of 'once for all' payment of 50,000 US dollars. In the assessment proceedings, assessee claimed this expenditure as revenue expenditure. The Income Tax Officer, on the other hand, took the view that the expenditure was incurred for the acquisition of an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit. Holding such expenditure to be capital in nature, the Income Tax Officer declined the deduction. This view of the Income Tax Officer was affirmed by the first appellate authorityi.e. Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The further appeal of the assessee was also dismissed by the ITAT. At the instance of the assessee, a reference was made to the High Court which was, however, decided in the negative against the assessee. It was thereafter that the matter travelled to this Court. [Para 23]

This Court after alluding to the judicial pronouncements on this point, observed that the idea of 'once for all' payment and 'enduring benefit' are not to be treated as something akin to statutory conditions. These concepts require flexibility and not a rigid approach. There is no single definitive criterion which by itself is determinative as to whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The 'once for all' payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect considered in a common sense way having regard to the business realities. [Para 23.1]

In the facts of that case, this Court held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for the better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should therefore be treated as revenue expenditure. Consequently, the appeal by the assessee was allowed and the question of law answered in the affirmative and against the revenue. [Para 23.2]

The next case that is adverted to is the case of CIT v. Madras Auto Service (P.) Ltd. [1998] 99 Taxman 575 (SC)/[1998] 233 ITR 468 (SC). In this case, the respondent assessee, a tenant, had incurred expenditure on demolition and construction of a new building which was to vest in the landlord. Assessee in lieu of incurring the actual cost of construction was entitled to use the premises for a period of 39 years at a reduced rent. The entire capital cost of construction was claimed by the assessee as revenue expenditure on the ground that the assessee had not acquired any new asset or such expenditure did not result in any enduring advantage to the assessee in the capital field. The above stand of the assessee was accepted by the ITAT and the High Court. When revenue came up in appeal before this Court, it was held that right from inception, the building was of the ownership of the lessor. Therefore, by spending this money, the assessee did not acquire any capital asset. The only advantage which the assessee derived by spending the money was that it got the lease of a new building at a low rent. From the business point of view, therefore, the assessee got the benefit of reduced rent. The High Court has, therefore, rightly considered this as obtaining a business advantage. The expenditure is, therefore, to be treated as revenue expenditure. [Para 24]

Having adverted to the relevant case laws, one may now examine the nature and character of non-compete fee; whether payment of non-compete fee is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure. Non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. It may be by way of a written agreement or by an oral understanding. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. Purpose of non-compete payment is to give a head start to the business of the payer. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the business of the payer or for enhancing the profitability of the business of the payer by insulating the payer from competition. [Para 25]

■

Thus non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance the profitability of the business, thereby facilitating the carrying on of the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, by restricting a competitor in business, is not in the capital field. [Para 26]

Though a payment may be a capital receipt in the hands of the recipient, it need not be a capital expenditure in the hands of the payer. In the instant case, out of three distributors two belonged to the same group of companies and the third distributor company consisted of persons belonging or known to the assessee group and, hence, there was no possibility of any hindrance or obstacle from the distributors that might arise when the agency was terminated. Further, it was not a case of mere termination of the distributorship agreements, but the assessee had acquired a large sales organisation and a marketing network belonging to the distributing agents and the entire profit-making apparatus of the distributors was taken over by the assessee along with well-trained manpower. It was not a case of mere termination of agreements, but the money was paid as consideration for the transfer of a profit-making apparatus of the distributing agents as there was transfer of staff, dealership network, brand image and other marketing infrastructure and there was also a restriction in the agreements that the distributors should not compete with the assessee for a period of few years from the date of termination. Therefore, it could not be said that no new asset was acquired by virtue of the termination. Further, the business of the distributorship agents was entirely different from the business of the assessee, though the agents might have dealt with the assessee’s own products. It was a case of acquisition of a profit-making apparatus of distributorship agency for which amounts were paid to the distributors and, hence, the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount paid was a capital expenditure. [Paras 5 and 7]

The relevant rules which deal with military contracts clearly provide that no person can run a canteen other than the one appointed by the military authorities and that the business was terminable at six months notice by the military authorities. There was thus no question of a free market and the business was in the nature of a monopoly of the military department. Consequently, any ideas of competition were foreign to the real nature of the business. Therefore, this payment to G could not be treated as the amount paid to avoid competition nor could this amount be said to have been paid by the assessee to buy the goodwill of G. The question of goodwill can arise only in connection with a business to carry on which a person has a right and in which continuity is expected. In asmuch as neither the assessee nor G nor anyone else had a legal right to run the business except for the year for which they had the contract, there was no guarantee in respect of the continuity of the business. There were therefore, no certain prospects to earn profits. The life of the business was only one year, i.e., the period for which the contract was given, and that too subject to cancellation by notice. No one could look forward to the prospects of earning profits as of right as there was no free market.

Ordinarily 'capital' means as asset which has an element of permanency about it and which is capable of being a source of income. Capital expenditure must, therefore, normally mean an acquisition of an asset of lasting value; while income or revenue expenses are generally running expenses incurred in earning profits or expenses incurred with the primary object of an immediate return or acquisition of assets which are not of lasting value and are likely to get exhausted or consumed in the process of the return or a very limited number of returns. The amount paid by the assessee to G was by way of satisfaction of the claim of G to the profits in the business. Therefore, it was an expenditure of a non-recurring nature.

For the above reasons, the Tribunal was right in holding that the payment in question was a capital expense and, hence, not admissible under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

There is no dispute that if a particular expenditure or payment results in an enduring benefit to the assessee or acquisition of any asset or benefit of permanent nature (in the absence of special circumstances leading to an opposite conclusion), the expenditure cannot be held to be revenue expenditure but it would be an expenditure of capital nature. Legal expenses per se can neither be revenue nor capital. It will depend on the facts of each case. The purpose for which the expenses have been incurred will be the relevant factor. If the expenses have been incurred in the course of running the business or for protecting the business, it will be a revenue expenditure but if it is in connection with the acquisition of a benefit of enduring nature or an asset of permanent character, then the legal expenditure would partake of the character of capital expenditure.

In the instant case, even according to the assessee itself, the object and purpose of the amalgamation was to take over the existing distribution organisation of a marketing company. It was also an admitted position that distribution of the product of the assessee was earlier done by the marketing company M which was an independent business establishment. As a result of the amalgamation, the entire business establishment with the well-established marketing network came in the hands of the assessee. which, according to the assessee itself, was the main purpose of the amalgamation. The Tribunal considered all these relevant factors and came to a definite finding that as a result of the amalgamation there was a radical alteration in the framework of the business of the assessee-company. In truth and substance, the purpose of the assessee was to acquire the running business of distributorship of the marketing company which was an independent business. The fact that the acquisition was intended to increase the profitability of the assessee could not convert the capital expenditure into revenue expenditure. That will be stretching the 'profitability test' too far. There is a thin line of demarcation between capital and revenue expenditure because the object of every business concern or assessee, who is carrying on business, is to increase or enhance its profits. That, by itself, cannot convert expenditure incurred for acquiring capital asset or benefit of enduring nature or setting up plant or machinery as revenue expenditure. No test is of universal application. Its application will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In order to hold a particular expenditure to be revenue expenditure the nexus between the expenditure and the profitability should be direct and proximate. In the instant case, there was no such direct nexus. The object and purpose of the amalgamation was to acquire the distribution net work of the other company which was a capital asset and advantage of enduring nature. The expenditure in question resulted in the addition to or expansion of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee.

In view of the above the legal expenses incurred in connection with the amalgamation of company M with the assessee had been rightly held by the Tribunal to be capital expenditure.

It is well settled that expenditure laid out for the acquisition or improvement of a fixed capital asset or for perfecting title or for getting rid of a defect in the title, would be capital expenditure. However, if it is incurred to protect the trade or business of the assessee or to protect his assets from attack, then it would be revenue expenditure.

In considering the nature of the expenditure, it would not be proper to proceed on the basis of the correctness of the pleadings in the suit, as the matter was not adjudicated upon by the Court. The pleadings represent mere allegations and unless the statements were proved they would merely remain as allegations. So long as there was no adjudication on the conduct of the assessee, the allegations made should not colour the determination of the issue.

In the instant case both parties to the litigation had given the go-by to their respective pleadings when they entered into a mutual compromise. There was nothing express or implied in the terms of the compromise to suggest that the impugned payment was towards payment of the balance of the purchase price of the deceased partner's share in the business. The assessee had already become the owner of the assets long ago and he had to defend the attack on the assets. This was, thus, clearly a case where the expenditure had not brought into existence any capital asset or enduring benefit. It would, therefore, be safe and reasonable to hold that qua the assessee the suit was an attack }on the title to his business and the impugned payment warded off that attack. The Tribunal was not justified in assuming that the payment under the compromise decree was the means by which the assessee had acquired full title to the business.

In this view of the matter, the impugned amount was a revenue expenditure.

The doctrine that a larger Bench of the Supreme Court has more authoritative force than a smaller Bench is relevant only as between cases which yield different ratio decidendi, and not where the one hands down a decision and the other merely lays down a dictum.

In determining whether a particular item of expenditure comes under the category of "capital" or "revenue" it is necessary to consider carefully the nature of the concern, the ordinary course of business, usually adopted by such firms, the object with which an expense is incurred and the actual effect thereof. It is only then that it can be decided under what category a particular expenditure falls. In instant case, the goodwill of the firm in which M was interested had for a separate consideration been transferred to the assessee entitling the latter to the benefit of the connections of M with 'R' Brothers. The annuity, which was made payable to M and to his wife, was in consideration of M not entering into competition during his lifetime with assessee. There was no question that under this latter provision a benefit accrued in favour of assessee, but was it of an enduring nature ? One very important provision was introduced in the agreement which must not be overlooked. The payments were made contingent upon the receipt by assessee of a certain amount from R Brothers with the further proviso that under certain circumstances the entire annuity might be stopped, irrespective of the fact whether or not assessee, continue to receive brokerage from R Brothers or whether annuities continued to be paid till the end of the two lives. M was restrained from entering into competition with the assessee-firm till the end of his natural life. There could be no question that M was definitely and permanently kept out of the filed of competition.

On the special facts arising in instant case and on the interpretation of the terms of contract as evidenced by the agreements, it must be held that the amount in question was not an item of capital expenditure but was a revenue expenditure allowable as an admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xii) of 1922 Act as it stood before its amendment in 1946.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee had purchased the goodwill and other rights for Rs. 10 lakhs which was treated to be capital expenditure. The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

In the instant case the most important circumstance that had to be borne in mind was that the ferry contract was only for a period of one year. The amounts paid by the assessee to buy off competition were paid only for the purpose of securing that advantage during that year. It could not, therefore, be said that these amounts were paid for securing an enduring advantage. They were paid in order to enable the assessee to derive more profits in the business by reducing the lease amount payable to the Government for operating the ferry. It was thus an amount paid for the purpose of the business. It could not be said that it was paid for the purpose of acquiring the business and not for the purpose of running it.

It was not contended that the lease amount paid for obtaining the right to operate the ferry was not in the nature of a revenue expenditure and was not deductible. There was no difference in the instant case between the lease amount and the amount paid to the other intended bidders in order to prevent them from competing and thus reduce the lease amount so that ultimately the assessee could derive more profits.

The question whether a particular expenditure is revenue expenditure incurred for the purposes of business must be determined on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances, and by the application of principles of commercial trading. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

Viewing the expenditure incurred in the instant case in such a context that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

the payment to the two employees was in consideration of the past services rendered by them to the firm and, therefore, to the assessee-company, was incorrect. It was held that the payment made to the two employees was primarily in consideration of the past services rendered by them to the firm, the business of which was taken over by the assessee. If so, the payment would be for purposes of business and in the nature of business expenditure and would not partake of the nature of capital expenditure. All that the assessee was attempting to do when it put down clause (11) in the terms of the agreement between the two employees and the assessee was to protect their good-will and defend it against possible competition. Their capital asset and their goodwill remained exactly the same as before and there was no addition or acquisition to those capital assets. Therefore, even assuming that this was an expenditure made to protect their capital assets, still it could be classed as a business expenditure.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee was saddled with the duty to establish that the expended amount fell in the revenue field. Admittedly the payment was for the purpose of business of the assessee. The payment was expended to ward off the competition in the field of the assessee’s business. Admittedly this restriction to compete or, in other words, the non-compete fee was paid by the assessee to retrain payee from the competitive business for a definite period of five years. The non-compete fee payment made by the assessee to ‘S’ gave enduring benefit to the assessee in its business. Thus, the payment of non-compete fee fell within the capital field which was not an allowable expenditure. [Para 10]

It is true that a sum paid by a company to a retiring director in consideration of the director's covenant not to compete with the company is capital expenditure. Similar expenditure for buying off potential competitors that improves the value of an assessee's goodwill has been considered and advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and of the nature of capital expenditure. But, the question ultimately depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In that connection, what is always of importance is to ascertain the true object and purpose for which the expenditure in question is incurred.

The payment of the sum of Rs. 50,000 to ‘P’ was towards remuneration and/or salary. The incidental result of the employment of ‘P’ with the condition that he would have no right of private practice was that from 28-3-1957, he would not be able to give advice to outsiders including competitors of the assessee-company in its business. That this result did not bring into existence any asset of any kind was quite clear. That by employment of ‘P’ the assessee-company could improve its own business prospects and could avoid excessive expenditure by use of indigenous machinery was merely incidental to the contract of employment. That this advantage did not deprive the competitors of the assessee-company from gathering similar and same kinds of advice from other consulting engineers was a fact of great importance. There was no evidence on record to show that more competent and/or equally competent consulting engineers were not available to the assessee-company's rival competitors. Ordinarily, negative covenants of this kind contained in service contracts do not result in any acquisition of assets of enduring and/or lasting character to an employer. If the negative covenant that was subsequently agreed in March, 1957, had been part of the contract of employment of 'P' from the very inception, the revenue would not have made the arguments which now it found possible to do having regard to the circumstances of this case. The admission, if any, made on behalf of the assessee that the assessee-company wanted to ensure that ‘P’ would not offer his services as a consulting engineer to rival concerns did not make any difference to the findings made above. The duration of ‘P’’s employment was to end on 30-6-1959. By continuing ‘P’ in its employment from 28-3-1957 to 30-6-1959, on the conditions agreed in March, 1957, the assessee-company did not acquire any asset of lasting or enduring character and did not improve the value of its own goodwill and did not buy off any competitors. Therefore, payment in question was a revenue expenditure.

Note : Decision was in favour of the assessee.

If the revenue wanted to hold that the consideration paid by the assessee as per the agreement was for the transfer of the business being undertaken by Tata-IBM Ltd., then such receipts should have been held as capital in the hands of the recipient. However, in the case of the recipient, the revenue had treated the receipts as revenue receipts and included those in the income. The matter had travelled up to the Tribunal and the Tribunal had held that the receipts were revenue in nature. The revenue could not blow hot and cold at the same time. Once it had taken the stand that the receipts in the hands of the recipient were revenue in nature, then such payments could not be held as capital in the hands of the payer representing the consideration paid for the transfer of business. In the instant case, the recipient had not been taxed under the head 'Capital gain' on the transfer of the business. Hence, the action of the Assessing Officer in holding that the receipts represented the receipts on account of transfer of business could not be upheld. [Para 7.1]

It was also not the case of the revenue that the payments had been made before the commencement of business. In the instant case, the business was being carried out by Tata-IBM. As per the agreement, it was clear that IBM and Tata had agreed to carry out certain activities through the assessee. The issue of commencement of business in respect of purchase of an existing undertaking by an assessee was before the Mumbai Bench in the case of Vidarbha Irrigation Development Corpn. v. Jt. CIT [2006] 102 ITD 1 (Mum.). In view of the said case, the expenditure under reference in the instant case could not be termed as an expenditure incurred before the commencement of the business. [Para 7.2]

The revenue had relied on the treatment given to such expenses by the assessee in its books of account. It is now well settled law that if according to the revenue law, the assessee is entitled to treat a sum as revenue expenditure, then the legal right of the assessee is not self-estopped by the treatment given by the assessee to it in its own books of account. [Para 7.3]

The assessee had treated the expenditure as deferred revenue expenditure. Such term presupposes that concerned expenditure creates a benefit in revenue field. Such benefit may be of an enduring nature but if it does not create any asset, then it cannot be treated as capital expenditure. [Para 7.4]

The Tribunal in the case of IBM India Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 105 ITD 1, had an occasion to consider as to whether the expenditure incurred in acquiring certain application software is revenue or capital. It was held in that case that in case the expenses are once and for all and may give advantage of an enduring benefit but are not with a view to bringing into existence any asset, then the expenditure cannot be classified as capital expenditure. The Supreme Court in the case of Allembic Chemical Co. [1989] 177 ITR 377/43 Taxman 312 held that the concept of payment made once and for all and of an enduring benefit must respond to the changing economic realities of the business. [Para 7.5]

Payment which frees an assessee from liability to make recurring revenue payments is revenue expenditure. But such test will fail in case an asset is acquired. If a labour saving machinery is purchased, then revenue expenditure is reduced in respect of new labour bill but the cost of machine cannot be treated as revenue expenditure as it brings into existence an asset. So far as payment made for getting the domestic customer database was concerned, it was clear that the assessee had only got right to use that database; the company which had provided such data-base was not precluded from using such database and, hence, the expenditure incurred was for use of database and not for its acquisition. In view of decision of the Bangalore Bench in the case of Wipro GE Medical System Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2003] 80 TTJ (Bang.) 55, it was to be held that the payment made for using the database was revenue in nature and was allowable as deduction. [Para 7.6]

So far as the unabsorbed revenue expenditure on development of designs and models of integral coaches, was concerned, HAL had not claimed it earlier because it was following the amortisation principle of accounting. But that was no bar for the assessee (BEML) to claim the amount in toto in the assessment year in question as business expenditure, since the amount was admittedly paid in the relevant year for the purpose of its business.

The main reason given by the Tribunal for disallowing the claim of the assessee, viz., that the assets taken over by the assessee in consideration for the payment representing this expenditure were mainly of an intangible nature, was inaccurate. The assessee paid that amount towards unabsorbed expenditure incurred by HAL on development of designs and development of various models of rail coaches, etc., taken over by the assessee. In the case of HAL, similar claim had been allowed by the revenue accepting the amortisation basis. There was, therefore, no justification for denying the claim of the assessee, in the instant case.

Regarding the payment made for technical know-how, the decision relied upon by the Tribunal had since been overruled and in Mysore Kirloskar Ltd. v . CIT [1978] 114 ITR 443 (Kar.) , the Full Bench had taken the view that payments made under agreement for acquisition of technical know- how should be considered as business expenditure. Therefore, the payment made in the instant case towards technical assistance fee must be regarded as revenue expenditure. The distinction made by the Tribunal between initial outlay of expenditure and current needs of the business of the assessee was equally untenable. In fact, no distinction can be made between initial investment to commence busi- ness and current expenses for continuing production. The nature of the expenditure for obtaining technical know-how cannot ordinarily depend upon the time at which the collaboration agreement came into existence. It may depend upon the purposes for which it was entered into and the benefits derived therefrom.

So far as the nature of the amount paid by the assesses to HAL towards the expenditure incurred by the latter on training the officers was concerned, the reasoning of the Tribunal was right, so that the relevant amount had been rightly disallowed.

The nature of services provided by 'E' was related to the reorganization of the staff and redrawing of line of responsibility which amounted to an internal improvement in the working method. There was no element of capital expenditure involved. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit, may, nonethe-less, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down. It is not every advantage of enduring nature acquired by an assessee that brings the case within the principle laid down in this test. What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The test of enduring benefit is, therefore, not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal rights, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

In view of the above discussion, the amount paid to 'E' was essentially revenue expenditure insofar as the same was spent for improving the working of the company's staff, thereby facilitating the assessee's trading operation while leaving the fixed capital untouched. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly allowed the assessee's claim.

Thus non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance the profitability of the business, thereby facilitating the carrying on of the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, by restricting a competitor in business, is not in the capital field. [Para 26] ■

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates in carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring of such expenditure. [Para 27]

■

The non-compete compensation from the stand point of the payer of such compensation is so paid in anticipation that absence of a competition from the other party may secure a benefit to the party paying the compensation. However, there is no certainty that such benefit would accrue. Notwithstanding such an arrangement, the payer (assesee) may still not achieve the desired result. In so far the present case is concerned, on account of payment of non-compete fee, the assessee had not acquired any new business and there is no addition to the profit making apparatus of the assessee. The assets remained the same. The expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of the same business. Further, there is no complete elimination of competition. Such payment made by the appellant to L&T did not create a monopoly of the appellant over the business of electronic products/ equipments. Payment was made to L&T only to ensure that the appellant operated the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment made to L&T cannot, therefore, be considered to be for acquisition of any capital asset or towards bringing into existence a new profit earning apparatus. [Para 28]

■

That being the position, it is opined that payment made by the appellant to L&T as non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1). [Para 29]

■

Consequently, the impugned judgment and order of the Delhi High Court dated 5-11-2012 passed in Income Tax Appeal No. 492/2012 is hereby set aside. The question framed is thus answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 30]

■

As regards the remaining appeals, it is viewed that it would be appropriate if the matters are remanded back to the respective ITATs, all appeals/ cross-appeals filed are revived and heard afresh having regard to the ratio laid down in this judgment. [Para 32]

Ordered accordingly. [Para 33]

expenditure, be it capital or revenue;

(v )where the expenditure has a direct nexus, connection or relation to the carrying on or conducting the business of the assessee, it must be regarded as an integral part of the profit-making process and in such a case it must be held to be a revenue expenditure; and

(vi )the period for which a right or benefit is available is not relevant because if the expenditure is found to have direct nexus with the profitability, then that test must fail. If the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores incurred by the assessee had been considered in the light of the assessee’s necessity or commercial expediency, it would be found that it satisfied both the tests because as admitted by the revenue authorities, the non-competition agreement was to enhance the assessee’s sales of relevant two chemicals in central and eastern parts of India without any competition. Even otherwise, the benefit to be procured by the assessee for a period of five years could not be said to be of ‘enduring nature’, and since the revenue authorities had rejected the assessee’s claim solely on the ground that the benefit procured by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’, the orders of the revenue authorities could not be upheld.

Even if the benefits derived by the assessee in the instant case were of enduring nature, then also the assessee was to succeed because of the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 /3 Taxman 69 and the findings to the effect that the effect of the agreement in question being directly related to the sale and production capacity of two chemicals, which in turn had effect of carrying on the assessee’s business efficiently and profitably in central and eastern parts of India and the test of enduring nature would fail and the expenditure had to be held as revenue expenditure.

Therefore, the expenditure incurred by the assessee by entering into a non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ was of revenue nature and, hence, an allowable deduction.

The another observation of the Assessing Officer for holding the expenditure in question to be capital expenditure was that there was no fear of competition from ‘V’ or that ‘V’ would not have been able to compete within a period of 5 years and that the assessee was to continue to get the benefit, even after 5 years, which was of ‘enduring nature’. However, the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) had considered the threat of competition only with reference to ‘V’ and not with reference to its founder ‘M’ in his individual capacity and, therefore, the conclusion arrived at by them could not be sustained in law. Further, the chemicals produced by ‘V’ before sale of the manufacturing plant to the assessee were being sold in a particular area, i.e., in the central and eastern parts of India and probably without any brand which would mean that whatever market ‘V’ and its founder had captured was only because of their personal rapport with the consumers of these two chemicals and, therefore, in the presence of other manufacturers of these two chemicals situated in that area ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ could enter into market for selling the chemicals produced by those manufacturers and were definitely a potential threat at least in central and eastern parts of India. Consequently, the revenue authorities’ observation that the benefit to be derived by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’ because ‘V’ was not in a position to compete during the period of 5 years because it could not start manufacturing these chemicals within 5 years and by that the assessee would get established itself so well in the market that it would be difficult to dislodge was misplaced, without any basis or reasoning and devoid of any merit. The expenditure had to be seen from the angle of the business or the businessman and not from the revenue’s attitude and it is so because had the assessee any mala fide intention to reduce its tax burden, it could have easily included the payment of Rs. 6 crores in purchase price of the manufacturing plant itself and could have purchased the plant for Rs. 35 crores instead of Rs. 29 crores. In that case, the assessee would have got depreciation on whole of the amount, i.e., including payment of Rs. 6 crores and in that situation nobody was going to question the assessee’s bona fide and, therefore, to term the expenditure as of capital nature, only because the assessee had claimed the payments separately, was not justified.

The amount paid was but a part of the money paid by it for acquiring assets and goodwill as also to avoid competition in trade by the vendor. The payment made as compensation was clearly an expenditure of capital nature as the right acquired was of enduring benefit, the vendor having undertaken not to market the milk in the Madras city.

Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in not allowing the same.

One of the tests to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure is whether the expenditure in question was for bringing into existence an asset or an advantage of an ‘enduring nature’ and was made once and for all meaning thereby an expenditure made once for all for procuring an enduring benefit. The expressions ‘enduring benefit’ and ‘rights of a permanent nature’ are only descriptive and not definitive and are related in meaning not synonymous with perpetual or everlasting. [Para 7]

In the instant case, BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products. Even though the period of two years was mentioned in the agreement, the predominant intention and purpose, as discernible from the stipulations in the agreement, clearly indicated that the assessee-company had obtained the monopoly rights on a permanent basis and BSL went out of its business of dealing in test and measurement products, of HP, inasmuch as it released its entire workforce connected with the line of business started by the assessee. Expenditure in question was clearly of a capital nature inasmuch as the assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years. The disallowance of expenditure was, therefore, justified. [Paras 8 and 12]

For the aforesaid reason finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 13]

To decide whether an expenditure of this nature is a capital expenditure or not would depend on the facts of the case. However, it is necessary to know whether the advantage derived by the payer is of an enduring nature, and for this, one of the considerations is the length of time for which the non-compete agreement would operate, although that is not decisive. While the length of time for which competition is eliminated may not strictly be decisive in all cases, yet, at the same time, it should not be so brief as to be virtually transitory. [Para 12]

In the instant case, the assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making the payment of non-compete fee. It merely eliminated competition in the two-wheeler business, for a while. From the record, it was not clear how long the restrictive covenant was to last, but it was neither permanent nor ephemeral. In that sense, the advantage was not of an enduring nature. There was also nothing to show that the amount of Rs. 4 crores was drawn out of the capital of the assessee. On a cumulative appreciation of the facts, it was clear that the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal did not err in concluding that the payment of non-compete fee by the assessee was a business expenditure and not a capital expenditure. [Para 17]

Therefore, the appeal was to be dismissed.

There could be no doubt that the payment of Rs. 40,100 which the assessee made to ‘MK’ Ltd. for procuring exclusively for its benefit the services, experience and technical knowledge of ‘B’ for the manufacture of castings, that is to say, for the purpose of setting the profit-earning machinery in motion, was an expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee-company. But an expenditure for the purpose of business may be of a capital nature; and if it is of that nature, then it cannot be claimed as deduction under section 37. The question, therefore, was whether the amount of Rs. 40,100 expended by the assessee was in the nature of capital expenditure or a revenue disbursement. The expenditure was incurred by the assessee once and for all for procuring the benefit and use of ‘B’s service, technical knowledge and experience. It was not any recurring expenditure in the nature of ‘operational expenses’. With that expenditure the assessee acquired an asset in the shape of ‘B’s technical knowledge and practical experience for the purpose of manufacturing castings and certain parts of diesel engines. The expenditure was not incurred for the purpose of earning profits in the conduct of the assessee’s business. The asset, which the assessee acquired, no doubt could not be compared with factory or office buildings, plant or machinery. The technical knowledge and practical experience of ‘B’ was an intangible ambience pervading the production and manufacturing organisation of the assessee. The benefit of the services, technical knowledge and experience of ‘B’ which the assessee acquired exclusively after paying Rs. 40,100 to ‘MK’ Ltd. was an advantage or asset for the enduring benefit of the assessee’s business. So long as the assessee retained the services of ‘B’, for its exclusively productive and manufacturing purposes and expressed its value in its products, it was, a fixed capital of the assessee. The assessee acquired a source of knowledge and experience helpful in the manufacture of the castings and certain parts of diesel engines; and thus by making a payment of Rs. 40,100 secured an enduring advantage and an asset, which was a capital asset of its business.

For all these reasons, the sum of Rs. 40,100 paid to ‘B’ was a capital expenditure in respect of which the assessee could not claim any deduction under section 37.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1/3 Taxman 69, held that it is not a universally true proposition that what may be a capital receipt in the hands of the payee must necessarily be capital expenditure in relation to the payer. The fact that a certain payment constitutes income or capital receipt in the hands of the recipient is not material in determining whether the payment is revenue or capital disbursement qua the payer. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit may, nonetheless, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down; if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operation or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee’s business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal right, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

By applying these principles to the facts of the instant case, the payment made by the assessee was incurred for the purpose of preserving an existing asset and not for the purpose of acquiring any new benefit of an enduring nature. The two employees had access to the secret formula used by the assessee in its manufacturing process and by retaining them in the service of the company even after retirement, the company ensured that there would not be any competition from these persons by setting up rival manufacturing concerns. Thus, the company was only trying to protect its existing asset so that its business could be carried on smoothly without the apprehended competition from its own retired personnel. It is well-settled in law that expenditure incurred for preserving or protection of a business asset is revenue in nature and not capital expenditure. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in sustaining the addition made by the Assessing Officer.
