The High Court ruled that Tiger Global's transaction was legitimate and not aimed at tax avoidance, allowing it to claim tax benefits under the treaty's 'grandfathering clause' for capital gains on shares acquired before April 1, 2017. The court rejected the AAR's view that Tiger Global was merely a "see-through entity" controlled by a US-based individual. The High Court acknowledged Tiger Global's significant economic activities, compliance with the required thresholds for expenses and liabilities, and the legitimacy of its Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) as proof of its bona fide status in Mauritius. The court further held that treaty shopping is not inherently objectionable unless explicitly shown to be solely for tax evasion.

3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

4. Section 44C covers head office expenses, whether common or solely for Indian branches: SC

Director of Income-tax (IT)-I, Mumbai v. American Express Bank Ltd. [2025] 181 taxmann.com 433 (SC)

The assessee, a non-resident banking company, filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year. While computing the income, the assessee claimed a deduction for expenses incurred at the head office directly related to the Indian branches.

The Assessing Officer (AO) contended that the expenses in question should be subject to the ceiling specified in Section 44C. The assessee claimed that the expenses in question could not have been classified as head office expenditure for the reason that Section 44C presupposes that at least a part of the expenditure is attributable to the business outside India. If this presumption does not hold, and the entire expenditure is incurred solely for the business in India, Section 44C would not apply.

The AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section.

CIT [1981] 127 ITR 746 /6 Taxman 50 (Delhi), it was held that if the collaboration agreement results in the absolute transfer of technical knowledge, etc., to the assessee, the assessee could be said to have acquired an asset or enduring advantage and the expenditure incurred may be of capital nature. On the other hand, where the payment is made only for obtaining access to information which does not become its own, the expenditure is of the revenue nature. In CIT v. Premier Automobiles Ltd. [1994] 206 ITR 1/[1993] 70 Taxman 495 (Bom.) there were two issues : For an earlier year the amount paid for acquisition of drawings, blue prints, specifications, process sheets and technical data had already been allowed as the revenue expenditure; therefore, there was no question of allowing depreciation thereon. During the year the assessee had purchased know-how from a manufacturer in England. It was held to be ‘plant’ following the decisions of the Supreme Court in Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 86 /[1985] 23 Taxman 66 and CIT v. Elecon Engg. Co. Ltd. [1987] 166 ITR 66 .

In Elecon Engg. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra), it was held, following the decisionin Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd.’s case (supra) that drawings and patterns constituted ‘plant’, and the appeal filed to the Supreme Court was dismissed.

It was held in Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd.’s case (supra) that drawings, designs, charts, plans, processing data, constituted a ‘book’ and fell within the definition of ‘plant’ under section 43(3). With the aid of these documents the assessee was able to commence its manufacturing activity and these documents formed the basis of manufacturing the products in question. That by themselves these documents did not perform any mechanical operation or process did not militate against their being plant since they were in a sense the basic tools of the assessee’s trade having a fairly enduring utility.

Tests laid down by the Supreme Court to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure

3. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency. If the outgoing expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-earning process and not for the acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition for carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as the revenue expenditure - Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (1953) (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC).

In cases where the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for extension of a business or a substantial replacement of equipment, there is no doubt that it is capital expenditure. Where the expenditure is incurred while the business is going on and is not incurred either for extension of the business or for substantial replacement of the equipment, if it is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is properly attributable to capital and is of the nature of capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is made not for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage, but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. The aim and object of the expenditure would determine the character of the expenditure, whether it is capital or revenue expenditure. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may go to the test of fixed and circulating capital. If the expenditure incurred was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be of the nature of capital expenditure and if it was part of its circulating capital, it would be of the nature of the revenue expenditure. These tests are mutually exclusive - Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). The expression ‘asset or advantage of endur- ing nature’ was evolved to emphasise the element of a sufficient degree of durability appropriate to the context. There is also no single defi- nite criterion which, by itself, is determinative whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The ‘once for all’ payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way, having regard to the business realities. On facts it was held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should, therefore, be held to be revenue expenditure. Further, as the agreement pertained to a product already in the line of the assessee’s business and not to a new product, it indicated that what was stipulated was for an improvement in the operations of the existing business and its efficiency and profitability - Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 / 43 Taxman 312 (SC).

Simultaneously, it must be noted that the expenditure did not bring into existence any capital asset as far as the lessee-company is concerned. The asset created by spending the amount did not belong to the assessee but the assessee got the business advantage of using modern premises at a low rent, thus, saving considerable revenue expenditure for the next 39 years. How will cases of this type be dealt with under the amended section 2(11)? Will this type of expenditure get the benefit of depreciation at 25 per cent? Obviously, further amendment is called for to take care of similar situations in the future. Otherwise, if the claim for depreciation under the amended law as it stands is denied, companies can continue to take advantage of the ruling of the Supreme Court and claim the entire amount as revenue expenditure. Much more thought has to be bestowed on the issue of business or commercial rights forming part of the block of assets. There is also an urgent need to look into the definition of ‘plant’ in section 43(3).

Capital v. Revenue expenditure

8. The question whether payment made for acquiring technical know-how will fall for deduction as revenue expenditure was considered in detail by the Supreme Court. In Ciba’s case that was a case where the Indian subsidiary made contributions at fixed percentages on sale in consideration of technical consultancy services, use of trade marks, etc., to the Swiss Principal. There was also an agreement to keep information confidential. The patents and trade marks were to be returned to the Swiss company on termination of the agreement. The agreement was to be in force for five years. The Supreme Court held that the amount should be allowed as business expenditure. The Indian company did not become entitled exclusively to the patents and trade marks at any time. It had merely access to the technical knowledge and experience of the Swiss Major. The Indian company was a mere licensee.

Will the present amendment supersede this ruling of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 ? Obviously not. The very concept of depreciation pre-supposes at least limited ownership or title. If the collaboration agreement is drafted in the manner done by Ciba of India Ltd., obviously the entire payment will have to be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On the other hand, if the company acquires complete title over the process or patents different considerations will arise. In Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC), the question was whether know-how obtained on ‘once for all’ payment for increasing the yield of penicillin in the existing plant with an undertaking regarding confidentiality would help the company to claim the expenditure in the revenue field.

The Supreme Court held that there was no material for the Tribunal to hold that the area of improvisation was not a part of the existing business or that the entire gamut of the existing manufacturing operations for the commercial production of penicillin in the assessee’s existing plant had become obsolete or inappropriate in relation to the exploitation of the new sub-cultures of the high yielding strains of penicillin supplied by the foreign firm and that the mere introduction of the new bio synthetic source required the erection and commissioning of a totally new and different type of plant and machinery.

The ‘once for all’ payment test was also inconclusive. What was relevant was the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of ‘enduring benefit’ might break down. Hence, it was revenue expenditure.

Despite the provision made for allowing depreciation on know-how, patent, etc., under the latest Finance Act, the field is still open for enterprising companies to take advantage of the rulings of the courts and make claims for deduction of the entire expenditure as revenue expenditure. This will, of course, have to be decided on various circumstances of the case. The amendment is only an enabling provision. The expenditure on know-how will hereafter have to be allowed either over a period of four years or in the year of acquisition itself depending on the facts of the case.

Brands and goodwill

9. The current financial year has seen a rush for amortisation of Brands and Goodwill. Brand valuation is now the buzz word in the corporate world. Both Goodwill and Brands are intangible. It is not easy to value the same in the balance sheet. Companies can capitalise brands in the balance sheet and reduce taxable income by claiming depreciation against such capitalised value.

. Deccan Sugars & Abkhari & Co. Ltd. [1986] 157 ITR 467 /[1987] 33 Taxman 28 allowed the loss suffered by its employees’ cooperative stores from the taxable income of the assessee by holding that running of the stores was a welfare measure which the assessee had to undertake to keep the workmen contended and, hence, the expenditure should be taken to be "for the purpose of the assessee’s business". Expenditure incurred by the assessee-cooperative-society for the purpose of presents to be given to its members on the occasion of its silver jubilee was held to be allowable as it was meant to kept alive its image amongst its members, generate goodwill and ensure continuity of business with the member societies as before. It was so held in (i) CIT v. Dascroi Taluka Co-operative Purchase & Sales Union Ltd. [1980] 126 ITR 413 /[1981] 5 Taxman 160 (Guj.), ( ii) Andhra Sugars Ltd. v. CIT [1988] 171 ITR 209 /[1987] 34 Taxman 431 (AP); (iii) Karjan Co-Op. Cotton Sales Ginning & Pressing Society v. CIT [1993] 199 ITR 17/ 69 Taxman 304 (Guj.) (FB). Similarly, presentation of wristwatches to employees is held to be in the nature of an incentive to encourage employees to attend to work punctually, to keep them happy and to earn their goodwill towards the company and therefore, held to be deductible - CIT v. Hayward Waldia Refinery Ltd. [1994] 209 ITR 159/[1995] 78 Taxman 558 (Cal.). Where the managing agents of a company, on the eve of the latter’s golden jubilee, gave a donation of Rs. 1 lakh which was utilized, though not earmarked for building a worker’s canteen, the expenditure was held to be allowable - CIT v. Tata Sons (P.) Ltd. [1978] 111 ITR 290 (Bom.). Likewise, the amount of corpus of a trust for providing financial assistance and affording higher education to the needy children of the employees of the assessee-company and the amount incurred for forming the trust were held to be deductible - CIT v. Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. [1988] 169 ITR 139 /[1987] 35 Taxman 294 (AP).

One has to view as to what is conveyed or rendered by employees in consideration of availing a benefit of ESOS/ESOP at a concessional price. Irrefutably it can be said that the benefit that is availed by employees is only in recognition of their services to the company and in return of which what is normally paid is salary or anything incidental like production incentive or bonus which could be tagged on to the salary alone. Therefore, the nature of benefit provided by a company is only a revenue expenditure and by no stretch of imagination the same can be treated as capital expenditure or capital loss. This could be culled out from out of the clauses of the Guidelines framed by the SEBI in this regard as the same was meant exclusively for the benefit of the employees. For this lone reason, no employee as per clause 11 of the scheme shall be entitled to transfer the option in favour of any other.

The nature of receipt of payment - whether it be of capital or revenue in the hands of the payee - is not determinative of as to whether the same is capital expenditure or revenue expenditure in the hands of the payer. This position was made clear by the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. (supra). Further, the reasoning of the Calcutta High Court in CIT v. Shalimar Industries (P.) Ltd. [1995] 78 Taxman 521 and Indian Commerce & Industries Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 78 Taxman 179 (Mad.) respectively, is worthy to note in this context. The facts in the aforesaid cases were that the assessee received shares in consideration of services rendered under a technical collaboration agreement with a foreign company and had shown their value as its income in the year of receipt. Subsequently, on account of the loss suffered by the foreign company and its name having been struck-off from the Register of Companies, there was no chance of any recovery. On these facts, the loss was held allowable as revenue loss despite the fact that the shares were shown in the assessee’s balance sheet in the year of their receipt as investment.

This prima facie appeals to any person as though it is gratuitous but the intendement ex facie behind it is only in recognition of the long-standing services of employees in a graded manner and also to keep the work force of the company more efficient by creating an affable environment so as to enable them to increase productivity and profitability of a company.

Therefore, the author is of the view that ESOS/ESOP benefit provided by a company to its employees as per the approved Guidelines framed by SEBI is well in accordance with the law and, accordingly, a company is entitled to claim the deferred-employees ESOS/ESOP compensation expenditure as business expenditure incurred by it wholly and exclusively for the purpose of its business.

it is said that the same cannot be allowed, even on amortization basis, as the payment relates to a benefit of an enduring nature. Such distinction now needs to be removed in view of the liberal approach followed in regard to capital payments covered under sections 35,35A, 35AB, 35D and36 (1)(ix) discussed earlier. It has also to be appreciated that the lease period which started with 99 years is getting reduced to much less number of years now. The issue needs to be considered from another angle also. In CIT v. Bombay State Trasport Corpn. [1979] 118 ITR 399 (Bom.), it has been said that for determining the true profits in the business sense or under proper principles of accountancy, the wear and tear of the assets utilised by an assessee for the purpose of earning his profits will have to be considered and allowance will have to be made for the wear and tear. That is what is notionally understood as depreciation on the assets utilised in business.

Accounting Standard (AS 6) on depreciation issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India defines the term 'depreciation' as follows:

"3.1 'Depreciation' is a measure of the wearing out, consumption or other loss of. value of a depreciable asset arising from use, effluxion of time or obsolescence through technology and market charges. Depreciation is allocated so as to charge a fair proportion of the depreciable amount in each accounting period during the expected useful life of the asset. Depreciation includes amortization of assets whose useful life is pre-determined.

It is true that strictly speaking, the concept of 'depreciation' cannot apply to lease premiums as depreciation is admissible, in terms of section 32, in regard only to buildings, machinery, plant and furniture. But viewed as an integrated part, lease hold lands can be said to form part of buildings' as their value is only for a limited period. In deciding the question of depreciation on the cost of land used for a building, and of the land appurtenant thereto, one has to decide whether such land forms part of the building. One can inarguably hold that such land is very much an element of building like cement and bricks. And if cement and bricks, etc., lose their identity and are no longer to be included as an asset (designated as building), there is no reason why the land (taken on lease for a limited period) should not be taken to have depreciated and lost its value and hence, lease hold premiums paid should be allowed as a revenue expenditure.

It may also be stated that there is very thin line of distinction between 'amortization' and 'depreciation'. The dictionary meaning of the word 'depreciation' has already been given earlier. 'Amortize' according to Webster's New International Dictionary, means: to make as if dead, destroy, to clear off, liquidate or otherwise extinguish - 'Amortization' or 'amortisation' is the "act or process of amortizing lands....". [Emphasis supplied]

If premium for land is to get liquidated after a certain number of years, then it is in no way different from depreciation and should be treated on the same footing. Thus, if 'lease premium' is not to be allowed as revenue expenditure then it should be depreciated along with the structure on it or even independently for the period for which the payment is to be valid.

Thus, the concept of lease premium being of a 'capital' nature or providing benefit of an enduring nature needs reconsideration. Ordinarily 'capital asset' means an asset which has an element of permanency about it and 'capital expenditure' must, therefore, generally mean an acquisition of an asset and the asset must be of lasting value; while income or revenue expenses are generally running expenses incurred in earning profits or expenses incurred with the primary object of an immediate return or acquisition of assets which are not of lasting value and are likely to get exhausted or consumed in the process of the return or a very limited number of returns - R.S. Radha Kishan Kapoor v. CIT [1963] 47 ITR 938 (All.) and Jagat Bus Service v. CIT [1950] 18 ITR 13 (All.). Further, it would be wrong to say that in all cases securing a benefit for the business is, prima facie, capital expenditure. A benefit which is merely transitory and has no endurance cannot be considered as a capital expenditure. In Anglo-Persian Oil Company Ltd. v. Dale [1932] 16 Tax Cas. 253, it has been said that if the payment of a lump sum closes the liability to make repeated and periodic payments in the future, it may generally be regarded as a payment of a revenue character. The amount and extent of a particular expenditure cannot determine its character. If an expenditure is made in connection with business itself in the sense that it is an integral part of the profit-earning process in that business, it is allowable as deduction under section 37. The payment of lease premium is certainly an integral part of the profit-earning process.

Conclusion

5. The foregoing discussion would show that there is a strong case for allowing lease premium as a revenue expenditure. This can be done in any of the following ways:

elastic in application and has to be construed in a business sense. Simply because payment has been made in lump sum, it cannot be inferred that the expenditure is of a capital nature. A lump sum payment can be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual revenue payments and a recurring periodic payment may be capital expenditure when it represents the payment by instalments of a capital nature -I.R. v. Ramsay 20 TC 79.

Expenditure on acquisition of land 3. Expenditure on acquiring land is one expenditure where there has been no difference of opinion regarding its character. Land has always been held to be a capital asset and expenditure on its acquisition has always been held to be expenditure of a capital nature. This asset has been held to be not entitled even for depreciation because the popular view has been that land does not depreciate in value by user. This has also been judicially recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v . Alps Theatre [1967] 65 ITR 377 .

Lease premium and rent

4. However, over the years, the practice of getting ownership rights over land by outright payment is disappearing fast. With the availability of land becoming scarce, the system of giving land on lease is now becoming the common practice. Ownership rights on land are now, generally, not granted, The Government institutions, being the major owners of vacant lands, give land only on lease for definite periods on payments which vary from outright lump sum payments to periodical payments. In some cases, both these practices are combined, i.e., the lessee is required to pay lump sum as also periodical rents - sometimes nominal and sometimes substantial. The land reverts back to the owner after the stipulated period and the payments made in lump sum are designated as 'lease premium'. Such premiums are, in essence, in the nature of consolidated rent paid in advance for a fixed period for the use of land during such period.

A 'lease', in a legal sense, is a transaction, in which a party owning the asset (called the lessor or landlord or owner) provides the asset for use over a certain period of time for a consideration which may be in the form of periodic payments (called rent) with or without a further down payment (called premium). The International Accounting Standard No. 17 defines it as an agreement whereby the lessor conveys to the lessee in return for rent, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time. Thus, the payments made under a lease agreement are for the use of the land not for acquiring an asset or a benefit of a enduring nature. If consideration paid is a return for the use and occupation of the land or premises demised, it is generally known as rent - M. Subbiah Nadar v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 58 (Mad.).

Periodical rent paid as lease rent is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act, being laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession - CIT v. R. Tolat & Co. [1980] 126 ITR 551 (Guj.). The same consideration should apply, when instead of rent being paid periodically, a lump sum is paid when the agreement is executed (usually referred to as premium) for the use of the land. In such a situation, great hardship is caused to the taxpayers, when such expenditure is not permitted to be amortised in the same manner as expenditure of the nature already referred to earlier which is allowed to be amortised. The character of an expenditure whether it is capital or revenue should be judged from its intrinsic nature rather than by the fact of its being a lump sum. It has been held that a lump sum payment bears the same character as that of a periodic sum which it replaces or substitutes - Vanden Berghes Ltd. v. Clark, ITC 390 (HL). Also see Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd. [1965] 58 ITR 241 (PC) and Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). As per observations in Indian Molasses Co. ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 66 (SC) and Bean v. Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries Ltd. [1946] 27 Tax Cas. 296, the fact of non-recurrence may signify an expenditure's nature to be of a capital nature, but it is not always decisive.

In this context, it may be mentioned that the Chokshi Committee had made the following recommendations in respect of amortisation of capital expenditure:

The payment is made "for the purposes of carrying on business or trading activity" and, therefore, it partakes the character of revenue expenditure. In Fenner Woodroffe & Co. Ltd. v. Almost on similar lines, observations have been made in the case of CIT v. Aluminium Corpn. of India Ltd. [1973] 92 ITR 563 (Cal.) by (Late) J. Sabyasachi Mukerjee, as he then was, who said that an expenditure would be considered to be an expenditure of a capital nature only when the purpose of the expenditure is the acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character. There is no permanency in leasehold rights.

Much importance is attached in this context to the phrase 'advantage of an enduring nature' used in section 37(1). 'Enduring benefit' is a relative term of contextual interpretation. It is not the law that in every case, if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure would be of a capital nature. In Girdhari Doss & Sons v. CIT [1976] 105 ITR 339 (All.), it has been observed at page 342 that the word 'enduring' means in the way the fixed capital endures and it does not connote a benefit that endures in the sense that for a good number of years, it relieves the assessee of a revenue payment.

Enduring benefit is not the acid test of capital expenditure in all cases. Even the celebrated author Viscount Cave, while laying down this test in Atherton v. British Insulated & Helsby Cables Ltd. [1925] 10TC 155 (HL) did not mean to propound a doctrine in unqualified terms. The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 had an occasion to consider these observations and it explained that this dictum is to be interpreted to see whether the benefit enures in a capital field or in a non-capital field. Where the expenditure, although enduring in character, has its impact on the running of the business, it would be an expenditure of a revenue nature.

However, the courts have treated as capital payments the leasehold premiums for acquiring rights in land. In Ramakrishna & Co. v. CIT [1973] 88 ITR 406 (Mad.), amount paid as consideration for obtaining the lease (as opposed to rent/ hire) has been held to be for the acquisition of a capital asset and, therefore, a capital expenditure. In CIT v. Banshidhar Sewbhagawan & Co. [1977] 109 ITR 828 (Gauhati), even advance rent has been held to be capital expenditure. In CIT v. Project Automobiles [1987] 167ITR 7811 (MP), lease premium for securing lease of land for 30 years has been held to be not allowable as revenue expenditure.

In the following cases amounts paid as annual rents were allowed even where the leases were for long periods:

(a) Singareni Collieries Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 553 (AP) - Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

(b) Braithwaite & Co (India ) Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 111 ITR542 (Cal.) -Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

From the above, it would be seen that there is an unreasonable discrimination between assessee having arrangement of annual lease rent and assessees paying advance lease rent in the form of lease premium as the former gets deduction under Income-tax Law while in regard to the latter, it is said that the same cannot be allowed, even on amortization basis, as the payment relates to a benefit of an enduring nature. Such distinction now needs to be removed in view of the liberal approach followed in regard to capital payments covered under sections 35,35A, 35AB, 35D and36 (1)(ix) discussed earlier. It has also to be appreciated that the lease period which started with 99 years is getting reduced to much less number of years now.

Section 37 of the Act is a residuary section extending the allowance of items of business expenditures which are not covered by sections 30 to 36.

The Court correctly held that law pertaining to the enduring benefit concept for disallowing deduction is no longer foolproof. The test of an enduring benefit can be traced from the decision of the Supreme Court in Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. In the words of the Supreme Court it was held that :

"What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. Business Combination Accounting Aspects Under IND-AS

4. An entity accounts for business combinations under Ind AS using the acquisition method of accounting.

4.1 Accounting Aspects for business combinations - The cost of a business combination is measured as the aggregate of the fair values of assets given, liabilities incurred or assumed and equity instruments issued. Costs directly attributable to the business combination are expensed as incurred, except the costs to issue debt that are amortized as part of the effective interest and costs to issue equity, which are included within equity.

4.2 Practice Aspects - Contingent consideration, if any, to be transferred by the entity is recognized at fair value at the acquisition date. Subsequent changes to the fair value of the contingent consideration that is deemed to be an asset or a liability are recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss. Contingent consideration that is classified as equity is not re-measured and its subsequent settlement is accounted for within equity.

The acquiree-company's identifiable assets, liabilities and contingent liabilities that meet the accounting recognition criteria are recognized at their fair values at the acquisition date, except for non-current assets that are classified as held-for sale in accordance with the standard, Non Current Assets Held for Sale and Discontinued Operations, which are recognized at fair value less costs to sell.

Contingent liabilities are only included in the identifiable assets and liabilities of the acquiree where there is a present obligation at the acquisition date.

On acquisition, a company is required to assess the classification of the acquire-company's assets and liabilities and is required to reclassify them if such classification is inappropriate at the group level.

Non-controlling interests arising from a business combination, which are present ownership interests, and entitle their holders to a proportionate share of the entity's net assets in the event of liquidation, can be measured either at the present ownership interest's proportionate share in the recognized amounts of the acquiree's identifiable net assets or at fair value. Such treatment under Ind AS is not an accounting policy choice but is selected for each individual business combination, and is to be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements.

In situations where the company held a non-controlling shareholding in the acquiree prior to obtaining control, such interest is required to be measured to fair value as at acquisition date. The measurement to fair value is included in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period.

Goodwill arising in a business combination is determined as the consideration paid, plus the fair value of any shareholding held prior to obtaining control, plus non-controlling interest and less the fair value of the identifiable assets and liabilities of the acquire. If the total of consideration transferred, non-controlling interest recognized and previously held interest measured is less than the fair value of the net assets of the subsidiary acquired in the case of a bargain purchase, the difference is recognized in equity (Capita reserve).

Goodwill should not be amortized but is required to be tested for impairment on an annual basis. If goodwill is assessed to be impaired, that impairment is not subsequently reversed.

Goodwill arising on acquisition of foreign entities is considered as an asset of the foreign entity. In such cases, the goodwill is translated to the functional currency at the end of each reporting period with the adjustment recognized in equity through other comprehensive income.

The High Court, relying on the decisions placed before the Court by the assessee and stating the categories of a computer software and their functions, has held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee on software and professional expenses were of revenue in nature and did not provide any enduring benefit to the assessee.

Facts of the case

2. The appeal was filed by the Revenue in the Delhi High Court against the order of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal ('ITAT') under section 260A of the Income-tax Act ('the Act'). The assessee was into the business of manufacturing safety glass for automobiles. In the financial year 1996-97, it had entered into an agreement with Arthur Anderson & Associates for installation of software and professional services. The software was based on application software, commonly known as Oracle Application. Another agreement was entered into between the assessee and Oracle Software India Pvt. Ltd. to grant license to the assessee for use of the software. The assessee in respect of the aforesaid transaction had incurred an expenditure to the tune of Rs. 1,36,77,664 and Rs. 1,70,68,811 in the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 respectively. However, in the books of account for the assessment year 1997-98, the assessee had not written off any sum towards the aforesaid expenditure and in the succeeding year had written off only a part of the expenditure. While computing taxable income, the assessee claimed entire expenditure as deduction for both the assessment years.

The Assessing Officer rejected the claims of the assessee on the ground that the said expenditure had resulted in an enduring benefit to the assessee. On appeal to the Commissioners (Appeal) the claim of the assessee was allowed on the ground that the said expenses did not result in creation of a new asset or a new source of income and the expenses incurred were recurring in nature to upgrade the system.

3. Contentions made

3.1 By the revenue - The case of the Revenue was that the expenditure incurred by the assessee was capital in nature, as it would endure to the assessee benefit for a long period. It was also contended that as huge amount of expense had been incurred in the assessment year 1998-99, it would tantamount to show that the expenditure was not incurred for the purposes of upgradation or for correction of the deficiencies. In the author's view this contention had no legal basis as amount of expenditure is no criteria for claiming deduction under section 37 of the Act.

3.2 By the assessee - It was contended on behalf of the assessee that merely because an expenditure results in an enduring benefit it would not be sufficient reason to treat the expenditure incurred as one expended on capital account. For this reasoning the assessee had cited various decisions of the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court and of the other High Courts. Relying upon the decisions cited, it was contended that what has to be deciphered in facts and circumstances of the each case is the real intent and purpose of the expenditure so as to ascertain, as to whether it had resulted in bringing into existence a capital asset?

4. An analysis of the judgment

4.1 Ruling by the High Court - The Delhi High Court ('the Court') was supplied with impeccable judgments of the Supreme Court and the other High Courts which addressed to the issue in favour of the assessee. The High Court after due consideration of these judgments stated as under :

"What is required to be seen is the real intent and purpose of the expenditure and whether the expenditure results in creation of fixed capital for the assessee? It is important to bear in mind that what is required to be seen is not whether the advantage obtained lasts forever but whether the expense incurred does away with a recurring expenses defrayed towards running a business as against an expense undertaken for the benefit of the business as a whole?"

Know-how and its treatment in Accountancy 4. The assessment year involved in the case was 1985-86. For the assessment years 1986-87 to 1997-98 ‘know-how’ has been defined in the Explanation to section 35AB, to mean any industrial information or technique likely to assist in the manufacture or processing of goods or in the working of a mine. The definition of ‘know-how’ for the purposes of section 32 in Explanation 4 is the same with effect from April 4, 1999. ‘Know-how’ is broadly speaking a ‘fund of technical knowledge’ - Rolls Royce Ltd. v. Jeffrey (Inspector of Taxes) [1965] 56 ITR 580 (HL).

According to ‘Accounting Standard-10 - Accounting for Fixed Assets’, know-how is generally of two types : relating to manufacturing processes; and relating to plans, designs and drawings of buildings or plant and machinery. Know-how related to plans, designs and drawings of buildings or plant and machinery is capitalised under the relevant asset heads and depreciation calculated on the total cost, including the cost of the know-how capitalised. Know-how relating to manufacturing processes is usually expensed in the year in which it is incurred.

What is the apposite test in Rajasthan High Court’s case ?

5. Know-how is a ‘fund of knowledge’; it is ‘any industrial information or technique likely to assist in the manufacture. . . or mining’. The pocket Oxford Dictionary meaning of technique is mechanical part of an art and craft; (loosely) method of achieving one’s purpose.

Drawings, designs, patterns, specifications, etc., are embodiments of know-how. Transfer of know-how results in a benefit or advantage to the transferor and involves a cost to the transferee. One characteristic of such know-how is that at the time of its acquisition, it holds a potential and a promise; it is only when the requisite machinery, plant and buildings are in place, that the process can be actually utilised either in the existing line of manufacture or in a new one. As far as plant and machinery and building are concerned, there is no doubt that they are capital assets; but the expenditure on the know-how can, as it were, be detached from those assets and its nature independently assessed - whether revenue or capital - by applying the tests laid down, by the Supreme Court.

The rules in AS-10, are simple. If the know-how relates to plans, designs, and drawings of buildings or plant and machinery, its cost is to be capitalised and added to the cost of the latter assets, and depreciation provided thereon. On the other hand, if the know-how relates to manufacturing processes, it has to be treated as the revenue expenditure.

Introduction

1.Direct tax laws, by their very nature, cannot remain static for long. These have to change to cater to various considerations arising consequent to change in policies, political philosophies, needs of the society, changing concepts in law, economic theories and practices, accounting principles, international relations, acts of God, need for revenue and similar other such situations. In fact, the history of federal taxes mirrors the history of a nation and by going through details concerning tax changes, one can feel the pulse of a country's development and other happenings.

Accounting concepts and practices have important bearing on taxation of incomes though accounting practices followed by taxpayers have been held to be not finally decisive in tax matters - Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v . SA.L. Narayan Row, CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 (SC) and CIT v. Cocanada Radhaswami Bank Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 306 (SC). In the matter of expenditure, accounting principles imply that all expenditure that is incurred for generating incomes it should be deducted for finding out what has been the net gain or loss. But in determining taxable incomes or losses, all expenses incurred are not deductible. Hence, in many situations, incomes, profits or losses for tax purposes are different from the actual results.

Capital v. Revenue

2. A very common controversy that arises in tax proceedings relates to concepts concerning 'capital' and 'revenue'. The disputes generally relate to whether particular receipts or expenditure are of capital or revenue nature. Normally, expenses of a capital nature are not allowed as deduction for computing taxable income. But there are provisions where expenditures which, prima facie, appear to be of a capital nature are, by express provisions in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act') either allowed as deduction in one year, or such expenditure is phased out (amortised) over a number of years. Some instances, where statute permits deduction of capital expenditure either in one stroke or over a few years, are considered below:

(i)Where the assessee incurs any expenditure of a capital nature on scientific research related to his business, the whole of such expenditure (excluding expenditure on acquisition of land) incurred in any previous year is allowable as deduction in that previous year - Section 35(1)(iv).

(ii)Capital expenditure on acquisition of patent rights or copy rights are allowable as business expenditure in equal instalments over a period of 14 years or over the unexpired life of the patent right or copy right – Section 35A.

(iii) Lump sum consideration paid for acquiring know-how for the purpose of business is allowed as deduction by spreading it equally over 6 years -Section 35AB.

(iv)Certain preliminary expenses incurred by an Indian company or resident non-corporate assessee are permitted to be amortised over a period of 10 years - Section 35D.

(v)An expenditure of a capital nature incurred by a corporate assessee for promoting family planning is allowable as a deduction in a period of 5 years - Section 36(1)(ix) .

Thus, the expression 'capital expenditure' is elastic in application and has to be construed in a business sense. Simply because payment has been made in lump sum, it cannot be inferred that the expenditure is of a capital nature. A lump sum payment can be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual revenue payments and a recurring periodic payment may be capital expenditure when it represents the payment by instalments of a capital nature -I.R. v. Conclusion

5. The Act is very clear as to which payments have to be classified as one on account of capital or revenue expenditure with respect to expenditure incurred for computer software. The test of an enduring benefit is not appropriate for the purpose of classifying the nature of the expenditure. In order to claim a particular item of expenditure which is deductible under section 37 of the Act the following condition should be satisfied :

(i) The expenditure should not be of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 of the Act;

(ii) It should have been incurred in that accounting year;

(iii) It should be in respect of a business which was carried on by the assessee and the profits of which are to be computed and assessed and should be incurred after setting-up of the business;

(iv) It should not be in the nature of personal expenses of the assessee;

(v) It should have been laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of such business; and

(vi) It should not be in the nature of a capital expenditure.

Accounting practices 12.1 General- Accounting practices are those which are followed as a matter of convention in contrast to standards which have been prescribed and are mandatory. A few of such items like treatment of deferred revenue expenditure, chit loss, and interest received during construction period are dealt with below :

12.2 Deferred revenue expenditure - Items like capital issue expenditure, preliminary expenses, technical know-how fee, etc., are treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the accounts, considering that they result in enduring benefit. However, under the Act, there is no concept of deferred revenue expenditure except when specially provided for like under sections 35A, 35AB, 35D, 35E, etc. Hence, expenditure of revenue nature, though treated as deferred revenue in accounts, should be claimed as a deduction for income-tax purposes entirely in the year in which the expenditure is actually incurred. Examples of such items are repairs and maintenance of ocean-going vessels like ships and dredgers; technical know-how fee; huge publicity campaign expenses, etc. Deductibility of know-how as a revenue expenditure and its capitalisation as plant and machinery have generated a lot of controversy. The leading authority for the proposition that technical know-how in the form of designs, drawings, etc., constitutes plant and is entitled to depreciation is the case of Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 86 . In this judgment, the Supreme Court upheld the assessee's claim for depreciation on expenditure capitalised as plant and there was no occasion to examine whether such expenditure constituted revenue or capital expenditure. The same, therefore, cannot be considered an authority for the proposition that technical know-how constitutes capital expenditure. In the following cases, lump sum/annual payments made for technical know-how even resulting in enduring benefit for periods ranging from five to ten years were held to be revenue in nature – CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 (SC), Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC), CIT v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. (P.) Ltd. [1980] 123 ITR 538 (Bom.), Praga Tools Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 123 ITR 773 (AP)(FB), Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 207 ITR 1017 (Bom.), etc. There are many cases in which this proposition was upheld and it was held that in these days of fast changing world technology, the frontiers of scientific and technical knowledge shift rapidly, the state of the art technology of modern times can neither be deemed to be permanent, nor of an enduring nature, so as to satisfy the enduring asset test. Thus, even though technical know-how acquired for improvement of technology is considered deferred revenue expenditure in accounts on the ground that the benefit accrues over a period of time, it is to be noted that under the Act, there being no provision for such concept, it has to be claimed as revenue expenditure in the year of incurring itself.

The other important issue in the context of deferred revenue expenditure is, again related to know-how, deductible under section 35AB, i.e., whether the said section applies only to capital expenditure or even to revenue expenditure. The popular opinion in this regard is that it applies to only capital expenditure, as it is an enabling section and not a disabling one and, hence, it does not cover revenue expenditure which, as it is, is allowable under section 37. Reference may be made to a recent decision in Wellman Incandescent India Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [1995] 55 ITD 338 (Cal.) upholding this contention. Yet another important issue to be considered is that technical know-how acquired for expansion of existing business by way of setting up a new project is allowable under section 35AB over a numbers of years from the income of existing business, though the new project is not commissioned and though such amount is treated as capital in the books, as discussed above. In these days of rapid and fast technology upgradation, such expenditure has to be carefully analysed and considered appropriately both in accounts and for tax purposes as between capital, revenue or combination of both. As is the case with the allowability of any expenditure under the Act, it is imperative that the deduction in this regard should also be claimed in the proper year based on express provisions and judicial precedents.

On the other hand, regular corporate tax provisions revolve around the idea of revenue vs capital items which requires mainly interpreting the text within tax law. Another example involves depreciation. While its calculation varies for accounting and tax purposes, usage of the TNMM method requires reference to depreciation as per the accounting standards and not the tax law. Having said this, any decision on treatment of a particular transaction/ issue should be looked at from both regular tax and TP perspectives. TP in tax is not an exact science and TP regulations are more subjective and prone to interpretation than regular corporate tax provisions. Also, considering TP regulations are relatively newer, there are lesser ambiguous TP issues that have been settled by courts than regular corporate tax ones.

Intersection of Business and Tax Worlds

Let us now look at how the tax and business worlds interact in relation to TP.

One can say from above discussions that both these worlds seem aligned to the arm's length principle. As seen in the example of the steel and car assembly businesses, the Business World would prefer independent pricing. The Tax World clearly prefers ALP in relation to TP. So, the basic rationale/ logic is the same in both these worlds. Further, the Tax World talks of a functional, asset and risk analysis before profiling a particular entity/ transaction and then comparing it with other independent entities/ transactions. The OECD TP Guidelines also specify that the remuneration for a transaction must be commensurate to the activities involved. The Business World talks of pricing and other processes based on whether the unit is a revenue, cost, investment or profit center. They are again talking of similar rationales. In fact, in many jurisdictions, the corporate law, i.e., not pertaining to income tax, requires companies to prove to regulators that controlled transactions were undertaken at arm's length. This governance mechanism helps protect the interests of minority shareholders.

While at a broad and general level, both the business and tax worlds are talking of the same logics for TP, it is possible that sometimes either tax or business requirements take precedence while deciding on TP issues. Tax regulations do not like that taxation is the primary rationale behind a particular arrangement. Similarly, business decisions must not be oblivious to tax implications. With increased and more robust TP compliance frameworks, tech-savvy tax authorities, and greater experience and knowledge, there is an increased need for business arrangements to be aligned with tax principles of TP.

Conclusion

The tax and business worlds of TP are not the same though they talk of the same concepts and logics. As tax regulations and scrutiny are getting sophisticated and business models are also becoming more dynamic and complicated, it is important that business decisions related to TP are taken in cognizance of tax implications. That business decisions are taken across the globe for MNEs, and tax functions are generally centralized and considered to be administrative, creates a challenge that every MNE must consider based on their facts and circumstances.

Often companies need to have their employees undergo specific trainings in order to fulfil the requirements of or in order to upskill them to fulfil a revenue contract with a customer. This may be required as a specific requirement of the customer or in order to skill the employees to execute the customer contract.

The accounting of such training costs can be debatable and often companies have treated specific training costs as a part of the contract cost.

Under Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 2015, Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers sets forth the following guidance for contract fulfilment costs:

95 If the costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer are not within the scope of another Standard (for example, Ind AS 2, Inventories, Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment or Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets), an entity shall recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract only if those costs meet all of the following criteria:

(a)

the costs relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that the entity can specifically identify (for example, costs relating to services to be provided under renewal of an existing contract or costs of designing an asset to be transferred under a specific contract that has not yet been approved);

(b)

the costs generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying (or in continuing to satisfy) performance obligations in the future;

and

(c)

the costs are expected to be recovered.

96 For costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer that are within the scope of another Standard, an entity shall account for those costs in accordance with those other Standards.

97 Costs that relate directly to a contract (or a specific anticipated contract) include any of the following:

(a)

direct labour (for example, salaries and wages of employees who provide the promised services directly to the customer);

(b)

direct materials (for example, supplies used in providing the promised services to a customer);

(c)

allocations of costs that relate directly to the contract or to contract activities (for example, costs of contract management and supervision, insurance and depreciation of tools and equipment used in fulfilling the contract);

(d)

costs that are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract; and

(e)

other costs that are incurred only because an entity entered into the contract (for example, payments to subcontractors).

98 An entity shall recognise the following costs as expenses when incurred:

(a)

general and administrative costs (unless those costs are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract, in which case an entity shall evaluate those costs in accordance with paragraph 97);

(b)

costs of wasted materials, labour or other resources to fulfil the contract that were not reflected in the price of the contract;

(c)

costs that relate to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations) in the contract (ie costs that relate to past performance);

and

(d)

costs for which an entity cannot distinguish whether the costs relate to unsatisfied performance obligations or to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations).

Therefore, based on the above guidance, if an entity incurs costs for training its staff specifically in order to execute a revenue contract with customers or as a requirement of the customer contracts, the cost may fit into a contract fulfilment cost. This is because, the training costs would relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that can be specifically identified and would generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying performance obligations towards the customers in the future.

However, the conflict arises in Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets, which states as follows:

5 This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (eg a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, ie the knowledge embodied in it.

Ind AS 38 acknowledges that an entity usually has insufficient control over the future economic benefits arising from an assembled workforce (i.e. a team of skilled workers, or specific management or technical talent) or from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset.

Therefore, this guidance would require specific training costs to be recognised as expense as incurred.

A question, therefore, arises as to whether such training costs can be capitalised under Ind AS 115 since they would fulfil the definition of fulfilment costs.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

CBDT's Error 10. The CBDT's Circular No. 599 dated April 24, 1991 is of course right in saying that broken period interest is not taxable. But the reason given is wrong. It says that interest paid as part of the purchase price is a revenue item and this should be set off against the interest received. It is here that the CBDT has fallen foul of the Supreme Court. The interest paid along with the purchase price is capital expenditure as rightly held by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra). The real reason why the broken period interest is not taxable, as canvassed in this article, is that when interest is received, the portion relating to the broken period, is actually a recovery of cost and must, therefore, be set off against the purchase price. To take a concrete example, if a bank purchases a security for Rs. 120 including Rs. 20 as broken period interest and subsequently receives Rs. 25 as interest from the issuer of the security, according to the CBDT, the cost is Rs. 100 only and the revenue is only Rs. 5, i.e., Rs. 25 - Rs. 20. According to the Supreme Court, the cost is Rs. 120 and the revenue is Rs. 25. According to accounting authorities, while the cost is no doubt Rs. 120 initially, it gets reduced to Rs. 100 subsequently on receipt of interest including the portion relating to the broken period. Since out of Rs. 25 received, Rs. 20 is credited to the investment account, Rs. 5 alone is revenue. Thus, arithmetically, the CBDT was right, but the principles employed were wrong.

The author here deals with the issue as to when capital reserve can be used to set off losses. The highlights of the article are the definition of ‘capital reserve’, circumstances in which it is created and its utilisation. In this context, the author has analysed the judgment of the Delhi High Court in Allianz Capital & Management Services Ltd., In re [2005] 63 SCL 496 wherein it has been held that after obtaining the Government’s approval, capital profits can be used to set off loss, and submits that this decision is binding within jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court only.

What is capital reserve

1. Reserve is profit retained or ploughed back in the business and accumulated over the years. Reserves are of two kinds (1) Revenue reserve and (2) Capital reserve. A reserve created out of trading profits is revenue reserve.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve. The Companies Act, 1956 does not directly define the term ‘capital reserve’. But according to Part III of Schedule VI of the Act, "the expression ‘capital reserve’ shall not include any amount regarded as free for distribution through the profit and loss account; and the expression ‘revenue reserve’ shall mean any reserve other than a capital reserve." In reality, the capital reserve is at time distributable as dividends among shareholders. But normally, it is not so distributed. The capital reserve is not created by transferring the profit through the appropriation account as is the case of the revenue or the general reserve. But, it is created out of the profits of a capital nature.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve.

How a capital reserve is created

2. The capital reserve is created out of the capital profits. Some of the circumstances under which the capital reserve is created are as under:

(a) Premiums received on the issue of shares and debentures are capital profits. They are considered as the capital reserve.

(b) Balance to the credit of forfeited shares account after the re-issue of such forfeited shares is transferred to the capital reserve.

(c) Profit on the redemption of debentures at a discount is considered as a capital profit and is transferred to the capital reserve.

(d) When on purchase of a business the purchase price is less than the value of the net assets acquired, the difference is normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(e) Similarly the profits prior to the incorporation of the limited company are considered capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve.

(f) Profits which are of an exceptional nature and which have not been earned during the regular course of business are at times considered as capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve. But it is not so treated always.

(g) Where the company sells its fixed assets at an amount which is higher than their cost, the excess over cost is considered as a capital profit. This profit is not earned during the regular course of business. Hence, such profits are normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(h) Sometimes a company may revalue its fixed assets as a result of appreciation in their value. The amount of appreciation is normally transferred to the capital reserve. Revaluation of fixed assets is made by following the Accounting Standard-10 accounting for fixed assets. Revaluation of assets should be done of a class of assets and not individual assets.

(i) If directed by the articles of association, certain profits may not be available for distribution among shareholders. In other words, such profits are not free for distribution through the profit and loss account. Such profits are transferred to the capital reserve.

(j) Certain capital gains and other items of profits which are not regarded as available for distribution as dividend are transferred to the capital reserve. (Adapted from Auditing Principles and Practice by V.H Krishnadwala pg. 2.265)

Disclosure of capital reserve in the balance sheet

3. According to Part I of Schedule VI to the Act, the capital reserve should be shown as a separate item under the head ‘Reserves and surplus’. It should not be mixed up with the revenue reserves. The share premium account is a capital profit, but it is shown as a separate item in the balance sheet.

Utilisation of capital profits (and hence the capital reserve)

4. Capital profits can be utilised for writing off intangible assets like the preliminary expenses, share/debenture issue expenses, goodwill, etc.

The share premium account can be applied for the following purposes as directed by section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 :

(a) in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to its shareholders as fully paid bonus shares,

(b) in writing off preliminary expenses,

of an intangible. Development of a trademark or goodwill takes place over a passage of time and is a slow ongoing process. In cases of well-known trademarks, the trademark is already recognised in the market. In such cases the expenditure incurred for promoting products, with a trademark, is really for exploitation of the trademark rather than for development of the value of the trademark. Brand value, therefore, does not represent trademark as a standalone asset. It is difficult and complex to determine and segregate its value. Therefore, it is not correct to assert that brand building is a substantial attribute of advertisement and sale promotion. Brand building represents a coordinated synergetic impact created largely by reputation and quality. There are good number of examples where brands have been built without incurring substantial advertisement or promotion expenses. Equally, there also are cases where, in spite of extensive and large scale advertisements, brand values have not been created. Hence, it would be erroneous and fallacious to treat brand building as counterpart of advertisement expenses. Advertisements may be the quickest and effective way to tell a brand story to a large audience, but just that is not enough to create or build a brand.

The High Court has also highlighted the fact that the Delhi High Court has repeatedly held that advertisement expenditure should not be generally treated as capital expenditure incurred or made for creating an intangible capital asset – see CIT v. Monto Motors Ltd. [2012] 206 Taxman 43/19 taxmann.com 57 (Delhi); CIT v. Spice Distribution Ltd. [2015] 229 Taxman 400/54 taxmann.com 325; and CIT v. Salora International Ltd. [2009] 308 ITR 199 (Delhi).

From the abovementioned observations of the High Court, on Brand and Brand Building, we may infer that AMP expenses incurred by an Indian Distributor AE are not necessarily for creation of marketing intangibles for Foreign AE. Where the brand of the Foreign AE is well-known and recognised, we may say that the Indian Distributor AE incurs AMP expenses for exploiting the brand for its own distribution business. In such a case the Indian Distributor AE will not be entitled to a separate remuneration for AMP functions. Of course, the Gross Profit (under RPM) and Net Profit (under TNMM) realised by the Indian Distributor should be in line with the comparables.

3.1.9 Economic Ownership of Brand:The Special Bench had rejected the concept of economic ownership of brand, in the context of Transfer Pricing. That concept has been now appreciated by the High Court. The High Court has held that the economic ownership of a brand name or trademark is accepted in international taxation as one of the components of determining the transfer price of goods.

Economic ownership when pleaded can be accepted if it is proved by the assessee. The burden is on the assessee. It cannot be assumed.

Economic ownership of a brand is an intangible asset, just as legal ownership is. On this point we may draw an inference from the High Court's observation, that in long-term distribution-cum-marketing arrangements, with the Foreign AE, the Indian Distributor (the purchasing AE) may acquire economic ownership of the brand – such ownership, however, has to be proved by the Indian Distributor. In that case the Indian Distributor does acquire the right to exploit the intangible property, like trademark or logo, embedded or affixed on the distributed goods. Therefore, in such a case we may assert that the AMP expenses are incurred by the Indian Distributor for its own benefit, as economic owner of the trademark or the logo. So, no separate AMP remuneration is due from the Foreign AE.

But what would be the appropriate remuneration in such a case, for AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributor? The appropriate remuneration would be the premium profits realised from exploitation of the brand. Such premium profits would be reflected in higher Gross Profit margins or higher Net Profit margins realised by the Indian Distributor, as compared to comparable distributors.

3.1.10 Direct Marketing Expenses:The High Court has rejected the Revenue's contention that direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, would form part of the AMP expenses.

Distribution and marketing exercise in case of tangible goods requires transfer or sale of goods to third parties, be it sub-distributors or retailers. That transaction is in the nature of sale of goods for consideration. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to sub-distributors or retailers are not in the nature and character of 'brand promotion'. They are not directly or immediately related to 'brand building' exercise, but have a live link and direct connection with marketing and increased volume of sales or turnover. The 'brand building' connect is too remote and faint.

To include and treat the direct marketing expenses, like trade discount or volume discount or incentive, as 'brand building' exercise would be contrary to common sense and would be highly exaggerated. The expenses being in the nature of selling expenses have an immediate connect with price or consideration payable for the goods sold. They are not incurred for publicity or advertisement.

Based on the above reasoning, the High Court has held that the direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, should not form part of the AMP expenses.

Classification of expenditure under income-tax law 8. For purposes of levy of income-tax, expenditure is classified into two categories, i.e., capital and revenue. The Income-tax Act does not recognise the third category, viz., deferred revenue expenditure. This is because under the cash system of accounting once expenditure is incurred and in the mercantile system once liability towards expenditure had accrued even though it is discharged on a future date, they are admissible as a deduction in computing income. Deferred revenue expenditure isrevenue expenditure incurred in one accounting period the benefit of which is applicable either wholly or in part to future periods. ‘As a rule an item falling under this heading is a fictitious asset, i.e., although it is shown as an asset in the balance sheet, it is not really an asset at all but a capital or abnormal loss which has not been written off’ [Accountancy by William Pickles, Fourth Edition, page 0804]. Thus, deferred revenue expenditure was unknown in income-tax matters and this has also been judicially recognised as discussed hereunder. Only where there is a specific provision like section 35A, 35AB, 35D or rule 9A, 9B, the expenditure is allowed to be amortised in more than one year.

In the case of Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd., In re [1952] 21 ITR 353 (All.), it was held that where the expenditure is of a heavy character and the benefits thereof were likely to extend beyond the year in question, the entire expenditure is deductible in the year of incurring it without any spreadover to future years, as there is no provision in law for spreading out. [Emphasis supplied] This decision was being followed without demur by the department for more than four decades. The Board Instruction No. 943, dated April 2, 1976 reiterates the abovenoted principle. As per this instruction, it is open to a subscriber to claim the entire amount paid under the OYT scheme in the year in which payment is made. Where the installation of telephone is in the previous year subsequent to the previous year in which the deposit is made, the deduction for payment should be allowed in the year of payment irrespective of the fact whether the telephone has been installed or not.

However, in a recent judgment in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340, the Apex Court has opened the Pandora’s box on this well-settled issue. The Apex Court observed that ordinarily revenue expenditure which is incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business must be allowed in its entirety in the year in which it is incurred. It cannot be spread over a number of years even if the assessee had written it off in his books over a period of years. Having said so, the Apex Court went on to say that the facts may justify an assessee who has incurred expenditure in a particular year to spread and claim it over a period of ensuing years. In fact, allowing the expenditure in one year might give a distorted picture of the profits of a particular year. The decision in Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd.’s case (supra) has not been cited in the above-mentioned case. The Tribunal has in fact allowed the entire expenditure in one year on the same reasoning as in Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd.’s case (supra). Here one is not able to reconcile the situation with the dictum laid down by the Apex Court. Has any assessee a choice to decide as to how his expenditure should be allowed ? The Apex Court having observed that normally such expenditure is allowable in one year cannot vary the principle merely on the ground that the profits will get distorted. This view looks based more on equity than law. Can this be a yardstick in fiscal matters to decide about the allowance of expenditure ? The principle upheld earlier in Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd.’s case (supra) and followed by the Tribunal is in conformity with the earlier decision in Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) to the effect that the nature of entries made by an assessee in his books is not decisive or conclusive of a matter. A time-tested practice has been given the go-by with the result that the assessing authorities will start disallowing expenditure on a subjective assessment presuming benefit as extending beyond the accounting year. The decision will spawn more litigation at a time when the Finance Minister is hoping to settle disputes by the Kar Vivad Samadhan Scheme. It would be necessary to issue a circular if harassment by way of disallowances/litigation are to be avoided. This decision itself needs a review. Till then it must be held as confined to the facts of the particular case.

FAQ 86. Whether details regarding GST have to be reported in Clause 27(a) as a clause in Form 3CD requires details of CENVAT but in schema requires for CENVAT/ITC?

FAQ 87. If the statutory auditor does not consider an item as a prior period expense, whereas the tax auditor feels that such item should be considered as a prior period, should that expense be disclosed in Clause 27(b) of Form 3CD?

It may be noted that there is a difference between the expenditure of any earlier year debited to the profit and loss account and the expenditure relating to an earlier year, which has crystallised during the relevant year. An expense, though related to previous periods, which has been determined in the current period, would not be considered a prior period item.

In such cases, though the expenditure may relate to the earlier year, it can be considered as arising during the year on the basis that the liability materialised or crystallised during the year, and such cases will not be reported under this clause.

FAQ 88. Mr. A, a sole proprietor, agreed to transfer his personal property to Mr. X and received some non-refundable advance against such a deal. The sale could not materialise as Mr. X could not pay the whole amount, and the advance money was forfeited by Mr. A. What are the disclosure requirements?

Section 56(2)(ix) of the Income-tax Act provides for taxability of any sum received as an advance in the course of negotiations for the transfer of a capital asset, and such sum was forfeited due to non-transfer of such capital asset. A new Clause 29A to Form 3CD has been inserted to report any advance received from the buyer but forfeited due to the non-materialisation of a deal to the sale of the capital asset.

The auditor is not required to report any such forfeited amount in respect of a personal capital asset or stock-in-trade. Any advances received and forfeited towards the sale of stock-in-trade would be taxable under section 28(i), and would not be required to be reported since the amount would be credited to the profit & loss account.

The requirement of reporting arises only on forfeiture of advance. If an advance has been received and has been outstanding for a considerable time, there is no requirement to report such amount unless and until it is forfeited by an act of the assessee.
