On reference :

■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal of the assessee as being devoid of any merit. The High Court opined that expenditure incurred by the assessee by way of non-compete fee paid to L&T could not be claimed as a revenue expenditure as it was clearly a capital expenditure. Despite holding the expenditure to be capital in nature, the High Court was of the further view that the non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for 7 years did not result in depreciable intangible asset. It was held that the right acquired by the assessee by payment of non-compete fee was a right in personam only against L&T for a period of 7 years. It was not a right in rem.

■

Adverting to the expression 'similar business or commercial rights' appearing in section 32(1)(ii), the High Court opined that it has to necessarily result in an intangible asset against the entire world to qualify for depreciation under the said provision. The High Court therefore dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

On second appeal :

The assessee was a firm of exchange brokers. One 'M' was also carrying on business in co-partnership as exchange brokers. 'M' and his partner were exchange partner of firm namely 'R' brothers – In year 1927, an agreement was entered into between assessee-firm and 'M'. As per terms of said agreement, 'M' was to transfer four seats in the Calcutta Exchange Brokers' Association, belonging to the firm of which he was partner, in favour of the assessee-firm. The goodwill of the firm was to be absolutely transferred in favour of the assessee-firm. The consideration mentioned in the agreement was £4,000 for transferring the four seats in the association and for the sale of the goodwill. It was further agreed that 'M' would not in future and at any time work as exchange broker or in any way compete with the assessee-firm, and the consideration for such agreeing not to enter into competition with the assessee-firm as exchange brokers in Calcutta were annuities payable during the lifetime of 'M' to him and after his death to his wife. The payment of the annuities was made contingent and payable 'only and so long as the brokerage earned from 'R' Brothers was not less than the double of the amount of such payment of annuity in each year. In certain circumstances the annuity was to be proportionately reduced and if the firm 'R' Brothers ceased to carry on business in Calcutta, the annuities would forthwith cease.

In view of aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held that the payment in question constituted revenue expenditure which, having admittedly been laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business, was properly allowable as an admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xii) of the 1922 Act.

On reference :

The assessee entered into agreements with two foreign companies for obtaining technical knowledge and information, training of Indian employees abroad and for use of trade name. In one case, the assessee was to establish a factory for the manufacture of trucks and other automotive products. For this, the payment was to be a percentage of net sales prices and net profits of the assessee's particular products. In the other case the foreign company's assistance was sought to start the operation of assessee-company's steel foundry for bringing it into effective commission. In the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee had paid towards fees Rs. 29,59,608 as share of profits to one company and Rs. 2,99,158 as lump sum fees to the other company. The assessee also incurred Rs. 1,69,925 as expenses on training its employees abroad by the foreign companies. All the three items were claimed as revenue expenditure but the ITO treated them as capital expenditure. On appeal, the AAC accepted the assessee's claim and allowed the appeal. On Department's appeal, the Tribunal considered the terms of the two agreements and found that, under one agreement, the assessee only got technical assistance and knowledge in regard to truck manufacture and the right to use its trade name for a specific period. It was thus really a case of fees being paid for user of technical know-how and trade name. Under the other agreement, it was the right to trade for purposes of carrying on its business upon the technical knowledge of the foreign company in regard to foundry business. In both the cases, the Tribunal opined that these items of expenditure had not resulted in acquisition or bringing into existence an asset or capital of enduring nature. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the payments were deafly revenue expenditure. Similarly, the expenditure on training was for running the business more efficiently so as to earn higher profits and was revenue in nature.

On reference :

The assessee-company, whose main business was as contractors, became a partner in a firm on 1-4-1980, with the sole intention of taking over the firm’s business, which comprised, inter alia, business in cotton and kapas. On the dissolution of the firm on 11-11-1980, the assessee took over the firm’s business, and its share in the firm’s business amounted to a loss of Rs. 16,005. The assessee claimed set off of this loss against its business income, but the ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that, since it related to the acquisition of a business, it was a capital expenditure. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the assessee’s claim.

On the revenue’s appeal:

The assessee carried on business as a dealer in motor vehicles. During the relevant period it was a dealer of Telco, under an agreement with that company, for the sale of Mercedes Benz trucks. The agreement required the assessee to maintain at its own expense an organization for the sale of vehicles, providing for maintenance of show rooms, service centers, repair shops, etc. and an adequate staff of trained salesman and a staff of trained technical service personnel. According to the agreement, the training was actually imparted by Telco which charged the assessee on that account. Under the training scheme, Telco proposed to build a hostel for the apprentices and to recover the entire cost of the hostel from its several dealers. The assessee paid Telco certain amount during the relevant accounting year and claimed that amount was a deduction from its assessable profits for the assessment year 1961-62. The ITO was of the view that the payment was made as the assessee's contribution towards the construction of the hostel, that the hostel would be the property of Telco and that, therefore, it was not a business expenditure. Accordingly, he rejected the assessee's claim.

The AAC allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that although the said amount was a contribution towards the construction of the hostel it was not an expense of a capital nature but was a revenue expense incurred in connection with the business of the assessee.

The Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO, holding that the amount was a capital expenditure.

On reference :

The assessee-firm took over as a new line of business, a gas distribution agency, from a company, under an agreement. By a letter dated 4-12-1974, the company informed the assessee-firm that it was prepared to relinquish the said agency, and it will be the responsibility of the assessee to get the agency from the principals. Accordingly, the assessee acquired the distri-bution rights from the principals. Being new and inexperienced in this line of business, the assessee took the assistance, help and guidance of the company for running the business and claimed the technical fees paid for this purpose under an agreement as revenue expenditure. The ITO, however, took the view (i) that the business had merely changed hands ; (ii) that no technical services would be required for carrying on a running and established business ; and (iii) that mention about technical services in the agreement, though apparent, was not real, and the payment was obviously in the nature of goodwill. The ITO, therefore, disallowed the claim by treating it as capital expenditure. The AAC, however, agreed with the assessee that this was a different line of the assessee’s business, which required technical assistance, apart from observance of certain regulations stipulated by the principals, and allowed the assessee’s claim.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company had a collaboration agreement with 'GIC' which trained its personnel in the operation and maintenance of float glass plant and also in its manufacturing and marketing. The training was given by 'GIC' before the plant was set up by the assessee. The amount paid to 'GIC' for imparting training was claimed by the assessee in the relevant assessment year on the ground that since the invoice was received from 'GIC' during the previous year, liability had crystallized only during the previous year. The Assessing Officer held that since those expenses were prior to setting up of plant, they were capital expenditures and were to be capitalized. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products. During the year under consideration, the assessee company had acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by the assessee with the latter. The consideration for such transfer was stated as Rs. 18.92 crores which included a sum of Rs. 5.94 crores by way of non-compete fee which was limited for a period of 5 years. For the assessment year 2005-06, the assessee filed its return of income, wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay, non-allowable under section 37. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by the assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as the period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years. The Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by the assessee was capital in nature, as such it disallowed the claim. Further, while dealing with the cross-objection filed by the assessee, the Tribunal restored the alternate plea in respect of allowance of depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) to the file of the Assessing Officer for deciding it.

On appeal:

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business as a book binder and publisher. It entered into an agreement dated 15-11-1958, with ‘B’ under which it obtained the right to run the business of a publication concern for a consideration of a fixed sum of Rs. 5,000 per annum plus a sum equivalent to 10 per cent of the net profits of each year of business. During the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1962-63, the assessee paid a total sum of Rs. 15,497 to ‘B’ as per the terms of the agreement dated 15-11-1958, and claimed the said amount as a business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the claim, as in his opinion the amount in question constituted consideration for the purchase of the business and was, therefore, in the nature of capital expenditure. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the disallowance made by the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was an outright sale of the business by ‘B’ in favour of the assessee but that the payment of Rs. 15,497 was allowable as revenue expenditure, in view of the decision in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. 36/49 Holdings Ltd. [1943] 25 TC 173 (CA) and in Travancore Sugars and Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 62 ITR 556 (SC).

On reference:

During the relevant accounting year, the assessee company had paid certain amount to its Ex-Managing-Director as non-compete fee on his retirement from the services. That fee represented compensation for not joining any company or share any expertise with companies having same business for a period of three years. Since such a payment was made to Ex-Managing Director to restrict him to share his experience and expertise for a period of 3 years, so that there was no immediate threat to the interest of assessee's business, therefore, the same was business expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer held that such payment of non-compete fee would result into enduring benefits to the assessee. Accordingly, the same was treated as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such a payment was paid for a restriction of three years and therefore, there is no question of any enduring benefit coming to the assessee. Moreover, the said Ex-Managing Director expired before the said period of three years, thus, such a payment was nothing but revenue expenditure.

On appeal by the Revenue:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of development of minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc., including extraction of fluorspar. It held a mining lease on Survey No. 40 in a certain village. Another company MMC held a prospecting licence for extracting fluorspar from the adjacent Survey No. 30 and applied for a mining lease thereon and prepared a prospecting report also. Under section 11(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, MMC had a preferential right for obtaining such a lease, but the Government rejected its application whereupon it went to Court for redress and obtained interim orders restraining the Government from giving the said Survey No. 30 on lease to any other party. Meanwhile the assessee-corporation had also applied for a mining lease on the said Survey No. 30. It had spent considerable amount on erecting its beneficiation plant for fluorspar which could run for the desired number of years only if it could get raw material from Survey No. 40 as well as Survey No. 30. The assessee-corporation, therefore, with a view to expanding its business, avoiding competition on the adjacent land and getting the required raw material for the desired number of years, entered into an agreement with MMC whereby it paid a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs to MMC on latter agreeing to withdraw the pending legal proceedings and give up its claim to Survey No. 30 to clear the assessee's path for obtaining a lease thereon. The assessee claimed, the aforesaid payment of Rs. 3 lakhs as revenue expenditure in the assessment year 1970-71. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim, holding the expenditure to be of capital nature. The AAC upheld the ITO's order on the ground that the benefit derived from the payment was of an enduring nature. The Tribunal confirmed the AAC's order.

On reference:

The assessee-firm purchased the business of export of hides and skins carried on by one G as a sole proprietary concern. Under the terms of the purchase, the take over by the assessee-firm was of the business as a whole including goodwill, trade mark, import and export quota rights as well as trade outstandings and trade debts. Subsequent to the take over of the business, the assessee-firm had to settle claims of certain foreign buyers in respect of short supply of goods sold by the assessee's predecessor and made payments to them, which it claimed as a business outgoing. On appeal, the ITO and the AAC rejected the assessee's claim for deduction. On further appeal the Tribunal, however, held that the amount paid was an item of business expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred by the assessee for the purpose of its business, and that the expenditure was not of a capital nature.

On reference, the revenue argued that the payment was not admissible as expenditure as it was not a legal or commercial obligation of the assessee and that, in any case, it was of a capital nature.

The assessee paid certain amount for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division of 'N' Chemicals.

The Assessing Officer opined that the expenses were incurred to bring new assets into existence, resulting in the benefit of enduring nature. He, therefore, treated those expenses as capital in nature.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that payment in question was allowable as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee purchased a hotel which had remained closed due to labour problems. At the time of purchase, the assessee had to pay Rs. 6.31 lakhs as compensation to the employees who were retrenched by the earlier management, as per agreement with the representatives of the workmen. The assessee contended that as the liability had to be incurred in order to run the business, it should be allowed as revenue expenditure. Alternatively, it was contended that it should be allowed as a capital expenditure and depreciation should be allowed on it. The Assessing Officer treated it as a capital expenditure but did not allow depreciation in respect thereof. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the Assessing Officer's order holding that the expenditure was not part of the purchase consideration and the payment was not as per agreement between the transferor and the assessee. The Tribunal, however, was of the view that since the assessee could not have conducted the business unless the compensation was paid, it was capital expenditure incurred in connection with or incidental to the acquisition cost of the asset and allowed assessee's claim for depreciation.

On reference :

The assessee had set up two new two star hotels during the relevant assessment year. Certain expenses in the form of salaries, training and development of general managers, service engineers, etc,. were incurred by the assessee after the setting up of its business but before the date of commencement of business to enable smooth functioning of the activities post commencement of business to provide uninterrupted and better services to the guests in the hotel without any obstruction.

These expenses though treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the books of account, but for the purpose of income tax, the same were claimed as revenue expenditure in full in the year of incurrence.

The Assessing Officer disallowed said expenditure by treating the same as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition.

On revenue's appeal:

held.text:
•

As far as the question as to whether an expenditure could be a capital expenditure or revenue expenditure is concerned, the concept that the expenditure yielding an advantage of enduring nature would be only a capital expenditure, has been fine-tuned, that even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one of revenue account. [Para 14]

•

It is not denied by the revenue that 'U' was the chairman and managing director of some of the companies which got merged with the assessee-company. 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to the clientele and the products, including the pricing of the products. By a process of amalgamation, the assessee had acquired the business of the amalgamating companies. However, for the fruitful exercise of its business as a business proposition, the assessee thought it fit to enter into a non-compete agreement with a person who had the knowledge of the entire operations, so as to get the full yield of the amalgamated company's business. In that context, rightly, the assessee took a commercial decision to pay non-compete fee to 'U' and going by the decision of the Apex Court, that the payment was in respect of the performing of the business of the assessee, it was to be held that the expenditure is only on revenue account and not on capital account. In the circumstances, the order of the Tribunal was set aside. [Para 19]

The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

If the expenditure relates to the domain of running the business concern, then, ordinarily, it would be revenue expenditure. If, on the other hand, the expenditure is made to acquire a certain business to free the business of the assessee from competition, then the expenditure is one of a capital nature. The ultimate conclusion would depend on the character of the expenditure.

In instant case, the assessee-company acquired the unexpired permits and thereby got rid of competition from private operators who were on the field prior to the acquisition. The investment was clearly one of a capital nature.

That being the conclusion, the amount was rightly not allowed as a deduction.

Note : The case was decided against assessee.

The amount in question was paid only to those members whose trucks were not booked. But for this payment, they would have otherwise competed in the business with the assessee. The object of the payment was to eliminate those competitors and to carry on the business unfettered by competition. The assessee made the payment to acquire this right of these persons. This led to enhance the value of its existing assets to make them more profit-yielding. The expense, therefore, could not be a revenue expense but was of a capital nature. The Tribunal was therefore right, in holding that amount so paid was not a permissible deduction for the purpose of income-tax.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

It could not be gainsaid that in agreeing on the price at which the business was taken over by the assessee from the vendor all the liabilities as well as the assets of the firm had been taken into account. One of the liabilities obviously was the liability towards bonus for the period preceding the date of the takeover. It was known to the assessee that as consideration for the takeover, it would have to incur a liability to the full extent finally determined as the amount payable as bonus for the period preceding the takeover. The amount, thus, spent in payment of bonus for that period was not an amount expended by the assessee to carry on, and earn the profits or gains of the business which it took over, but an amount expended to obtain the business which it purchased. That was not an expenditure, which partook the character of revenue, but it was clearly a capital expenditure. Therefore, the balance bonus paid during the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1975-76 was not a revenue expenditure.

It was not possible for G’s group to recognise the past services of R as already both the groups were having serious disputes and the matter was pending before the High Court. G’s group had removed R from his position in the assessee-company and Board of Directors and restrained R from operating bank accounts of four companies of this group and from attending day-to-day work. No specific amount had been earmarked for alleged past services. Further R being MD of the assessee must have been getting salaries for the services rendered by him in the past and question of any amount being assigned for such past services did not arise. There was no scope for recognising the past services of R and to allocate any amount out of the impugned amount given to R.

The assessee-company had not brought anything on record to show that R acquired special expertise or experience in the bus-body building activities. It was not the case of the assessee that R had got any special training in India or abroad in the bus-body building operation or he himself had made any research or was personally involved in such activities. If these were the facts, then this was not a ground for giving the amount to R. The assessee was running in losses and even if some salary was being given to R, a sum of Rs. 1.29 crores shall not be in any manner near to the amounts R would have earned as profit from company or would have got emoluments to that extent. What was the criterion of assessee-company to arrive at this figure of Rs. 1.29 crores was not explained.

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Admittedly, the assessee was participating in an auction to obtain the privilege of vending liquor. The question was whether elimination of a rival from competing with the auction will be opposed to public policy. This question cannot be considered in isolation de hors the nature of the trade, privilege or the right with respect to which the auction is held. If the subject-matter involved is a trade which could be normally considered as a lawful trade and the individual has a fundamental right to carry on such a trade, eliminating a rival trader from operating in the same field will be incidental to the exercise of that fundamental right. On the other hand, if the subject-matter is loosely referred to as trade or business but actually is not recognised as trade or business in respect of which no fundamental right exists and only the State has the exclusive privilege to indulging in such a trade or business, different considerations should prevail. In the latter case, the State may engage in this trade of a pernicious character only because it is inevitable to do so having regard to the public interest such as the absolute need to raise revenue for the State which in turn is utilised for the public welfare. It may also be a case where the State engages itself in such a business or trade to minimise the public harm, which otherwise would result to the public, if the trade or business is carried on by the citizens at large.

It is now quite firmly established that none has a fundamental right to carry on the trade in vending liquor. The right given to trade in this regard is actually a privilege conferred by the State and normally these privileges are conferred by auctioning the right to vend, in the case of arrack.

What the bidder pays to the State is not only towards the liquor to be obtained but it would include normally the price for the privilege which he obtains by being the successful bidder in the auction.

It is clear, therefore, that there should be a fair auction of the right to vend liquor and the fairness should be decided not only with reference to the competing bidders but also with reference to public interest. The public revenue is affected either way as a result of the auction. Any attempt made which has a bearing on the ultimate result of the auction and the net revenue that will be collected by the State will be an attempt on public interest. It is of utmost importance that there should be as many bidders as possible in such an auction, so that maximum revenue could be obtained by the State. Purchasing of rival bidders, therefore, on the face of it, will be harmful to public interest and the very object of conducting the auction gets defeated or diluted when intending bidders are sought to be kept away by one of the bidders.

In the instant case, the assessee had purchased a rival bidder so that he could not come forward to participate in the auction. This was contrary to public interest as well as public welfare and, therefore, opposed to public policy. The payment made which, on the face of it was contrary to public policy could not be recognized as a valid payment for the purpose of the Act. Whatever is expended to obtain an asset used in a trade or business is a capital expenditure; however, if the expenditure is incurred in the course of the business to earn the current income, prima facie it may be a revenue expenditure.

The test for determining whether an expenditure is capital or revenue, varies depending upon the nature of the business acquired. When the period of the business and the duration during which the right to carry on the trade is itself limited, the elimination of a rival from competing, while obtaining the right to trade has nothing to do with the expenditure incurred in the course of carrying on the trade. The expenditure here is incurred at the threshold to obtain the right to vend liquor. It was in the nature of investment made to set up the business and, therefore, should be treated as a capital investment. The expenditure incurred in the instant case was incurred once and for all with a view to bring into existence the asset or the advantage of obtaining the privilege to vend liquor for one year. The entire business itself was of one year's duration. The expenditure incurred to obtain this right or privilege cannot be just treated as expenditure incurred only for one year because the very business asset had a life of one year only. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure could not be accepted.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the Revenue.

Coming to the nature of expenditure in question, it can be seen from the various tests laid down in the earlier decided cases that broadly the basic tests to determine the nature of an expenditure remain the same even in the context of a modern situation and those tests include the test of initial outlay of the business, the aim and object of the expenditure, enduring benefit test and the test of fixed and circulating capital. [Para 122] Applying the aforementioned tests to the facts of the instant case, it may be stated that the so-called 'non-compete agreement' was part & parcel of the entire transaction. The assessee had acquired a business concern in India with its outlay (more particularly described elsewhere in this order) and the entire transaction was outlined in the MoU dated 4-11-1996. The aggregate amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was determined as the total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets referred to in article 1 and the Ballabgarh land and building referred to in article 2. The purchase price itself stated that the amount of Rs. 52.5 crores was to be paid as total purchase price for the Compressor Division's assets and Ballabgarh land and building. [Para 123]

It can be seen that non-compete agreement was made Appendix 'M' to the agreement dated 2-11-1997 and was, thus, part and parcel of the main agreement, the signing and execution whereof was a condition precedent. [Para 124.1]

It could be mentioned here that the total purchase price of Rs. 52.5 crores envisaged in MoU vide clause 3 included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores which was to be paid for non-compete agreement. The other sum of Rs. 49.85 crores was to be paid in respect of various assets. If these two sums were aggregated, then the total amount would come to Rs. 52.5 crores which was the agreed purchase price. The assessee-company was incorporated for the purpose of effectuating the transactions agreed in the MoU. The purpose of the assessee-company for which it was incorporated was that 'Tecumseh USA', being a leading global compressor manufacturer, was interested in purchasing compressor related operations of Whirlpool India for the Indian compressor market. Thus, the very intention and purpose was to establish business in India by taking over the compressor and related operations of Whirlpool India in India. The non-compete agreement was part and parcel of the whole transaction and could not be treated to be a separate transaction. [Para 125]

The case of the assessee would fall under the test which describes that if the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for the expansion of the business or a substantial replacement of the equipment, then it would fall under the capital expenditure. It was not an expenditure incurred while the business was being carried on. Though it had been the contention of the assessee that non-compete agreement was executed subsequent to the date of main agreement, yet such contention of the assessee could not be accepted as in the main agreement itself the non-compete agreement was appended as 'M' without which the transaction was not complete, as by including the amount paid for non-compete agreement the purchase price as stated in MoU could be arrived at. [Para 126]

The incurring of expenditure also brought an enduring benefit to the assessee if the same was examined from the proposition of law laid down in the case of Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC) wherein their Lordships have considered the period of five years as providing an enduring advantage to the assessee irrespective of the fact that the payment was to be made annually. [Para 127]

It is well-settled that expenditure incurred on warding off competition in the business even to a rival dealer will constitute capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure it is not necessary that non-compete fee be paid to create monopoly rights. [Para 129]

In view of aforesaid, it was to be held that the expenditure of Rs. 2.65 crores claimed by the assessee in pursuance of non-compete agreement dated 10-7-1997 was capital expenditure, the deduction of which could not be granted to the assessee as revenue expenditure. [Para 131]

EDITOR'S NOTE

Following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Punjab State Industrial Development Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT[1997] 225 ITR 792 / 93 Taxman 5, it was to be held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee on increasing its authorized share capital was a capital expenditure and could not be allowed as deduction.

Under section 37(1) any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession is allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", provided it is not in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee. The line that divides revenue expenditure from capital expenditure is often very thin and hazy. None of the tests evolved from time to time determine what is attributable to capital and what to revenue is either exhaustive or of universal application. Each case depends on its own facts. To decide, therefore, on which side of the line the expenditure falls, it is necessary to look at the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure and the nature of the right acquired. If it is incurred by the assessee for the purpose of creating, curing or competing his title to capital, it must be regarded as capital expenditure. But, if it is for the purpose of protecting his business, it would be considered as revenue expenditure. Moreover, it is the true nature of the expenditure that is relevant and not the description given to it by the assessee in his books of account or other documents.

In the instant case, the said payment was required to be made by the assessee for acquisition of the interest of his brother. In the partnership to enable him to become the sole owner of the business hitherto run in partnership with him. It was not a payment made for the purpose of protecting the business, as contended by the assessee and described in the cash book of the assessee. Such payment could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of running the business. In truth and substance, it was in the nature of capital expenditure, because the real purpose of this payment was to acquire the interest of his brother in the business of the said firm, which was a profit-yielding asset and was, therefore, in the nature of capital expenditure which was not allowable as deduction under section 37(1).

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature. This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

The problem of deciding whether any given item of business expenditure is capital or revenue would depend for its solution on a consideration of and depends upon a multitude of factual and other circumstances. As an elementary proposition it may be said that where a business is acquired or where there is a substantial addition to the capital equipment of a business or where there is an increase in the capital structure of an existing business, then the outgoing in all these cases, must be regarded as capital outlay and not as revenue expenditure. On the other side, again as an elementary proposition, it may be said that all current or day to day or running expenses in a business must be regarded as items of revenue expenditure.

In the instant case there was not a direct item of expenditure connected with any such capital item such as acquisition of a capital asset or its expansion. The item of expenditure in question was no doubt connected with the amalgamation of the two business concerns, but was directly incurred in meeting legal charges and court expenses.

In such a situation, the expenses incurred by the assessee in connection with amalgamation of another company with it, should be allowed as revenue expenditure.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

The non-competition fee of Rs. 3.25 crores paid by the assessee was allowable as revenue expenditure of the business of the assessee. The non-competition agreement entered into by the assessee with KHPL was to prevent R. Raju from establishing a power plant in Andhra Pradesh for a period of three years. The amount was paid, and a non-competition agreement was entered into, is not in dispute. The law declared by the judgment of the Supreme Court, and the Delhi High Court, is that it is only if the non-competition agreement is of a permanent or an enduring nature can it be said to be a capital expenditure. The agreement prevented R. Raju from establishing a power plant only for a period of three years from the date of the agreement. The restrictive covenant was neither permanent nor was the advantage derived by the assessee therefrom of an enduring nature. The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in holding that the assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making payment of a non-competition fee; and it merely eliminated competition in its business for a while. [Para 10]

The appeal fails and is, accordingly, dismissed. [Para 12]

The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

But, it could not be said that the expenditure should be treated as capital expenditure only for the reason that the assessee had not obtained an enduring benefit. Both the agreements and payments were made contemporaneously, as the assessee had acquired the brand right of the new product in its entirety and the non-compete clause was separately deduced in another agreement. Therefore, the non-compete agreement was, in fact, a part and parcel of the main contract of acquiring the brand right. The agreement whereby the assessee acquired the brand right for Rs. 85 lakhs and the non-compete agreement executed after paying Rs. 40 lakhs, both were to be considered and understood in unison. The two agreements were not representing two different events. The subject-matter of both the agreements was one and the same and for the purpose of declaring that the assessee had acquired the brand right of the product known as Lacto Calamine. When both the agreements were taken together, it was clear that payment of Rs. 40 lakhs was nothing but a part of the consideration for acquiring the brand right of the product. Instead of executing a single agreement for the entire amount of Rs. 125 lakhs, the assessee had executed two agreements for Rs. 85 lakhs and Rs. 40 lakhs, qualifying the latter amount as paid for non-compete agreement. The reason for splitting up the agreement was best known to the assessee. As matter of fact, it was clear that by executing both the agreements the assessee had transacted only one business, i.e., the business of acquiring exclusive brand name of the product ‘Lacto Calamine’. [Para 24]

A perusal of the agreement clearly points to the fact that while the consideration of Rs.1.30 crores was towards the net value of assets, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is "for obligations and covenants". [Para 13]

The clauses of the agreement go to show that the amount of Rs.70 lakhs is not merely payment towards the non-compete clause but also towards various other obligations which were imposed upon SML and had a direct bearing on the final execution and implementation of the agreement. To argue that the entire consideration was towards the non-compete fee would, therefore, be an incorrect statement, inasmuch as the clauses of the agreement do not reflect so. The emphasis in the agreement is towards the takeover of the assets of SML, and it was to ensure that the agreement bears fruition that the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs has been apportioned for various obligations and covenants imposed on SML. [Para 14]

Under these circumstances, the question that is to be decided is whether the expenditure of Rs.70 lakhs incurred is of capital or revenue nature. The consideration of Rs.70 lakhs was clearly towards ensuring that there will be no impediment in the smooth transfer of SML's factory to the assessee. It should be complete and final. From the facts placed before the Court, there really did not appear to be any serious threat whatsoever in order for the assessee to pay the non-compete fee to SML which had not even commenced its manufacturing. From the nature of the transaction, it is clear that the acquisition of SML's unit was, for expansion purposes. It was to expand and increase production by acquiring a new undertaking. The entire business with capital assets was acquired. The payment was bifurcated into two parts, Rs. 130 lakhs towards net assets and Rs.70 lakhs for other obligations and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about the agreement as also all the intellectual property and other data and information. The said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards the non-compete obligation. [Para 15]

Even the non-compete obligations in clause 11 appear to be illusory in nature and restricted to 'constant velocity joints or any other competitive products'. Clearly, the same is of limited nature and there was also no obligation of non-compete imposed upon the promoter directors of SML. In fact, as stated during the course of arguments, the managing director of SML became the corporate director of the assessee. Thus, the non-compete clause and the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs are not completely and exclusively inter-linked. The payment of Rs.70 lakhs, which is a substantial sum, i.e., more than half of the consideration paid for the net assets of the unit itself, was for a multitude of obligations and covenants which were fastened upon SML and not only towards the non-compete obligations. [Para 16]

It is clear that the consideration of Rs. 70 lakhs was not expressly towards the non-compete obligation, but towards smoothening the process of acquisition of the asset, i.e., the unit of SML in Madras as approvals that were required from the financial institutions, income tax authorities and other governmental authorities were towards the finalisation and closure of the acquisition process. Other covenants and obligations imposed upon SML, i.e., warranties, confidentiality, etc., added value to the asset being acquired. There is no doubt that in the facts of the present case, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is a capital expenditure and hence the question of law is answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 18]

It is now well settled that the character of expenditure will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case not by the application of rigid tests, but by deriving support from many aspects of the whole lot of circumstances and the ultimate answer would depend upon a commonsense appreciation of the guiding features.

In the instant case, the assessee had established a good reputation and market for writing inks by the manufacture and sale of ink, under the brand name 'quink'. In the agreement, there was a recognition of the formation and establishment of the partnership by A for the manufacture and sale of writing inks, similar to those made and sold by the assessee and it being a powerful potential competitor.

The desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership was also clearly spelt out from the terms of the agreement. The negotiated settlement under the terms and conditions set out in the agreement, was clearly relatable to the desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership backed by the experience and expertise of the ex-managing director, whose wife and daughters were the partners in the same line of business activity as that of the assessee. Undoubtedly, the activity of the partnership in setting up a competitive business was harmful to the assessee and the agreement was the outcome of the prospect of power competition from the partnership and a desire on the part of the assessee to protect itself against that disadvantage. Further, the departure of A from the assessee-company and the prospect of his making available his experience and expertise in the manufacture and marketing of ink to his wife and daughters, who were the partners of the firm, would have rendered the goodwill of the assessee vulnerable, as the assessee, when it commanded the benefit of the services of A, was in an advantageous position. There was, thus, a positive detriment to the assessee due to the competition from the partnership and against such damaging competition, the assessee obtained the benefit of a restrictive covenant against such powerful competition. That resulted in the assessee buying of potential competition, which was a positive detriment owing to such competition, and had also enabled the assessee not only to safeguard its goodwill, but also to enhance it. The payment of Rs. 1,00,000 by the assessee to the partnership was to secure advantages resulting in the removal from the arena of a possible competition and securing the elimination of a risk or detriment to the assessee due to competition. Though under the terms of the agreement, the benefit of the restrictive covenant was to enure only for a period of five years, from the facts stated in the order of the Tribunal and also the terms of the dissolution deed, it was seen that the partnership, which was a potential competitor, had also vanished and A had also left the shores of India. That would clearly establish that what the assessee had paid for was of permanent or enduring quality, in the sense that the competition had been totally eliminated and a protection had been acquired for the business of the assessee as a whole. In other words, the amount paid by the assessee was no part of the working or operational expenses of the assessee, but its aim and object was acquisition of an advantage of enduring nature, viz., freedom from competition from the partnership for the rest of the period of the business activities of the assessee.

Therefore, the consideration paid in terms of agreement was an expenditure of capital nature.

In order to determine the nature of expenditure, one has to examine the facts of the each case independently. No hard and fast rule can be laid down to determine the nature of expenditure. If an assessee acquires any capital asset or enduring benefit for a longer period, the expenditure may be called to be a ‘capital expenditure’. In the instant case, the assessee had purchased the shipping business from the vendor against a lumpsum consideration of Rs. 43,47,000 comprising of cost of goodwill of Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 38,47,000 for non-competition covenant fees for a period of 5 years. From a perusal of the non-competition clause contained in the agreement, it was clear that in lieu of receipt of a non-competition fees, the vendor was restrained from doing similar type of business in any capacity for a period of 5 years within India. This condition would not apply to a business carried on by the vendor outside the India. Period of condition was fixed up to 5 years and, thereafter, the vendor was at liberty to enter into similar type of business activity. Further from the other provisions of the agreement, it was not borne out that the vendor was permanently restrained from doing the shipping business in future. Meaning thereby, it was a temporary arrangement made with the vendor in order to settle down its new business of shipping. It has been repeatedly held by the Apex Court and various High Courts that an expenditure incurred to avoid competition, if dictated by business necessity and commercial exigencies, would be allowable as a revenue expenditure as the benefit derived out of it is directly related to the enhancement of profitability of business. In the instant case, by avoiding a main competition from the vendor, the assessee had derived the benefits out of it to enhance its profitability only and it was not a case that the competition was eliminated permanently or for a longer period. Moreover, it was not a case of the revenue that the vendor was only competitor in this line of business. There were other business constituents who were engaged in the similar type of business and a threat of competition was also there to be faced by the assessee from those business constituents. This covenant was executed only for a period of 5 years and that too only for Indian territory. If the assessee intended to do its business outside Indian territory, it had to face the competition from the vendor also. Meaning thereby, this covenant was not executed for a permanent elimination of the competition from the seller. Therefore, the benefit was derived by the assessee for a limited period of 5 years and that too only in Indian territory. Therefore, the non-competition covenant fees paid by the assessee to the vendor could not be treated as capital expenditure. The covenant was executed on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down the assessee in a new acquired business of shipping and the benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability. As such, the expenditure incurred by the assessee was a revenue expenditure and the same was to be allowed as a business expenditure. [Para 23]

Further, since the assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, this expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and the corresponding expenditure be allowed in every year. Therefore, the impugned order was to be set aside and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to allow the total expenditure over a period of 5 years in which the non-competition covenant fees remained in force. [Para 24]

Where the assessee had not furnished any details in respect of sundry expenses either before the lower authorities or before the Tribunal, the lower authorities were justified in disallowing 10 per cent of sundry expenses.

In the instant case the assessee had paid non-compete fee to its Ex-Managing Director for restrciting him to share his expertise or to join any other company in a similar line of business of chemicals for a period of three years on certain consideration. Since the agreement for restrictive covenant was only for the period of three years to ward off a potential threat or completion, it was held that there could be no question of enduring benefit for a long period. [Para 18]

However, such a payment is also to be seen from the context of commercial and business expediency. If the outgoing expenditure is so inextricably linked or related to carrying on or conduct of the business, that is, it can be regarded as integral part of the profit earning process and not for any acquisition of asset or a right of permanent character and incurring of the expenditure is a condition for carrying on the business, then such an expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure. In the instant case the agreement for payment of non-compete fee was only to protect the existing business for a temporary period to ward off completion so that assessee could get stabilizing period without its long serving MD. Here no new assets of any enduirng benefit had arisen to the assessee on such payment. If the advantage was not for longer period and not enduring in nature, then such a payment of non-compete fee was nothing but business expenditure which was on revenue account. On similar facts and circumstances, the Delhi High Court also in the case of Eicher Ltd. (supra), after discussing various case laws came to the conclusion that payment of non-compete fee for eliminating competition in the two wheeler business cannot be held that assessee has acquired capital asset of enduring nature. Thus on these facts, it was held that such a payment of non-compete fee was allowable as a revenue expenditure and the order of Commissioner (Appeals) on this score was confirmed. Revenue's ground was thus dismissed. [Para 19]

In the instant case, insofar as payment for getting domestic customer database is concerned, it is clear that, assessee has only got right to use that database, the company which has provided such database is not precluded from using such database. Hence the expenditure incurred is for the use of database and not for acquisitions of such database. There is no question of acquisition of any assets when the access is made and the payment is made for the same. The said payment cannot (sic -can) be treated as revenue expenditure. There is no infirmity or irregularity in the said finding of the Tribunal. [Para 12]

In respect of payment made towards transfer of human skill is concerned, it has been made towards the expenses incurred for training and on recruitment. Such expenses were under revenue field, and therefore the payments have been made to save such revenue expenses as per the agreement. TATA IBM has spent lot of money to give training to those employees who were transferred to the assessee-company. They are trained in the field of software. They have opted for employment with assessee-company and for their past services in TATA IBM, expenditure has been incurred. Such expenditure cannot be termed as expenditure laid for carrying on the business.

The advantages obtained by TATA IBM can be treated as services rendered by those employees to TATA IBM. The concept of payment made once and for all and of the enduring benefit respond to the changing economic realities of business and hence the expenditure incurred on processing domestic customer database and transfer of human skill is a revenue expenditure, though the benefit may be of enduring in nature. Hence, the said expenditure has to be treated as revenue expenditure. The order passed by the Assessing Officer to disallow said expenditure is erroneous in law. [Para 13]

In the result, the revenue's appeal is dismissed.
