Introduction

1.Direct tax laws, by their very nature, cannot remain static for long. These have to change to cater to various considerations arising consequent to change in policies, political philosophies, needs of the society, changing concepts in law, economic theories and practices, accounting principles, international relations, acts of God, need for revenue and similar other such situations. In fact, the history of federal taxes mirrors the history of a nation and by going through details concerning tax changes, one can feel the pulse of a country's development and other happenings.

Accounting concepts and practices have important bearing on taxation of incomes though accounting practices followed by taxpayers have been held to be not finally decisive in tax matters - Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v . SA.L. Narayan Row, CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 (SC) and CIT v. Cocanada Radhaswami Bank Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 306 (SC). In the matter of expenditure, accounting principles imply that all expenditure that is incurred for generating incomes it should be deducted for finding out what has been the net gain or loss. But in determining taxable incomes or losses, all expenses incurred are not deductible. Hence, in many situations, incomes, profits or losses for tax purposes are different from the actual results.

Capital v. Revenue

2. A very common controversy that arises in tax proceedings relates to concepts concerning 'capital' and 'revenue'. The disputes generally relate to whether particular receipts or expenditure are of capital or revenue nature. Normally, expenses of a capital nature are not allowed as deduction for computing taxable income. But there are provisions where expenditures which, prima facie, appear to be of a capital nature are, by express provisions in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act') either allowed as deduction in one year, or such expenditure is phased out (amortised) over a number of years. Some instances, where statute permits deduction of capital expenditure either in one stroke or over a few years, are considered below:

(i)Where the assessee incurs any expenditure of a capital nature on scientific research related to his business, the whole of such expenditure (excluding expenditure on acquisition of land) incurred in any previous year is allowable as deduction in that previous year - Section 35(1)(iv).

(ii)Capital expenditure on acquisition of patent rights or copy rights are allowable as business expenditure in equal instalments over a period of 14 years or over the unexpired life of the patent right or copy right – Section 35A.

(iii) Lump sum consideration paid for acquiring know-how for the purpose of business is allowed as deduction by spreading it equally over 6 years -Section 35AB.

(iv)Certain preliminary expenses incurred by an Indian company or resident non-corporate assessee are permitted to be amortised over a period of 10 years - Section 35D.

(v)An expenditure of a capital nature incurred by a corporate assessee for promoting family planning is allowable as a deduction in a period of 5 years - Section 36(1)(ix) .

Thus, the expression 'capital expenditure' is elastic in application and has to be construed in a business sense. Simply because payment has been made in lump sum, it cannot be inferred that the expenditure is of a capital nature. A lump sum payment can be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual revenue payments and a recurring periodic payment may be capital expenditure when it represents the payment by instalments of a capital nature -I.R. v. Ramsay 20 TC 79.

However, there is no authority to proposition raised hereinbelow. There is a possibility to raise an argument that the license fee paid by the assessee was in the nature of royalty for the right to use the software. The recent ruling of the Karnataka High Court in CIT v. Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd.9 supports the same but the Delhi High Court has taken a different view in the case of DIT v. Ericsson A.B.10 . The license fee paid for use of the copyright or a software can be contended to be royalty, therefore, same may be of capital in nature, as royalty per se may constitute a right acquired by a person to use someone else's property. The Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) of the Act defines royalty as 'for the purposes of this clause, "royalty" means consideration (including any lump sum consideration but excluding any consideration which would be the income of the recipient chargeable under the head "Capital gains") for—

'(v) the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of any copyright, literary, artistic or scientific work including films or video tapes for use in connection with television or tapes for use in connection with radio broadcasting, but not including consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films ;'

Only support can be drawn from the judgment of the Supreme Court in Jonas Woodhead & Sons Ltd. v. CIT 11 where for composite payment for supply of technical know-how and services for setting-up plant and manufacture of products, made to a non-resident, it was held that the entire payment made could not be held to be revenue expenditure, merely because the payment was required to be made at a certain percentage of the gross turnover of the products as royalty. The disallowance of 25 per cent of the sum paid as royalty by the appellant to the English company as capital expenditure was not allowable as a revenue expenditure. This decision might have brought some exchequer to the Revenue.

On the other hand, in the decision of the Delhi High Court in CIT v. G4S Securities System (India)( P.) Ltd.12 it was held that where the payment of royalty was to be made on year-to-year basis on the net sales of the assessee, at no point of time was the assessee entitled to become the exclusive owner of the know-how and the trademark. Hence, the expenditure incurred by the assessee as royalty was revenue expenditure and was deductible under section 37(1) of the Act. The view taken by the Delhi High Court is not in consonance with that of the Supreme Court. However, the decision of the Supreme Court was on the basis that supply of technical know-how and services for setting-up plant and manufacture of products had resulted in an enduring benefit to the assessee. The Supreme Court had not considered its earlier view taken in Ciba of India Ltd.13 wherein it was held that in view of the rapid technological obsolescence, technical know-how has a short life and that it should ordinarily be revenue expenditure as held for industries like manufacture of pharmaceuticals.

Keeping in view the decision of the Supreme Court in Jonas Woodhead & Sons Ltd. (supra) it might have been possible to argue that the license fee paid by Asahi India Safety Glass Ltd. (supra) was in nature of royalty resulting in an enduring benefit, but relying on the decision of Ciba of India Ltd. ( supra) it may not be correct to contend the same. The view taken in Ciba of India Ltd. ( supra) has been followed by the other High Courts14.

Conclusion

5. The Act is very clear as to which payments have to be classified as one on account of capital or revenue expenditure with respect to expenditure incurred for computer software. The test of an enduring benefit is not appropriate for the purpose of classifying the nature of the expenditure. In order to claim a particular item of expenditure which is deductible under section 37 of the Act the following condition should be satisfied :

(i) The expenditure should not be of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 of the Act;

(ii) It should have been incurred in that accounting year;

(iii) It should be in respect of a business which was carried on by the assessee and the profits of which are to be computed and assessed and should be incurred after setting-up of the business;

(iv) It should not be in the nature of personal expenses of the assessee;

(v) It should have been laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of such business; and

(vi) It should not be in the nature of a capital expenditure.

Accounting practices 12.1 General- Accounting practices are those which are followed as a matter of convention in contrast to standards which have been prescribed and are mandatory. A few of such items like treatment of deferred revenue expenditure, chit loss, and interest received during construction period are dealt with below :

12.2 Deferred revenue expenditure - Items like capital issue expenditure, preliminary expenses, technical know-how fee, etc., are treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the accounts, considering that they result in enduring benefit. However, under the Act, there is no concept of deferred revenue expenditure except when specially provided for like under sections 35A, 35AB, 35D, 35E, etc. Hence, expenditure of revenue nature, though treated as deferred revenue in accounts, should be claimed as a deduction for income-tax purposes entirely in the year in which the expenditure is actually incurred. Examples of such items are repairs and maintenance of ocean-going vessels like ships and dredgers; technical know-how fee; huge publicity campaign expenses, etc. Deductibility of know-how as a revenue expenditure and its capitalisation as plant and machinery have generated a lot of controversy. The leading authority for the proposition that technical know-how in the form of designs, drawings, etc., constitutes plant and is entitled to depreciation is the case of Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 86 . In this judgment, the Supreme Court upheld the assessee's claim for depreciation on expenditure capitalised as plant and there was no occasion to examine whether such expenditure constituted revenue or capital expenditure. The same, therefore, cannot be considered an authority for the proposition that technical know-how constitutes capital expenditure. In the following cases, lump sum/annual payments made for technical know-how even resulting in enduring benefit for periods ranging from five to ten years were held to be revenue in nature – CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 (SC), Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC), CIT v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. (P.) Ltd. [1980] 123 ITR 538 (Bom.), Praga Tools Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 123 ITR 773 (AP)(FB), Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 207 ITR 1017 (Bom.), etc. There are many cases in which this proposition was upheld and it was held that in these days of fast changing world technology, the frontiers of scientific and technical knowledge shift rapidly, the state of the art technology of modern times can neither be deemed to be permanent, nor of an enduring nature, so as to satisfy the enduring asset test. Thus, even though technical know-how acquired for improvement of technology is considered deferred revenue expenditure in accounts on the ground that the benefit accrues over a period of time, it is to be noted that under the Act, there being no provision for such concept, it has to be claimed as revenue expenditure in the year of incurring itself.

The other important issue in the context of deferred revenue expenditure is, again related to know-how, deductible under section 35AB, i.e., whether the said section applies only to capital expenditure or even to revenue expenditure. The popular opinion in this regard is that it applies to only capital expenditure, as it is an enabling section and not a disabling one and, hence, it does not cover revenue expenditure which, as it is, is allowable under section 37. Reference may be made to a recent decision in Wellman Incandescent India Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [1995] 55 ITD 338 (Cal.) upholding this contention. Yet another important issue to be considered is that technical know-how acquired for expansion of existing business by way of setting up a new project is allowable under section 35AB over a numbers of years from the income of existing business, though the new project is not commissioned and though such amount is treated as capital in the books, as discussed above. In these days of rapid and fast technology upgradation, such expenditure has to be carefully analysed and considered appropriately both in accounts and for tax purposes as between capital, revenue or combination of both. As is the case with the allowability of any expenditure under the Act, it is imperative that the deduction in this regard should also be claimed in the proper year based on express provisions and judicial precedents.

Intersection of Business and Tax Worlds

Let us now look at how the tax and business worlds interact in relation to TP.

One can say from above discussions that both these worlds seem aligned to the arm's length principle. As seen in the example of the steel and car assembly businesses, the Business World would prefer independent pricing. The Tax World clearly prefers ALP in relation to TP. So, the basic rationale/ logic is the same in both these worlds. Further, the Tax World talks of a functional, asset and risk analysis before profiling a particular entity/ transaction and then comparing it with other independent entities/ transactions. The OECD TP Guidelines also specify that the remuneration for a transaction must be commensurate to the activities involved. The Business World talks of pricing and other processes based on whether the unit is a revenue, cost, investment or profit center. They are again talking of similar rationales. In fact, in many jurisdictions, the corporate law, i.e., not pertaining to income tax, requires companies to prove to regulators that controlled transactions were undertaken at arm's length. This governance mechanism helps protect the interests of minority shareholders.

While at a broad and general level, both the business and tax worlds are talking of the same logics for TP, it is possible that sometimes either tax or business requirements take precedence while deciding on TP issues. Tax regulations do not like that taxation is the primary rationale behind a particular arrangement. Similarly, business decisions must not be oblivious to tax implications. With increased and more robust TP compliance frameworks, tech-savvy tax authorities, and greater experience and knowledge, there is an increased need for business arrangements to be aligned with tax principles of TP.

Conclusion

The tax and business worlds of TP are not the same though they talk of the same concepts and logics. As tax regulations and scrutiny are getting sophisticated and business models are also becoming more dynamic and complicated, it is important that business decisions related to TP are taken in cognizance of tax implications. That business decisions are taken across the globe for MNEs, and tax functions are generally centralized and considered to be administrative, creates a challenge that every MNE must consider based on their facts and circumstances.

7. The Supreme Court in its recent ruling in Madras Auto Service (P.) Ltd. [1998] 233 ITR 468, has considered the issue from a practical standpoint. Often companies need to have their employees undergo specific trainings in order to fulfil the requirements of or in order to upskill them to fulfil a revenue contract with a customer. This may be required as a specific requirement of the customer or in order to skill the employees to execute the customer contract.

The accounting of such training costs can be debatable and often companies have treated specific training costs as a part of the contract cost.

Under Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 2015, Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers sets forth the following guidance for contract fulfilment costs:

95 If the costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer are not within the scope of another Standard (for example, Ind AS 2, Inventories, Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment or Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets), an entity shall recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract only if those costs meet all of the following criteria:

(a)

the costs relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that the entity can specifically identify (for example, costs relating to services to be provided under renewal of an existing contract or costs of designing an asset to be transferred under a specific contract that has not yet been approved);

(b)

the costs generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying (or in continuing to satisfy) performance obligations in the future;

and

(c)

the costs are expected to be recovered.

96 For costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer that are within the scope of another Standard, an entity shall account for those costs in accordance with those other Standards.

97 Costs that relate directly to a contract (or a specific anticipated contract) include any of the following:

(a)

direct labour (for example, salaries and wages of employees who provide the promised services directly to the customer);

(b)

direct materials (for example, supplies used in providing the promised services to a customer);

(c)

allocations of costs that relate directly to the contract or to contract activities (for example, costs of contract management and supervision, insurance and depreciation of tools and equipment used in fulfilling the contract);

(d)

costs that are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract; and

(e)

other costs that are incurred only because an entity entered into the contract (for example, payments to subcontractors).

98 An entity shall recognise the following costs as expenses when incurred:

(a)

general and administrative costs (unless those costs are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract, in which case an entity shall evaluate those costs in accordance with paragraph 97);

(b)

costs of wasted materials, labour or other resources to fulfil the contract that were not reflected in the price of the contract;

(c)

costs that relate to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations) in the contract (ie costs that relate to past performance);

and

(d)

costs for which an entity cannot distinguish whether the costs relate to unsatisfied performance obligations or to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations).

Therefore, based on the above guidance, if an entity incurs costs for training its staff specifically in order to execute a revenue contract with customers or as a requirement of the customer contracts, the cost may fit into a contract fulfilment cost. This is because, the training costs would relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that can be specifically identified and would generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying performance obligations towards the customers in the future.

However, the conflict arises in Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets, which states as follows:

5 This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (eg a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, ie the knowledge embodied in it.

Ind AS 38 acknowledges that an entity usually has insufficient control over the future economic benefits arising from an assembled workforce (i.e. a team of skilled workers, or specific management or technical talent) or from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset.

Therefore, this guidance would require specific training costs to be recognised as expense as incurred.

A question, therefore, arises as to whether such training costs can be capitalised under Ind AS 115 since they would fulfil the definition of fulfilment costs.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

CBDT's Error 10. The CBDT's Circular No. 599 dated April 24, 1991 is of course right in saying that broken period interest is not taxable. But the reason given is wrong. It says that interest paid as part of the purchase price is a revenue item and this should be set off against the interest received. It is here that the CBDT has fallen foul of the Supreme Court. The interest paid along with the purchase price is capital expenditure as rightly held by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra). The real reason why the broken period interest is not taxable, as canvassed in this article, is that when interest is received, the portion relating to the broken period, is actually a recovery of cost and must, therefore, be set off against the purchase price. To take a concrete example, if a bank purchases a security for Rs. 120 including Rs. 20 as broken period interest and subsequently receives Rs. 25 as interest from the issuer of the security, according to the CBDT, the cost is Rs. 100 only and the revenue is only Rs. 5, i.e., Rs. 25 - Rs. 20. According to the Supreme Court, the cost is Rs. 120 and the revenue is Rs. 25. According to accounting authorities, while the cost is no doubt Rs. 120 initially, it gets reduced to Rs. 100 subsequently on receipt of interest including the portion relating to the broken period. Since out of Rs. 25 received, Rs. 20 is credited to the investment account, Rs. 5 alone is revenue. Thus, arithmetically, the CBDT was right, but the principles employed were wrong.

Capital Reserve can be Used to Set off Loss, with Company Court’s Approval

S. VENUGOPALAN

The author is a Company Secretary.

The author here deals with the issue as to when capital reserve can be used to set off losses. The highlights of the article are the definition of ‘capital reserve’, circumstances in which it is created and its utilisation. In this context, the author has analysed the judgment of the Delhi High Court in Allianz Capital & Management Services Ltd., In re [2005] 63 SCL 496 wherein it has been held that after obtaining the Government’s approval, capital profits can be used to set off loss, and submits that this decision is binding within jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court only.

What is capital reserve

1. Reserve is profit retained or ploughed back in the business and accumulated over the years. Reserves are of two kinds (1) Revenue reserve and (2) Capital reserve. A reserve created out of trading profits is revenue reserve.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve. The Companies Act, 1956 does not directly define the term ‘capital reserve’. But according to Part III of Schedule VI of the Act, "the expression ‘capital reserve’ shall not include any amount regarded as free for distribution through the profit and loss account; and the expression ‘revenue reserve’ shall mean any reserve other than a capital reserve." In reality, the capital reserve is at time distributable as dividends among shareholders. But normally, it is not so distributed. The capital reserve is not created by transferring the profit through the appropriation account as is the case of the revenue or the general reserve. But, it is created out of the profits of a capital nature.

A reserve which is created out of capital profits is a capital reserve.

How a capital reserve is created

2. The capital reserve is created out of the capital profits. Some of the circumstances under which the capital reserve is created are as under:

(a) Premiums received on the issue of shares and debentures are capital profits. They are considered as the capital reserve.

(b) Balance to the credit of forfeited shares account after the re-issue of such forfeited shares is transferred to the capital reserve.

(c) Profit on the redemption of debentures at a discount is considered as a capital profit and is transferred to the capital reserve.

(d) When on purchase of a business the purchase price is less than the value of the net assets acquired, the difference is normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(e) Similarly the profits prior to the incorporation of the limited company are considered capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve.

(f) Profits which are of an exceptional nature and which have not been earned during the regular course of business are at times considered as capital profits and are transferred to the capital reserve. But it is not so treated always.

(g) Where the company sells its fixed assets at an amount which is higher than their cost, the excess over cost is considered as a capital profit. This profit is not earned during the regular course of business. Hence, such profits are normally transferred to the capital reserve.

(h) Sometimes a company may revalue its fixed assets as a result of appreciation in their value. The amount of appreciation is normally transferred to the capital reserve. Revaluation of fixed assets is made by following the Accounting Standard-10 accounting for fixed assets. Revaluation of assets should be done of a class of assets and not individual assets.

(i) If directed by the articles of association, certain profits may not be available for distribution among shareholders. In other words, such profits are not free for distribution through the profit and loss account. Such profits are transferred to the capital reserve.

(j) Certain capital gains and other items of profits which are not regarded as available for distribution as dividend are transferred to the capital reserve. (Adapted from Auditing Principles and Practice by V.H Krishnadwala pg. 2.265)

Disclosure of capital reserve in the balance sheet

3. According to Part I of Schedule VI to the Act, the capital reserve should be shown as a separate item under the head ‘Reserves and surplus’. It should not be mixed up with the revenue reserves. The share premium account is a capital profit, but it is shown as a separate item in the balance sheet.

Utilisation of capital profits (and hence the capital reserve)

4. Capital profits can be utilised for writing off intangible assets like the preliminary expenses, share/debenture issue expenses, goodwill, etc.

The share premium account can be applied for the following purposes as directed by section 78 of the Companies Act, 1956 :

(a) in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to its shareholders as fully paid bonus shares,

(b) in writing off preliminary expenses,

of an intangible. Development of a trademark or goodwill takes place over a passage of time and is a slow ongoing process. In cases of well-known trademarks, the trademark is already recognised in the market. In such cases the expenditure incurred for promoting products, with a trademark, is really for exploitation of the trademark rather than for development of the value of the trademark. Brand value, therefore, does not represent trademark as a standalone asset. It is difficult and complex to determine and segregate its value. Therefore, it is not correct to assert that brand building is a substantial attribute of advertisement and sale promotion. Brand building represents a coordinated synergetic impact created largely by reputation and quality. There are good number of examples where brands have been built without incurring substantial advertisement or promotion expenses. Equally, there also are cases where, in spite of extensive and large scale advertisements, brand values have not been created. Hence, it would be erroneous and fallacious to treat brand building as counterpart of advertisement expenses. Advertisements may be the quickest and effective way to tell a brand story to a large audience, but just that is not enough to create or build a brand.

The High Court has also highlighted the fact that the Delhi High Court has repeatedly held that advertisement expenditure should not be generally treated as capital expenditure incurred or made for creating an intangible capital asset – see CIT v. Monto Motors Ltd. [2012] 206 Taxman 43/19 taxmann.com 57 (Delhi); CIT v. Spice Distribution Ltd. [2015] 229 Taxman 400/54 taxmann.com 325; and CIT v. Salora International Ltd. [2009] 308 ITR 199 (Delhi).

From the abovementioned observations of the High Court, on Brand and Brand Building, we may infer that AMP expenses incurred by an Indian Distributor AE are not necessarily for creation of marketing intangibles for Foreign AE. Where the brand of the Foreign AE is well-known and recognised, we may say that the Indian Distributor AE incurs AMP expenses for exploiting the brand for its own distribution business. In such a case the Indian Distributor AE will not be entitled to a separate remuneration for AMP functions. Of course, the Gross Profit (under RPM) and Net Profit (under TNMM) realised by the Indian Distributor should be in line with the comparables.

3.1.9 Economic Ownership of Brand:The Special Bench had rejected the concept of economic ownership of brand, in the context of Transfer Pricing. That concept has been now appreciated by the High Court. The High Court has held that the economic ownership of a brand name or trademark is accepted in international taxation as one of the components of determining the transfer price of goods.

Economic ownership when pleaded can be accepted if it is proved by the assessee. The burden is on the assessee. It cannot be assumed.

Economic ownership of a brand is an intangible asset, just as legal ownership is. On this point we may draw an inference from the High Court's observation, that in long-term distribution-cum-marketing arrangements, with the Foreign AE, the Indian Distributor (the purchasing AE) may acquire economic ownership of the brand – such ownership, however, has to be proved by the Indian Distributor. In that case the Indian Distributor does acquire the right to exploit the intangible property, like trademark or logo, embedded or affixed on the distributed goods. Therefore, in such a case we may assert that the AMP expenses are incurred by the Indian Distributor for its own benefit, as economic owner of the trademark or the logo. So, no separate AMP remuneration is due from the Foreign AE.

But what would be the appropriate remuneration in such a case, for AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributor? The appropriate remuneration would be the premium profits realised from exploitation of the brand. Such premium profits would be reflected in higher Gross Profit margins or higher Net Profit margins realised by the Indian Distributor, as compared to comparable distributors.

3.1.10 Direct Marketing Expenses:The High Court has rejected the Revenue's contention that direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, would form part of the AMP expenses.

Distribution and marketing exercise in case of tangible goods requires transfer or sale of goods to third parties, be it sub-distributors or retailers. That transaction is in the nature of sale of goods for consideration. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to sub-distributors or retailers are not in the nature and character of 'brand promotion'. They are not directly or immediately related to 'brand building' exercise, but have a live link and direct connection with marketing and increased volume of sales or turnover. The 'brand building' connect is too remote and faint.

To include and treat the direct marketing expenses, like trade discount or volume discount or incentive, as 'brand building' exercise would be contrary to common sense and would be highly exaggerated. The expenses being in the nature of selling expenses have an immediate connect with price or consideration payable for the goods sold. They are not incurred for publicity or advertisement.

Based on the above reasoning, the High Court has held that the direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, should not form part of the AMP expenses.

In this case, this issue was dealt with extensively. A similar view was expressed in CIT v. G.T. Industries [1993] 203 ITR 538 (Bom.).

(ii) Interest on borrowings for expansion of existing business - There is a very important distinction between the provisions of the Act and accounting principles so far as interest on borrowings utilised for expansion of existing business is concerned, which probably has contributed to substantial tax saving, particularly in the case of companies regularly undertaking expansion schemes. According to clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 36, interest paid in respect of capital borrowed for the purpose of business is allowable as a deduction. It has been held in several decisions that undertaking a new project for manufacture of a product different from the existing line of manufacture also constitutes the same business as long as there is unified management reflected by a single set of accounts, dovetailing of business activity through flow of funds, etc., and that interest paid on borrowings utilised in such project under construction, though capitalised in books, is allowable as revenue expenditure under the Act - CIT v. Classification of expenditure under income-tax law 8. For purposes of levy of income-tax, expenditure is classified into two categories, i.e., capital and revenue. The Income-tax Act does not recognise the third category, viz., deferred revenue expenditure. This is because under the cash system of accounting once expenditure is incurred and in the mercantile system once liability towards expenditure had accrued even though it is discharged on a future date, they are admissible as a deduction in computing income. Deferred revenue expenditure isrevenue expenditure incurred in one accounting period the benefit of which is applicable either wholly or in part to future periods. ‘As a rule an item falling under this heading is a fictitious asset, i.e., although it is shown as an asset in the balance sheet, it is not really an asset at all but a capital or abnormal loss which has not been written off’ [Accountancy by William Pickles, Fourth Edition, page 0804]. Thus, deferred revenue expenditure was unknown in income-tax matters and this has also been judicially recognised as discussed hereunder. Only where there is a specific provision like section 35A, 35AB, 35D or rule 9A, 9B, the expenditure is allowed to be amortised in more than one year.

In the case of Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd., In re [1952] 21 ITR 353 (All.), it was held that where the expenditure is of a heavy character and the benefits thereof were likely to extend beyond the year in question, the entire expenditure is deductible in the year of incurring it without any spreadover to future years, as there is no provision in law for spreading out. [Emphasis supplied] This decision was being followed without demur by the department for more than four decades. The Board Instruction No. 943, dated April 2, 1976 reiterates the abovenoted principle. As per this instruction, it is open to a subscriber to claim the entire amount paid under the OYT scheme in the year in which payment is made. Where the installation of telephone is in the previous year subsequent to the previous year in which the deposit is made, the deduction for payment should be allowed in the year of payment irrespective of the fact whether the telephone has been installed or not.

However, in a recent judgment in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340, the Apex Court has opened the Pandora’s box on this well-settled issue. The Apex Court observed that ordinarily revenue expenditure which is incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business must be allowed in its entirety in the year in which it is incurred. It cannot be spread over a number of years even if the assessee had written it off in his books over a period of years. Having said so, the Apex Court went on to say that the facts may justify an assessee who has incurred expenditure in a particular year to spread and claim it over a period of ensuing years. In fact, allowing the expenditure in one year might give a distorted picture of the profits of a particular year. This view looks based more on equity than law. Can this be a yardstick in fiscal matters to decide about the allowance of expenditure ? The principle upheld earlier in Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd.’s case (supra) and followed by the Tribunal is in conformity with the earlier decision in Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) to the effect that the nature of entries made by an assessee in his books is not decisive or conclusive of a matter. A time-tested practice has been given the go-by with the result that the assessing authorities will start disallowing expenditure on a subjective assessment presuming benefit as extending beyond the accounting year. The decision will spawn more litigation at a time when the Finance Minister is hoping to settle disputes by the Kar Vivad Samadhan Scheme. It would be necessary to issue a circular if harassment by way of disallowances/litigation are to be avoided. This decision itself needs a review. Till then it must be held as confined to the facts of the particular case.

FAQ 87. If the statutory auditor does not consider an item as a prior period expense, whereas the tax auditor feels that such item should be considered as a prior period, should that expense be disclosed in Clause 27(b) of Form 3CD?

It may be noted that there is a difference between the expenditure of any earlier year debited to the profit and loss account and the expenditure relating to an earlier year, which has crystallised during the relevant year. An expense, though related to previous periods, which has been determined in the current period, would not be considered a prior period item.

In such cases, though the expenditure may relate to the earlier year, it can be considered as arising during the year on the basis that the liability materialised or crystallised during the year, and such cases will not be reported under this clause.

In case of any conflict in the opinion of the statutory auditor and tax auditor, the opinion of the tax auditor shall prevail, and the information thereof shall be reported in Form 3CD.

FAQ 88. Mr. A, a sole proprietor, agreed to transfer his personal property to Mr. X and received some non-refundable advance against such a deal. The sale could not materialise as Mr. X could not pay the whole amount, and the advance money was forfeited by Mr. A. What are the disclosure requirements?

Section 56(2)(ix) of the Income-tax Act provides for taxability of any sum received as an advance in the course of negotiations for the transfer of a capital asset, and such sum was forfeited due to non-transfer of such capital asset. A new Clause 29A to Form 3CD has been inserted to report any advance received from the buyer but forfeited due to the non-materialisation of a deal to the sale of the capital asset.

The auditor is not required to report any such forfeited amount in respect of a personal capital asset or stock-in-trade. Any advances received and forfeited towards the sale of stock-in-trade would be taxable under section 28(i), and would not be required to be reported since the amount would be credited to the profit & loss account.

The requirement of reporting arises only on forfeiture of advance. If an advance has been received and has been outstanding for a considerable time, there is no requirement to report such amount unless and until it is forfeited by an act of the assessee.

Reporting obligation under Clause 29 is triggered if a closely held company issues unquoted shares at a premium. In such case, the excess of the premium over the fair market value of the shares shall be taxable as income from other sources in the hands of the company.

AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section. The Explanation prescribes a tripartite test to determine if an expense qualifies as 'head office expenditure' - (i) The expenditure was incurred outside India; (ii) The expenditure is in the nature of 'executive and general administration' expenses; and (iii) The said executive and general administration expenditure is of the specific kind enumerated in clauses (a), (b), or (c) respectively of the Explanation, or is of the kind prescribed under clause (d).

This means that even if such head office expenditure can be allowed as a deduction under Section 37(1), it would not be permitted if it exceeds the ceiling limit set under Section 44C. Section 44C of the Income Tax Act does not create a distinction between common and exclusive head office expenditure. It applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches. The term 'attributable' in Clause (c) does not create a statutory distinction between 'common' and 'exclusive' expenditure.

Thus, the question of law is answered in favour of the Revenue, and it was held that Section 44C applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches.

5. Reduction in share capital of subsidiary & subsequent reduction in shareholding is 'transfer' under Section 2(47): SC

Jupiter Capital (P.) Ltd. v. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 170 taxmann.com 305 (SC)

The assessee held shares in an Indian company. The company filed a petition before the High Court for a reduction of its share capital to set off the loss against the paid-up equity share capital. The High Court ordered for a reduction in the share capital of the company. The assessee's share was reduced proportionately, and the company paid an amount to the assessee as consideration. During the year, the assessee claimed a long-term capital loss accrued on the reduction in share capital from the sale of shares of such company.

However, the Assessing Officer (AO) contended that although the number of shares got reduced by virtue of reduction in share capital of the company, yet the face value of each share as well as shareholding pattern remained the same. Thus, reduction in shares of the subsidiary company did not result in the transfer of a capital asset as envisaged in section 2(47).

The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that section 2(47) is an inclusive definition providing that relinquishment of an asset or extinguishment of any right therein amounts to a transfer of a capital asset. While the taxpayer continues to remain a shareholder of the company even with the reduction of share capital, it could not be accepted that there was no extinguishment of any part of his right as a shareholder qua the company.

The expression 'extinguishment of any right therein' is of wide import. It covers every possible transaction which results in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise, of all or any of the bundle of rights, qualitative or quantitative, which the assessee has in a capital asset, whether such asset is corporeal or incorporeal.

In the instant case, the face value per share remained the same before the reduction of share capital and after the reduction of share capital. However, as the total number of shares were reduced.

Relying upon the decision in case of Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. Commissioner of Income Tax reported in (1997) 7 SCC 524, it was held that reduction of right in a capital asset would amount to 'transfer' under section 2(47). Sale is only one of the modes of transfer envisaged by section 2(47). Relinquishment of any rights in it, which may not amount to sale, can also be considered as transfer and any profit or gain which arises from the transfer of such capital asset is taxable under section 45.

Also, a company under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 has a right to reduce the share capital, and one of the modes which could be adopted is to reduce the face value of the preference share. When as a result of the reducing of the face value of the share, the share capital is reduced, the right of the preference shareholder to the dividend or his share capital and the right to share in the distribution of the net assets upon liquidation is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in the capital. Such a reduction of the right of the capital asset clearly amounts to a transfer within the meaning of section 2(47).

Thus, it was held that the reduction in share capital of the subsidiary company and subsequent proportionate reduction in the shareholding of the assessee would be squarely covered within the ambit of the expression 'sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset' used in section 2(47).

TAXABLE INCOME

3. The chasm between the taxable income and the accountant’s or legal concept of income is very wide, more because of the numerous deeming provisions in the tax statute, which nullify them. Tax on capital gains itself is a glaring example of taxing what is not income. Deeming provisions even in respect of salary income treating terminal benefits as normal income, subject, no doubt, to measured relief and various other provisions like anti-compete fee under section 28 of the Act besides such income as from lotteries under section 56, are again other capital receipts, which are treated as revenue receipts, contrary to accepted understanding of revenue as against capital receipts. Provisions for deemed dividend and deeming accrual on receipt basis are other instances.

Some items of revenue expenditure are deemed to be capital expenditure allowed to be amortised over the years as in the case of expenses on mergers and demergers under section 35DD of the Act or VRS payments under section 35DDA of the Act. What makes the taxable income even more distorted making a sweeping departure from real income is the deeming provision like disallowance of what is deemed to be illegal under Explanation to section 37(1) of the Act. Expenditure from which tax is failed to be deducted at source is disallowed under section 40(a) of the Act. Even where mercantile system is followed, cash system is substituted under section 43B, so as to legitimise hybrid system to revenue’s advantage in the matter of taxes, interest to banks and financial institutions and welfare dues. What is worse is the provision to treat cash expenditure above the limit of Rs. 20,000 under section 40A(3) of the Act with minor exceptions on the understanding, that expenditure would include purchases. Apart from what is collected as tax, penalty is collected on deposits and repayments in cash under section 269SS and 269T of the Act, unless reasonable cause is established. Both sections 40A(3) and 269SS and 269T would strangely target genuine transactions, because expenditure, which is not genuine and deposits which are not genuine are taxable as income. The complexity of our laws is more evident in the matters of cross-border transactions with Double Tax Avoidance Agreements hardly touching the existing problems with transfer pricing adding to the existing confusion. Almost every Finance Act would add to the list of deeming provisions.

DISCRIMINATORY TREATMENT OF CORPORATE SECTOR

4. Our system of corporate taxation is highly discriminatory making corporations liable for additional burden by way of book profits tax on one hand and dividend distribution tax on the other. Tax on dividend is a double taxation of corporate income, whether the dividends are assessed in the hands of shareholder or company. Loans and advances are deemed as dividend income of the shareholder or a concern in which the shareholder is interested under section 2(22)( e) of the Act. Right of set off on actual distributed dividend in a later year as provided in the section makes no sense, when such dividend is taxed in the hands of an interested concern, so that it is another instance of double taxation in shareholder’s hands once as deemed dividend and again in the hands of the interested concern, when there is actual distribution of dividend. Deeming loss under the head ‘Capital gains’ on share transactions as speculative under Explanation to section 73 of the Act is a special provision targetting corporations. Fringe Benefits Tax though not limited to corporations imposes further burden especially on manufacturing companies with a large work force.

Non-cash consideration like securities issued by SPV should be recorded at the lowest of : (a) fair value of such consideration; (b) carrying value (net) of securitized assets; and (c) net realizable value of securitized assets. In case of a mix of cash and non-cash consideration, the non-cash consideration will be recorded as aforesaid subject to the cash component being reduced from the value of securitized assets. All costs like legal expenses, etc., incurred on a ‘true-sale’ securitisation transaction should be fully and immediately recognized in the profit and loss statement. Obligations accepted by the originator (for example, recourse obligation) should be valued and expected losses, if any, should be provided in the profit and loss statement.

If, however, the securitisation transaction is not a ‘true-sale’, the securitized asset should continue to be carried in the balance sheet of the originator and the consideration received should be shown as ‘borrowings’ with appropriate disclosure about security, i.e., assets securitised. Costs like legal fees, etc., incurred on such transaction could be either recognized fully and immediately in the profit and loss statement or amortized over the life of such borrowing.

4.4 Income-tax treatment - The income-tax treatment primarily depends on the nature of the assets of the originator. In a true sale transaction, if the securitised asset is a trade receivable (‘trading portfolio’), then the ‘securitised result’ should be considered as the ‘business income’. As a corollary, if the securitised asset is an investment, i.e., a capital asset for the originator, then the ‘securitised result’ should be considered as ‘capital gains’. Classification of ‘securitisation result’ is important as capital loss can be recouped only against capital gains and not against any other income. So, in absence of sufficient taxable ‘capital gains’ accruing to the originator either in the year of securitisation or eight succeeding tax years thereafter, the un-recouped ‘capital loss’ arising on securitisation will be a dead tax loss for the originator. Such loss will increase the cost of securitisation.

An alternate view, on securitisation of a ‘trading portfolio’, could be that since the originator severs his income-generating asset, the ‘securitisation result’ should be considered as being on ‘capital’ account. However, the better view appears to be that since securitisation is akin to realisation of a trading asset, any resultant gains or loss should be considered as ‘business income’ and not ‘capital gains’.

The servicing fee received by the originator (in case he services the assets) should be treated as ‘business income’ where it relates to securitisation of ‘trading portfolio’. Similarly, interest on cash collateral and/or subordinate securities should be considered as ‘business income’ of the originator. Legal fees and related securitisation costs should, therefore, be considered as tax-deductible business expenditure.

In case of securitisation of ‘capital asset’, the service fee/interest income from cash collateral/subordinate securities could be classified as ‘income from other sources’. The legal fees and related costs may be deductible against capital gains on the basis that they are wholly and exclusively incurred for transfering the ‘capital asset’. However, dispute with the tax authorities on this count cannot be fully ruled out.

Whether reimbursement of expenses is not subject to service tax?

Upto April 18, 2006, service tax is payable only on gross amount charged for service rendered. Before April 18, 2006, there was a Board circular stating that reimbursable expenses were not included in the assessable value for the purpose of levy of service tax. If a service provider incurs some expenditure on behalf of customer, that amount is not part of service provided and will not be taxable. The expenses which are reimbursed by the client are taxable only from April 18, 2006, i.e., as per Service tax (Determination of value) Rules, 2006.

As per rule 5(1) of the Service tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, the cost or expenditure which is incurred by the service provider in the course of providing taxable service is to be included in the value of taxable services.

In Malabar Management Services (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2008] 14 STT 107 - The assessee was providing Business Auxiliary Services to the ICICI Bank to market the bank’s personal loans. They were reimbursed by the bank in respect of expenses on salary of personnel, infrastructural expenses like rent, electricity, telephone charges, stationary, etc. But the bank charged service tax only on the consideration and not on the reimbursed expenses. As per the agreement made between bank and the assessee, there was a fixed rate of commission which was mentioned in the agreement. The department demanded service tax on the reimbursed amount. Finally, the Tribunal held that reimbursable expenses were not part of the assessable value in view the fact that the consideration was already fixed in the agreement.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

Internationally, the IFRS Interpretations Committee had received a request in 2019 about training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. In the fact pattern described in the request:

a. an entity enters into a contract with a customer that is within the scope of IFRS 15. The contract is for the supply of outsourced services.

b.

to be able to provide the services to the customer, the entity incurs costs to train its employees (as described in paragraph 15 of IAS 38 Intangible Assets) so that they understand the customer's equipment and processes. Applying IFRS 15, the entity does not identify the training activities as a performance obligation.

c.

the contract permits the entity to charge to the customer the costs of training (i) the entity's employees at the beginning of the contract, and (ii) new employees that the entity hires as a result of any expansion of the customer's operations.

The request asked whether the entity recognises the training costs as an asset or an expense when incurred.

Which IFRS Standard applies to the training costs?

Paragraph 95 of IFRS 15 requires an entity to recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer not within the scope of another IFRS Standard, only if those costs meet all three criteria specified in paragraph 95. Consequently, before assessing the criteria in paragraph 95, the entity first considers whether the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract are within the scope of another IFRS Standard.

Paragraph 5 of IAS 38 states that 'this Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities'. Accordingly, the Committee concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity applies IAS 38 in accounting for the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract with the customer.

Application of IAS 38

Paragraph 69(b) of IAS 38 lists 'expenditure on training activities' as an example of expenditure that an entity recognises as an expense when incurred. Paragraph 15 of IAS 38 explains that 'an entity usually has insufficient control over the expected future economic benefits arising from a team of skilled staff and from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset'.

In addition, in explaining the requirements in IFRS 15 regarding costs to fulfil a contract, paragraph BC307 of IFRS 15 states that 'if the other Standards preclude the recognition of any asset arising from a particular cost, an asset cannot then be recognised under IFRS 15'.

Accordingly, the Committee, in its September 2019 meeting, concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity recognises as an expense when incurred the training costs to fulfil the contract with the customer.

The Committee concluded that the principles and requirements in IFRS 15 and IAS 38 provide an adequate basis for an entity to determine its accounting for training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. Consequently, the Committee decided not to add this matter to its standard-setting agenda.

Therefore, based on this interpretation, such specific training costs shall be expensed as incurred and can not be capitalised.

FAQ 45. Section 43B specifically disallows the interest expense which is converted into a loan. Whether such disallowance shall be permanent?

Circular No.7/2006 dated 17-07-2006 clarifies that the unpaid interest, whenever actually paid to the bank or financial institution, will be in the nature of revenue expenditure deserving deduction in the computation of income. Therefore, the converted interest, by whatever name called, in the wake of its conversion into a loan or borrowing or advance, will be eligible for deduction in the computation of income of the previous year in which the converted interest is 'actually paid'.

In other words, the nomenclature of the sum of converted interest will make no difference as the payment of converted interest will not represent the repayment of the principal. The circular clarifies that the fundamental principle remains that once an amount has been determined as interest payable to the banks or financial institutions, any subsequent change of nomenclature of interest will not affect its allowability and deduction in terms of section 43B will have to be allowed on its actual payment. However, the Assessing Officer can ask for a certificate from the assessee to be obtained from the lender bank or financial institution, etc., as evidence of 'actual payment' of interest to banks or financial institutions.

FAQ 46. Will the sum payable to Indian Railways for advertisement at railway stations be disallowed under section 43B?

If an advertising agency is making payment to the railways for putting up hoardings or display panels on railway premises, such payment would be deemed to be the payment for the use of railway assets, as the payment is for the use of space on the premises. However, where an advertiser is making payment to the railways for the display of advertisements on hoardings or displays in railway premises, such a payment is in the nature of payment for the services of advertisement and not for the use of railway assets.

Any sum payable to Indian Railways for the use of railways assets shall be allowed on a payment basis. Any sum payable to Indian Railways for its services shall be allowed as per the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee.

FAQ 73. If the statutory auditor does not consider an item as a prior period expense, whereas the tax auditor feels that such item should be considered as a prior period, should that expense be disclosed in Clause 27(b) of Form 3CD?

It may be noted that there is a difference between the expenditure of any earlier year debited to the profit and loss account and the expenditure relating to an earlier year, which has crystallised during the relevant year. An expense, though related to previous periods, which has been determined in the current period, would not be considered a prior period item.

In such cases, though the expenditure may relate to the earlier year, it can be considered as arising during the year on the basis that the liability materialised or crystallised during the year, and such cases will not be reported under this clause.

In case of any conflict in the opinion of the statutory auditor and tax auditor, the opinion of the tax auditor shall prevail, and the information thereof shall be reported in Form 3CD.

Examples 18 and 21

Example 18

Birincil acquires 100 per cent of the equity in Company T, which has developed several promising technologies but which has only minimal sales. A PPA is carried out which attributes 20 of the price to tangible and identified intangible property, and 80 to goodwill and going concern. The intangibles owned by T are subsequently transferred to another associated enterprise (S) which takes over responsibility for ongoing RD. The Revised Discussion Draft states that: "… a substantial portion of the value described in the purchase price allocation as goodwill of Company T may be seen transferred to Company S with the other Company T intangibles…. Company T should be entitled to compensation for such value either as part of the price paid by Company S for the transferred rights to technology intangibles, or through the compensation Company T is paid in years following the transaction for the RD services of its workforce. It should generally be assumed that value does not disappear, not is it destroyed, as part of an internal business restructuring." (Paragraph 292).

Example 21

Osnovni acquired Company S for 160. Prior to the acquisition, Company S shares were trading at 100; other buyers were willing to pay between 120 and 130. Presentations to the board of directors state that Osnovni was willing to pay the high price of 160 because of the complementary nature of the existing products in the Osnovni group with the products and potential products of Company S.

Osnovni arranges for the transfer of the European and Asian intangibles that S owns to its subsidiary T. The Revised Discussion Draft states that, to the extent that the premium reflects the complementary nature of the Osnovni and S intangibles in Europe and Asia, the purchase price premium should be reflected in the payment by T for S intangibles; to the extent that the premium arises because of complementarities outside of T's territory, it should not.

Comment

Both of these examples ignore the fundamental difference between the price paid in an acquisition – which is based on the value of the target to the MNE group as whole – and the value of specific assets transferred between two associated members of the group. Consider the following. Independent Company S has intangible assets with a market value of 100 and Company T has intangible assets, also with a market value of 100, while the two companies operate as separate companies. When the intangible assets of the two companies are combined (either by S buying the equity in T or T buying the equity in S), the combined value of the intangibles s and t increases from 200 to 300 because of synergies.

For simplicity, assume that the entire value of S and T is derived from the intangible assets that they own. Given this, we know that the price that S will pay for T (or which T will pay for S) is at least 100 (the standalone value of their intangible assets) but no more than 200 (the standalone value plus total value of all synergies). Now consider two situations:

(1)

S acquires T for 200 and transfers T's intangible asset, to itself. If S uses the price paid in the acquisition to determine the payment to T for intangible asset, S pays T 200 and T receives the entire benefit of the synergy. The implied price for the value of S's own intangible asset is 100. Or,

(2)

T acquires S for 200 and transfers to itself. If T uses the price paid in the acquisition to determine the payment to S for intangible assets, T pays S 200 and S receives the entire benefit of the synergy. The implied price for the value of T's own intangible asset is 100.

Note that in these two situations, the value of the intangibles based purely on the acquisition price would be different depending on which company was the acquirer and which was the target, which does not make intuitive sense.

The expenditure incurred by an assessee will be under examination as per section 40A(2)(b) in terms of reasonableness, not being excessive and as per the business needs. Three criteria have been laid down for verification by an assessing officer and he would be justified to disallow expenditure as being excessive or unreasonable, having regard to -

(a)

The fair market value of the goods, services or facilities for which the payment is made; or

(b)

The legitimate business needs of the assessee's business or profession; or

The benefit derived by or accruing to the assessee from the payment

The Supreme Court also referred to two popular treatises dealing with book-keeping and accounting principles in Spicer and Pegler's Book-keeping and Accounts and Batliboi's Principles and Practice of Auditing, and observed that in the former work the principle that discount on debentures is to be treated as interest and in the latter, an observation that it can be charged on a proportionate basis during the period of its life has relevance in cases of this kind. Therefore, though an assessee would not be justified in claiming deduction of the entire amount of discount in the accounting year in question, it would be entitled to proportionate deduction spread over the period for which the bonds remain outstanding."

""The expression 'expenditure' is not defined in the Act, as such. In the context of different statutes, the expression 'expenses' have been construed. Carmarthen Corporation [1841] 10 LJ Exch. 401, the expression 'expenses' meant actual disbursements not allowances for loss of time. Therefore, a charge by a town clerk for preparing lists of Parliamentary voters was not 'expense incurred' by him within the Parliamentary Voters Registration Act, 1843. But, again, in the case of R. v. It, therefore, appears that the expression must be understood in the context in which it is used."

"Reference in this connection may be made to section 37 of the Act which enjoins that any expenditure not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession should be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'. In sections 30 to 36, the expressions 'expenses incurred ' as well as 'allowances and depreciation' had been used. For example, depreciation and allowances have been dealt with in section 32. Therefore, the Legislature was using the expression 'any expenditure' in section 37 to cover both.""

The Explanation 3 to section 43A strengthens further the argument that the capitalisation approach is available for all assets.

5. The following points emerge from the foregoing discussion :

-Capitalisation of exchange fluctuation loss to the cost of fixed assets creates value distortion. This approach as suggested in the company law is divergent from the International Accounting Standard, and also defies the standard asset valuation norm.

-Any exchange fluctuation loss should be immediately expensed unless it qualifies for capitalisation, being (i) a loss arising out of severe devaluation or depreciation of the reporting currency against which there was no means of heading, (ii) the fixed asset was acquired recently, and (iii) the capitalisation would not push up the carrying amount of fixed assets beyond lower of the current cost or realisable value.

-The requirement of AS - 11, that allows extension of the capitalisation of exchange fluctuation even to fixed assets acquired in India utilising foreign currency loan should be scrapped.

-Expenses or loss arising out of forward cover arrangement against foreign currency liability is essentially an event of currency risk management. This should not be treated as capital expense or capital loss. Rather it should be immediately expensed.

-In section 43A, this capitalisation approach has been made applicable to any asset, but it should be restricted only to capital expenditure or capital asset. It is possible to apply the special meaning of actual cost as explained in section 43A for the purpose of finding out the actual cost of imported stock. Unless the imported stock is sold, the relevant currency loss would not be expensed.

-AS - 11 has perhaps exceeded the spirit of the company law, a situation which should be immediately rectified.

The expression 'enduring advantage' is a relative term, not enduring in the sense of its being permanent, but is sufficiently durable depending upon the nature of the terms upon which it can be acquired [Devidas Vithaldas & Co. v. To decide whether an expenditure is capital or revenue in nature, what is decisive is the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure, the nature of the right acquired, and their relation, inter se, and this is the only key to resolve the issue in the light of the general principles, which are followed in such cases [K. T. M. T. M. Abdul Kayoom v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 689 (SC)].

To find out whether an expenditure is on the capital account or on revenue, one must consider the expenditure in relation to the business. Since all payments reduce capital in the ultimate analysis, one is apt to consider a loss as amounting to a loss of capital. But this is not true of all losses, because losses in the running of the business cannot be said to be of capital. The questions to consider in this connection are: For what was the money laid out? Was it to acquire an asset of an enduring nature for the benefit of the business, or was it an outgoing in the doing of the business? If money be lost in the first circumstance, it is a loss of capital, but if lost in the second circumstance, it is a revenue loss. In the first, it bears the character of an investment, but in the second, to use a commonly understood phrase, it bears the character of current expenses [CIT v. Mysore Sugar Co. Ltd. [1962] 46 ITR 649 (SC)].

Whether an expenditure incurred by an assessee in any AY is an expenditure of revenue or capital nature leads to the following conclusions:—

(1)

If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business asset, it would be 'capital expenditure'. If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(2)

If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operations, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(3)

Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired for payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trademarks, it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(4)

If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with the net sales. The outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of 'capital expenditure'.

(5)

If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled, the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the 'capital' nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(6)

A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be 'revenue expenditure' or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment. Thus, if the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(7)

An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a 'capital expenditure'.
