On reference :

HELD: It could not be gainsaid that in agreeing on the price at which the business was taken over by the assessee from the vendor all the liabilities as well as the assets of the firm had been taken into account. One of the liabilities obviously was the liability towards bonus for the period preceding the date of the takeover. It was known to the assessee that as consideration for the takeover, it would have to incur a liability to the full extent finally determined as the amount payable as bonus for the period preceding the takeover. The amount, thus, spent in payment of bonus for that period was not an amount expended by the assessee to carry on, and earn the profits or gains of the business which it took over, but an amount expended to obtain the business which it purchased. That was not an expenditure, which partook the character of revenue, but it was clearly a capital expenditure. Therefore, the balance bonus paid during the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1975-76 was not a revenue expenditure.

The assessee had purchased the goodwill and other rights for Rs. 10 lakhs which was treated to be capital expenditure. The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-Assesses took over as sole proprietor, business of firm in which he was partner, consequent on its dissolution due to death of one partner-Later, he converted business into partnership firm by admitting his son as partner-Still later, sons of deceased partner filed suit against assessee for reopening of earlier dissolution and for restraining assessee from carrying on business-Suit settled by compromise decree under which assessee paid lump sum to plaintiffs as final settlement-Whether sum so paid was allowable as revenue expenditure-Held, on facts, yes
Rule of practice-Stare decisis-Applicability as between decisions of larger bench of supreme court and smaller bench.

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a partnership concern. When the firm dissolved due to death of one partner, the assessee took over the business as a going concern after paying certain money to the deceased's heirs towards purchase of their interests in the partnership assets. He carried on the business for some time as a sole proprietor and, thereafter, converted it into a partnership by taking his son as partner. Later on, the assessee was faced with a suit instituted by some of the minor sons of the deceased-partner of the erstwhile partnership, demanding reopening of earlier dissolution and restraining the assessee from carrying on business. The suit was eventually compromised, when the assessee agreed to pay them Rs. 40,000 in full settlement. He claimed the payment as an admissible deduction, but the ITO disallowed the claim since it did not relate to the partnership business then carried on by the assessee. While the AAC allowed the impugned claim, the Tribunal negatived the same, holding that the expenditure was incurred by the assessee to protect his business and, hence, was capital in nature.

On reference :

HELD: It is well settled that expenditure laid out for the acquisition or improvement of a fixed capital asset or for perfecting title or for getting rid of a defect in the title, would be capital expenditure. However, if it is incurred to protect the trade or business of the assessee or to protect his assets from attack, then it would be revenue expenditure.

In considering the nature of the expenditure, it would not be proper to proceed on the basis of the correctness of the pleadings in the suit, as the matter was not adjudicated upon by the Court. The pleadings represent mere allegations and unless the statements were proved they would merely remain as allegations. So long as there was no adjudication on the conduct of the assessee, the allegations made should not colour the determination of the issue.

In the instant case both parties to the litigation had given the go-by to their respective pleadings when they entered into a mutual compromise. There was nothing express or implied in the terms of the compromise to suggest that the impugned payment was towards payment of the balance of the purchase price of the deceased partner's share in the business. The assessee had already become the owner of the assets long ago and he had to defend the attack on the assets. This was, thus, clearly a case where the expenditure had not brought into existence any capital asset or enduring benefit. It would, therefore, be safe and reasonable to hold that qua the assessee the suit was an attack }on the title to his business and the impugned payment warded off that attack. The Tribunal was not justified in assuming that the payment under the compromise decree was the means by which the assessee had acquired full title to the business.

In this view of the matter, the impugned amount was a revenue expenditure.

The doctrine that a larger Bench of the Supreme Court has more authoritative force than a smaller Bench is relevant only as between cases which yield different ratio decidendi, and not where the one hands down a decision and the other merely lays down a dictum.

In the instant case the most important circumstance that had to be borne in mind was that the ferry contract was only for a period of one year. The amounts paid by the assessee to buy off competition were paid only for the purpose of securing that advantage during that year. It could not, therefore, be said that these amounts were paid for securing an enduring advantage. They were paid in order to enable the assessee to derive more profits in the business by reducing the lease amount payable to the Government for operating the ferry. It was thus an amount paid for the purpose of the business. It could not be said that it was paid for the purpose of acquiring the business and not for the purpose of running it.

It was not contended that the lease amount paid for obtaining the right to operate the ferry was not in the nature of a revenue expenditure and was not deductible. There was no difference in the instant case between the lease amount and the amount paid to the other intended bidders in order to prevent them from competing and thus reduce the lease amount so that ultimately the assessee could derive more profits.

The question whether a particular expenditure is revenue expenditure incurred for the purposes of business must be determined on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances, and by the application of principles of commercial trading. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

Viewing the expenditure incurred in the instant case in such a context that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

The assessee-company was doing financing business and its main source of income was dividend and interest. The board of directors of the assessee-company decided to enter into the new business of entertainment. Therefore, the assessee-company amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’, which was owned by the film star Amitabh Bachchan, and this was approved by the jurisdictional High Court. The assessee paid certain lump sum amount to the two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for the next ten years. The assessee claimed deduction of the same as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and treated the expenditure in question as a capital expenditure. He held that the payment in question was made for acquiring a new asset, i.e., the brand/copyright, that is to say, a source of earning profit itself. The Assessing Officer further held that the revenue expenditure would be incurred every year, whereas the payment to both the stars was for once and for all and it was, therefore, a payment of enduring nature and also a source itself. The Assessing Officer also rejected the contention of the assessee that the artists were not prevented totally in carrying on their profession as artists, holding that, in fact, by virtue of the aforesaid agreements the assessee had an exclusive control over the services of the artists. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee had now entered into a new field of entertainment business and this was not an expansion of existing business, but a new line of business.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the artists had agreed to perform the diverse acts for the assessee, whereby the assessee could generate revenues from them and also copyrights on the products. Thus, it was the user of brand equity obtained by the assessee and not any capital asset as such. He further held that the expenditure incurred in acquiring goodwill of course was capital expenditure, but the payment made towards user of goodwill was of revenue nature and allowable as such. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, held that the expenditure in question incurred by the assessee definitely was not of capital nature, but of revenue. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340 further held that the payment was made for the right to use the artists for ten years and, hence, the payment in question was to be spread over every year equally.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

FACT: On incorporation the assessee-company became one of the partners of the firm 'NS', with effect from 1-8-1976. That firm was dissolved on 31-12-1976 and as a consequence the assets and liabilities of the erstwhile firm along with the business vested with the assessee-company. The dissolution deed that was drawn up, specified about the royalty that would be payable to the retiring partners for not doing such business for fifteen years arising out of the business of firm. The assessee by virtue of the dissolution deed, which was agreed to by it, provided royalty in its books by crediting to the two retired partners. The amount of royalty which was so shown as payable to the two retired partners for various assessment years, was claimed as revenue expenditure; but that was not accepted by the ITO. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On reference:

HELD: Whether the expenditure was in the nature of a capital expenditure or a business expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee’s business, one must not confine oneselves only to the agreements between the parties. The question must be determined in the light of all the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no rule that if there is a written agreement between the parties the authorities and the High Court must look only to that written agreement and nothing else.

It is now settled law that the question whether the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each case.

The assessee-company was floated by the holding company to do the chit fund business exclusively in northern Telangana Districts. The agreement was also liable to be terminated at any time with a notice of 10 months by either parties. The payment made by the assessee was claimed to be revenue in nature on the ground that the payment was not only for non-competing, but was also for several other services rendered by the holding company to the assessee. It was also submitted that the assessee did not derive any benefit of enduring nature and, therefore, it could not be termed as capital expenditure.

The Assessing Officer was not convinced with the assessee's contentions. He held that the non-compete fee was capital in nature and, hence, disallowed the same and brought it to tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was saddled with the duty to establish that the expended amount fell in the revenue field. Admittedly the payment was for the purpose of business of the assessee. The payment was expended to ward off the competition in the field of the assessee’s business. Admittedly this restriction to compete or, in other words, the non-compete fee was paid by the assessee to retrain payee from the competitive business for a definite period of five years. The non-compete fee payment made by the assessee to ‘S’ gave enduring benefit to the assessee in its business. Thus, the payment of non-compete fee fell within the capital field which was not an allowable expenditure. [Para 10]

The assessee purchased two distilleries. As per the agreement, an amount of Rs. 10 crores was given to their promoters for the restrictive covenant not to compete with the assessee for 10 years with a view to facilitate its profits by eliminating competition from the promoters. The Assessing Officer observed that there were limits to the price of shares of a company determined by market forces and in the instant case it was difficult to imagine that such limits would not have been operative and the assessee was left with no option but to pay the cost of acquisition over and above the price paid for the acquisition of the shares of these companies to their promoters; that, in order to claim the payments as allowable deduction, the transaction was given the colour of payments as non-competition fees, but, in fact, the real purpose of those payments was to compensate the promoters of the companies owning the two distilleries for the cost of the distilleries; that it was not the case of the assessee that the payments were made to any distillery owner or business rival and it was also not the case of the assessee that the persons who were paid the said amounts possessed special expertise and skill so as to threaten the business of the assessee; and that the circumstance that these persons’ companies/ distilleries did not produce any brand of liquor with national market presence, did not support the case of the assessee as to the real purpose or motive of the said payments. He, therefore, held that the claim of the assessee for allowability of Rs. 10 crores as business expenditure was nothing but part of the cost of distilleries and added it to the income of the assessee. On appeal, it was submitted that agreement for non-competition fees was for 5 years and based on certain decisions, it was claimed that where the benefit was not of enduring nature but was to exhaust in a short period, the expenditure was of revenue nature. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the payment could not be taken as the revenue expenditure because the agreements were to run for a long duration of 10 years unfettered by any stipulation of termination; that payment of non-competition fees could have some rationale if the competition was between equals producing the same commodity and that the promoters of the two distilleries taken over were no match for the assessee who had monopoly of manufacturing and marketing its own brand names. He, therefore, held that there was no business necessity for making the non-competition fees of Rs. 10 crores and upheld the disallowance.

On further appeal :

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 - Assessee-company acquired brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement - Under a separate non-compete agreement, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company as consideration for restraining it from competing in business of products similar to Lacto Calamine for a period of ten years - Amount paid as non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure by assessee - Whether in cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and benefit of restrain acquired by assessee for period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit - Held, yes - Whether therefore, by paying non-compete fee, it could be said that assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by assessee was in nature of capital expenditure and not revenue in character as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of manufacture of medicines and Lacto Calamine, purchased the brand name ‘Lacto Calamine’ from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement. Subsequently, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company under a non-compete agreement for restraining it from competing directly or indirectly in the business activities carried on by the assessee. The payment so made for the purchase of brand name was accounted for by the assessee as an item of capital expenditure but the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs paid as non-compete fee was claimed as a deduction being revenue in nature under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer, however, rejected the assessee’s said claim by holding that non-compete fee paid by it to ‘D’ was a capital expenditure inasmuch as by making said payment the assessee had acquired an advantage of an enduring nature by way of freedom from competition that would have been induced by ‘D’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1990-91 - Assessee was a representative agent of HP products in India - In order to ensure its monopoly status and eliminate any competition in its business for two years assessee entered into an agreement under which it agreed to pay consideration to BSL - BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products - Whether expenditure in question was of capital nature inasmuch as assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of selling, marketing and distribution of various products of Hewlett Packard (HP). It was a representative agent of HP products in India. In order to ensure its monopoly status and eliminate any competition in its business for two years the assessee entered into an agreement with BSL under which the assessee paid a consideration of Rs. 1.68 crore immediately and an equal amount was payable after one year. It was debited to profit and loss account as a proportionate amount for five months treating it as business expenditure in the year ended 31-3-1990. The Assessing Officer disallowed by holding that the said expenditure was capital in nature as it resulted in benefit of enduring nature. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) endorsed the finding of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: One of the tests to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure is whether the expenditure in question was for bringing into existence an asset or an advantage of an ‘enduring nature’ and was made once and for all meaning thereby an expenditure made once for all for procuring an enduring benefit. The expressions ‘enduring benefit’ and ‘rights of a permanent nature’ are only descriptive and not definitive and are related in meaning not synonymous with perpetual or everlasting. [Para 7]

In the instant case, BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products. Even though the period of two years was mentioned in the agreement, the predominant intention and purpose, as discernible from the stipulations in the agreement, clearly indicated that the assessee-company had obtained the monopoly rights on a permanent basis and BSL went out of its business of dealing in test and measurement products, of HP, inasmuch as it released its entire workforce connected with the line of business started by the assessee. Expenditure in question was clearly of a capital nature inasmuch as the assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years. The disallowance of expenditure was, therefore, justified. [Paras 8 and 12]

For the aforesaid reason finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 13]

The assessee was a manufacturer of tractors, jeeps and motorvehicles. It incurred expenses to the tune of Rs. 7.97 crores, towards acquiring various companies and entities, Indian and overseas. The assessee claimed such expenditure to be revenue in nature, incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee. The Assessing Officer, however, denied the claim and held the expenditure to be capital in nature.

FACT: • The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

HELD: Nature of expenditure incurred by assessee

• In the present case, the assessee is a joint venture between 'S' corporation and L&T. Apparently, the agreement entered into with the L&T in view of the changed relationship ensures that the latter does not enter into the same business. Although it is contended that the advantage is only by way of facilitation of the assessee's business and ensuring greater efficiency as well as profitability, on the other side, what can be seen is that the arrangement was to endure for a substantial period, i.e. 7 years coupled with the fact that the L&T had its own presence in consumer goods sector and would be able to put up an effective competition for business engaged in by the assessee, there is no doubt that the amount is to ensure a certain position in the market by keeping-out L&T. In such circumstances, it is opined that the deduction cannot be claimed as a revenue expenditure, it clearly falls within the capital field. [Para 10]

Depreciation in case of intangible asset

• The question arises as to whether a non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for seven years amounts to a depreciable intangible asset. Each of the species of rights spelt-out in section 32(1)(ii), i.e. know-how, patent, copyright, trademark, license or franchise as or any other right of a similar kind which confers a business or commercial or any other business or commercial right of similar nature has to be 'intangible asset'. The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the ownership. In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance 'in rem'.

• However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity. The right can be asserted in the present instance only against L&T and in a sense, the right 'in personam'.

revenue receipt in the hands of the payee. For example, in the hands of the purchaser of a machinery, the payment would be capital in nature, while in the hands of the seller, it could be revenue receipt. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that because the receipt in the hands of the recipient i.e. the holding company has been accepted as a revenue receipt, it should be treated as revenue expenditure in the hands of the assessee is not acceptable. [Para 5] In case of CIT v. Andhra Fuels (P.) Ltd. [2016] 70 taxmann.com 271/240 Taxman 280 (AP), the jurisdictional High Court was considering the case of an assessee who had entered into a non-compete fee agreement for a period of 3 years to ward off competition in the territories of the AP and the consideration paid for such non-competition was claimed as a deduction as the revenue expenditure. The High Court held that the restrictive covenant of non-competition for a period of 3 years from the date of agreement was neither permanent nor was an advantage of an enduring nature derived by the assessee and therefore, the payment was allowable as a deduction. [Para 7]

The nature and character of the payment in the hands of the assessee would depend upon the purpose of the payment and the nature of the benefit enured to the assessee by such payment. On formation of assessee-company, the holding company wanted the assessee-company to benefit by taking over its business in northern Telangana Districts. By virtue of the non-compete agreement, the holding company has lost part of its territory and consequently, a source of income and it is compensated by receipt of 1 per cent of the annual turnover. What is to be seen in this case is whether the assessee has gained anything by virtue of this agreement. The assessee has gained the business of the holding company i.e. the income generating area and also not having its holding company as its competitor. Whether this benefit is enduring in nature. Perhaps not. Because, by the agreement the period of non-competing was 5 years only. It was further extended by a further period of 5 years and the payment is payable every year. Thus, the payment is forwarding off competition from its holding company in a particular area and thereby generating revenue therefrom. [Para 8]

The agreement is for a period of 5 years and the assessee has also filed a copy of the agreement by which the agreement has been extended by a further period of five years. The second agreement also contains the same terms & conditions as in the first agreement. Without going into the second agreement, which is additional evidence filed. It is found that various clauses in the first agreement itself demonstrate that the agreement was initially for a period of 5 years and even the consideration is an annual payment based on the annual turnover. Therefore, it appears to be a payment for loss of revenue to the holding company and is dependent upon the business carried on by the assessee. The restrictive covenant is only for a period of 5 years and is extendable by a further period as mutually agreed to by both the parties. The agreement is also liable to be terminated with prior notice of 10 months. The agreement also includes various other services to be provided by the holding company to the assessee company and the payment was not just for non-competition. In this view of the matter also, the payment made by the assessee to the holding company is revenue expenditure as without the said payment, the assessee could not have carried on its business more efficiently and profitably. Therefore, the payment is in the nature of revenue expenditure and is an allowable deduction under section 37(1). [Para 9]

In the result, assessee's appeal is allowed. [Para 10]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Where assessee-firm took over running business of a trust and transfer was irrevocable, recurring payment made by assessee to trust for use of goodwill and other assets of trust could only be treated as capital expenditure
The assessee-firm had taken over a hotel and restaurant under the name ‘Vishala’ which was acquired in pursuance of an agreement between the assessee-firm and S. Family Trust. Earlier to the agreement, the aforesaid trust was carrying on business under the name and style of ‘Vishala’. Even in the assessee-firm, the trust was one of the partners. It was claimed by the assessee that the assessee had to pay a recurring expense of Rs. 1 lakh or 5 per cent of its sale, whichever was more, per year, for the use of goodwill and other assets of the trust under agreement, dated 2-6-1983. This payment was claimed to be of revenue nature and, therefore, to be deducted while computing appellant’s income.
Held that, in the instant case, there was transfer of a running business with all assets and liabilities including goodwill. There was absolutely no clause in the agreement which would indicate that transferor on the happening of a particular event was entitled to get back the running business or any part thereof. The party of the first part had no right at all to terminate the agreement. Therefore, there was complete transfer of running business from party of first part to party of second part for a consideration as provided in clause (8) of the agreement. The consideration as provided in the above clause was the total consideration for all assets including building, furniture and other assets and goodwill. The right vested in the party of first part in no way affected the passing of the property from the said party to party of second part. The mere fact that consideration was to be paid annually or through instalment would not affect the transfer of asset and the running business which was clearly of capital nature.
The conduct on the part of the assessee clearly clinched the issue that a capital asset in the shape of running business of restaurant and hotel was transferred to the assessee under the agreement. On building and other assets the assessee claimed depreciation as owner for the consideration paid as per clause (8) of the agreement. Having regard to the fact that amount in question was paid for acquiring an asset of enduring nature, the payment was rightly held to be of capital nature and not deductible.

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-During 1960 assessee-company entered into a 20-year agreement with foreign company for obtaining technical consultation and training facilities-Assesses paid Rs. 12 lakhs in lump sum initially and was to reimburse actual expenses incurred by foreign company from time to time in rendering stipulated services-Tribunal allowed assessee to spread said expenditure of Rs. 12 lakhs over 20-year period of agreement, treating it as revenue expenditure and thereby rejecting revenue's stand that it was capital expenditure which could not be spread over above-said period-Whether tribunal's view legally correct-Held, on facts, yes

lot of circumstances and the ultimate answer would depend upon a commonsense appreciation of the guiding features.

In the instant case, the assessee had established a good reputation and market for writing inks by the manufacture and sale of ink, under the brand name 'quink'. In the agreement, there was a recognition of the formation and establishment of the partnership by A for the manufacture and sale of writing inks, similar to those made and sold by the assessee and it being a powerful potential competitor. The desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership was also clearly spelt out from the terms of the agreement. The negotiated settlement under the terms and conditions set out in the agreement, was clearly relatable to the desire of the assessee to avoid competition from the partnership backed by the experience and expertise of the ex-managing director, whose wife and daughters were the partners in the same line of business activity as that of the assessee. Undoubtedly, the activity of the partnership in setting up a competitive business was harmful to the assessee and the agreement was the outcome of the prospect of power competition from the partnership and a desire on the part of the assessee to protect itself against that disadvantage. Further, the departure of A from the assessee-company and the prospect of his making available his experience and expertise in the manufacture and marketing of ink to his wife and daughters, who were the partners of the firm, would have rendered the goodwill of the assessee vulnerable, as the assessee, when it commanded the benefit of the services of A, was in an advantageous position. There was, thus, a positive detriment to the assessee due to the competition from the partnership and against such damaging competition, the assessee obtained the benefit of a restrictive covenant against such powerful competition. That resulted in the assessee buying of potential competition, which was a positive detriment owing to such competition, and had also enabled the assessee not only to safeguard its goodwill, but also to enhance it. The payment of Rs. 1,00,000 by the assessee to the partnership was to secure advantages resulting in the removal from the arena of a possible competition and securing the elimination of a risk or detriment to the assessee due to competition. Though under the terms of the agreement, the benefit of the restrictive covenant was to enure only for a period of five years, from the facts stated in the order of the Tribunal and also the terms of the dissolution deed, it was seen that the partnership, which was a potential competitor, had also vanished and A had also left the shores of India. That would clearly establish that what the assessee had paid for was of permanent or enduring quality, in the sense that the competition had been totally eliminated and a protection had been acquired for the business of the assessee as a whole. In other words, the amount paid by the assessee was no part of the working or operational expenses of the assessee, but its aim and object was acquisition of an advantage of enduring nature, viz., freedom from competition from the partnership for the rest of the period of the business activities of the assessee.

Therefore, the consideration paid in terms of agreement was an expenditure of capital nature.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1995-96 - Whether payment made to avail possibility of 
 an advantage should be considered as a payment made to remove a possible disadvantage and it is not a payment to acquire an enduring advantage - Held, yes - Assessee-company which was doing only financing business amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’ carrying on business of entertainment and paid certain amount to two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan, by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for next ten years - Assessee-company claimed deduction of amount paid as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Assessing Officer disallowed assessee’s claim and treated expenditure as capital expenditure for a new distinct business - Whether since Memorandum of Association authorized transferee-company to carry on business of transferor-company, it could not be said that payment was made by assessee for new and distinct business - Held, yes - Whether services of artists were obtained for ten years, but for facilitating their continued co-operation, which would go to increase assessee’s profitability, it was for 120 days in a year and artists were free to work anywhere else and, therefore, payment made to artists was for user of brand equity or talents and not for acquisition of capital asset as such - Held, yes - Whether assessee made payment to avail performance of artists when it was expedient to get artists in interest of trade and, therefore, same was allowable as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since expenditure was incurred in year under consideration, same was to be allowed in year of payment itself - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was doing financing business and its main source of income was dividend and interest. The board of directors of the assessee-company decided to enter into the new business of entertainment. Therefore, the assessee-company amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’, which was owned by the film star Amitabh Bachchan, and this was approved by the jurisdictional High Court. The assessee paid certain lump sum amount to the two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for the next ten years. The assessee claimed deduction of the same as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and treated the expenditure in question as a capital expenditure. He held that the payment in question was made for acquiring a new asset, i.e., the brand/copyright, that is to say, a source of earning profit itself. The Assessing Officer further held that the revenue expenditure would be incurred every year, whereas the payment to both the stars was for once and for all and it was, therefore, a payment of enduring nature and also a source itself. The Assessing Officer also rejected the contention of the assessee that the artists were not prevented totally in carrying on their profession as artists, holding that, in fact, by virtue of the aforesaid agreements the assessee had an exclusive control over the services of the artists. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee had now entered into a new field of entertainment business and this was not an expansion of existing business, but a new line of business.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the artists had agreed to perform the diverse acts for the assessee, whereby the assessee could generate revenues from them and also copyrights on the products. Thus, it was the user of brand equity obtained by the assessee and not any capital asset as such. He further held that the expenditure incurred in acquiring goodwill of course was capital expenditure, but the payment made towards user of goodwill was of revenue nature and allowable as such. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, held that the expenditure in question incurred by the assessee definitely was not of capital nature, but of revenue. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340 further held that the payment was made for the right to use the artists for ten years and, hence, the payment in question was to be spread over every year equally.

On cross appeals :

HELD: The Memorandum of Association authorized the transferee-company to carry on the business of transferor-company. Hence, the view canvassed by the revenue that the payment was made by the assessee for a new and distinct business, was liable to be rejected. [Para 56]

HEADNOTE: III-Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Whether amount of fee paid by assessee company to its Ex-Managing Director on his retirement to restrict him to share his experience and expertise for a period of 3 years, was an allowable revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee] [Paras 18 and 19]

FACT: During the relevant accounting year, the assessee company had paid certain amount to its Ex-Managing-Director as non-compete fee on his retirement from the services. That fee represented compensation for not joining any company or share any expertise with companies having same business for a period of three years. Since such a payment was made to Ex-Managing Director to restrict him to share his experience and expertise for a period of 3 years, so that there was no immediate threat to the interest of assessee's business, therefore, the same was business expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer held that such payment of non-compete fee would result into enduring benefits to the assessee. Accordingly, the same was treated as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such a payment was paid for a restriction of three years and therefore, there is no question of any enduring benefit coming to the assessee. Moreover, the said Ex-Managing Director expired before the said period of three years, thus, such a payment was nothing but revenue expenditure.

On appeal by the Revenue:

HELD: In the instant case the assessee had paid non-compete fee to its Ex-Managing Director for restrciting him to share his expertise or to join any other company in a similar line of business of chemicals for a period of three years on certain consideration. Since the agreement for restrictive covenant was only for the period of three years to ward off a potential threat or completion, it was held that there could be no question of enduring benefit for a long period. [Para 18]

However, such a payment is also to be seen from the context of commercial and business expediency. If the outgoing expenditure is so inextricably linked or related to carrying on or conduct of the business, that is, it can be regarded as integral part of the profit earning process and not for any acquisition of asset or a right of permanent character and incurring of the expenditure is a condition for carrying on the business, then such an expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure. In the instant case the agreement for payment of non-compete fee was only to protect the existing business for a temporary period to ward off completion so that assessee could get stabilizing period without its long serving MD. Here no new assets of any enduirng benefit had arisen to the assessee on such payment. If the advantage was not for longer period and not enduring in nature, then such a payment of non-compete fee was nothing but business expenditure which was on revenue account. On similar facts and circumstances, the Delhi High Court also in the case of Eicher Ltd. (2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure. (3) If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operation, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit, may, nonethe-less, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down. It is not every advantage of enduring nature acquired by an assessee that brings the case within the principle laid down in this test. What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The test of enduring benefit is, therefore, not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal rights, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

In view of the above discussion, the amount paid to 'E' was essentially revenue expenditure insofar as the same was spent for improving the working of the company's staff, thereby facilitating the assessee's trading operation while leaving the fixed capital untouched. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly allowed the assessee's claim.

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal of the assessee as being devoid of any merit. The High Court opined that expenditure incurred by the assessee by way of non-compete fee paid to L&T could not be claimed as a revenue expenditure as it was clearly a capital expenditure. Despite holding the expenditure to be capital in nature, the High Court was of the further view that the non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for 7 years did not result in depreciable intangible asset. It was held that the right acquired by the assessee by payment of non-compete fee was a right in personam only against L&T for a period of 7 years. It was not a right in rem.

■

Adverting to the expression 'similar business or commercial rights' appearing in section 32(1)(ii), the High Court opined that it has to necessarily result in an intangible asset against the entire world to qualify for depreciation under the said provision. The High Court therefore dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

The non-compete compensation from the stand point of the payer of such compensation is so paid in anticipation that absence of a competition from the other party may secure a benefit to the party paying the compensation. In so far the present case is concerned, on account of payment of non-compete fee, the assessee had not acquired any new business and there is no addition to the profit making apparatus of the assessee. Such payment made by the appellant to L&T did not create a monopoly of the appellant over the business of electronic products/ equipments. Payment was made to L&T only to ensure that the appellant operated the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment made to L&T cannot, therefore, be considered to be for acquisition of any capital asset or towards bringing into existence a new profit earning apparatus. [Para 28]

■

That being the position, it is opined that payment made by the appellant to L&T as non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1). [Para 29]

■

Consequently, the impugned judgment and order of the Delhi High Court dated 5-11-2012 passed in Income Tax Appeal No. 492/2012 is hereby set aside. The question framed is thus answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 30]

■

As regards the remaining appeals, it is viewed that it would be appropriate if the matters are remanded back to the respective ITATs, all appeals/ cross-appeals filed are revived and heard afresh having regard to the ratio laid down in this judgment. [Para 32]

■

Ordered accordingly. [Para 33]

(v )where the expenditure has a direct nexus, connection or relation to the carrying on or conducting the business of the assessee, it must be regarded as an integral part of the profit-making process and in such a case it must be held to be a revenue expenditure; and

(vi )the period for which a right or benefit is available is not relevant because if the expenditure is found to have direct nexus with the profitability, then that test must fail. If the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores incurred by the assessee had been considered in the light of the assessee’s necessity or commercial expediency, it would be found that it satisfied both the tests because as admitted by the revenue authorities, the non-competition agreement was to enhance the assessee’s sales of relevant two chemicals in central and eastern parts of India without any competition. Even otherwise, the benefit to be procured by the assessee for a period of five years could not be said to be of ‘enduring nature’, and since the revenue authorities had rejected the assessee’s claim solely on the ground that the benefit procured by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’, the orders of the revenue authorities could not be upheld.

Even if the benefits derived by the assessee in the instant case were of enduring nature, then also the assessee was to succeed because of the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 /3 Taxman 69 and the findings to the effect that the effect of the agreement in question being directly related to the sale and production capacity of two chemicals, which in turn had effect of carrying on the assessee’s business efficiently and profitably in central and eastern parts of India and the test of enduring nature would fail and the expenditure had to be held as revenue expenditure.

Therefore, the expenditure incurred by the assessee by entering into a non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ was of revenue nature and, hence, an allowable deduction.

The another observation of the Assessing Officer for holding the expenditure in question to be capital expenditure was that there was no fear of competition from ‘V’ or that ‘V’ would not have been able to compete within a period of 5 years and that the assessee was to continue to get the benefit, even after 5 years, which was of ‘enduring nature’. However, the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) had considered the threat of competition only with reference to ‘V’ and not with reference to its founder ‘M’ in his individual capacity and, therefore, the conclusion arrived at by them could not be sustained in law. Further, the chemicals produced by ‘V’ before sale of the manufacturing plant to the assessee were being sold in a particular area, i.e., in the central and eastern parts of India and probably without any brand which would mean that whatever market ‘V’ and its founder had captured was only because of their personal rapport with the consumers of these two chemicals and, therefore, in the presence of other manufacturers of these two chemicals situated in that area ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ could enter into market for selling the chemicals produced by those manufacturers and were definitely a potential threat at least in central and eastern parts of India. Consequently, the revenue authorities’ observation that the benefit to be derived by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’ because ‘V’ was not in a position to compete during the period of 5 years because it could not start manufacturing these chemicals within 5 years and by that the assessee would get established itself so well in the market that it would be difficult to dislodge was misplaced, without any basis or reasoning and devoid of any merit. The expenditure had to be seen from the angle of the business or the businessman and not from the revenue’s attitude and it is so because had the assessee any mala fide intention to reduce its tax burden, it could have easily included the payment of Rs. 6 crores in purchase price of the manufacturing plant itself and could have purchased the plant for Rs. 35 crores instead of Rs. 29 crores. In that case, the assessee would have got depreciation on whole of the amount, i.e., including payment of Rs. 6 crores and in that situation nobody was going to question the assessee’s bona fide and, therefore, to term the expenditure as of capital nature, only because the assessee had claimed the payments separately, was not justified.
