Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income (Revenue or capital receipt) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2008-09 - Assessee paid an amount of Rs. 1.30 crores for purpose of taking liner business of a German company from their existing agent and same was transferred to assessee's name - Later on, assessee lost business to Agent of German Company - On termination of agency, assessee received compensation of Rs. 59.96 lakhs from parent company - Assessee set off compensation received out of payment made for purpose of securing agency business and claimed balance amount as revenue expenditure - It was observed that compensation received by assessee was not from person to whom payment of Rs. 1.30 crores was made for securing agency business and, thus, had nothing to do with acquiring of agency - Whether treatment given by Assessing Officer of expenses incurred for securing agency business as capital expenditure and receipt of compensation on termination of agency business as revenue in nature was justified - Held, yes [Para 29] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: HAL was a government company. The rail coach division which was functioning as a unit of HAL was transferred on 1-1-1965 as a going concern to BEML, another government company, which was the present assessee HAL had incurred development expenditure towards designs and models of integral coaches which it had amortised and had been claiming and was allowed deduction on amortisation principle. At the time of transfer of the division, there was unabsorbed expenditure of a certain amount in the books of HAL, which, according to the terms of the transfer was also taken over by BEML and reimbursed to HAL. Originally, the assessee (BEML) claimed only a part of the amount as deduction in the relevant assessment year on the amortization principle. Subsequently it claimed the entire amount as revenue expenditure in its assessment for the assessment year 1965-66. The ITO dissallowed the first claim and did not consider the second. On appeal, the AAC allowed part of the expenditure on amortisation basis, but the Tribunal accepted the revenue's appeal and restored the ITO's order.

HAL had also executed preliminary works relating to manufacture of heavy earth moving equipment unit and had incurred expenditure of a certain amount, a major portion of which represented technical assistance fee paid to the collaborator. On transfer of this unit to BEML, the latter reimbursed this expenditure to HAL and claimed it as deduction in its assessment. The claim was not allowed by the ITO and the assessee's appeals to the AAC and the Tribunal were also rejected. For its conclusion that the expenditure was of capital nature and, therefore, not allowable, the Tribunal followed the Karnataka High Court's decision in Mysore Kirloskar v. CIT [1968] 67 ITR 23 . The other reason for the Tribunal upholding the disallowance was that at the time the collaboration agreement was entered into, the HAL was not manufacturing any article of the type of earth moving equipment, and the expenditure on drawings, etc., was initial outlay of the business. The remaining expenditure was on training of officers and, according to the Tribunal, the experience gained by them was an intangible asset of the assessee-company and, hence the expenditure was of capital nature.

On reference:

HELD: So far as the unabsorbed revenue expenditure on development of designs and models of integral coaches, was concerned, HAL had not claimed it earlier because it was following the amortisation principle of accounting. But that was no bar for the assessee (BEML) to claim the amount in toto in the assessment year in question as business expenditure, since the amount was admittedly paid in the relevant year for the purpose of its business.

The main reason given by the Tribunal for disallowing the claim of the assessee, viz., that the assets taken over by the assessee in consideration for the payment representing this expenditure were mainly of an intangible nature, was inaccurate. The assessee paid that amount towards unabsorbed expenditure incurred by HAL on development of designs and development of various models of rail coaches, etc., taken over by the assessee. In the case of HAL, similar claim had been allowed by the revenue accepting the amortisation basis. There was, therefore, no justification for denying the claim of the assessee, in the instant case.

Regarding the payment made for technical know-how, the decision relied upon by the Tribunal had since been overruled and in Mysore Kirloskar Ltd. v . CIT [1978] 114 ITR 443 (Kar.) , the Full Bench had taken the view that payments made under agreement for acquisition of technical know- how should be considered as business expenditure. Therefore, the payment made in the instant case towards technical assistance fee must be regarded as revenue expenditure. The distinction made by the Tribunal between initial outlay of expenditure and current needs of the business of the assessee was equally untenable. In fact, no distinction can be made between initial investment to commence busi- ness and current expenses for continuing production. The nature of the expenditure for obtaining technical know-how cannot ordinarily depend upon the time at which the collaboration agreement came into existence. It may depend upon the purposes for which it was entered into and the benefits derived therefrom.

So far as the nature of the amount paid by the assesses to HAL towards the expenditure incurred by the latter on training the officers was concerned, the reasoning of the Tribunal was right, so that the relevant amount had been rightly disallowed.

The assessee was a firm of exchange brokers. One 'M' was also carrying on business in co-partnership as exchange brokers. 'M' and his partner were exchange partner of firm namely 'R' brothers – In year 1927, an agreement was entered into between assessee-firm and 'M'. As per terms of said agreement, 'M' was to transfer four seats in the Calcutta Exchange Brokers' Association, belonging to the firm of which he was partner, in favour of the assessee-firm. The goodwill of the firm was to be absolutely transferred in favour of the assessee-firm. The consideration mentioned in the agreement was £4,000 for transferring the four seats in the association and for the sale of the goodwill. It was further agreed that 'M' would not in future and at any time work as exchange broker or in any way compete with the assessee-firm, and the consideration for such agreeing not to enter into competition with the assessee-firm as exchange brokers in Calcutta were annuities payable during the lifetime of 'M' to him and after his death to his wife. The payment of the annuities was made contingent and payable 'only and so long as the brokerage earned from 'R' Brothers was not less than the double of the amount of such payment of annuity in each year. In certain circumstances the annuity was to be proportionately reduced and if the firm 'R' Brothers ceased to carry on business in Calcutta, the annuities would forthwith cease.

In view of aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held that the payment in question constituted revenue expenditure which, having admittedly been laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business, was properly allowable as an admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xii) of the 1922 Act.

On appeal by the department : HELD: The auditors of the assessee-company had treated the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores as deferred revenue expenditure to be amortised over a period of 3 years and it was, accordingly, debited to ‘Deferred revenue expenditure account’. Accordingly, in the balance-sheet and profit and loss account as at 31-3-1998 an amount of Rs. 71,66,667 was written off and balance of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was shown as balance under the head ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. It showed that in the profit and loss account only a claim of Rs. 71,66,667 was made as per auditor’s note. However, in computation of income, the assessee added Rs. 71,66,667 to the declared loss and claimed the entire sum as deduction. The balance sum of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was taken in the balance-sheet under the head ‘Miscellaneous expenditure’ stating that sum as ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. Thus, after adding the said sum, the assessee claimed, in the computation of income, the entire sum of Rs. 2.15 crores as revenue expenditure in the relevant assessment year. [Paras 10, 11 and 12]

The facts in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were entirely different from those of the instant case. Thus, the assessee’s reliance on the said decisions and then claiming the entire amount paid in purchasing new business as revenue expenditure was misplaced and incorrect. [Para 16]

In the instant case, the assessee purchased (i) a running business, (ii) right to publish two titles and (iii) complete and exclusive ownership basis along with all the rights and benefits attached thereto. As an ancillary to the purchase of titles and running business, the assessee also got detailed list of subscribers, advertisers and employees, who wanted to continue with the assessee after takeover. Thus, in addition to titles, the assessee also purchased something akin to goodwill. Same customers and advertisers would remain attached to the titles. [Para 18]

The tests to come to the conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature are that the expenditure is incurred to :

(i )set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in the same line.

(ii )commence a business.

(iii )acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity.

(iv )acquire an asset.

(v )acquire a source of generating income.

All the tests led to one inescapable conclusion that what the assessee had spent was for acquiring a new business/new assets/an enduring benefit and a source of income. From all the tests, the expenditure incurred could not have been considered under section 37(1) under which claim was made.

Hence, the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores was a capital expenditure. [Para 20]

The decisions in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were not even remotely connected with the assessee’s case. An issue on which the Tribunal has expressed an opinion in favour of the assessee or which has been regarded as debatable by any court would certainly be debatable on which there can be another opinion. There could not be second opinion, and had not been, on the facts of the assessee’s case, that the expenditure incurred on acquiring a new business, a source of income, an asset and benefit of enduring nature could not be revenue in nature. Hence, there was no debatable issue in the instant case. [Para 21]

In the instant case, the facts missing from the return filed were : (i) to whom the payment of Rs. 2.15 crores was made, when and how. (ii ) copy of agreement with the seller [which was given at the time of scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) only]. (iii) that the assessee was purchasing a new business. (iv) the names of the journals and the fact that the titles were purchased on an exclusive ownership for all the time to come along with all the paraphernalia of employees and space on rent. Thus, the claim of the assessee that the expenditure in question was a revenue expenditure was not bona fide. [Paras 24 and 25]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee was engaged in business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products - Assessee-company acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by assessee with latter - Consideration for such transfer included certain non-compete fee which was limited for a period of five years - For assessment year 2005-06, assessee filed its return of income wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, however, disallowed same on ground that payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay - Commissioner (Appeals) held that expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years - On second appeal, Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by assessee was capital in nature, as such disallowed claim - It was noted that assessee itself treated expenditure as capital in books of account - Likewise, in schedule 2 to balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets' - This also showed that assessee treated this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature - Whether in view of above, Tribunal rightly held expenditure as capital in nature - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products. During the year under consideration, the assessee company had acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by the assessee with the latter. The consideration for such transfer was stated as Rs. 18.92 crores which included a sum of Rs. 5.94 crores by way of non-compete fee which was limited for a period of 5 years. For the assessment year 2005-06, the assessee filed its return of income, wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay, non-allowable under section 37. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by the assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as the period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years. The Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by the assessee was capital in nature, as such it disallowed the claim. Further, while dealing with the cross-objection filed by the assessee, the Tribunal restored the alternate plea in respect of allowance of depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) to the file of the Assessing Officer for deciding it.

On appeal:

HELD: Re: non-compete fee, whether capital or revenue:

The assessee itself treated the expenditure as capital in the books of account. However, at the same time, it was maintained that since it was paid for loss of business that 'KOAL' would suffer, the same was treated as revenue in nature. Likewise, in schedule 2 to the balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets'. This also showed that the assessee treats this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature. [Para 12]

In view of above, the Tribunal rightly held that the expenditure was capital in nature. [Para 14]

The assessee entered into agreements with two foreign companies for obtaining technical knowledge and information, training of Indian employees abroad and for use of trade name. In one case, the assessee was to establish a factory for the manufacture of trucks and other automotive products. For this, the payment was to be a percentage of net sales prices and net profits of the assessee's particular products. In the other case the foreign company's assistance was sought to start the operation of assessee-company's steel foundry for bringing it into effective commission. In the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee had paid towards fees Rs. 29,59,608 as share of profits to one company and Rs. 2,99,158 as lump sum fees to the other company. The assessee also incurred Rs. 1,69,925 as expenses on training its employees abroad by the foreign companies. All the three items were claimed as revenue expenditure but the ITO treated them as capital expenditure. On appeal, the AAC accepted the assessee's claim and allowed the appeal. On Department's appeal, the Tribunal considered the terms of the two agreements and found that, under one agreement, the assessee only got technical assistance and knowledge in regard to truck manufacture and the right to use its trade name for a specific period. It was thus really a case of fees being paid for user of technical know-how and trade name. Under the other agreement, it was the right to trade for purposes of carrying on its business upon the technical knowledge of the foreign company in regard to foundry business. In both the cases, the Tribunal opined that these items of expenditure had not resulted in acquisition or bringing into existence an asset or capital of enduring nature. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the payments were deafly revenue expenditure. Similarly, the expenditure on training was for running the business more efficiently so as to earn higher profits and was revenue in nature.

On reference :

The amount paid was but a part of the money paid by it for acquiring assets and goodwill as also to avoid competition in trade by the vendor. The payment made as compensation was clearly an expenditure of capital nature as the right acquired was of enduring benefit, the vendor having undertaken not to market the milk in the Madras city.

Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in not allowing the same.

One of the tests to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure is whether the expenditure in question was for bringing into existence an asset or an advantage of an ‘enduring nature’ and was made once and for all meaning thereby an expenditure made once for all for procuring an enduring benefit. The expressions ‘enduring benefit’ and ‘rights of a permanent nature’ are only descriptive and not definitive and are related in meaning not synonymous with perpetual or everlasting. [Para 7]

In the instant case, BSL had released its entire workforce and the marketing establishment relating to test and measurement products and closed its business of dealing in the said products. Even though the period of two years was mentioned in the agreement, the predominant intention and purpose, as discernible from the stipulations in the agreement, clearly indicated that the assessee-company had obtained the monopoly rights on a permanent basis and BSL went out of its business of dealing in test and measurement products, of HP, inasmuch as it released its entire workforce connected with the line of business started by the assessee. Expenditure in question was clearly of a capital nature inasmuch as the assessee had obtained an enduring benefit of eliminating competition in its line of business not over a period of two years only but also for succeeding years. The disallowance of expenditure was, therefore, justified. [Paras 8 and 12]

For the aforesaid reason finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether once expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred restraining recipient for a short or limited period, expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase profitability of assessee and is not a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Assessee purchased running business of a firm along with its goodwill and paid certain amount to partners of that firm for not carrying on same line of business for five years - Whether expenditure incurred by assessee was revenue in nature and, hence, allowable - Held, yes - Whether, however, since expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in relevant assessment year as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: During the relevant assessment year, the assessee purchased goodwill along with the running business from a firm for Rs. 10 lakhs. The assessee further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of said firm for not carrying on same line of business and other related fields for 5 years. In the computation of income, the assessee claimed the expenditure of Rs. 5 lakhs as revenue expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer treated the said expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee had purchased the goodwill and other rights for Rs. 10 lakhs which was treated to be capital expenditure. The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

IT: Where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietary concern, and in terms of agreement, company did not acquire copyright, but only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, license fee paid would be a revenue expenditure

To decide whether an expenditure of this nature is a capital expenditure or not would depend on the facts of the case. However, it is necessary to know whether the advantage derived by the payer is of an enduring nature, and for this, one of the considerations is the length of time for which the non-compete agreement would operate, although that is not decisive. While the length of time for which competition is eliminated may not strictly be decisive in all cases, yet, at the same time, it should not be so brief as to be virtually transitory. [Para 12]

In the instant case, the assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making the payment of non-compete fee. It merely eliminated competition in the two-wheeler business, for a while. From the record, it was not clear how long the restrictive covenant was to last, but it was neither permanent nor ephemeral. In that sense, the advantage was not of an enduring nature. There was also nothing to show that the amount of Rs. 4 crores was drawn out of the capital of the assessee. On a cumulative appreciation of the facts, it was clear that the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal did not err in concluding that the payment of non-compete fee by the assessee was a business expenditure and not a capital expenditure. [Para 17]

Therefore, the appeal was to be dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance - Before final acquisition, assessee was appointed as an administrator of company and was put in charge of establishment - Assessee paid certain amount to 'M' being deprivation charges and claimed said amount as revenue expenditure - Whether since amount had been paid as compensation for deprivation of income which 'M' would have earned, had it not been deprived of possession and no part of said amount was paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of undertaking of 'M', amount paid by assessee was in nature of revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance. During the period of litigation before final acquisition, the assessee was appointed as administrator of 'M' and it was put in charge of the establishment. The assessee paid a total consideration of Rs. 320.79 lakhs to 'M' out of which Rs. 122.79 lakhs (at the rate of Rs.11.39 lakhs per annum) was for deprivation of management and Rs. 198 lakhs was for acquisition of the undertaking. The assessee claimed that amount of Rs. 122.79 lakhs paid by it was a revenue expenditure. The Commissioner disallowed the assessee's claim and treated the entire amount as a capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal found that out of the amount of Rs. 320.79 lakhs, the amount of Rs. 198 lakhs was a capital expenditure, but the another sum of Rs. 122.79 lakhs, being deprivation charges, was in the nature of revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: From the calculation of the compensation, as broken up, it was clear that Rs. 198 lakhs was paid for acquisition of the undertaking of 'M'. Obviously, that was a capital expenditure, which was no more in dispute, and so far as that amount was concerned, admittedly, the title passed on from 'M' to the assessee, only by virtue of section 7 of the Metal Corporation (Nationalization and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 meaning thereby that till then the entire undertaking continued to be the property of 'M'. Notwithstanding that, since 'M' was deprived of the management and possession, as an administrator was appointed, who had run the industry during the intervening period, and who might have earned profit or might have incurred losses, but then the fact did remain, that 'M' could not run the undertaking, and earn any income therefrom. It appeared that said factor which had been taken into consideration, and it appeared to be agreed upon that 'M' would have earned the profits at the rate of Rs. 11.39 lakhs per annum, had it not been deprived of the possession and, therefore, it was directed to be compensated for the period during which it stood deprived of the possession and management. [Para 5]

If the acquisition would not have gone through, or would have ultimately failed, even then, 'M' would have been entitled to compensation for the deprivation, obviously, in which event the amount would not have been capable of being described as capital expenditure. Obviously, therefore, if the things went through, then too, that part of the amount could not be said to be the capital expenditure. Yet, another aspect of the matter was that no part of the amount of Rs. 122.79 lakhs was shown to have been intended, or have been contended by the parties, as paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of the undertaking of 'M'. [Para 6]

In that view of the matter, considering from any stand point, said amount could not be said to be a capital expenditure, and the Tribunal had rightly found so. The appeal, thus, having no force, was to be dismissed. [Para 7]

There could be no doubt that the payment of Rs. 40,100 which the assessee made to ‘MK’ Ltd. for procuring exclusively for its benefit the services, experience and technical knowledge of ‘B’ for the manufacture of castings, that is to say, for the purpose of setting the profit-earning machinery in motion, was an expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee-company. But an expenditure for the purpose of business may be of a capital nature; and if it is of that nature, then it cannot be claimed as deduction under section 37. The question, therefore, was whether the amount of Rs. 40,100 expended by the assessee was in the nature of capital expenditure or a revenue disbursement. The expenditure was incurred by the assessee once and for all for procuring the benefit and use of ‘B’s service, technical knowledge and experience. It was not any recurring expenditure in the nature of ‘operational expenses’. With that expenditure the assessee acquired an asset in the shape of ‘B’s technical knowledge and practical experience for the purpose of manufacturing castings and certain parts of diesel engines. The expenditure was not incurred for the purpose of earning profits in the conduct of the assessee’s business. The asset, which the assessee acquired, no doubt could not be compared with factory or office buildings, plant or machinery. The technical knowledge and practical experience of ‘B’ was an intangible ambience pervading the production and manufacturing organisation of the assessee. The benefit of the services, technical knowledge and experience of ‘B’ which the assessee acquired exclusively after paying Rs. 40,100 to ‘MK’ Ltd. was an advantage or asset for the enduring benefit of the assessee’s business. So long as the assessee retained the services of ‘B’, for its exclusively productive and manufacturing purposes and expressed its value in its products, it was, a fixed capital of the assessee. The assessee acquired a source of knowledge and experience helpful in the manufacture of the castings and certain parts of diesel engines; and thus by making a payment of Rs. 40,100 secured an enduring advantage and an asset, which was a capital asset of its business.

For all these reasons, the sum of Rs. 40,100 paid to ‘B’ was a capital expenditure in respect of which the assessee could not claim any deduction under section 37.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1/3 Taxman 69, held that it is not a universally true proposition that what may be a capital receipt in the hands of the payee must necessarily be capital expenditure in relation to the payer. The fact that a certain payment constitutes income or capital receipt in the hands of the recipient is not material in determining whether the payment is revenue or capital disbursement qua the payer. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit may, nonetheless, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down; if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operation or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee’s business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal right, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

By applying these principles to the facts of the instant case, the payment made by the assessee was incurred for the purpose of preserving an existing asset and not for the purpose of acquiring any new benefit of an enduring nature. The two employees had access to the secret formula used by the assessee in its manufacturing process and by retaining them in the service of the company even after retirement, the company ensured that there would not be any competition from these persons by setting up rival manufacturing concerns. Thus, the company was only trying to protect its existing asset so that its business could be carried on smoothly without the apprehended competition from its own retired personnel. It is well-settled in law that expenditure incurred for preserving or protection of a business asset is revenue in nature and not capital expenditure. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in sustaining the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

Pavan Vad for the Appellant. R.K. Patel for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Holding company was doing business of chit fund in undivided State of Andhra Pradesh - Assessee-company was floated by holding company to do chit fund business exclusively in northern Telangana Districts - Holding company and assessee entered into a business agreement by which holding company rendered various services - In this agreement, both assessee and its holding company demarcated areas in which they shall carry out business operations - Assessee had to pay 1 per cent of its annual turnover to its holding company - Initially agreement was for a period of five years - Assessing Officer held that this agreement was for giving non-compete fee by assessee to its holding company which was capital in nature and hence, he disallowed same - Whether since agreement in question also included various other services to be provided by holding company to assessee company and payment was not just for non-competition agreement, payment made by assessee to its holding company was revenue expenditure as without payment of such non-compete fee, assessee could not carry on its business more efficiently and profitably - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure

FACT: The holding company was doing chit fund business in the undivided state of Andhra Pradesh. The assessee-company was floated by the holding company to do the chit fund business exclusively in northern Telangana Districts. Both the holding company and the subsidiary company entered into an agreement, according to which the assessee had to pay 1 per cent of its annual turnover for a period of five years as non-compete fee to the holding company for not carrying out its business in northern Telangana Districts. The agreement was also liable to be terminated at any time with a notice of 10 months by either parties. The payment made by the assessee was claimed to be revenue in nature on the ground that the payment was not only for non-competing, but was also for several other services rendered by the holding company to the assessee. It was also submitted that the assessee did not derive any benefit of enduring nature and, therefore, it could not be termed as capital expenditure.

The Assessing Officer was not convinced with the assessee's contentions. He held that the non-compete fee was capital in nature and, hence, disallowed the same and brought it to tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: As per various clauses of the agreement the holding company and the assessee herein have demarcated the areas and territory in which they shall operate and each of the two shall not carry out the operations in the areas allocated to each of them. The consideration to be paid by the assessee to its holding company for such restriction on its activities is at 1 per cent of the annual turnover. It is the case of the assessee that though the resolutions passed by the Board of Directors of the holding company was that the non-compete fee agreement is valid till 31-12-2060. The agreement was for a fixed period of 5 years only and the agreement was also liable to be terminated at any time with a notice of 10 months by either parties. [Para 4]

The first argument of the assessee was that, the holding company has offered the receipt to tax in its hands and therefore, it should be treated as revenue expenditure in the hands of the assessee as well. But, whether such treatment in the hands of the recipient would clinch the issue? It would not, because the nature of the payment could be capital in the hands of the payer, while it could be revenue receipt in the hands of the payee. For example, in the hands of the purchaser of a machinery, the payment would be capital in nature, while in the hands of the seller, it could be revenue receipt. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that because the receipt in the hands of the recipient i.e. the holding company has been accepted as a revenue receipt, it should be treated as revenue expenditure in the hands of the assessee is not acceptable. [Para 5]

The assessee-company, whose main business was as contractors, became a partner in a firm on 1-4-1980, with the sole intention of taking over the firm’s business, which comprised, inter alia, business in cotton and kapas. The assessee claimed set off of this loss against its business income, but the ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that, since it related to the acquisition of a business, it was a capital expenditure. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the assessee’s claim.

On the revenue’s appeal:

the OTCEI only enables one to do trading of securities through a network of computers of OTCEI dealers, located in different cities, which are connected to the Central Computer of the OTCEI through a satellite link up. In that sense, it, thus, helps the dealer in carrying on or running or managing the business of share dealer/dealings or share brokerage efficiently and profitably without creating in his favour any advantage of enduring benefit on capital field. [Para 7.30] It was not in dispute that the said dealership was not transferable and neither the admission fee was refundable in any case. Even if the assessee decided or forced to terminate the dealership or if the OTCEI terminated the dealership, the admission fee was not refundable to the assessee as was clearly evident from the terms and conditions of appointment as a dealer of OTCEI. Similarly, the payment of technology cost for providing training to the assessee’s employees for the purpose of making them qualified as per OTCEI’s qualification procedure was found to be necessary or condition precedent for carrying on day-to-day business as a dealer on OTCEI and to operate the counter thereof. The aim and object of the aforesaid expenditures were, thus, for carrying on the assessee’s business and as such those were of the revenue in nature. On the facts of the case, there was no reason to hold that the assessee had derived an advantage of enduring nature on capital field or otherwise had acquired any capital asset. [Para 7.31]

The appointment as a dealer on the OTCEI could not be equated to the Stock Exchange membership of the Calcutta Stock Exchange. It is settled that if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee’s business to be carried on more effectively or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on the revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The criteria of ‘once and for all’ payment did not render the payments in question as of capital in nature as it is settled that the expression ‘once and for all’ is used to denote an expenditure which is made once and for all for procuring an enduring benefit to business in capital filed as distinguished from a recurring expenditure in the nature of operational expenses. In the instant case, the expenditure had been incurred for running the business of share dealing and share brokerage as an integral part of the profit-earning process or operation. What was material was the nature and substance of the payment. The purport and object of becoming dealer on OTCEI was to facilitate the assessee’s trading operations or to enable the assessee to carry on its business more efficiently, extensively and profitably in the background of rapidly changing and advancing economic realities of stock business. [Para 7.32]

Therefore, the payment of admission fee to become a dealer on OTCEI and to operate the counter, and the payment for imparting training to the assessee’s employees so as to make them qualified as per guidelines laid down by OTCEI were to be held as the revenue expenditure and the orders of the authorities below were to be set aside on that issue. [Para 7.34]

No doubt, the amount received by Telco was intended to meet the cost of construction of the hostel, and the hostel was to be Telco's property. And when the assessee made the payment, it was aware that it would be so applied by Telco. But so far as the assessee was concerned, it paid to Telco for the training imparted to the apprentices sent by the assessee. It paid the amount as training charge, and so far as the assessee was concerned, it remained a training charge, even though Telco applied it to the construction of the hostel and the assessee knew that it would be so applied.

The AAC had held that the amount represented payment made by the assessee to Telco in respect of the training scheme. That finding was not upset by the Tribunal. But, the Tribunal proceeded on the basis that under the training scheme the assessee was obliged to contribute towards the construction of the hostel. What the Tribunal omitted to consider was that the entire object of the scheme was the training of the assessee's apprentices and it was for that reason that payment was made by the assessee. There was no dispute that if Telco had not undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices there would have been no obligation on the assessee to pay the amount. One could not ignore that payment was made because Telco had undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices.

If expenditure is incurred for the purpose of increasing the profits while carrying on the business it must be treated as revenue expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee made payment to Telco on account of the training imparted by Telco to the assessee's apprentices. Trained personnel were necessary for the purpose of the assessee's business. It was necessary because a condition of the agency agreement with Telco required the assessee to have trained personnel. It was necessary also because the staff of trained personnel obviously induced better sales. There was no question here of the assessee acquiring any asset or advantage of an enduring nature. There was nothing to show that the personnel so trained were under bond to serve the assessee for a long term of years.

There was no question of the assessee acquiring any "know-how" from Telco which would become it property subsequently. The assessee had entered into an agreement to sell vehicles manufactured by Telco, and for the purpose of ensuring compliance with the agreement requiring the assessee to maintain a staff of trained personnel, it secured the training of its personnel form Telco and made payment thereof to it. It was open to the assessee to have its personnel trained from any other suitable center. There was nothing in the agreement binding the assessee to have its personnel trained by Telco. If it selected Telco for that purpose it was obviously persuaded by the circumstance that the vehicles in which it dealt were manufactured by Telco.

The payment made by the assessee to Telco was payment made wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business and it was not of a capital nature. The payment should have been allowed as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee carried on business as a dealer in motor vehicles. During the relevant period it was a dealer of Telco, under an agreement with that company, for the sale of Mercedes Benz trucks. The agreement required the assessee to maintain at its own expense an organization for the sale of vehicles, providing for maintenance of show rooms, service centers, repair shops, etc. and an adequate staff of trained salesman and a staff of trained technical service personnel. According to the agreement, the training was actually imparted by Telco which charged the assessee on that account. Under the training scheme, Telco proposed to build a hostel for the apprentices and to recover the entire cost of the hostel from its several dealers. The assessee paid Telco certain amount during the relevant accounting year and claimed that amount was a deduction from its assessable profits for the assessment year 1961-62. The ITO was of the view that the payment was made as the assessee's contribution towards the construction of the hostel, that the hostel would be the property of Telco and that, therefore, it was not a business expenditure. Accordingly, he rejected the assessee's claim.

The AAC allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that although the said amount was a contribution towards the construction of the hostel it was not an expense of a capital nature but was a revenue expense incurred in connection with the business of the assessee.

The Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO, holding that the amount was a capital expenditure.

The auditors of the assessee-company had treated the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores as deferred revenue expenditure to be amortised over a period of 3 years and it was, accordingly, debited to ‘Deferred revenue expenditure account’. Accordingly, in the balance-sheet and profit and loss account as at 31-3-1998 an amount of Rs. 71,66,667 was written off and balance of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was shown as balance under the head ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. It showed that in the profit and loss account only a claim of Rs. 71,66,667 was made as per auditor’s note. However, in computation of income, the assessee added Rs. 71,66,667 to the declared loss and claimed the entire sum as deduction. The balance sum of Rs. 1,43,33,333 was taken in the balance-sheet under the head ‘Miscellaneous expenditure’ stating that sum as ‘Deferred revenue expenditure’. Thus, after adding the said sum, the assessee claimed, in the computation of income, the entire sum of Rs. 2.15 crores as revenue expenditure in the relevant assessment year. [Paras 10, 11 and 12]

The facts in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were entirely different from those of the instant case. Thus, the assessee’s reliance on the said decisions and then claiming the entire amount paid in purchasing new business as revenue expenditure was misplaced and incorrect. [Para 16]

In the instant case, the assessee purchased (i) a running business, (ii) right to publish two titles and (iii) complete and exclusive ownership basis along with all the rights and benefits attached thereto. As an ancillary to the purchase of titles and running business, the assessee also got detailed list of subscribers, advertisers and employees, who wanted to continue with the assessee after takeover. Thus, in addition to titles, the assessee also purchased something akin to goodwill. Same customers and advertisers would remain attached to the titles. [Para 18]

The tests to come to the conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature are that the expenditure is incurred to :

(i )set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in the same line.

(ii )commence a business.

(iii )acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity.

(iv )acquire an asset.

(v )acquire a source of generating income.

All the tests led to one inescapable conclusion that what the assessee had spent was for acquiring a new business/new assets/an enduring benefit and a source of income. From all the tests, the expenditure incurred could not have been considered under section 37(1) under which claim was made.

Hence, the expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores was a capital expenditure. [Para 20]

The decisions in the cases of Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. (supra ) and Aquapump Industries (supra ) were not even remotely connected with the assessee’s case. An issue on which the Tribunal has expressed an opinion in favour of the assessee or which has been regarded as debatable by any court would certainly be debatable on which there can be another opinion. There could not be second opinion, and had not been, on the facts of the assessee’s case, that the expenditure incurred on acquiring a new business, a source of income, an asset and benefit of enduring nature could not be revenue in nature. Hence, there was no debatable issue in the instant case. [Para 21]

In the instant case, the facts missing from the return filed were : (i) to whom the payment of Rs. 2.15 crores was made, when and how. (ii ) copy of agreement with the seller [which was given at the time of scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) only]. (iii) that the assessee was purchasing a new business. (iv) the names of the journals and the fact that the titles were purchased on an exclusive ownership for all the time to come along with all the paraphernalia of employees and space on rent. Thus, the claim of the assessee that the expenditure in question was a revenue expenditure was not bona fide. [Paras 24 and 25]

The facts, which are not accurate, will be inaccurate. Accurate facts are those to which, if further facts are supplemented, would not alter the decision. Facts disclosed would be inaccurate if on further supplementing the facts, the decision would be reversed. Accurate facts also mean full and true facts, which have a material bearing on making computation of income. The facts disclosed by the assessee were half truth and, hence, not accurate, i.e., inaccurate. [Para 27]

The assessee-firm took over as a new line of business, a gas distribution agency, from a company, under an agreement. By a letter dated 4-12-1974, the company informed the assessee-firm that it was prepared to relinquish the said agency, and it will be the responsibility of the assessee to get the agency from the principals. Accordingly, the assessee acquired the distri-bution rights from the principals. Being new and inexperienced in this line of business, the assessee took the assistance, help and guidance of the company for running the business and claimed the technical fees paid for this purpose under an agreement as revenue expenditure. The ITO, however, took the view (i) that the business had merely changed hands ; (ii) that no technical services would be required for carrying on a running and established business ; and (iii) that mention about technical services in the agreement, though apparent, was not real, and the payment was obviously in the nature of goodwill. The ITO, therefore, disallowed the claim by treating it as capital expenditure. The AAC, however, agreed with the assessee that this was a different line of the assessee’s business, which required technical assistance, apart from observance of certain regulations stipulated by the principals, and allowed the assessee’s claim.

On second appeal :

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether to come to conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature, tests to be applied are where expenditure is incurred to set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in same line, to commence a business, to acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity, to acquire an asset and to acquire a source of generating income - Held, yes - Assessee purchased right, titles and ownership of two magazines/periodicals and agreement entered into between assessee and seller of two titles provided, inter alia, that seller was owner and publisher of titles, which were free from all charges, liens and encumbrances and assessee could, after purchase, use title and information in course of its
 business - Assessee claimed sum of Rs. 2.15 crores paid for acquiring titles of two magazines as revenue expenditure - Whether all tests led to one inescapable conclusion that what assessee had spent was for acquiring a new business/new assets/an enduring benefit and a source of income - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, expenditure of Rs. 2.15 crores was a capital expenditure not allowable under section 37(1) - Held, yes

The Memorandum of Association authorized the transferee-company to carry on the business of transferor-company. Hence, the view canvassed by the revenue that the payment was made by the assessee for a new and distinct business, was liable to be rejected. [Para 56]

It could not be said that the payment received by the artists, i.e., Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan, had already been held as capital receipt in the hands of the recipients and, therefore, it should naturally be treated as capital payment in the hands of the assessee as well. If the assessee had not paid a lump sum amount, the assessee was bound to make the payment as and when the engagements arose. The assessee had retained the senior artists. The artists are human beings. It is difficult to equate the performance of the artists on par with the use of some capital assets as such. [Para 57]

The transferor-company ‘S’ was in the field of entertainment business. As such, it was difficult to hold that the assessee was also not in the field of entertainment after the amalgamation, as approved by the jurisdictional High Court. It was true that the assessee’s only source of income was dividend and interest, but that finding of the Assessing Officer did not bring out the facts in its entirety. [Para 58]

Undoubtedly, the payment to acquire right, title and interest exclusively of cinema theatre can only be treated as acquisition of source itself. However, the payment to Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan, artists, was a payment for use of their artistic talents. It was not acquisition of source itself. Source would exist independently and they were also free to perform for others, except for the time and duration which was acquired by the assessee by virtue of the payments in question. [Para 59]

The agreement was for the performance of 120 days in a year for ten years and the payment was made in lump sum. For each year, the artists were exclusively available to the assessee. For the remaining days over the entire period of ten years they were free to perform for others. It was an agreement to pay for the performance and the assessee had no exclusive hold on them. The assessee was free to enter into agreement with other artists even for similar nature of performance. Had the assessee engaged the artists without this agreement for each and every engagement, the assessee had to make independent payment. In the instant case, the payment was consolidated and paid in lump sum. By making that payment in lump sum the assessee, in fact, saved a recurring payment, which was otherwise to be treated as revenue payment. [Para 60]

The assessee made the payment to avail the performance of the artists when it was expedient to get the artists in the interest of trade and, therefore, the same was deductible expenditure. The payment made to avail the possibility of an advantage should be considered as a payment made to remove a possible disadvantage and it is not a payment to acquire an enduring advantage. [Para 62]

Hence, the payment in question was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). [Para 64]

The decision relied upon by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. (supra) did not support the case of the revenue. The Commissioner (Appeals) had omitted a part of the said decision, which makes it clear that if an assessee claims expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the business purpose in the normal course, it should be allowed in the very same year. The Supreme Court has further held that it cannot be spread over a number of years, even if the assessee has written it off in its books of account over a period of years. That observation makes it clear that this cannot be allowed so because the assessee might be doing this purposely with an intention to have a distorted figure and claim the benefit or the assessee’s liability to pay tax may get a distorted picture. In the instant case, there was no evidence to show that this was actually the intention of the assessee. In the year under consideration, the expenditure was incurred and the assessee was claiming it. [Para 92]

In the instant case, the services of the artists were obtained for ten years, but for facilitating their continued co-operation, which would go to increase the assessee’s profitability, it was for 120 days in a year and the artists were free to work anywhere else. Thus, it was for user of brand equity or talents and not for acquisition of capital as such. [Para 93]

Thus, the payment made to the artists was not of capital nature because it was for the user of the talents and not for the acquisition of capital as such. [Para 94]

Therefore, the expenditure as claimed by the assessee was to be allowed in the year of payment itself. [Para 96]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1978-79 - Whether compensation paid for acquiring assets, goodwill and to avoid competition in trade by vendor, being expenditure to acquire right of enduring benefit, would be capital expenditure in nature - Held, yes

It was essential in the first instance to determine what was the real nature of the transaction between the parties which gave rise to this question, whether expenditure in question was in the nature of capital expenditure or revenue expenditure and the nature of the transaction that was to be considered was the agreement of sale by which G sold his whole undertaking to the assessee company. The first question for consideration was what was the price that the company had to pay to G for this undertaking? Now, in taxation matters it is not necessary to construe documents from their purely legal aspect. It is open to courts not merely to look at the documents themselves, but also to consider the surrounding circumstances so as to arrive at a conclusion as to what was the real nature of the transaction from the point of view of two businessmen who were carrying out this transaction. In all taxation matters more emphasis must be placed upon the business aspect of the transaction rather than on the purely legal and technical aspect; if and considering the transaction from that point of view, it was clear that the consideration for the sale of this undertaking could clearly be divided into two categories; first payment of a specific sum of Rs. 75,000 and the allocation of 500 preference shares to G; the second category consisted of the payment of a commission every year on the production by the company of coal. Now two or three important factors must be born in mind with regard to part of the consideration that fell under the second category: (1) the payment of commission was for an indefinite period. There was no limitation of time attached to it. (2) the payment of this commission had no bearing to profits but was related to the turnover of the assessee company. (3) no specific amount was mentioned in relation to which the payment of commission was to be attributed. Now a purchaser may buy a going concern and may fix a certain price and that price may be payable in a lump sum or it may be payable by instalments. The mere fact that a capital sum is payable by instalments spread over a certain length of time will not convert the nature of that payment from a capital expenditure into a, revenue expenditure; but the payment of instalments would always have some relationship to the actual price fixed for the sale of the particular undertaking. In the instant case, under the agreement the parties agreed that an indefinite sum for an indefinite period should be paid by the purchaser to the vendor so long as the collieries were in a working condition.

As the payment made by the assessee was a payment made for an indefinite period, a payment made in relation to the turnover of the company and not in relation to its profits, and as this payment had no bearing to any specific sum fixed as part of the price for the purchase of the undertaking, this payment was in the nature of revenue payment and not capital payment. Therefore, it could be concluded that the Tribunal was justified in holding that commission or annual payment made by the assessee company on the basis of coal raised from the colliery was revenue expenditure.

Note : The case was decided infavour of the assessee.

The assessee-company had a collaboration agreement with 'GIC' which trained its personnel in the operation and maintenance of float glass plant and also in its manufacturing and marketing. The assessee was engaged in the business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products. During the year under consideration, the assessee company had acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by the assessee with the latter. The consideration for such transfer was stated as Rs. 18.92 crores which included a sum of Rs. 5.94 crores by way of non-compete fee which was limited for a period of 5 years. For the assessment year 2005-06, the assessee filed its return of income, wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay, non-allowable under section 37. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by the assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as the period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years. The Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by the assessee was capital in nature, as such it disallowed the claim. Further, while dealing with the cross-objection filed by the assessee, the Tribunal restored the alternate plea in respect of allowance of depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) to the file of the Assessing Officer for deciding it.

On appeal:

INCOME TAX: Where assessee paid a non-compete fee to restrain another party from operating in same business segment, such payment merely protected or enhanced assessee’s business profitability and facilitated more efficient conduct of business, and though it could confer an enduring advantage, same was not in capital field and did not result in creation of any new asset or accretion to profit-earning apparatus; therefore, non-compete fee was allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1)

In the instant case the non-compete fee although identified separately by the valuer but it was inbuilt in the lump sum consideration. The assessee split the lump sum consideration in various tangible and intangible assets on the basis of report of the valuers which was not doubted either by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the present case, the only dispute was relating to the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores, the said amount was difference in the value of tangible/intangible assets of the going concern which was purchased by the assessee and the lump sum amount paid for taking over the business, so it was in the nature of the goodwill and since the assessee was having the enduring benefit particularly when there was a covenant on the seller for not to run the similar type of business for three years. Therefore, the said amount cannot be considered as revenue in nature as has been held by the Commissioner (Appeals). Since the amount under consideration was in excess of the value of tangible and intangible asset and was a part of the lump sum consideration for acquiring the business, so it was a goodwill. [Para 30]

Therefore, by considering the totality of the facts, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside on this issue and the view taken by the Assessing Officer that the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores was nothing but goodwill of the business and a capital expenditure is upheld.

Now question arises as to whether the assessee is eligible for depreciation on the goodwill. In this regard, it is relevant to point out that the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. SMIF Securities Ltd. [SLP (Civil) No. 35600 of 2009] held that the goodwill is eligible for depreciation under section 32. [Para 32]

In view of the above, it is held that the non-compete fee amounting to Rs. 6.80 crore paid by the assessee was capital in nature and was eligible for depreciation under section 32. [Para 33]

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business as a book binder and publisher. It entered into an agreement dated 15-11-1958, with ‘B’ under which it obtained the right to run the business of a publication concern for a consideration of a fixed sum of Rs. 5,000 per annum plus a sum equivalent to 10 per cent of the net profits of each year of business. On further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was an outright sale of the business by ‘B’ in favour of the assessee but that the payment of Rs. 15,497 was allowable as revenue expenditure, in view of the decision in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. 36/49 Holdings Ltd. [1943] 25 TC 173 (CA) and in Travancore Sugars and Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 62 ITR 556 (SC).

During the relevant accounting year, the assessee company had paid certain amount to its Ex-Managing-Director as non-compete fee on his retirement from the services. That fee represented compensation for not joining any company or share any expertise with companies having same business for a period of three years. Since such a payment was made to Ex-Managing Director to restrict him to share his experience and expertise for a period of 3 years, so that there was no immediate threat to the interest of assessee's business, therefore, the same was business expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer held that such payment of non-compete fee would result into enduring benefits to the assessee. Accordingly, the same was treated as capital expenditure.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such a payment was paid for a restriction of three years and therefore, there is no question of any enduring benefit coming to the assessee. Moreover, the said Ex-Managing Director expired before the said period of three years, thus, such a payment was nothing but revenue expenditure.

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of development of minerals and mines, extraction of ores, etc., including extraction of fluorspar. It held a mining lease on Survey No. 40 in a certain village. Another company MMC held a prospecting licence for extracting fluorspar from the adjacent Survey No. 30 and applied for a mining lease thereon and prepared a prospecting report also. Under section 11(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, MMC had a preferential right for obtaining such a lease, but the Government rejected its application whereupon it went to Court for redress and obtained interim orders restraining the Government from giving the said Survey No. 30 on lease to any other party. It had spent considerable amount on erecting its beneficiation plant for fluorspar which could run for the desired number of years only if it could get raw material from Survey No. 40 as well as Survey No. 30. The assessee-corporation, therefore, with a view to expanding its business, avoiding competition on the adjacent land and getting the required raw material for the desired number of years, entered into an agreement with MMC whereby it paid a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs to MMC on latter agreeing to withdraw the pending legal proceedings and give up its claim to Survey No. 30 to clear the assessee's path for obtaining a lease thereon. The Assessing Officer found during the course of assessment proceedings that a sum of Rs. 2.5 crores was reflected as a cost of office building purchased as on 31-3-2000. But in a subsequent year the company classified the amount as 'loans and advances' and added back the depreciation claimed on the office building. On the change of the stand, the assessee explained that a sum of Rs. 2.5 crores was given by an earlier company, namely, JI Ltd. for acquiring the use of premises for business purposes. This advance was given by JI Ltd. when it was not amalgamated with the assessee-company. After amalgamation, the claim of depreciation which continued to be passed on to the assessee-company was claimed but the error was rectified by filing the revised return. Thus, an error had crept in classifying the sum of Rs. 2.5 crores as an asset which was thereafter reclassified as 'loans and advances'. The Assessing Officer, however, did not agree with this explanation and held that the assessee-company had made advances to one of the directors of the company by camouflaging it as a security deposit. The company had paid huge interest on its borrowings to the extent of Rs. 83,42,846. He also held that reclassification of fixed assets into 'advances' was done with a mala fide intent to evade payment of tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim on the ground that expenditure of Rs. 2.5 crores was incurred out of share capital raised by JI Ltd. and it had no element of cost.  Held that investment in the property was done by JI Ltd. prior to its amalgamation with assessee-company and was out of funds raised in public issue by that company. Later on, this company merged with the assessee resulting in transfer of asset to the present company. Even though reclassification from 'asset' to 'loans and advances' may not be free from doubt but the fact that the investment in the property was clearly out of interest-free funds being the share capital raised by earlier company. Therefore, the question of disallowing interest paid by the assessee-company did not arise. The expression 'enduring advantage' is a relative term, not enduring in the sense of its being permanent, but is sufficiently durable depending upon the nature of the terms upon which it can be acquired [Devidas Vithaldas & Co. v. CIT [1972] 84 ITR 277 (SC)]. To decide whether an expenditure is capital or revenue in nature, what is decisive is the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure, the nature of the right acquired, and their relation, inter se, and this is the only key to resolve the issue in the light of the general principles, which are followed in such cases [K. T. M. T. M. Abdul Kayoom v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 689 (SC)].

To find out whether an expenditure is on the capital account or on revenue, one must consider the expenditure in relation to the business. Since all payments reduce capital in the ultimate analysis, one is apt to consider a loss as amounting to a loss of capital. But this is not true of all losses, because losses in the running of the business cannot be said to be of capital. The questions to consider in this connection are: For what was the money laid out? Was it to acquire an asset of an enduring nature for the benefit of the business, or was it an outgoing in the doing of the business? If money be lost in the first circumstance, it is a loss of capital, but if lost in the second circumstance, it is a revenue loss. In the first, it bears the character of an investment, but in the second, to use a commonly understood phrase, it bears the character of current expenses [CIT v. Mysore Sugar Co. Ltd. [1962] 46 ITR 649 (SC)].

Whether an expenditure incurred by an assessee in any AY is an expenditure of revenue or capital nature leads to the following conclusions:—

(1)

If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business asset, it would be 'capital expenditure'. If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(2)

If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operations, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(3)

Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired for payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trademarks, it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(4)

If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with the net sales. The outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of 'capital expenditure'.

(5)

If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled, the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the 'capital' nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(6)

A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be 'revenue expenditure' or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment. Thus, if the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(7)

An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a 'capital expenditure'.

The question identified by the Court to be answered by it was as under—

Whether amount of owelty i.e., compensation deposited to equalize partition represents immovable property and would attract capital gain tax?

The High Court held as under— "The payment of Rs. 24 crores to Group A is to equalize the inequalities in partition of the assets of 'H' Ltd. The amount so paid is immovable property. If such amount is to be treated as income liable to tax, the inequalities would set in as the share of the recipient will diminish to the extent of tax. Since the amount paid during the course of partition is to settle the inequalities in partition, it is deemed to be immovable property. Such amount is not an income liable to tax. Thus, the amount of owelty i.e., compensation deposited by Group B, is to equalize the partition represents immovable property and will not attract capital gain. With regard to the argument that the assessee is liable to tax being interest on cash, suffice it to say, that such question or fact does not arise from the orders of the Tribunal. Consequently, it is held that the amount of compensation paid to the assessee to settle inequalities in partition, thus, a provision of owelty, represents immovable property and is not an income exigible to tax."

"Owelty" means the difference which is paid or secured by one coparcener to another, for the purpose of equalizing a partition: a lien created or a pecuniary sum paid by order of the Court to effect an equitable partition of property (as in divorce) when such a partition in kind would be impossible, impracticable, or prejudicial to one of the parties. In other words, it is a payment to balance (both) sides involved in a dispute.
