IMPROVEMENT OF TITLE

Section 55(1)(b)(2) speaks of 'expenditure of a capital nature incurred in making any additions or alterations to the capital asset'. Improving the owner's title to the asset is different from improving the asset itself. Therefore, the amount paid as and by way of settlement of a claim to a person who disputes the title of the assessee, cannot be said to be an expenditure by way of any improvement to the asset as such [CIT v. V. Indira [1980] 3 Taxman 155 (Mad.)].

In the case which arose before the Madras High Court in Kumudam Printers (P.) Ltd v. CIT [1997] 92 Taxman 372 (Mad.) the assessee-company purchased certain land and buildings under a registered sale deed for Rs. 11 lakhs. The Assessing Officer being of the view that the fair market value of said property was Rs. 16.94 lakhs and, hence, purchase consideration was understated in the sale deed, initiated proceedings for acquisition of the property. As a result of discussion between the vendor and department, the vendor agreed to pay capital gains tax that would arise in respect of the transaction on the basis that sale consideration was Rs. 16.94 lakhs, which came to Rs. 1.75 lakhs. To avoid acquisition proceedings, however, the assessee paid this amount on behalf of vendor and claimed the same as deduction for the assessment year 1975-76. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that expenditure was not incurred in the course of business of the assessee or for the purpose of earning income from its business and also because it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal agreed with the findings of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) that the liability to pay the capital gains tax was a statutory liability of the vendor and not of the assessee-company and, hence, as far as the assessee-company was concerned, the liability was that of a third party and further there was no stipulation at the time of sale to bind the assessee-company towards the tax liability of the vendor and the payment was made because of the interest which the persons in the management of the assessee-company had in the vendor and not because of any liability or threatened liability which had come upon the assessee-company and which the assessee tried to evade or avoid by agreeing to bear the liability. According to the Tribunal, the assessee never treated this amount as capital expenditure but wrote off the amount in its profit and loss account as a revenue expenditure and, hence, the amount could not be treated to go to enhance the cost of asset and the question of grant of depreciation on that amount would not arise.

On reference the Madras High Court held as under-

"At the stage of discussion between the vendor and the department, pursuant to which the vendor agreed to pay the capital gains tax on the transaction on the basis that the property had been transferred for the fair market value of Rs. 16.94 lakhs as determined by the Department, the assessee-company was never in the picture. It was only later that the assessee-company agreed with the vendor, a close relative of the purchaser, to effect payment of the said sum of Rs. 1.75 lakhs. The finding of the lower authorities was that the assessee had agreed to effect this payment because of its close relationship with the vendor. Whatever might have been the reason, the fact remained that the liability was not of the assessee and the assessee did not have anything to do with the said liability of the vendor. If the assessee-company had not agreed to effect the payment, the vendor would have to effect the payment. The payment of amount by the purchaser/assessee was only a voluntary and gratuitous payment of liability of a third party, i.e., the vendor. In view of the assessee having become the owner of the property on registration of sale deed, its title was complete and perfect and also its title to property was never questioned by anyone. In such circumstances, the question of treating the payment of liability of a third party as an expenditure of the assessee-company, much less for the purpose of business, could not at all arise. The Tribunal was, thus, right in holding that the said payment could not be allowed as cost of the asset.

In deciding that lump sum amount paid as lease premiums are expenditure of a capital nature much stress is laid on the magnitude of payments. However, in decided cases, much relevance has not been attached to the quantum of payments. In Cameron v. Prendergrast (Inspector of Taxes) [1940] 8 ITR Suppl. 75 (HL), it has been said that the magnitude of the payment is immaterial in determining whether certain expenditure is revenue or capital as the magnitude is a relative term.

In Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. v. CIT [1969] 74 ITR 484 , the Punjab & Haryana High Court has said that a lump sum payment may be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual rent payments and even a recurring periodic payment of instalments of a capital sum.

Justice H.R. Khanna in M.k. Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1972] 86 ITR 38 (SC), has made the following classical observation in the context of an expenditure being revenue or capital:

"The answer to the question as to whether an amount paid is a revenue expenditure or capital expenditure depends not so much upon the fact as to whether the amount paid is large or small or whether it has been paid in lump sum or by instalments, as it does upon the purpose for which the payment has been made and expenditure incurred. It is the real nature and quality of the payment and not the question or the manner of the payment which would prove decisive. If the subject of making the payment is to acquire a capital asset, the payment would partake of the character of a capital payment even though it is made not in lump sum but by instalments over a period of time. On the contrary, payment made in the course of and for the purpose of carrying on business or trading activity would be revenue expenditure even though the payment is of a large amount and has not to be made periodically." 3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

4. Section 44C covers head office expenses, whether common or solely for Indian branches: SC

Director of Income-tax (IT)-I, Mumbai v. American Express Bank Ltd. [2025] 181 taxmann.com 433 (SC)

The assessee, a non-resident banking company, filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year. While computing the income, the assessee claimed a deduction for expenses incurred at the head office directly related to the Indian branches.

The Assessing Officer (AO) contended that the expenses in question should be subject to the ceiling specified in Section 44C. The assessee claimed that the expenses in question could not have been classified as head office expenditure for the reason that Section 44C presupposes that at least a part of the expenditure is attributable to the business outside India. If this presumption does not hold, and the entire expenditure is incurred solely for the business in India, Section 44C would not apply.

The AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section.

Tests laid down by the Supreme Court to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure

3. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency. If the outgoing expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-earning process and not for the acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition for carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as the revenue expenditure - Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (1953) (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC).

In cases where the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for extension of a business or a substantial replacement of equipment, there is no doubt that it is capital expenditure. Where the expenditure is incurred while the business is going on and is not incurred either for extension of the business or for substantial replacement of the equipment, if it is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is properly attributable to capital and is of the nature of capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is made not for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage, but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. The aim and object of the expenditure would determine the character of the expenditure, whether it is capital or revenue expenditure. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may go to the test of fixed and circulating capital. If the expenditure incurred was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be of the nature of capital expenditure and if it was part of its circulating capital, it would be of the nature of the revenue expenditure. These tests are mutually exclusive - Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). The expression ‘asset or advantage of endur- ing nature’ was evolved to emphasise the element of a sufficient degree of durability appropriate to the context. There is also no single defi- nite criterion which, by itself, is determinative whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The ‘once for all’ payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way, having regard to the business realities. On facts it was held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should, therefore, be held to be revenue expenditure. Further, as the agreement pertained to a product already in the line of the assessee’s business and not to a new product, it indicated that what was stipulated was for an improvement in the operations of the existing business and its efficiency and profitability - Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 / 43 Taxman 312 (SC).

An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a 'capital expenditure'.

(8) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be 'revenue expenditure'. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which has to be dressed up or processed before it is converted into stock-in-trade, the expenditure incurred over it would be 'capital expenditure'.

The above principles are neither exhaustive nor intended to be. They only serve as guidelines to solve the problems that is before the Court [Hylam Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 310 (AP)].

Capital expenditure cannot become revenue expenditure simply on reason that it was incurred in connection with business activities which ultimately resulted in efficiently carrying on day-to-day business. Thus, the question of voluntary and/or involuntary payment is not material for determining capital or revenue nature of expenditure [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 63 Taxman 493 (SC)].

Ultimately, the question whether an expenditure is revenue in nature or capital in nature will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case taking into account the quality and quantity of the amount, the position of the parties, the object of the transaction which has impact on the business, the nature of trade for which the expenditure is incurred and the purpose thereof, etc. Simultaneously, each factor, by itself, is not decisive. It is the cumulative effect of all the facts and circumstances that would afford the prime guiding factor [J. K. Cotton Manufacturers Ltd. v. CIT [1975] 101 ITR 221 (SC)].

Test of enduring benefit not a conclusive test - It would be misleading to suppose that, in all cases, securing a benefit for the business would be prima facie capital expenditure so long as the benefit is not so transitory as to have no endurance at all. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, may, nonetheless, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down. It is not every advantage of enduring nature acquired by an assessee that brings the case within the principle laid down in this test. What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a, commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The test of enduring benefit is, therefore, not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case [Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 3 Taxman 69 (SC)].

Once for all payment test is also inconclusive - Capital expenditure is a thing that is going to be spent once and for all and income expenditure is a thing which is going to recur every year, but added that it was not and was not meant to be a decisive test. However, when an expenditure is made, not only once and for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, I think that there is very good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to an opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as properly attributable not to revenue but to capital [Vallambrosa Rubber Co. v. Farmer,(1910) 5 Tax Cas. 529].

There is also no single definite criterion which, by itself, is determinative whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The 'once for all' payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a common-sense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of enduring benefit might break down [Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC)].

Case Study 5.10.1.4 : PQR &Co. firm plans to construct a hotel on a site which is currently occupied by the residents of a small town. The firm agrees to pay the cost of relocating the residents to another site. Whether, as per ICDS-V(Revised), the cost of relocating should be capitalised as part of the cost of land for the hotel or as part of the hotel building?

Answer: The relocation is a direct result of the decision to acquire the land. Therefore, cost of relocating existing residents is directly attributable cost to make the land ready for its intended use. Therefore, cost of relocating should be capitalised as part of cost of land, not as part of cost of the hotel building.

Case Study 5.10.1.5 : A public sector company is engaged in refining and marketing of petroleum products. The company has entered into engineering agreements with a foreign licensor for transfer of know-how for installation of petrochemical plant at one of its refineries. The know-how can be used only for the company's own use and cannot be sold or transferred or leased to others. As per the agreement, the licensor will provide engineering and technical services in connection with the design of the plant. Whether, as per ICDS-V(Revised), the cost of technical know-how fee related to plant design incurred under the engineering agreement is to be capitalised as a part of the relevant plant? Or is it to be capitalised as a distinct asset i.e. intangible asset?

Answer: ICDS-I(Revised) requires treatment in accordance with substance of transaction and not merely its legal form. Therefore, in order to determine whether know-how should be capitalised as an intangible asset or as a part of relevant plant, judgment needs to be exercised as to which element is more significant, the PPE/TFA element or intangible element. The company should evaluate whether, in substance, any intangible part is actually integral to the larger asset or whether it is really a separate asset in its own right. In the present case, the technical know-how is integral to the plant which is required for installation of the petrochemical plant. The know-how can be used only for the company's own use and cannot be sold or transferred or leased to others. Since know-how has been acquired and will be used for installation of this plant only, the cost of knowhow should be capitalised as part of cost of relevant plant as directly attributable cost.

Case Study 5.10.1.6 : A manufacturing company contracted with a supplier to procure equipments over a period of 3 years. If company wishes to terminate the contract, company has to pay cancellation fees in respect of those equipments which are not procured by the Company as per the contract. The Company decides to terminate the contract at the end of year 1 since it has identified another supplier which would result in a significant reduction in cost for the company. It pays the cancellation fees in respect of the remaining equipments not yet procured. Whether, in terms of ICDS-V(Revised), the cancellation fee paid by the Company should be capitalised as part of the cost of the equipment purchased from the new supplier?

Answer: The cancellation fee is not directly attributable cost it is not directly related to the acquisition of the equipment and is not required to make equipment from the new supplier ready for its intended use. Hence, the cancellation fee should not be capitalised as part of the cost of the equipments purchased from new supplier. Rather, it should be expensed off as and when incurred.

The terms of the agreement clearly specify that the liquidated damages are paid as compensation for failure to meet performance conditions in terms of the desired quality and level of output subsequent to commissioning of the plant. The damages will be calculated based on the shortfall in the output as a percentage of the contract price. Whether such liquidated damages received be deducted from the cost of the related asset or offered to tax as income under the ICDSs?

Capital v. Revenue expenditure

8. The question whether payment made for acquiring technical know-how will fall for deduction as revenue expenditure was considered in detail by the Supreme Court. In Ciba’s case that was a case where the Indian subsidiary made contributions at fixed percentages on sale in consideration of technical consultancy services, use of trade marks, etc., to the Swiss Principal. There was also an agreement to keep information confidential. The patents and trade marks were to be returned to the Swiss company on termination of the agreement. The agreement was to be in force for five years. The Supreme Court held that the amount should be allowed as business expenditure. The Indian company did not become entitled exclusively to the patents and trade marks at any time. It had merely access to the technical knowledge and experience of the Swiss Major. The Indian company was a mere licensee.

Will the present amendment supersede this ruling of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 ? Obviously not. The very concept of depreciation pre-supposes at least limited ownership or title. If the collaboration agreement is drafted in the manner done by Ciba of India Ltd., obviously the entire payment will have to be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On the other hand, if the company acquires complete title over the process or patents different considerations will arise. In Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC), the question was whether know-how obtained on ‘once for all’ payment for increasing the yield of penicillin in the existing plant with an undertaking regarding confidentiality would help the company to claim the expenditure in the revenue field.

The Supreme Court held that there was no material for the Tribunal to hold that the area of improvisation was not a part of the existing business or that the entire gamut of the existing manufacturing operations for the commercial production of penicillin in the assessee’s existing plant had become obsolete or inappropriate in relation to the exploitation of the new sub-cultures of the high yielding strains of penicillin supplied by the foreign firm and that the mere introduction of the new bio synthetic source required the erection and commissioning of a totally new and different type of plant and machinery.

The ‘once for all’ payment test was also inconclusive. What was relevant was the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of ‘enduring benefit’ might break down. Hence, it was revenue expenditure.

Despite the provision made for allowing depreciation on know-how, patent, etc., under the latest Finance Act, the field is still open for enterprising companies to take advantage of the rulings of the courts and make claims for deduction of the entire expenditure as revenue expenditure. This will, of course, have to be decided on various circumstances of the case. The amendment is only an enabling provision. The expenditure on know-how will hereafter have to be allowed either over a period of four years or in the year of acquisition itself depending on the facts of the case.

Betterment charges - Betterment charges on account of increase in the valuation of the land of the assessee should not be held as a revenue expenditure although general improvement of the area might have an impact on better running of the business [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 63 Taxman 493 (SC)].

Business expansion - The nature of the new business is not a decisive test for determining whether or not there is an expansion of an existing business. The nature of the business could be as distinct as a jewellery business and a business of cinematographic films; it could be as different as manufacture of metal alloys and manufacture of rubber products. What is of importance is that the control of both the ventures, the existing venture as well as the new venture, must be in the hands of one establishment or management or administration. The place of business of the existing business and the new business may not be in close proximity - it could be as far apart as Baroda and Bangalore. However, the funds utilised for the management of both the concerns must be common as reflected in the balance sheet of the company [Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. CIT [2008] 166 Taxman 55 (Delhi)].

Expenditure in connection with expansion of existing business would be allowed as revenue expenditure notwithstanding that same have been capitalised in the books of account [CIT v. Nirma Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 125/229 Taxman 535 (Guj.)]. However, where expenditure incurred by assessee for expansion of business had no nexus with business carried on by assessee, same held to be not allowable [United Breweries Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 8/229 Taxman 113 (Kar.)].

Business exploration expenses - Where the assessee, had paid a sum of Rs. 75 lakhs to management consultants, as professional fees for assessment of market attractiveness of assessee's business in terms of gaining global market, evaluation of assessee's business ability to compete, analysis of business's future growth trend, and development of detailed business strategies for the assessee to grow in the dynamic business environment, the said payment was fully deductible as revenue expenditure, since the assessee, with an intention of bringing about improvements in the way it did its business, had sought for and obtained reports of the consultant [CIT v. Carborandum Universal Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 347 (Mad.)].

Expenditure incurred by assessee on market survey report obtained during course of business activities of assessee for exploring further business is allowable [CIT v. Nuchem Ltd. [2015] 59 taxmann.com 455 (P&H)].

Decree to protect property/name - Payment by assessee to satisfy decree passed by the High Court against it in order to protect its property and name is allowable as business expenditure [CIT v. Hitachi Koki India Ltd. [2015] 56 taxmann.com 8/230 Taxman 643 (Kar.)].

What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a common-sense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of enduring benefit might break down [Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC)]. Fixed and circulating capital - 'Fixed capital' is what the assessee turns into profit by keeping it in his own possession and 'circulating capital' is what he makes profit of by parting with it and letting it change masters. Thus, an item of disbursement may be regarded as of a capital nature when it is relatable to a fixed asset or capital, whereas the circulating capital or stock-in-trade would be treated as revenue receipt [John Smith & Son v. Moore, (1921) 12 TC 266 (HL)]. So long as the expenditure in question can be clearly referred to the acquisition of an asset which falls within one or the other of these two categories, such a test would be a critical one. But this test also sometimes breaks down because there are many forms of expenditure which do not fall easily within these two categories and not infrequently, the line of demarcation is difficult to draw and leads to subtle distinctions between profit that is made 'out of assets' and profit that is made 'upon' assets or 'with' assets. Moreover, there may be cases where expenditure, though referable to or in connection with fixed capital, is nevertheless allowable as revenue expenditure [Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 3 Taxman 69 (SC)].

Treatment in books of account is not relevant - Where expenditure is revenue in nature, it can be claimed as deduction u/s 37 regardless of treatment given to said expenditure in assessee's books of account [CIT v. Gaja Advisors (P.) Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 389 (Delhi)].

No concept of deferred revenue expenditure - In the income-tax law, there is no concept of deferred revenue expenditure. Once the assessee claims the deduction for the whole amount of an expenditure, even in the year in which it is incurred, and the expenditure fulfils the test laid down u/s 37, it has to be allowed [CIT v. Citi Financial Consumer Fin. Ltd. [2012] 20 taxmann.com 452 (Delhi)]. Also see, PCIT v. Manugraph India (P.) Ltd. [2019] 111 taxmann.com 145/267 Taxman 437 (Bom.).

Revenue expenditure cannot be spread over a number of years even if assessee has written it off in its books over a period of a number of years [CIT v. Jai Parabolic Springs Ltd. [2008] 172 Taxman 258 (Delhi)].

PERSONAL EXPENSES

Meaning - Personal expenses include only expenses on the person of the assessee or to satisfy his personal needs such as clothes, food, etc., or for purposes not related to the business for which the deduction is claimed. Every expense to discharge a personal obligation does not become a personal expense [State of Madras v. G. J. Coehlo [1964] 53 ITR 186 (SC)].

Gifts on marriage, etc. - Expenditure on gifts made on the occasion of marriages in the families of directors of the companies with which the assessee has business dealings, friends and relatives, cannot qualify as business expenditure [CIT v. Jeevandas Laljee & Sons [1999] 106 Taxman 139 (Mad.)].

Treatment of human body part - Expenditure incurred on assessee's heart surgery was not an expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of his profession [Shanti Bhushan v. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 181/199 Taxman 280 (Delhi)]. Also see, Dhimant Hiralal Thakar v. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 177/[2016] 236 Taxman 181 (Bom.).

'Wholly and exclusively', meaning of - The expression 'wholly and exclusively' does not mean 'necessarily'. Ordinarily, it is for the assessee to decide whether any expenditure should be incurred in the course of his or its business. Such expenditure may be incurred voluntarily and without any necessity and if it is incurred for promoting the business and to earn profits, the assessee can claim deduction even though there was no compelling necessity to incur such expenditure [Sassoon J. David & Co. P. Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 1 Taxman 485 (SC)].

The word 'wholly' refers to quantum of expenditure. The word 'exclusively' refers to the motive, objective and purpose of the expenditure and gives jurisdiction to the taxing authorities to examine these matters [CIT v. Delhi Safe Deposit Co. Ltd. [1982] 8 Taxman 1 (SC)].

CIT [1989] 47 Taxman 244 (P&H)]. Consultancy fee paid towards preparation of a report on diversification of the assessee's new business activity is to be disallowed as capital expenditure [Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. v. CIT [1987] 35 Taxman 406 (AP)].

Consultancy charges on account of drawings and designs prepared by a particular agency in respect of computer software cannot be treated as capital expense [PCIT v. TIL Ltd. [2018] 93 taxmann.com 394/255 Taxman 373 (Cal.)].

Defending auditors in disciplinary proceedings - Expenses incurred by assessee-company in defending disciplinary proceedings by shareholders against its auditors are not allowable as decision of such proceedings, one way or other, would not have affected assessee's business [CIT v. Priya Village Roadshows Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 44 (Delhi)].

Where the assessee-company incurred expenses on obtaining a project report in connection with setting up another unit at a different place, the expenditure incurred by the assessee-company would be capital in nature [CIT v. J. K. Chemicals Ltd. [1994] 207 ITR 985 (Bom.)].

Capital or revenue expenditure

For computation of income under the Income-tax Act, money laid out wholly or exclusively for the purposes of business is allowed as expenditure. What is the money laid wholly and exclusively laid out is a question which must be determined upon the principles of commercial trading. In the ultimate analysis the moot question is as to whether it is the expenditure laid out as a part of the process of profit earning [see Tata Hydro-Electric Agencies Ltd. v. CIT [1937] 5 ITR 202 (PC)]. If the expenses are entailed for initiation of business, or for extension of business, or for substantial replacement of equipment, they would be capital in nature. However, in the case of a running business, where they are not entailed for extension of business, or for substantial replacement of equipment, they may be treated as properly attributable to capital when they are made not only once for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade/business. If they are not entailed for the extension of business or for advantage of the enduring benefit to the business, but made for the purposes of running the business or working it with a view to producing profits, they would be chargeable to revenue account. The aim and object of the expenditure would determine the character of the expenses. It is only in those cases where these tests also fail the Court may consider as to whether the expenditure incurred was a part of the fixed capital of the business, or part of the circulating capital [see Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)]. The words "as being of permanent or enduring nature" are not to be understood in the sense that the advantage which would be obtained would last forever. In certain circumstances, the test of bringing into existence an advantage of enduring nature may not serve the purpose. There may be cases where the expenditure expenses, even if resulting in the advantage of enduring benefit, may be properly chargeable to revenue account if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operations, or enabling him to manage and conduct his business more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched [see Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 (SC)]. If the outgoing or expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process, and not for the acquisition of an asset, or a right of permanent character, the possession of which is a condition of carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure [see Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (1953) (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)]. One of the relevant questions which the court has to ask is that : is the disbursement made for acquisition of a source of profit or income, or is it for facilitating the trading operation or carrying it on in a more efficient manner? [see Empire Jute Co. Ltd.’s case (supra)]

The word 'capital' connotes permanency and capital expenditure is, therefore, closely akin to the concept of securing something, tangible or intangible property, or corporeal or incorporeal rights, so that they could be of a lasting or enduring benefit to the enterprise in issue. Revenue expenditure, on the other hand, is operational in its perspective and solely intended for the furtherance of the enterprise. To put it differently, capital means an asset which has an element of permanency about it and which is capable of being a source of income and capital expenditure must, therefore, generally mean acquisition of an asset and the asset must be intended to be of a lasting value, while revenue expenses are generally running expenses incurred in earning profit or expenses incurred with the primary object of an immediate return or acquisition of assets which are not of lasting value and are likely to get exhausted or consumed in the process of the return or a very limited number of returns.

The nature of receipt of payment - whether it be of capital or revenue in the hands of the payee - is not determinative of as to whether the same is capital expenditure or revenue expenditure in the hands of the payer. This position was made clear by the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. (supra). Further, the reasoning of the Calcutta High Court in CIT v. Shalimar Industries (P.) Ltd. [1995] 78 Taxman 521 and Indian Commerce & Industries Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 78 Taxman 179 (Mad.) respectively, is worthy to note in this context. The facts in the aforesaid cases were that the assessee received shares in consideration of services rendered under a technical collaboration agreement with a foreign company and had shown their value as its income in the year of receipt. Subsequently, on account of the loss suffered by the foreign company and its name having been struck-off from the Register of Companies, there was no chance of any recovery. On these facts, the loss was held allowable as revenue loss despite the fact that the shares were shown in the assessee’s balance sheet in the year of their receipt as investment.

This prima facie appeals to any person as though it is gratuitous but the intendement ex facie behind it is only in recognition of the long-standing services of employees in a graded manner and also to keep the work force of the company more efficient by creating an affable environment so as to enable them to increase productivity and profitability of a company.

Therefore, the author is of the view that ESOS/ESOP benefit provided by a company to its employees as per the approved Guidelines framed by SEBI is well in accordance with the law and, accordingly, a company is entitled to claim the deferred-employees ESOS/ESOP compensation expenditure as business expenditure incurred by it wholly and exclusively for the purpose of its business.

CIT [2000] 243 ITR 158, held that cancellation of sale of assets cannot be such a subsequent event so as to change the nature of the receipt of the forfeited amount. 6.15-2e WHETHER A RECEIPT IS CAPITAL OR REVENUE - The principles that can be deduced from various decisions of the Indian and the foreign courts for determining whether a particular amount received by an assessee is capital or revenue in nature are as under :

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

■ Profit motive is not decisive of the question, whether a particular receipt is capital or income.7

■ The question whether the payer is compelled to pay has no relevance in the determination of the character of the receipt. It may be that the payee has no legal claim for payment and the payment is made voluntarily, yet the receipt may be of revenue character.8

A voluntary payment is a profit of employment if it accrues by virtue of the employment notwithstanding that there may not be any legal obligation to make the payment. If, however, the payment is in the nature of a personal gift to him, it is not regarded as a payment for services but as a mere present.8

■ The voluntary payment to a lawyer by a person who is not a client but who has benefited by the lawyer’s professional services to another is taxable.1

■ The fund out of which the money came is not material.2

■ General payments made by way of donation to a company out of benevolence or feeling of charity would not entail income in the hands of the recipient.3

■ Amounts received in settlement of a right under trading contract are trading receipts.4

6.15-2f COMPENSATION - WHETHER REVENUE OR CAPITAL - About the receipt of compensation the law is that as discussed below :

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

■ Compensation for surrender of industrial licence - In CIT v. Automobile Products of India Ltd.1, the Bombay High Court held that where the termination of the activity is not a necessary incident of the business of the assessee and the extinction and surrender of the industrial licence and the collaboration agreement have impaired the profit-making structure of the assessee, the amount received by it as compensation will be a capital receipt.

The following substantial question was referred to the High Court—

Fixed capital is what is retained by the owner and turned to profit while circulating capital is parted with in order to yield profit. The ITC had not (made) any fixed capital investment to run the hotel under the "Operating Licence Agreement". Such distinction now needs to be removed in view of the liberal approach followed in regard to capital payments covered under sections 35,35A, 35AB, 35D and36 (1)(ix) discussed earlier. It has also to be appreciated that the lease period which started with 99 years is getting reduced to much less number of years now. The issue needs to be considered from another angle also. In CIT v. Bombay State Trasport Corpn. [1979] 118 ITR 399 (Bom.), it has been said that for determining the true profits in the business sense or under proper principles of accountancy, the wear and tear of the assets utilised by an assessee for the purpose of earning his profits will have to be considered and allowance will have to be made for the wear and tear. That is what is notionally understood as depreciation on the assets utilised in business.

Accounting Standard (AS 6) on depreciation issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India defines the term 'depreciation' as follows:

"3.1 'Depreciation' is a measure of the wearing out, consumption or other loss of. value of a depreciable asset arising from use, effluxion of time or obsolescence through technology and market charges. Depreciation is allocated so as to charge a fair proportion of the depreciable amount in each accounting period during the expected useful life of the asset. Depreciation includes amortization of assets whose useful life is pre-determined.

It is true that strictly speaking, the concept of 'depreciation' cannot apply to lease premiums as depreciation is admissible, in terms of section 32, in regard only to buildings, machinery, plant and furniture. But viewed as an integrated part, lease hold lands can be said to form part of buildings' as their value is only for a limited period. In deciding the question of depreciation on the cost of land used for a building, and of the land appurtenant thereto, one has to decide whether such land forms part of the building. One can inarguably hold that such land is very much an element of building like cement and bricks. And if cement and bricks, etc., lose their identity and are no longer to be included as an asset (designated as building), there is no reason why the land (taken on lease for a limited period) should not be taken to have depreciated and lost its value and hence, lease hold premiums paid should be allowed as a revenue expenditure.

It may also be stated that there is very thin line of distinction between 'amortization' and 'depreciation'. The dictionary meaning of the word 'depreciation' has already been given earlier. 'Amortize' according to Webster's New International Dictionary, means: to make as if dead, destroy, to clear off, liquidate or otherwise extinguish - 'Amortization' or 'amortisation' is the "act or process of amortizing lands....". [Emphasis supplied]

If premium for land is to get liquidated after a certain number of years, then it is in no way different from depreciation and should be treated on the same footing. Thus, if 'lease premium' is not to be allowed as revenue expenditure then it should be depreciated along with the structure on it or even independently for the period for which the payment is to be valid.

Thus, the concept of lease premium being of a 'capital' nature or providing benefit of an enduring nature needs reconsideration. Ordinarily 'capital asset' means an asset which has an element of permanency about it and 'capital expenditure' must, therefore, generally mean an acquisition of an asset and the asset must be of lasting value; while income or revenue expenses are generally running expenses incurred in earning profits or expenses incurred with the primary object of an immediate return or acquisition of assets which are not of lasting value and are likely to get exhausted or consumed in the process of the return or a very limited number of returns - R.S. Radha Kishan Kapoor v. CIT [1963] 47 ITR 938 (All.) and Jagat Bus Service v. CIT [1950] 18 ITR 13 (All.). Further, it would be wrong to say that in all cases securing a benefit for the business is, prima facie, capital expenditure. A benefit which is merely transitory and has no endurance cannot be considered as a capital expenditure. In Anglo-Persian Oil Company Ltd. v. Dale [1932] 16 Tax Cas. 253, it has been said that if the payment of a lump sum closes the liability to make repeated and periodic payments in the future, it may generally be regarded as a payment of a revenue character. The amount and extent of a particular expenditure cannot determine its character. If an expenditure is made in connection with business itself in the sense that it is an integral part of the profit-earning process in that business, it is allowable as deduction under section 37. The payment of lease premium is certainly an integral part of the profit-earning process.

33.3.4-1 Tests evolved by judicial decisions to decide whether the expenditure is capital expenditure or not - The tests generally applied by courts to decide whether a particular expenditure is of a capital nature or not are set out below:

(1) Whether it brings into existence an asset or advantage of enduring benefit. The question of whether a particular benefit is of an enduring or permanent nature will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. (enduring benefit test)

Primary test is to see whether any enduring benefit has resulted; if this test is of no avail, test of fixed or circulating capital is to be applied. If the expenditure is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is not made for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may apply the test of fixed or circulating capital. If expenditure was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be capital expenditure, If it was part of its circulating capital, it would revenue expenditure. These tests are thus mutually exclusive and have to be applied to the facts of each particular case in the manner indicated above - Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC).

(2)

Whether it is referable to fixed capital or fixed assets in contrast to circulating capital or current assets. (fixed capital vs. circulating capital test)

(3)

Whether it relates to the very framework of the assessee's business. (framework test)

(4)

Whether it is an initial expenditure incurred in setting the profit-earning machinery in motion. (initial expenditure test)

(5)

Whether it is an expenditure to acquire a concern or goodwill (acquisition of concern/goodwill test).

CAPITAL GAIN ON INTANGIBLE ASSETS

31.1

WHAT IS AN INTANGIBLE ASSET?

An intangible asset is an asset that is not physical in nature. Goodwill, brand recognition and intellectual property, such as patents, trademarks, and copyrights, are all intangible assets. Intangible assets exist in opposition to tangible assets, which include land, vehicles, equipment, and inventory.

Additionally, financial assets such as stocks and bonds, which derive their value from contractual claims, are considered tangible assets.

31.1-1 Valuing Intangible Assets

Businesses can create or acquire intangible assets. For example, a business may create a mailing list of clients or establish a patent. If a business creates an intangible asset, it can write off the expenses from the process, such as filing the patent application, hiring a lawyer, and paying other related costs.

In addition, all the expenses along the way of creating the intangible asset are capitalised. However, intangible assets created by a company do not appear on the balance sheet and have no recorded book value. Because of this, when a company is purchased, often the purchase price is above the book value of assets on the balance sheet. The purchasing company records the premium paid as an intangible asset on its balance sheet.

31.1-2 Goodwill

The Apex Court in Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India [1970] 40 Comp. Cas. 325 has observed as below in respect of Goodwill:

"Goodwill of a business is an intangible asset: it is the whole advantage of the reputation and connections formed with the customers together with the circumstances making the connection durable. It is that component of the total value of the undertaking which is attributable to the ability of the concern to earn profits over a course of years or in excess of normal amounts because of its reputation, location and other features. Goodwill of an undertaking therefore is the value of the attraction to customers arising from the name and reputation for skill, integrity, efficient business management or efficient service".

Goodwill is an intangible asset. Where a business is taken over by way of amalgamation, the difference between the amount paid for the business and the net worth is treated as goodwill according to the requirements of accounting principles.

Section 55(2)(a) provides that in the case of acquisition of goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession by purchase from a previous owner, the cost of acquisition means the amount of purchase price. In any other case the cost of acquisition of goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession will be taken as nil.

Section 55(1)(b) provides that for the purposes of sections 48 and 49 'cost of any improvement' in relation to goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession will always be nil.

The present position relating to goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession is mentioned below:

(i)

where the goodwill is purchased from another person, the cost of acquisition of the goodwill will be taken to be the purchase price and the cost of improvement will be 'nil';

(ii)

where the goodwill is self-generated, the cost of acquisition of the goodwill will be nil and the cost of improvement will also be 'nil'.

While the questions relating to 'cost of acquisition' and 'cost of improvement' have been settled by these amendments the matter relating to taxability of the amount received for the goodwill is still not free from doubt. The point to note is that, most of the High Courts as well as the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 5 Taxman 1/128 ITR 294 (SC) held that in the case of self-generated goodwill, apart from the fact that the cost of acquisition and cost of improvement cannot be determined, it is not possible to determine the date as to when the asset comes into existence. The date of acquisition of the asset is a material factor in applying the computation provisions pertaining to capital gains and, hence, the computation provisions cannot be applied as it cannot be determined whether the goodwill is a long-term or a short-term capital asset. Of course, the department is likely to take the view that the benefit of doubt may be given to the assessee and the capital gains should be brought to tax at least as long-term capital gains.

The assessee cannot claim that he had spent out or away the amount which he seeks to get deduction of [Indian Molasses Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 66 (SC)]. Actual delivery or parting with money is not required - The expression 'expenditure' denotes 'spending' or 'paying out or away', i.e., something that goes out of the coffers of the assessee. A mere liability to satisfy an obligation by an assessee is undoubtedly not an 'expenditure': it is only when he satisfies the obligation by delivery of cash or property or by settlement of accounts, there is 'expenditure'. But 'expenditure' does not necessarily involve actual delivery of or parting with money or property. If there are cross-claims—one by the assessee against a stranger and the other by the stranger against the assessee—and as a result of accounting the balance due only is paid, the amount which is debited against the assessee in the settlement of accounts may appropriately be termed 'expenditure' [CIT v. Nainital Bank Ltd. [1966] 62 ITR 638 (SC)].

Liability - 'Expenditure' is not necessarily confined to the money which has been actually paid out. It covers a liability which has accrued or which has been incurred although it may have to be discharged at a future date [Madras Industrial Investment Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 91 Taxman 340 (SC)].

Contingent liability - Contingent liabilities do not constitute expenditure and cannot be the subject-matter of deduction even under the mercantile system of accounting. Expenditure which is deductible for income-tax purposes is towards a liability actually existing at the time but setting apart money which might become expenditure on the happening of an event is not expenditure [Shree Sajjan Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 23 Taxman 37 (SC)].

Contingent liability discounted and valued as necessary, can be taken into account as trading expenses if it is sufficiently certain to be capable of valuation and if profits cannot be properly estimated without taking it into consideration [Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Their Workmen [1969] 73 ITR 53 (SC)].

Loss - A distinction has to be made between an 'expenditure' and a 'loss' because both of them are not one and the same. Disbursement or expenditure of a trader or a businessman is something which comes out of his pocket whereas a loss is something different. Loss is not a thing which he expends or disburses. That is a thing which comes upon him ab extra. Expenditure must arise out of a voluntary act on the part of the assessee whereas loss is entirely involuntary [CIT v. S. C. Kothari [1971] 82 Taxman 794 (SC)]. However, the expression 'expenditure' may, in the circumstances of a particular case, cover an amount which is really a 'loss' even though the said amount has not gone out from the pockets of the assessee [M. P. Financial Corporation v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 42 (MP); CIT v. Woodward Governor India (P.) Ltd. [2009] 179 Taxman 326 (SC)].

CAPITAL/REVENUE EXPENDITURE

Tests to determine - If the expenditure is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is properly attributable to capital and is of the nature of capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is not made for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. If any such asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business is thus acquired or brought into existence, it would be immaterial whether the source of the payment was the capital or the income of the concern or whether the payment was made once and for all or was made periodically. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may go to the test of fixed or circulating capital and consider whether the expenditure incurred was part of the fixed capital of the business or part of its circulating capital. If it was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be of the nature of capital expenditure and if it was part of its circulating capital, it would be of the nature of revenue expenditure. These tests are thus mutually exclusive and have to be applied to the facts of each particular case in the manner indicated above [Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)]. The expression 'enduring advantage' is a relative term, not enduring in the sense of its being permanent, but is sufficiently durable depending upon the nature of the terms upon which it can be acquired [Devidas Vithaldas & Co. v. CIT [1972] 84 ITR 277 (SC)].

Lease premium and rent

4. However, over the years, the practice of getting ownership rights over land by outright payment is disappearing fast. With the availability of land becoming scarce, the system of giving land on lease is now becoming the common practice. Ownership rights on land are now, generally, not granted, The Government institutions, being the major owners of vacant lands, give land only on lease for definite periods on payments which vary from outright lump sum payments to periodical payments. In some cases, both these practices are combined, i.e., the lessee is required to pay lump sum as also periodical rents - sometimes nominal and sometimes substantial. The land reverts back to the owner after the stipulated period and the payments made in lump sum are designated as 'lease premium'. Such premiums are, in essence, in the nature of consolidated rent paid in advance for a fixed period for the use of land during such period.

A 'lease', in a legal sense, is a transaction, in which a party owning the asset (called the lessor or landlord or owner) provides the asset for use over a certain period of time for a consideration which may be in the form of periodic payments (called rent) with or without a further down payment (called premium). The International Accounting Standard No. 17 defines it as an agreement whereby the lessor conveys to the lessee in return for rent, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time. Thus, the payments made under a lease agreement are for the use of the land not for acquiring an asset or a benefit of a enduring nature. If consideration paid is a return for the use and occupation of the land or premises demised, it is generally known as rent - M. Subbiah Nadar v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 58 (Mad.).

Periodical rent paid as lease rent is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act, being laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession - CIT v. R. Tolat & Co. [1980] 126 ITR 551 (Guj.). The same consideration should apply, when instead of rent being paid periodically, a lump sum is paid when the agreement is executed (usually referred to as premium) for the use of the land. In such a situation, great hardship is caused to the taxpayers, when such expenditure is not permitted to be amortised in the same manner as expenditure of the nature already referred to earlier which is allowed to be amortised. The character of an expenditure whether it is capital or revenue should be judged from its intrinsic nature rather than by the fact of its being a lump sum. It has been held that a lump sum payment bears the same character as that of a periodic sum which it replaces or substitutes - Vanden Berghes Ltd. v. Clark, ITC 390 (HL). Also see Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd. [1965] 58 ITR 241 (PC) and Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). As per observations in Indian Molasses Co. ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 66 (SC) and Bean v. Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries Ltd. [1946] 27 Tax Cas. 296, the fact of non-recurrence may signify an expenditure's nature to be of a capital nature, but it is not always decisive.

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

Much importance is attached in this context to the phrase 'advantage of an enduring nature' used in section 37(1). 'Enduring benefit' is a relative term of contextual interpretation. It is not the law that in every case, if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure would be of a capital nature. In Girdhari Doss & Sons v. CIT [1976] 105 ITR 339 (All.), it has been observed at page 342 that the word 'enduring' means in the way the fixed capital endures and it does not connote a benefit that endures in the sense that for a good number of years, it relieves the assessee of a revenue payment.

Enduring benefit is not the acid test of capital expenditure in all cases. Even the celebrated author Viscount Cave, while laying down this test in Atherton v. British Insulated & Helsby Cables Ltd. [1925] 10TC 155 (HL) did not mean to propound a doctrine in unqualified terms. The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 had an occasion to consider these observations and it explained that this dictum is to be interpreted to see whether the benefit enures in a capital field or in a non-capital field. Where the expenditure, although enduring in character, has its impact on the running of the business, it would be an expenditure of a revenue nature.

However, the courts have treated as capital payments the leasehold premiums for acquiring rights in land. In Ramakrishna & Co. v. CIT [1973] 88 ITR 406 (Mad.), amount paid as consideration for obtaining the lease (as opposed to rent/ hire) has been held to be for the acquisition of a capital asset and, therefore, a capital expenditure. In CIT v. Banshidhar Sewbhagawan & Co. [1977] 109 ITR 828 (Gauhati), even advance rent has been held to be capital expenditure. In CIT v. Project Automobiles [1987] 167ITR 7811 (MP), lease premium for securing lease of land for 30 years has been held to be not allowable as revenue expenditure.

In the following cases amounts paid as annual rents were allowed even where the leases were for long periods:

(a) Singareni Collieries Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 553 (AP) - Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

(b) Braithwaite & Co (India ) Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 111 ITR542 (Cal.) -Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

From the above, it would be seen that there is an unreasonable discrimination between assessee having arrangement of annual lease rent and assessees paying advance lease rent in the form of lease premium as the former gets deduction under Income-tax Law while in regard to the latter, it is said that the same cannot be allowed, even on amortization basis, as the payment relates to a benefit of an enduring nature. Such distinction now needs to be removed in view of the liberal approach followed in regard to capital payments covered under sections 35,35A, 35AB, 35D and36 (1)(ix) discussed earlier. It has also to be appreciated that the lease period which started with 99 years is getting reduced to much less number of years now.

General - It is well-settled that the premium paid by the lessee for the grant of lease, whether payable in lump sum or in instalments over the whole period of the lease along with the rent, is normally capital expenditure. Had the assessee chosen to pay rent annually for each and every year of lease, such expenditure certainly would have to be regarded as revenue expenditure. 5.3.1a Treatment of free land provided by Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) to company engaged in manufacture and sale of CNG for the exclusive purpose of setting up of a CNG station at BMTC depots which shall be used exclusively for filling up of gas in the buses owned by BMTC---whether government grant and whether land is asset of the company?.-In the extant case, BMTC has given the land to the company (although free of cost) for the exclusive purpose of setting up of gas station and the same shall be used exclusively for filling up of gas in the buses owned by BMTC. Thus, although in form, it may appear that BMTC is providing grant in the form of land to the company, the substance is that it is an arrangement from which both the parties are mutually benefited, BMTC getting an exclusive supply of gas for its buses from the gas station set up by the company in its own premises and the company in the form of consideration for supply of gas to BMTC. Since government grant/assistance is generally non-gratuitous and non-reciprocal, the arrangement in the extant case should not be considered as that of government grant/assistance.

In the extant case, the ownership of the land is with BMTC itself and only right to use of land for limited purpose of supplying gas to BMTC buses has been transferred. Further, the company can use the land only for setting up CNG station and not for any other purpose such as, exchange, lease, use it to settle liability, or to distribute it to owners etc. Also, the company can use the CNG station set up on the land only for supplying CNG to the BMTC buses and it cannot use the same station to supply CNG to other customers. Therefore, the company in the extant case does not control the land transferred to it by BMTC and accordingly, the company cannot recognise the land as an asset in its financial statements. The substance of the transaction is that the company's assets (CNG station) are located at the customer's location to provide services exclusively to the customer and to facilitate the company in earning revenue from supply of CNG and from which BMTC is getting an exclusive availability of CNG for its buses in its own premises. 4.2 An analysis of the judgment - The Court upon analyzing the decisions of the Supreme Court and the other High Courts has rightly decided in favour of the assessee. Section 37 of the Act is a residuary section extending the allowance of items of business expenditures which are not covered by sections 30 to 36.

The Court correctly held that law pertaining to the enduring benefit concept for disallowing deduction is no longer foolproof. The test of an enduring benefit can be traced from the decision of the Supreme Court in Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT 4, wherein it was doubted and held that the test of an enduring benefit is not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case. In the words of the Supreme Court it was held that :

"What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitability while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future."

The case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. ( supra) is well-settled, though the application of the same will depend on facts and circumstances of the case.

1.9-4b DEFERRED REVENUE EXPENDITURE - The accounting theory and practice permit treatment of revenue expenditure as deferred revenue expenditure in certain circumstances including in particular when the benefit of such expenditure is likely to be derived over a period of years. Usually, such expenditure is written off in three to five years.

Accordingly, in the year in which the expenditure is incurred, the treatment in profit and loss account may be either of the following :

The amount is straightway debited to 'deferred revenue expenditure account' in the books. The appropriate portion is debited to Profit and Loss Account and balance is carried in balance sheet as deferred revenue expenditure under the head 'Miscellaneous Expenditure'.

Or

The whole of the amount is debited to profit and loss account and through the appropriation account, the appropriate portion is transferred to deferred revenue expenditure and carried to balance sheet.

Usually, it is observed that the former method is followed. In either case, an issue arises as to the treatment of the amount deferred in computing book profits.

As per the authorities so far available an adjustment to book profits can be made only in the following circumstances :

If the profit and loss account is not in accordance with the requirements of the Schedule; or

The provisions of section 115JA of the Act permit such adjustments.

Section 115JA of the Act, as such, does not permit any addition/reduction in respect of write off of deferred expenditure or expenditure deferred to subsequent year(s) ('either adjustment'). In that case, the only possible argument for making either adjustment could be that the method employed by the company does not reflect 'result of the working' as required by para 2(a)of Part II of the Schedule. Possibly, this argument may not stand and it could be contended that this is an acceptable accounting and commercial practice and therefore it cannot be certainly or reasonably said that the accounts do not reflect proper results of working.

A further question which could arise is that when such deferred expenditure is written off in the subsequent year, can such expenditure be added back ? Once again, it is felt that the above arguments would come into play and no such addition can be made on the ground that it does not pertain to the year.

As said earlier, it may be possible for a company to compile a different profit and loss account for the purpose of section 115JA from the one laid before AGM. If a company prepares a separate profit and loss account for section 115JA and debits entire deferred revenue expenditure to such profit and loss account, it would be in a position to claim the entire expenditure in computing book profit for the purpose of MAT. It appears that no adjustment in this behalf can be made inasmuch as it is not permitted as discussed earlier.

1.9-4c CAPITAL EXPENDITURE - As per accepted commercial and accounting principles, a capital expenditure, if written off, does not constitute a proper charge to the profit and loss account in arriving at working results. Accordingly, if such expenditure is written off, then it may have to be adjusted by adding it back to arrive at the net profit. At the same time, an amount of capital expenditure, which is not material, may be regarded as proper charge, once again, having regard to accepted accounting and commercial practices. Accordingly, such an amount cannot be added back.

1.9-5 Certain losses and its treatment - If a company has incurred loss on account of speculation or capital loss or other loss on account of fraud, etc., allowance thereof, under normal provisions of the Act, is subject to various provisions as well as compliance conditions.

However, if such a loss is provided in books of account, no adjustment in respect thereof can be made by adding the same back to net profit for the following reasons:

(a)

Such a provision would be in compliance with para 2 of Part II of the Schedule;

(b)

Section 115JA of the Act does not provide for adjustment of such loss; and

(c)

As discussed above, there can be adjustment only in respect of a liability either than ascertained liability and this permitted adjustment does not extend to such provision for loss.

Accordingly, the above types of loss can be deducted in computing the book profits for the purpose.
