FACT: • The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

HELD: Nature of expenditure incurred by assessee

• In the present case, the assessee is a joint venture between 'S' corporation and L&T. Apparently, the agreement entered into with the L&T in view of the changed relationship ensures that the latter does not enter into the same business. Although it is contended that the advantage is only by way of facilitation of the assessee's business and ensuring greater efficiency as well as profitability, on the other side, what can be seen is that the arrangement was to endure for a substantial period, i.e. 7 years coupled with the fact that the L&T had its own presence in consumer goods sector and would be able to put up an effective competition for business engaged in by the assessee, there is no doubt that the amount is to ensure a certain position in the market by keeping-out L&T. In such circumstances, it is opined that the deduction cannot be claimed as a revenue expenditure, it clearly falls within the capital field. [Para 10]

Depreciation in case of intangible asset

• The question arises as to whether a non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for seven years amounts to a depreciable intangible asset. Each of the species of rights spelt-out in section 32(1)(ii), i.e. know-how, patent, copyright, trademark, license or franchise as or any other right of a similar kind which confers a business or commercial or any other business or commercial right of similar nature has to be 'intangible asset'. The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the ownership. In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance 'in rem'.

• However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity. The right can be asserted in the present instance only against L&T and in a sense, the right 'in personam'.

However, the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) had considered the threat of competition only with reference to ‘V’ and not with reference to its founder ‘M’ in his individual capacity and, therefore, the conclusion arrived at by them could not be sustained in law. Further, the chemicals produced by ‘V’ before sale of the manufacturing plant to the assessee were being sold in a particular area, i.e., in the central and eastern parts of India and probably without any brand which would mean that whatever market ‘V’ and its founder had captured was only because of their personal rapport with the consumers of these two chemicals and, therefore, in the presence of other manufacturers of these two chemicals situated in that area ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ could enter into market for selling the chemicals produced by those manufacturers and were definitely a potential threat at least in central and eastern parts of India. 3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

FACT: During the relevant assessment year, the assessee purchased goodwill along with the running business from a firm for Rs. 10 lakhs. The assessee further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of said firm for not carrying on same line of business and other related fields for 5 years. In the computation of income, the assessee claimed the expenditure of Rs. 5 lakhs as revenue expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer treated the said expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee had purchased the goodwill and other rights for Rs. 10 lakhs which was treated to be capital expenditure. The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

It is true that a sum paid by a company to a retiring director in consideration of the director's covenant not to compete with the company is capital expenditure. Similar expenditure for buying off potential competitors that improves the value of an assessee's goodwill has been considered and advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and of the nature of capital expenditure. But, the question ultimately depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In that connection, what is always of importance is to ascertain the true object and purpose for which the expenditure in question is incurred.

The payment of the sum of Rs. 50,000 to ‘P’ was towards remuneration and/or salary. The incidental result of the employment of ‘P’ with the condition that he would have no right of private practice was that from 28-3-1957, he would not be able to give advice to outsiders including competitors of the assessee-company in its business. That this result did not bring into existence any asset of any kind was quite clear. That by employment of ‘P’ the assessee-company could improve its own business prospects and could avoid excessive expenditure by use of indigenous machinery was merely incidental to the contract of employment. That this advantage did not deprive the competitors of the assessee-company from gathering similar and same kinds of advice from other consulting engineers was a fact of great importance. There was no evidence on record to show that more competent and/or equally competent consulting engineers were not available to the assessee-company's rival competitors. Ordinarily, negative covenants of this kind contained in service contracts do not result in any acquisition of assets of enduring and/or lasting character to an employer. If the negative covenant that was subsequently agreed in March, 1957, had been part of the contract of employment of 'P' from the very inception, the revenue would not have made the arguments which now it found possible to do having regard to the circumstances of this case. The admission, if any, made on behalf of the assessee that the assessee-company wanted to ensure that ‘P’ would not offer his services as a consulting engineer to rival concerns did not make any difference to the findings made above. The duration of ‘P’’s employment was to end on 30-6-1959. By continuing ‘P’ in its employment from 28-3-1957 to 30-6-1959, on the conditions agreed in March, 1957, the assessee-company did not acquire any asset of lasting or enduring character and did not improve the value of its own goodwill and did not buy off any competitors. Therefore, payment in question was a revenue expenditure.

Note : Decision was in favour of the assessee.

Non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. It may be by way of a written agreement or by an oral understanding. There is a thin line of demarcation between capital and revenue expenditure because the object of every business concern or assessee, who is carrying on business, is to increase or enhance its profits. That, by itself, cannot convert expenditure incurred for acquiring capital asset or benefit of enduring nature or setting up plant or machinery as revenue expenditure. No test is of universal application. Its application will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In order to hold a particular expenditure to be revenue expenditure the nexus between the expenditure and the profitability should be direct and proximate. In the instant case, there was no such direct nexus. The object and purpose of the amalgamation was to acquire the distribution net work of the other company which was a capital asset and advantage of enduring nature. The expenditure in question resulted in the addition to or expansion of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee.

The expression 'enduring advantage' is a relative term, not enduring in the sense of its being permanent, but is sufficiently durable depending upon the nature of the terms upon which it can be acquired [Devidas Vithaldas & Co. v. CIT [1972] 84 ITR 277 (SC)]. To decide whether an expenditure is capital or revenue in nature, what is decisive is the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure, the nature of the right acquired, and their relation, inter se, and this is the only key to resolve the issue in the light of the general principles, which are followed in such cases [K. T. M. T. M. Abdul Kayoom v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 689 (SC)].

To find out whether an expenditure is on the capital account or on revenue, one must consider the expenditure in relation to the business. Since all payments reduce capital in the ultimate analysis, one is apt to consider a loss as amounting to a loss of capital. But this is not true of all losses, because losses in the running of the business cannot be said to be of capital. The questions to consider in this connection are: For what was the money laid out? Was it to acquire an asset of an enduring nature for the benefit of the business, or was it an outgoing in the doing of the business? If money be lost in the first circumstance, it is a loss of capital, but if lost in the second circumstance, it is a revenue loss. In the first, it bears the character of an investment, but in the second, to use a commonly understood phrase, it bears the character of current expenses [CIT v. Mysore Sugar Co. Ltd. [1962] 46 ITR 649 (SC)].

Whether an expenditure incurred by an assessee in any AY is an expenditure of revenue or capital nature leads to the following conclusions:—

(1)

If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business asset, it would be 'capital expenditure'. If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(2)

If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operations, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(3)

Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired for payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trademarks, it would be expenditure of a 'revenue' nature.

(4)

If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with the net sales. The outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of 'capital expenditure'.

(5)

If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled, the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the 'capital' nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(6)

A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be 'revenue expenditure' or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment. Thus, if the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be 'revenue expenditure'.

(7)

An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a 'capital expenditure'.

No doubt, the amount received by Telco was intended to meet the cost of construction of the hostel, and the hostel was to be Telco's property. And when the assessee made the payment, it was aware that it would be so applied by Telco. But so far as the assessee was concerned, it paid to Telco for the training imparted to the apprentices sent by the assessee. It paid the amount as training charge, and so far as the assessee was concerned, it remained a training charge, even though Telco applied it to the construction of the hostel and the assessee knew that it would be so applied.

The AAC had held that the amount represented payment made by the assessee to Telco in respect of the training scheme. That finding was not upset by the Tribunal. But, the Tribunal proceeded on the basis that under the training scheme the assessee was obliged to contribute towards the construction of the hostel. What the Tribunal omitted to consider was that the entire object of the scheme was the training of the assessee's apprentices and it was for that reason that payment was made by the assessee. There was no dispute that if Telco had not undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices there would have been no obligation on the assessee to pay the amount. One could not ignore that payment was made because Telco had undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices.

If expenditure is incurred for the purpose of increasing the profits while carrying on the business it must be treated as revenue expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee made payment to Telco on account of the training imparted by Telco to the assessee's apprentices. Trained personnel were necessary for the purpose of the assessee's business. It was necessary because a condition of the agency agreement with Telco required the assessee to have trained personnel. It was necessary also because the staff of trained personnel obviously induced better sales. There was no question here of the assessee acquiring any asset or advantage of an enduring nature. There was nothing to show that the personnel so trained were under bond to serve the assessee for a long term of years.

There was no question of the assessee acquiring any "know-how" from Telco which would become it property subsequently. The assessee had entered into an agreement to sell vehicles manufactured by Telco, and for the purpose of ensuring compliance with the agreement requiring the assessee to maintain a staff of trained personnel, it secured the training of its personnel form Telco and made payment thereof to it. It was open to the assessee to have its personnel trained from any other suitable center. There was nothing in the agreement binding the assessee to have its personnel trained by Telco. If it selected Telco for that purpose it was obviously persuaded by the circumstance that the vehicles in which it dealt were manufactured by Telco.

The payment made by the assessee to Telco was payment made wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business and it was not of a capital nature. The payment should have been allowed as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act.

Introduction

1.Direct tax laws, by their very nature, cannot remain static for long. These have to change to cater to various considerations arising consequent to change in policies, political philosophies, needs of the society, changing concepts in law, economic theories and practices, accounting principles, international relations, acts of God, need for revenue and similar other such situations. In fact, the history of federal taxes mirrors the history of a nation and by going through details concerning tax changes, one can feel the pulse of a country's development and other happenings.

Accounting concepts and practices have important bearing on taxation of incomes though accounting practices followed by taxpayers have been held to be not finally decisive in tax matters - Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v . SA.L. Narayan Row, CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 (SC) and CIT v. Cocanada Radhaswami Bank Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 306 (SC). In the matter of expenditure, accounting principles imply that all expenditure that is incurred for generating incomes it should be deducted for finding out what has been the net gain or loss. But in determining taxable incomes or losses, all expenses incurred are not deductible. Hence, in many situations, incomes, profits or losses for tax purposes are different from the actual results.

Capital v. Revenue

2. A very common controversy that arises in tax proceedings relates to concepts concerning 'capital' and 'revenue'. The disputes generally relate to whether particular receipts or expenditure are of capital or revenue nature. Normally, expenses of a capital nature are not allowed as deduction for computing taxable income. But there are provisions where expenditures which, prima facie, appear to be of a capital nature are, by express provisions in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act') either allowed as deduction in one year, or such expenditure is phased out (amortised) over a number of years. Some instances, where statute permits deduction of capital expenditure either in one stroke or over a few years, are considered below:

(i)Where the assessee incurs any expenditure of a capital nature on scientific research related to his business, the whole of such expenditure (excluding expenditure on acquisition of land) incurred in any previous year is allowable as deduction in that previous year - Section 35(1)(iv).

(ii)Capital expenditure on acquisition of patent rights or copy rights are allowable as business expenditure in equal instalments over a period of 14 years or over the unexpired life of the patent right or copy right – Section 35A.

(iii) Lump sum consideration paid for acquiring know-how for the purpose of business is allowed as deduction by spreading it equally over 6 years -Section 35AB.

(iv)Certain preliminary expenses incurred by an Indian company or resident non-corporate assessee are permitted to be amortised over a period of 10 years - Section 35D.

(v)An expenditure of a capital nature incurred by a corporate assessee for promoting family planning is allowable as a deduction in a period of 5 years - Section 36(1)(ix) .

Thus, the expression 'capital expenditure' is elastic in application and has to be construed in a business sense. Simply because payment has been made in lump sum, it cannot be inferred that the expenditure is of a capital nature. A lump sum payment can be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual revenue payments and a recurring periodic payment may be capital expenditure when it represents the payment by instalments of a capital nature -I.R. v. Ramsay 20 TC 79.

The assessee had further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of that firm whose goodwill and other rights were purchased, with an understanding that the partners would not enter in the same line of business at least for 5 years. So, whatever benefit was accrued to the assessee, was only for 5 years and not for an indefinite period. That fact was also strengthened from the agreement in which it had been set out that the recipient would not share, sell or use any information or knowledge in his possession regarding the optical trade business and related and incidental information of any manner, relating to firm, whether directly or indirectly, to or with any person or entity without the specific written prior permission of the assessee. That condition was imposed for a period of 5 years and during that period, if the partner would commit any default in observing the covenants set out in various clauses, the assessee was entitled to repayment of the whole of the said amount, meaning thereby, that the non-compete charges were paid to restrain the recipient from entering into similar type of trade or activities at least for 5 years. As such, by making that payment, assessee had not derived any enduring benefit for an unlimited period.

It has been repeatedly held by the various High Courts that once the expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred, restraining the recipient for a short or limited period, the expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase the profitability of the assessee and is not a capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee had incurred the expenditure to restrain the recipient for 5 years from entering into same trades and line of business in the same area, and, as such, the expenditure was revenue in nature and was allowable. However, since the expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in the impugned assessment year.

It may, by incurring this expenditure, ensure, at least insofar as the vendor is concerned, that the profit-making apparatus continues to yield returns, as envisaged, or in other words, continues to be as effective, and nothing more, i.e., is akin to a ‘maintenance’ expenditure. Such expenditure, as would be readily agreed, is incurred only to ensure the operational efficiency of the underlying subject or the income-yielding source. In marketing parlance, one may draw comparison (to the extent such comparisons can be validly drawn) to the profit of one’s understanding, with the expenditure on advertisement. One would easily recall a decline in the market share of a number of products in the public eye, consequent to a sudden or phased withdrawal of advertisement support. In fact, the advertisement also enables an ‘increase’ in the market share - without doubt - a prized capital asset/advantage; though, however, no firm or definite relationship can be established, in the nature of things, between the two; the success (including its level) or otherwise of an advertisement campaign depending upon a variety of disparate and subjective factors, including the intensity and appeal of that of the rival product(s). Admittedly, the assessee was participating in an auction to obtain the privilege of vending liquor. The question was whether elimination of a rival from competing with the auction will be opposed to public policy. This question cannot be considered in isolation de hors the nature of the trade, privilege or the right with respect to which the auction is held. If the subject-matter involved is a trade which could be normally considered as a lawful trade and the individual has a fundamental right to carry on such a trade, eliminating a rival trader from operating in the same field will be incidental to the exercise of that fundamental right. On the other hand, if the subject-matter is loosely referred to as trade or business but actually is not recognised as trade or business in respect of which no fundamental right exists and only the State has the exclusive privilege to indulging in such a trade or business, different considerations should prevail. In the latter case, the State may engage in this trade of a pernicious character only because it is inevitable to do so having regard to the public interest such as the absolute need to raise revenue for the State which in turn is utilised for the public welfare. It may also be a case where the State engages itself in such a business or trade to minimise the public harm, which otherwise would result to the public, if the trade or business is carried on by the citizens at large.

It is now quite firmly established that none has a fundamental right to carry on the trade in vending liquor. The right given to trade in this regard is actually a privilege conferred by the State and normally these privileges are conferred by auctioning the right to vend, in the case of arrack.

What the bidder pays to the State is not only towards the liquor to be obtained but it would include normally the price for the privilege which he obtains by being the successful bidder in the auction.

It is clear, therefore, that there should be a fair auction of the right to vend liquor and the fairness should be decided not only with reference to the competing bidders but also with reference to public interest. The public revenue is affected either way as a result of the auction. Any attempt made which has a bearing on the ultimate result of the auction and the net revenue that will be collected by the State will be an attempt on public interest. It is of utmost importance that there should be as many bidders as possible in such an auction, so that maximum revenue could be obtained by the State. Purchasing of rival bidders, therefore, on the face of it, will be harmful to public interest and the very object of conducting the auction gets defeated or diluted when intending bidders are sought to be kept away by one of the bidders.

In the instant case, the assessee had purchased a rival bidder so that he could not come forward to participate in the auction. This was contrary to public interest as well as public welfare and, therefore, opposed to public policy. The payment made which, on the face of it was contrary to public policy could not be recognized as a valid payment for the purpose of the Act. Whatever is expended to obtain an asset used in a trade or business is a capital expenditure; however, if the expenditure is incurred in the course of the business to earn the current income, prima facie it may be a revenue expenditure.

The test for determining whether an expenditure is capital or revenue, varies depending upon the nature of the business acquired. When the period of the business and the duration during which the right to carry on the trade is itself limited, the elimination of a rival from competing, while obtaining the right to trade has nothing to do with the expenditure incurred in the course of carrying on the trade. The expenditure here is incurred at the threshold to obtain the right to vend liquor. It was in the nature of investment made to set up the business and, therefore, should be treated as a capital investment. The expenditure incurred in the instant case was incurred once and for all with a view to bring into existence the asset or the advantage of obtaining the privilege to vend liquor for one year. The entire business itself was of one year's duration. The expenditure incurred to obtain this right or privilege cannot be just treated as expenditure incurred only for one year because the very business asset had a life of one year only. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that the expenditure was in the nature of a revenue expenditure could not be accepted.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the Revenue.

(7)

An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a 'capital expenditure'.

(8) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be 'revenue expenditure'. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which has to be dressed up or processed before it is converted into stock-in-trade, the expenditure incurred over it would be 'capital expenditure'.

The above principles are neither exhaustive nor intended to be. They only serve as guidelines to solve the problems that is before the Court [Hylam Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 310 (AP)].

Capital expenditure cannot become revenue expenditure simply on reason that it was incurred in connection with business activities which ultimately resulted in efficiently carrying on day-to-day business. Thus, the question of voluntary and/or involuntary payment is not material for determining capital or revenue nature of expenditure [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 63 Taxman 493 (SC)].

Ultimately, the question whether an expenditure is revenue in nature or capital in nature will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case taking into account the quality and quantity of the amount, the position of the parties, the object of the transaction which has impact on the business, the nature of trade for which the expenditure is incurred and the purpose thereof, etc. Simultaneously, each factor, by itself, is not decisive. It is the cumulative effect of all the facts and circumstances that would afford the prime guiding factor [J. K. Cotton Manufacturers Ltd. v. CIT [1975] 101 ITR 221 (SC)].

Test of enduring benefit not a conclusive test - It would be misleading to suppose that, in all cases, securing a benefit for the business would be prima facie capital expenditure so long as the benefit is not so transitory as to have no endurance at all. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, may, nonetheless, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down. It is not every advantage of enduring nature acquired by an assessee that brings the case within the principle laid down in this test. What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a, commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The test of enduring benefit is, therefore, not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case [Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 3 Taxman 69 (SC)].

Once for all payment test is also inconclusive - Capital expenditure is a thing that is going to be spent once and for all and income expenditure is a thing which is going to recur every year, but added that it was not and was not meant to be a decisive test. However, when an expenditure is made, not only once and for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, I think that there is very good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to an opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as properly attributable not to revenue but to capital [Vallambrosa Rubber Co. v. Farmer,(1910) 5 Tax Cas. 529].

There is also no single definite criterion which, by itself, is determinative whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The 'once for all' payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a common-sense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of enduring benefit might break down [Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC)].

Under section 37(1) any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession is allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", provided it is not in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee. The line that divides revenue expenditure from capital expenditure is often very thin and hazy. None of the tests evolved from time to time determine what is attributable to capital and what to revenue is either exhaustive or of universal application. Each case depends on its own facts. To decide, therefore, on which side of the line the expenditure falls, it is necessary to look at the nature of the business, the nature of the expenditure and the nature of the right acquired. If it is incurred by the assessee for the purpose of creating, curing or competing his title to capital, it must be regarded as capital expenditure. But, if it is for the purpose of protecting his business, it would be considered as revenue expenditure. Moreover, it is the true nature of the expenditure that is relevant and not the description given to it by the assessee in his books of account or other documents.

In the instant case, the said payment was required to be made by the assessee for acquisition of the interest of his brother. In the partnership to enable him to become the sole owner of the business hitherto run in partnership with him. It was not a payment made for the purpose of protecting the business, as contended by the assessee and described in the cash book of the assessee. Such payment could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of running the business. In truth and substance, it was in the nature of capital expenditure, because the real purpose of this payment was to acquire the interest of his brother in the business of the said firm, which was a profit-yielding asset and was, therefore, in the nature of capital expenditure which was not allowable as deduction under section 37(1).

Tests laid down by the Supreme Court to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure

3. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency. If the outgoing expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-earning process and not for the acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition for carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as the revenue expenditure - Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (1953) (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC).

In cases where the expenditure is made for the initial outlay or for extension of a business or a substantial replacement of equipment, there is no doubt that it is capital expenditure. Where the expenditure is incurred while the business is going on and is not incurred either for extension of the business or for substantial replacement of the equipment, if it is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is properly attributable to capital and is of the nature of capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is made not for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage, but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. The aim and object of the expenditure would determine the character of the expenditure, whether it is capital or revenue expenditure. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may go to the test of fixed and circulating capital. If the expenditure incurred was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be of the nature of capital expenditure and if it was part of its circulating capital, it would be of the nature of the revenue expenditure. These tests are mutually exclusive - Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). The expression ‘asset or advantage of endur- ing nature’ was evolved to emphasise the element of a sufficient degree of durability appropriate to the context. There is also no single defi- nite criterion which, by itself, is determinative whether a particular outlay is capital or revenue. The ‘once for all’ payment test is also inconclusive. What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way, having regard to the business realities. On facts it was held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should, therefore, be held to be revenue expenditure. Further, as the agreement pertained to a product already in the line of the assessee’s business and not to a new product, it indicated that what was stipulated was for an improvement in the operations of the existing business and its efficiency and profitability - Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 / 43 Taxman 312 (SC).

IT : Amount of fee paid to Ex-Managing Director on his retirement as non-compete fee is a revenue expenditure

Though a payment may be a capital receipt in the hands of the recipient, it need not be a capital expenditure in the hands of the payer. In the instant case, out of three distributors two belonged to the same group of companies and the third distributor company consisted of persons belonging or known to the assessee group and, hence, there was no possibility of any hindrance or obstacle from the distributors that might arise when the agency was terminated. Further, it was not a case of mere termination of the distributorship agreements, but the assessee had acquired a large sales organisation and a marketing network belonging to the distributing agents and the entire profit-making apparatus of the distributors was taken over by the assessee along with well-trained manpower. It was not a case of mere termination of agreements, but the money was paid as consideration for the transfer of a profit-making apparatus of the distributing agents as there was transfer of staff, dealership network, brand image and other marketing infrastructure and there was also a restriction in the agreements that the distributors should not compete with the assessee for a period of few years from the date of termination. Therefore, it could not be said that no new asset was acquired by virtue of the termination. Further, the business of the distributorship agents was entirely different from the business of the assessee, though the agents might have dealt with the assessee’s own products. It was a case of acquisition of a profit-making apparatus of distributorship agency for which amounts were paid to the distributors and, hence, the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount paid was a capital expenditure. [Paras 5 and 7]

The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

But, it could not be said that the expenditure should be treated as capital expenditure only for the reason that the assessee had not obtained an enduring benefit. Both the agreements and payments were made contemporaneously, as the assessee had acquired the brand right of the new product in its entirety and the non-compete clause was separately deduced in another agreement. Therefore, the non-compete agreement was, in fact, a part and parcel of the main contract of acquiring the brand right. The agreement whereby the assessee acquired the brand right for Rs. 85 lakhs and the non-compete agreement executed after paying Rs. 40 lakhs, both were to be considered and understood in unison. The two agreements were not representing two different events. The subject-matter of both the agreements was one and the same and for the purpose of declaring that the assessee had acquired the brand right of the product known as Lacto Calamine. When both the agreements were taken together, it was clear that payment of Rs. 40 lakhs was nothing but a part of the consideration for acquiring the brand right of the product. Instead of executing a single agreement for the entire amount of Rs. 125 lakhs, the assessee had executed two agreements for Rs. 85 lakhs and Rs. 40 lakhs, qualifying the latter amount as paid for non-compete agreement. The reason for splitting up the agreement was best known to the assessee. As matter of fact, it was clear that by executing both the agreements the assessee had transacted only one business, i.e., the business of acquiring exclusive brand name of the product ‘Lacto Calamine’. [Para 24]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Where assessee-firm took over running business of a trust and transfer was irrevocable, recurring payment made by assessee to trust for use of goodwill and other assets of trust could only be treated as capital expenditure
The assessee-firm had taken over a hotel and restaurant under the name ‘Vishala’ which was acquired in pursuance of an agreement between the assessee-firm and S. Family Trust. Earlier to the agreement, the aforesaid trust was carrying on business under the name and style of ‘Vishala’. Even in the assessee-firm, the trust was one of the partners. It was claimed by the assessee that the assessee had to pay a recurring expense of Rs. 1 lakh or 5 per cent of its sale, whichever was more, per year, for the use of goodwill and other assets of the trust under agreement, dated 2-6-1983. This payment was claimed to be of revenue nature and, therefore, to be deducted while computing appellant’s income.
Held that, in the instant case, there was transfer of a running business with all assets and liabilities including goodwill. There was absolutely no clause in the agreement which would indicate that transferor on the happening of a particular event was entitled to get back the running business or any part thereof. The party of the first part had no right at all to terminate the agreement. Therefore, there was complete transfer of running business from party of first part to party of second part for a consideration as provided in clause (8) of the agreement. The consideration as provided in the above clause was the total consideration for all assets including building, furniture and other assets and goodwill. The right vested in the party of first part in no way affected the passing of the property from the said party to party of second part. The mere fact that consideration was to be paid annually or through instalment would not affect the transfer of asset and the running business which was clearly of capital nature.
The conduct on the part of the assessee clearly clinched the issue that a capital asset in the shape of running business of restaurant and hotel was transferred to the assessee under the agreement. On building and other assets the assessee claimed depreciation as owner for the consideration paid as per clause (8) of the agreement. Having regard to the fact that amount in question was paid for acquiring an asset of enduring nature, the payment was rightly held to be of capital nature and not deductible.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-Assesses took over as sole proprietor, business of firm in which he was partner, consequent on its dissolution due to death of one partner-Later, he converted business into partnership firm by admitting his son as partner-Still later, sons of deceased partner filed suit against assessee for reopening of earlier dissolution and for restraining assessee from carrying on business-Suit settled by compromise decree under which assessee paid lump sum to plaintiffs as final settlement-Whether sum so paid was allowable as revenue expenditure-Held, on facts, yes
Rule of practice-Stare decisis-Applicability as between decisions of larger bench of supreme court and smaller bench.

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a partnership concern. When the firm dissolved due to death of one partner, the assessee took over the business as a going concern after paying certain money to the deceased's heirs towards purchase of their interests in the partnership assets. He carried on the business for some time as a sole proprietor and, thereafter, converted it into a partnership by taking his son as partner. Later on, the assessee was faced with a suit instituted by some of the minor sons of the deceased-partner of the erstwhile partnership, demanding reopening of earlier dissolution and restraining the assessee from carrying on business. The suit was eventually compromised, when the assessee agreed to pay them Rs. 40,000 in full settlement. He claimed the payment as an admissible deduction, but the ITO disallowed the claim since it did not relate to the partnership business then carried on by the assessee. While the AAC allowed the impugned claim, the Tribunal negatived the same, holding that the expenditure was incurred by the assessee to protect his business and, hence, was capital in nature.

On reference :

HELD: It is well settled that expenditure laid out for the acquisition or improvement of a fixed capital asset or for perfecting title or for getting rid of a defect in the title, would be capital expenditure. However, if it is incurred to protect the trade or business of the assessee or to protect his assets from attack, then it would be revenue expenditure.

In considering the nature of the expenditure, it would not be proper to proceed on the basis of the correctness of the pleadings in the suit, as the matter was not adjudicated upon by the Court. The pleadings represent mere allegations and unless the statements were proved they would merely remain as allegations. So long as there was no adjudication on the conduct of the assessee, the allegations made should not colour the determination of the issue.

In the instant case both parties to the litigation had given the go-by to their respective pleadings when they entered into a mutual compromise. There was nothing express or implied in the terms of the compromise to suggest that the impugned payment was towards payment of the balance of the purchase price of the deceased partner's share in the business. The assessee had already become the owner of the assets long ago and he had to defend the attack on the assets. This was, thus, clearly a case where the expenditure had not brought into existence any capital asset or enduring benefit. It would, therefore, be safe and reasonable to hold that qua the assessee the suit was an attack }on the title to his business and the impugned payment warded off that attack. The Tribunal was not justified in assuming that the payment under the compromise decree was the means by which the assessee had acquired full title to the business.

In this view of the matter, the impugned amount was a revenue expenditure.

The doctrine that a larger Bench of the Supreme Court has more authoritative force than a smaller Bench is relevant only as between cases which yield different ratio decidendi, and not where the one hands down a decision and the other merely lays down a dictum.

The nature of services provided by 'E' was related to the reorganization of the staff and redrawing of line of responsibility which amounted to an internal improvement in the working method. There was no element of capital expenditure involved. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit, may, nonethe-less, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down. It is not every advantage of enduring nature acquired by an assessee that brings the case within the principle laid down in this test. What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The test of enduring benefit is, therefore, not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal rights, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

In view of the above discussion, the amount paid to 'E' was essentially revenue expenditure insofar as the same was spent for improving the working of the company's staff, thereby facilitating the assessee's trading operation while leaving the fixed capital untouched. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly allowed the assessee's claim.

Thus, the expenditure was an item of capital expenditure. On second appeal, the Tribunal also held it as an expenditure of capital nature.

On reference:

HELD: It is now well settled that the character of expenditure will have to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case not by the application of rigid tests, but by deriving support from many aspects of the whole lot of circumstances and the ultimate answer would depend upon a commonsense appreciation of the guiding features.

In the instant case, the assessee had established a good reputation and market for writing inks by the manufacture and sale of ink, under the brand name 'quink'. In the agreement, there was a recognition of the formation and establishment of the partnership by A for the manufacture and sale of writing inks, similar to those made and sold by the assessee and it being a powerful potential competitor.

that the whole expenditure was deductible as revenue. It pointed out that the expenditure brought about some kind of enduring benefit for the ‘company’. Simultaneously, it must be noted that the expenditure did not bring into existence any capital asset as far as the lessee-company is concerned. The asset created by spending the amount did not belong to the assessee but the assessee got the business advantage of using modern premises at a low rent, thus, saving considerable revenue expenditure for the next 39 years. How will cases of this type be dealt with under the amended section 2(11)? Will this type of expenditure get the benefit of depreciation at 25 per cent? Obviously, further amendment is called for to take care of similar situations in the future. Otherwise, if the claim for depreciation under the amended law as it stands is denied, companies can continue to take advantage of the ruling of the Supreme Court and claim the entire amount as revenue expenditure. Much more thought has to be bestowed on the issue of business or commercial rights forming part of the block of assets. There is also an urgent need to look into the definition of ‘plant’ in section 43(3).

Capital v. Revenue expenditure

8. The question whether payment made for acquiring technical know-how will fall for deduction as revenue expenditure was considered in detail by the Supreme Court. In Ciba’s case that was a case where the Indian subsidiary made contributions at fixed percentages on sale in consideration of technical consultancy services, use of trade marks, etc., to the Swiss Principal. There was also an agreement to keep information confidential. The patents and trade marks were to be returned to the Swiss company on termination of the agreement. The agreement was to be in force for five years. The Supreme Court held that the amount should be allowed as business expenditure. The Indian company did not become entitled exclusively to the patents and trade marks at any time. It had merely access to the technical knowledge and experience of the Swiss Major. The Indian company was a mere licensee.

Will the present amendment supersede this ruling of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 ? Obviously not. The very concept of depreciation pre-supposes at least limited ownership or title. If the collaboration agreement is drafted in the manner done by Ciba of India Ltd., obviously the entire payment will have to be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On the other hand, if the company acquires complete title over the process or patents different considerations will arise. In Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC), the question was whether know-how obtained on ‘once for all’ payment for increasing the yield of penicillin in the existing plant with an undertaking regarding confidentiality would help the company to claim the expenditure in the revenue field.

The Supreme Court held that there was no material for the Tribunal to hold that the area of improvisation was not a part of the existing business or that the entire gamut of the existing manufacturing operations for the commercial production of penicillin in the assessee’s existing plant had become obsolete or inappropriate in relation to the exploitation of the new sub-cultures of the high yielding strains of penicillin supplied by the foreign firm and that the mere introduction of the new bio synthetic source required the erection and commissioning of a totally new and different type of plant and machinery.

The ‘once for all’ payment test was also inconclusive. What was relevant was the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of ‘enduring benefit’ might break down. Hence, it was revenue expenditure.

Despite the provision made for allowing depreciation on know-how, patent, etc., under the latest Finance Act, the field is still open for enterprising companies to take advantage of the rulings of the courts and make claims for deduction of the entire expenditure as revenue expenditure. This will, of course, have to be decided on various circumstances of the case. The amendment is only an enabling provision. The expenditure on know-how will hereafter have to be allowed either over a period of four years or in the year of acquisition itself depending on the facts of the case.

Brands and goodwill

9. The current financial year has seen a rush for amortisation of Brands and Goodwill. Brand valuation is now the buzz word in the corporate world. Both Goodwill and Brands are intangible. It is not easy to value the same in the balance sheet. Companies can capitalise brands in the balance sheet and reduce taxable income by claiming depreciation against such capitalised value.

On the revenue’s appeal:

the payment which would prove decisive. If the subject of making the payment is to acquire a capital asset, the payment would partake of the character of a capital payment even though it is made not in lump sum but by instalments over a period of time. On the contrary, payment made in the course of and for the purpose of carrying on business or trading activity would be revenue expenditure even though the payment is of a large amount and has not to be made periodically." (p. 38) When a person makes a payment for getting leasehold rights for use of land, he obviously, does not acquire a capital asset. The payment is made "for the purposes of carrying on business or trading activity" and, therefore, it partakes the character of revenue expenditure. In Fenner Woodroffe & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 102 ITR 665 (Mad.), V. Ramaswami, J. has observed that it is the aim and object of the expenditure that would determine the character of the sum, whether it is a capital or revenue expenditure and neither the source nor the manner of payment may be of any consequence. Almost on similar lines, observations have been made in the case of CIT v. Aluminium Corpn. of India Ltd. [1973] 92 ITR 563 (Cal.) by (Late) J. Sabyasachi Mukerjee, as he then was, who said that an expenditure would be considered to be an expenditure of a capital nature only when the purpose of the expenditure is the acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character. There is no permanency in leasehold rights.

Much importance is attached in this context to the phrase 'advantage of an enduring nature' used in section 37(1). 'Enduring benefit' is a relative term of contextual interpretation. It is not the law that in every case, if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure would be of a capital nature. In Girdhari Doss & Sons v. CIT [1976] 105 ITR 339 (All.), it has been observed at page 342 that the word 'enduring' means in the way the fixed capital endures and it does not connote a benefit that endures in the sense that for a good number of years, it relieves the assessee of a revenue payment.

Enduring benefit is not the acid test of capital expenditure in all cases. Even the celebrated author Viscount Cave, while laying down this test in Atherton v. British Insulated & Helsby Cables Ltd. [1925] 10TC 155 (HL) did not mean to propound a doctrine in unqualified terms. The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 had an occasion to consider these observations and it explained that this dictum is to be interpreted to see whether the benefit enures in a capital field or in a non-capital field. Where the expenditure, although enduring in character, has its impact on the running of the business, it would be an expenditure of a revenue nature.

However, the courts have treated as capital payments the leasehold premiums for acquiring rights in land. In Ramakrishna & Co. v. CIT [1973] 88 ITR 406 (Mad.), amount paid as consideration for obtaining the lease (as opposed to rent/ hire) has been held to be for the acquisition of a capital asset and, therefore, a capital expenditure. In CIT v. Banshidhar Sewbhagawan & Co. [1977] 109 ITR 828 (Gauhati), even advance rent has been held to be capital expenditure. In CIT v. Project Automobiles [1987] 167ITR 7811 (MP), lease premium for securing lease of land for 30 years has been held to be not allowable as revenue expenditure.

In the following cases amounts paid as annual rents were allowed even where the leases were for long periods:

(a) Singareni Collieries Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 553 (AP) - Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

(b) Braithwaite & Co (India ) Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 111 ITR542 (Cal.) -Annual lease rent is a revenue expenditure.

From the above, it would be seen that there is an unreasonable discrimination between assessee having arrangement of annual lease rent and assessees paying advance lease rent in the form of lease premium as the former gets deduction under Income-tax Law while in regard to the latter, it is said that the same cannot be allowed, even on amortization basis, as the payment relates to a benefit of an enduring nature. Such distinction now needs to be removed in view of the liberal approach followed in regard to capital payments covered under sections 35,35A, 35AB, 35D and36 (1)(ix) discussed earlier. It has also to be appreciated that the lease period which started with 99 years is getting reduced to much less number of years now.

CBDT's Error 10. The CBDT's Circular No. 599 dated April 24, 1991 is of course right in saying that broken period interest is not taxable. But the reason given is wrong. It says that interest paid as part of the purchase price is a revenue item and this should be set off against the interest received. It is here that the CBDT has fallen foul of the Supreme Court. The interest paid along with the purchase price is capital expenditure as rightly held by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra). The real reason why the broken period interest is not taxable, as canvassed in this article, is that when interest is received, the portion relating to the broken period, is actually a recovery of cost and must, therefore, be set off against the purchase price. To take a concrete example, if a bank purchases a security for Rs. 120 including Rs. 20 as broken period interest and subsequently receives Rs. 25 as interest from the issuer of the security, according to the CBDT, the cost is Rs. 100 only and the revenue is only Rs. 5, i.e., Rs. 25 - Rs. 20. According to the Supreme Court, the cost is Rs. 120 and the revenue is Rs. 25. According to accounting authorities, while the cost is no doubt Rs. 120 initially, it gets reduced to Rs. 100 subsequently on receipt of interest including the portion relating to the broken period. Since out of Rs. 25 received, Rs. 20 is credited to the investment account, Rs. 5 alone is revenue. Thus, arithmetically, the CBDT was right, but the principles employed were wrong.

A perusal of the agreement clearly points to the fact that while the consideration of Rs.1.30 crores was towards the net value of assets, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is "for obligations and covenants". [Para 13]

The clauses of the agreement go to show that the amount of Rs.70 lakhs is not merely payment towards the non-compete clause but also towards various other obligations which were imposed upon SML and had a direct bearing on the final execution and implementation of the agreement. To argue that the entire consideration was towards the non-compete fee would, therefore, be an incorrect statement, inasmuch as the clauses of the agreement do not reflect so. The emphasis in the agreement is towards the takeover of the assets of SML, and it was to ensure that the agreement bears fruition that the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs has been apportioned for various obligations and covenants imposed on SML. [Para 14]

Under these circumstances, the question that is to be decided is whether the expenditure of Rs.70 lakhs incurred is of capital or revenue nature. The consideration of Rs.70 lakhs was clearly towards ensuring that there will be no impediment in the smooth transfer of SML's factory to the assessee. It should be complete and final. From the facts placed before the Court, there really did not appear to be any serious threat whatsoever in order for the assessee to pay the non-compete fee to SML which had not even commenced its manufacturing. From the nature of the transaction, it is clear that the acquisition of SML's unit was, for expansion purposes. It was to expand and increase production by acquiring a new undertaking. The entire business with capital assets was acquired. The payment was bifurcated into two parts, Rs. 130 lakhs towards net assets and Rs.70 lakhs for other obligations and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about the agreement as also all the intellectual property and other data and information. The said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards the non-compete obligation. [Para 15]

Even the non-compete obligations in clause 11 appear to be illusory in nature and restricted to 'constant velocity joints or any other competitive products'. Clearly, the same is of limited nature and there was also no obligation of non-compete imposed upon the promoter directors of SML. In fact, as stated during the course of arguments, the managing director of SML became the corporate director of the assessee. Thus, the non-compete clause and the consideration of Rs.70 lakhs are not completely and exclusively inter-linked. The payment of Rs.70 lakhs, which is a substantial sum, i.e., more than half of the consideration paid for the net assets of the unit itself, was for a multitude of obligations and covenants which were fastened upon SML and not only towards the non-compete obligations. [Para 16]

It is clear that the consideration of Rs. 70 lakhs was not expressly towards the non-compete obligation, but towards smoothening the process of acquisition of the asset, i.e., the unit of SML in Madras as approvals that were required from the financial institutions, income tax authorities and other governmental authorities were towards the finalisation and closure of the acquisition process. Other covenants and obligations imposed upon SML, i.e., warranties, confidentiality, etc., added value to the asset being acquired. There is no doubt that in the facts of the present case, the payment of Rs.70 lakhs is a capital expenditure and hence the question of law is answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 18]

FACT: The assessee-company was doing financing business and its main source of income was dividend and interest. The board of directors of the assessee-company decided to enter into the new business of entertainment. Therefore, the assessee-company amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’, which was owned by the film star Amitabh Bachchan, and this was approved by the jurisdictional High Court. The assessee paid certain lump sum amount to the two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for the next ten years. The assessee claimed deduction of the same as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and treated the expenditure in question as a capital expenditure. He held that the payment in question was made for acquiring a new asset, i.e., the brand/copyright, that is to say, a source of earning profit itself. The Assessing Officer further held that the revenue expenditure would be incurred every year, whereas the payment to both the stars was for once and for all and it was, therefore, a payment of enduring nature and also a source itself. The Assessing Officer also rejected the contention of the assessee that the artists were not prevented totally in carrying on their profession as artists, holding that, in fact, by virtue of the aforesaid agreements the assessee had an exclusive control over the services of the artists. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee had now entered into a new field of entertainment business and this was not an expansion of existing business, but a new line of business.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the artists had agreed to perform the diverse acts for the assessee, whereby the assessee could generate revenues from them and also copyrights on the products. Thus, it was the user of brand equity obtained by the assessee and not any capital asset as such. He further held that the expenditure incurred in acquiring goodwill of course was capital expenditure, but the payment made towards user of goodwill was of revenue nature and allowable as such. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, held that the expenditure in question incurred by the assessee definitely was not of capital nature, but of revenue. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340 further held that the payment was made for the right to use the artists for ten years and, hence, the payment in question was to be spread over every year equally.

413. Mohanlal Hargovind of Jubbulpore v. CIT [1949] 17 ITR 473 (PC)

There is no definition of the expression 'capital expenditure' in the Act, and it must be construed in a business sense save insofar as there may be rules of construction applicable to it.

CIT v. Wolkem (P.) Ltd. Co. [2002] 258 ITR 350 (Raj.)

The expression 'capital expenditure' is not defined in the Income-tax Act and the words 'in the nature of capital expenditure' occurring in section 37(1) make the meaning of the expression more elastic in its application to the facts of each case. The consistent view of the Court is that the expression is to be construed in a business sense save insofar as there may be rules of construction applicable to it. The word 'capital' connotes permanency and capital expenditure is, therefore, closely akin to the concept of securing something, tangible or intangible property, corporeal or incorporeal right so that they could be of a lasting or enduring benefit to the enterprises in issue. Revenue nature expenditure, on the other hand, is operational in its perspective and solely intended for the furtherance of the enterprise.
