Expenditure on acquisition of land 3. Expenditure on acquiring land is one expenditure where there has been no difference of opinion regarding its character. Land has always been held to be a capital asset and expenditure on its acquisition has always been held to be expenditure of a capital nature. This asset has been held to be not entitled even for depreciation because the popular view has been that land does not depreciate in value by user. This has also been judicially recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v . Alps Theatre [1967] 65 ITR 377 .

Lease premium and rent

4. However, over the years, the practice of getting ownership rights over land by outright payment is disappearing fast. With the availability of land becoming scarce, the system of giving land on lease is now becoming the common practice. Ownership rights on land are now, generally, not granted, The Government institutions, being the major owners of vacant lands, give land only on lease for definite periods on payments which vary from outright lump sum payments to periodical payments. In some cases, both these practices are combined, i.e., the lessee is required to pay lump sum as also periodical rents - sometimes nominal and sometimes substantial. The land reverts back to the owner after the stipulated period and the payments made in lump sum are designated as 'lease premium'. Such premiums are, in essence, in the nature of consolidated rent paid in advance for a fixed period for the use of land during such period.

A 'lease', in a legal sense, is a transaction, in which a party owning the asset (called the lessor or landlord or owner) provides the asset for use over a certain period of time for a consideration which may be in the form of periodic payments (called rent) with or without a further down payment (called premium). The International Accounting Standard No. 17 defines it as an agreement whereby the lessor conveys to the lessee in return for rent, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time. Thus, the payments made under a lease agreement are for the use of the land not for acquiring an asset or a benefit of a enduring nature. If consideration paid is a return for the use and occupation of the land or premises demised, it is generally known as rent - M. Subbiah Nadar v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 58 (Mad.).

Periodical rent paid as lease rent is allowable as deduction under section 37 of the Act, being laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession - CIT v. R. Tolat & Co. [1980] 126 ITR 551 (Guj.). The same consideration should apply, when instead of rent being paid periodically, a lump sum is paid when the agreement is executed (usually referred to as premium) for the use of the land. In such a situation, great hardship is caused to the taxpayers, when such expenditure is not permitted to be amortised in the same manner as expenditure of the nature already referred to earlier which is allowed to be amortised. The character of an expenditure whether it is capital or revenue should be judged from its intrinsic nature rather than by the fact of its being a lump sum. It has been held that a lump sum payment bears the same character as that of a periodic sum which it replaces or substitutes - Vanden Berghes Ltd. v. Clark, ITC 390 (HL). Also see Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd. [1965] 58 ITR 241 (PC) and Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC). As per observations in Indian Molasses Co. ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 66 (SC) and Bean v. Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries Ltd. [1946] 27 Tax Cas. 296, the fact of non-recurrence may signify an expenditure's nature to be of a capital nature, but it is not always decisive.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

Internationally, the IFRS Interpretations Committee had received a request in 2019 about training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. In the fact pattern described in the request:

a. an entity enters into a contract with a customer that is within the scope of IFRS 15. The contract is for the supply of outsourced services.

b.

to be able to provide the services to the customer, the entity incurs costs to train its employees (as described in paragraph 15 of IAS 38 Intangible Assets) so that they understand the customer's equipment and processes. Applying IFRS 15, the entity does not identify the training activities as a performance obligation.

c.

the contract permits the entity to charge to the customer the costs of training (i) the entity's employees at the beginning of the contract, and (ii) new employees that the entity hires as a result of any expansion of the customer's operations.

The request asked whether the entity recognises the training costs as an asset or an expense when incurred.

Which IFRS Standard applies to the training costs?

Paragraph 95 of IFRS 15 requires an entity to recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer not within the scope of another IFRS Standard, only if those costs meet all three criteria specified in paragraph 95. Consequently, before assessing the criteria in paragraph 95, the entity first considers whether the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract are within the scope of another IFRS Standard.

Paragraph 5 of IAS 38 states that 'this Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities'. Accordingly, the Committee concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity applies IAS 38 in accounting for the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract with the customer.

Application of IAS 38

Paragraph 69(b) of IAS 38 lists 'expenditure on training activities' as an example of expenditure that an entity recognises as an expense when incurred. Paragraph 15 of IAS 38 explains that 'an entity usually has insufficient control over the expected future economic benefits arising from a team of skilled staff and from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset'.

In addition, in explaining the requirements in IFRS 15 regarding costs to fulfil a contract, paragraph BC307 of IFRS 15 states that 'if the other Standards preclude the recognition of any asset arising from a particular cost, an asset cannot then be recognised under IFRS 15'.

Accordingly, the Committee, in its September 2019 meeting, concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity recognises as an expense when incurred the training costs to fulfil the contract with the customer.

The Committee concluded that the principles and requirements in IFRS 15 and IAS 38 provide an adequate basis for an entity to determine its accounting for training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. Consequently, the Committee decided not to add this matter to its standard-setting agenda.

Therefore, based on this interpretation, such specific training costs shall be expensed as incurred and can not be capitalised.

The Supreme Court in the case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1/3 Taxman 69, held that it is not a universally true proposition that what may be a capital receipt in the hands of the payee must necessarily be capital expenditure in relation to the payer. The fact that a certain payment constitutes income or capital receipt in the hands of the recipient is not material in determining whether the payment is revenue or capital disbursement qua the payer. There may be cases where expenditure, even if incurred for obtaining an advantage of enduring benefit may, nonetheless, be on revenue account and the test of enduring benefit may break down; if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operation or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee’s business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. What is an outgoing of capital and what is an outgoing on account of revenue depends on what the expenditure is calculated to effect from a practical and business point of view rather than upon the juristic classification of the legal right, if any, secured, employed or exhausted in the process. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency.

By applying these principles to the facts of the instant case, the payment made by the assessee was incurred for the purpose of preserving an existing asset and not for the purpose of acquiring any new benefit of an enduring nature. It is well-settled in law that expenditure incurred for preserving or protection of a business asset is revenue in nature and not capital expenditure. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in sustaining the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

We accordingly recommend that all expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business or profession, other than personal expenditure of the taxpayer, should be allowed as a deduction in computing the profits and gains. In deciding that lump sum amount paid as lease premiums are expenditure of a capital nature much stress is laid on the magnitude of payments. However, in decided cases, much relevance has not been attached to the quantum of payments. In Cameron v. Prendergrast (Inspector of Taxes) [1940] 8 ITR Suppl. 75 (HL), it has been said that the magnitude of the payment is immaterial in determining whether certain expenditure is revenue or capital as the magnitude is a relative term.

In Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. v. CIT [1969] 74 ITR 484 , the Punjab & Haryana High Court has said that a lump sum payment may be a revenue expenditure when it represents the commutation of a series of annual rent payments and even a recurring periodic payment of instalments of a capital sum.

Justice H.R. Khanna in M.k. Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1972] 86 ITR 38 (SC), has made the following classical observation in the context of an expenditure being revenue or capital:

"The answer to the question as to whether an amount paid is a revenue expenditure or capital expenditure depends not so much upon the fact as to whether the amount paid is large or small or whether it has been paid in lump sum or by instalments, as it does upon the purpose for which the payment has been made and expenditure incurred. It is the real nature and quality of the payment and not the question or the manner of the payment which would prove decisive. If the subject of making the payment is to acquire a capital asset, the payment would partake of the character of a capital payment even though it is made not in lump sum but by instalments over a period of time. On the contrary, payment made in the course of and for the purpose of carrying on business or trading activity would be revenue expenditure even though the payment is of a large amount and has not to be made periodically." (p. 38)

Capital or revenue expenditure

For computation of income under the Income-tax Act, money laid out wholly or exclusively for the purposes of business is allowed as expenditure. What is the money laid wholly and exclusively laid out is a question which must be determined upon the principles of commercial trading. In the ultimate analysis the moot question is as to whether it is the expenditure laid out as a part of the process of profit earning [see Tata Hydro-Electric Agencies Ltd. v. CIT [1937] 5 ITR 202 (PC)]. If the expenses are entailed for initiation of business, or for extension of business, or for substantial replacement of equipment, they would be capital in nature. However, in the case of a running business, where they are not entailed for extension of business, or for substantial replacement of equipment, they may be treated as properly attributable to capital when they are made not only once for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade/business. If they are not entailed for the extension of business or for advantage of the enduring benefit to the business, but made for the purposes of running the business or working it with a view to producing profits, they would be chargeable to revenue account. The aim and object of the expenditure would determine the character of the expenses. It is only in those cases where these tests also fail the Court may consider as to whether the expenditure incurred was a part of the fixed capital of the business, or part of the circulating capital [see Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)]. The words "as being of permanent or enduring nature" are not to be understood in the sense that the advantage which would be obtained would last forever. In certain circumstances, the test of bringing into existence an advantage of enduring nature may not serve the purpose. There may be cases where the expenditure expenses, even if resulting in the advantage of enduring benefit, may be properly chargeable to revenue account if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operations, or enabling him to manage and conduct his business more efficiently or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched [see Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1 (SC)]. If the outgoing or expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process, and not for the acquisition of an asset, or a right of permanent character, the possession of which is a condition of carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure [see Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (1953) (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)]. One of the relevant questions which the court has to ask is that : is the disbursement made for acquisition of a source of profit or income, or is it for facilitating the trading operation or carrying it on in a more efficient manner? [see Empire Jute Co. Ltd.’s case (supra)]

The word 'capital' connotes permanency and capital expenditure is, therefore, closely akin to the concept of securing something, tangible or intangible property, or corporeal or incorporeal rights, so that they could be of a lasting or enduring benefit to the enterprise in issue. Revenue expenditure, on the other hand, is operational in its perspective and solely intended for the furtherance of the enterprise. To put it differently, capital means an asset which has an element of permanency about it and which is capable of being a source of income and capital expenditure must, therefore, generally mean acquisition of an asset and the asset must be intended to be of a lasting value, while revenue expenses are generally running expenses incurred in earning profit or expenses incurred with the primary object of an immediate return or acquisition of assets which are not of lasting value and are likely to get exhausted or consumed in the process of the return or a very limited number of returns.

The assessee-company was doing financing business and its main source of income was dividend and interest. The board of directors of the assessee-company decided to enter into the new business of entertainment. Therefore, the assessee-company amalgamated with a private limited company ‘S’, which was owned by the film star Amitabh Bachchan, and this was approved by the jurisdictional High Court. The assessee paid certain lump sum amount to the two film stars, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan by virtue of agreements for obtaining their services for 120 days for each year, for the next ten years. The assessee claimed deduction of the same as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and treated the expenditure in question as a capital expenditure. He held that the payment in question was made for acquiring a new asset, i.e., the brand/copyright, that is to say, a source of earning profit itself. The Assessing Officer further held that the revenue expenditure would be incurred every year, whereas the payment to both the stars was for once and for all and it was, therefore, a payment of enduring nature and also a source itself. The Assessing Officer also rejected the contention of the assessee that the artists were not prevented totally in carrying on their profession as artists, holding that, in fact, by virtue of the aforesaid agreements the assessee had an exclusive control over the services of the artists. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee had now entered into a new field of entertainment business and this was not an expansion of existing business, but a new line of business.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the artists had agreed to perform the diverse acts for the assessee, whereby the assessee could generate revenues from them and also copyrights on the products. Thus, it was the user of brand equity obtained by the assessee and not any capital asset as such. He further held that the expenditure incurred in acquiring goodwill of course was capital expenditure, but the payment made towards user of goodwill was of revenue nature and allowable as such. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, held that the expenditure in question incurred by the assessee definitely was not of capital nature, but of revenue. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340 further held that the payment was made for the right to use the artists for ten years and, hence, the payment in question was to be spread over every year equally.

5. The expenditure incurred in the execution/construction of BOT asset is directly related to the business of the sponsor’ s business and can only be viewed as a part of the process of carrying on business to earn profit and is revenue expenditure.

In the hands of the sponsor, the asset remains in his possession as a licencee for the limited period as laid down in the agreement. Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC), Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 1/3 Taxman 69 (SC), CIT v. Delhi Safe Deposit Co. Ltd. [1982] 133 ITR 756/8 Taxman 1 (SC).

METHOD OF ACCOUNTING

6. No accounting standards have been notified by the Central Government with respect to the treatment of the expenditure on the construction/completion of projects under the licence agreements under BOT system. However, the same having been incurred in the initial year(s), equity and fairness demand that the same be not claimed in entirety as revenue expenditure in the initial year(s), but the same be claimed proportionately in each year within the licence period against the revenue accruing from the project. This position would be in consonance with the concept that expenditure relating to the income accrued to the assessee/licencee in a particular year should be claimed in that year. If entire expenditure is claimed in the first year, it will give a very distorted picture of the profits in a particular year. The whole effort ought to be to bring the real income of the particular year to be taxed, this can only be achieved if the expenditure incurred in the initial year is spread over in the years during which benefit of the expenditure is to be received by the assessee. Even otherwise, there is no loss of the revenue, the proportionate cost of project gets adjusted against the revenue of that year.

In this connection, reference is invited to the judgment of the Apex Court in Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/91 Taxman 340 wherein it has been held, inter alia, as under:

"Section 37(1) further requires that the expenditure should not be of a capital nature. The question whether a particular expenditure is revenue expenditure incurred for the purpose of business must be determined on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances, and by the application of principles of commercial trading. The question must be viewed in the larger context of business necessity or expediency. If the outgoing or expenditure is so related to the carrying on, or conduct of the business, that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-making process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition of the carrying on of the business, the expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure. Any liability incurred for the business of obtaining a loan would be revenue expenditure.

Ordinarily, revenue expenditure which is incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business must be allowed in its entirety in the year in which it is incurred. It cannot be spread over a number of years even if the assessee has written it off in his books, over a period of years. However, the facts may justify an assessee who has incurred expenditure in a particular year to spread and claim it over a period of ensuring years. Issuing debentures is an instance where, although the assessee has incurred the liability to pay the discount in the year of issue of debentures, the payment is to secure a benefit over a number of years. There is a continuing benefit to the business of the company over the entire period. The liability should, therefore, be spread over the period of the debentures." (p. 802)

What is relevant is the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a common-sense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of enduring benefit might break down [Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC)]. Fixed and circulating capital - 'Fixed capital' is what the assessee turns into profit by keeping it in his own possession and 'circulating capital' is what he makes profit of by parting with it and letting it change masters. Thus, an item of disbursement may be regarded as of a capital nature when it is relatable to a fixed asset or capital, whereas the circulating capital or stock-in-trade would be treated as revenue receipt [John Smith & Son v. So long as the expenditure in question can be clearly referred to the acquisition of an asset which falls within one or the other of these two categories, such a test would be a critical one. No concept of deferred revenue expenditure - In the income-tax law, there is no concept of deferred revenue expenditure. PERSONAL EXPENSES

Meaning - Personal expenses include only expenses on the person of the assessee or to satisfy his personal needs such as clothes, food, etc., or for purposes not related to the business for which the deduction is claimed. Every expense to discharge a personal obligation does not become a personal expense [State of Madras v. G. J. Coehlo [1964] 53 ITR 186 (SC)].

Gifts on marriage, etc. - Expenditure on gifts made on the occasion of marriages in the families of directors of the companies with which the assessee has business dealings, friends and relatives, cannot qualify as business expenditure [CIT v. Jeevandas Laljee & Sons [1999] 106 Taxman 139 (Mad.)].

Treatment of human body part - Expenditure incurred on assessee's heart surgery was not an expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of his profession [Shanti Bhushan v. LAID OUT AND EXPENDED WHOLLY AND EXCLUSIVELY FOR THE PURPOSES OF BUSINESS OR PROFESSION

'Wholly and exclusively', meaning of - The expression 'wholly and exclusively' does not mean 'necessarily'. Ordinarily, it is for the assessee to decide whether any expenditure should be incurred in the course of his or its business. Such expenditure may be incurred voluntarily and without any necessity and if it is incurred for promoting the business and to earn profits, the assessee can claim deduction even though there was no compelling necessity to incur such expenditure [Sassoon J. David & Co. P. Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 1 Taxman 485 (SC)].

The word 'wholly' refers to quantum of expenditure. The word 'exclusively' refers to the motive, objective and purpose of the expenditure and gives jurisdiction to the taxing authorities to examine these matters [CIT v. Delhi Safe Deposit Co. Ltd. [1982] 8 Taxman 1 (SC)].

If this condition is not fulfilled and there is a possibility of there being a resulting trust in favour of the assessee, the money cannot be considered to have been spent by the assessee. The assessee cannot claim that he had spent out or away the amount which he seeks to get deduction of [Indian Molasses Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 66 (SC)]. Actual delivery or parting with money is not required - The expression 'expenditure' denotes 'spending' or 'paying out or away', i.e., something that goes out of the coffers of the assessee. A mere liability to satisfy an obligation by an assessee is undoubtedly not an 'expenditure': it is only when he satisfies the obligation by delivery of cash or property or by settlement of accounts, there is 'expenditure'. But 'expenditure' does not necessarily involve actual delivery of or parting with money or property. If there are cross-claims—one by the assessee against a stranger and the other by the stranger against the assessee—and as a result of accounting the balance due only is paid, the amount which is debited against the assessee in the settlement of accounts may appropriately be termed 'expenditure' [CIT v. Nainital Bank Ltd. [1966] 62 ITR 638 (SC)].

Liability - 'Expenditure' is not necessarily confined to the money which has been actually paid out. It covers a liability which has accrued or which has been incurred although it may have to be discharged at a future date [Madras Industrial Investment Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 91 Taxman 340 (SC)].

Contingent liability - Contingent liabilities do not constitute expenditure and cannot be the subject-matter of deduction even under the mercantile system of accounting. Expenditure which is deductible for income-tax purposes is towards a liability actually existing at the time but setting apart money which might become expenditure on the happening of an event is not expenditure [Shree Sajjan Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 23 Taxman 37 (SC)].

Contingent liability discounted and valued as necessary, can be taken into account as trading expenses if it is sufficiently certain to be capable of valuation and if profits cannot be properly estimated without taking it into consideration [Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Their Workmen [1969] 73 ITR 53 (SC)].

Loss - A distinction has to be made between an 'expenditure' and a 'loss' because both of them are not one and the same. Disbursement or expenditure of a trader or a businessman is something which comes out of his pocket whereas a loss is something different. Loss is not a thing which he expends or disburses. That is a thing which comes upon him ab extra. Expenditure must arise out of a voluntary act on the part of the assessee whereas loss is entirely involuntary [CIT v. S. C. Kothari [1971] 82 Taxman 794 (SC)]. However, the expression 'expenditure' may, in the circumstances of a particular case, cover an amount which is really a 'loss' even though the said amount has not gone out from the pockets of the assessee [M. P. Financial Corporation v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 42 (MP); CIT v. Woodward Governor India (P.) Ltd. [2009] 179 Taxman 326 (SC)].

CAPITAL/REVENUE EXPENDITURE

Tests to determine - If the expenditure is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is properly attributable to capital and is of the nature of capital expenditure. If, on the other hand, it is not made for the purpose of bringing into existence any such asset or advantage but for running the business or working it with a view to produce the profits, it is a revenue expenditure. If any such asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business is thus acquired or brought into existence, it would be immaterial whether the source of the payment was the capital or the income of the concern or whether the payment was made once and for all or was made periodically. It is only in those cases where this test is of no avail that one may go to the test of fixed or circulating capital and consider whether the expenditure incurred was part of the fixed capital of the business or part of its circulating capital. If it was part of the fixed capital of the business, it would be of the nature of capital expenditure and if it was part of its circulating capital, it would be of the nature of revenue expenditure. These tests are thus mutually exclusive and have to be applied to the facts of each particular case in the manner indicated above [Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)]. The expression 'enduring advantage' is a relative term, not enduring in the sense of its being permanent, but is sufficiently durable depending upon the nature of the terms upon which it can be acquired [Devidas Vithaldas & Co. v. CIT [1972] 84 ITR 277 (SC)].

Only support can be drawn from the judgment of the Supreme Court in Jonas Woodhead & Sons Ltd. v. CIT 11 where for composite payment for supply of technical know-how and services for setting-up plant and manufacture of products, made to a non-resident, it was held that the entire payment made could not be held to be revenue expenditure, merely because the payment was required to be made at a certain percentage of the gross turnover of the products as royalty. The disallowance of 25 per cent of the sum paid as royalty by the appellant to the English company as capital expenditure was not allowable as a revenue expenditure. This decision might have brought some exchequer to the Revenue.

On the other hand, in the decision of the Delhi High Court in CIT v. G4S Securities System (India)( P.) Ltd.12 it was held that where the payment of royalty was to be made on year-to-year basis on the net sales of the assessee, at no point of time was the assessee entitled to become the exclusive owner of the know-how and the trademark. Hence, the expenditure incurred by the assessee as royalty was revenue expenditure and was deductible under section 37(1) of the Act. The view taken by the Delhi High Court is not in consonance with that of the Supreme Court. However, the decision of the Supreme Court was on the basis that supply of technical know-how and services for setting-up plant and manufacture of products had resulted in an enduring benefit to the assessee. The Supreme Court had not considered its earlier view taken in Ciba of India Ltd.13 wherein it was held that in view of the rapid technological obsolescence, technical know-how has a short life and that it should ordinarily be revenue expenditure as held for industries like manufacture of pharmaceuticals.

Keeping in view the decision of the Supreme Court in Jonas Woodhead & Sons Ltd. (supra) it might have been possible to argue that the license fee paid by Asahi India Safety Glass Ltd. (supra) was in nature of royalty resulting in an enduring benefit, but relying on the decision of Ciba of India Ltd. ( supra) it may not be correct to contend the same. The view taken in Ciba of India Ltd. ( supra) has been followed by the other High Courts14.

Conclusion

5. The Act is very clear as to which payments have to be classified as one on account of capital or revenue expenditure with respect to expenditure incurred for computer software. The test of an enduring benefit is not appropriate for the purpose of classifying the nature of the expenditure. In order to claim a particular item of expenditure which is deductible under section 37 of the Act the following condition should be satisfied :

(i) The expenditure should not be of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 of the Act;

(ii) It should have been incurred in that accounting year;

(iii) It should be in respect of a business which was carried on by the assessee and the profits of which are to be computed and assessed and should be incurred after setting-up of the business;

(iv) It should not be in the nature of personal expenses of the assessee;

(v) It should have been laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of such business; and

(vi) It should not be in the nature of a capital expenditure.

There could be no doubt that the payment of Rs. 40,100 which the assessee made to ‘MK’ Ltd. for procuring exclusively for its benefit the services, experience and technical knowledge of ‘B’ for the manufacture of castings, that is to say, for the purpose of setting the profit-earning machinery in motion, was an expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee-company. But an expenditure for the purpose of business may be of a capital nature; and if it is of that nature, then it cannot be claimed as deduction under section 37. The question, therefore, was whether the amount of Rs. 40,100 expended by the assessee was in the nature of capital expenditure or a revenue disbursement. The expenditure was incurred by the assessee once and for all for procuring the benefit and use of ‘B’s service, technical knowledge and experience. It was not any recurring expenditure in the nature of ‘operational expenses’. With that expenditure the assessee acquired an asset in the shape of ‘B’s technical knowledge and practical experience for the purpose of manufacturing castings and certain parts of diesel engines. The expenditure was not incurred for the purpose of earning profits in the conduct of the assessee’s business. The asset, which the assessee acquired, no doubt could not be compared with factory or office buildings, plant or machinery. The technical knowledge and practical experience of ‘B’ was an intangible ambience pervading the production and manufacturing organisation of the assessee. The benefit of the services, technical knowledge and experience of ‘B’ which the assessee acquired exclusively after paying Rs. 40,100 to ‘MK’ Ltd. was an advantage or asset for the enduring benefit of the assessee’s business. So long as the assessee retained the services of ‘B’, for its exclusively productive and manufacturing purposes and expressed its value in its products, it was, a fixed capital of the assessee. The assessee acquired a source of knowledge and experience helpful in the manufacture of the castings and certain parts of diesel engines; and thus by making a payment of Rs. 40,100 secured an enduring advantage and an asset, which was a capital asset of its business.

For all these reasons, the sum of Rs. 40,100 paid to ‘B’ was a capital expenditure in respect of which the assessee could not claim any deduction under section 37.

CAPITAL GAIN ON INTANGIBLE ASSETS

31.1

WHAT IS AN INTANGIBLE ASSET?

An intangible asset is an asset that is not physical in nature. Goodwill, brand recognition and intellectual property, such as patents, trademarks, and copyrights, are all intangible assets. Intangible assets exist in opposition to tangible assets, which include land, vehicles, equipment, and inventory.

Additionally, financial assets such as stocks and bonds, which derive their value from contractual claims, are considered tangible assets.

31.1-1 Valuing Intangible Assets

Businesses can create or acquire intangible assets. For example, a business may create a mailing list of clients or establish a patent. If a business creates an intangible asset, it can write off the expenses from the process, such as filing the patent application, hiring a lawyer, and paying other related costs.

In addition, all the expenses along the way of creating the intangible asset are capitalised. However, intangible assets created by a company do not appear on the balance sheet and have no recorded book value. Because of this, when a company is purchased, often the purchase price is above the book value of assets on the balance sheet. The purchasing company records the premium paid as an intangible asset on its balance sheet.

31.1-2 Goodwill

The Apex Court in Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India [1970] 40 Comp. Cas. 325 has observed as below in respect of Goodwill:

"Goodwill of a business is an intangible asset: it is the whole advantage of the reputation and connections formed with the customers together with the circumstances making the connection durable. It is that component of the total value of the undertaking which is attributable to the ability of the concern to earn profits over a course of years or in excess of normal amounts because of its reputation, location and other features. Goodwill of an undertaking therefore is the value of the attraction to customers arising from the name and reputation for skill, integrity, efficient business management or efficient service".

Goodwill is an intangible asset. Where a business is taken over by way of amalgamation, the difference between the amount paid for the business and the net worth is treated as goodwill according to the requirements of accounting principles.

Section 55(2)(a) provides that in the case of acquisition of goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession by purchase from a previous owner, the cost of acquisition means the amount of purchase price. In any other case the cost of acquisition of goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession will be taken as nil.

Section 55(1)(b) provides that for the purposes of sections 48 and 49 'cost of any improvement' in relation to goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession will always be nil.

The present position relating to goodwill of a business or goodwill of a profession is mentioned below:

(i)

where the goodwill is purchased from another person, the cost of acquisition of the goodwill will be taken to be the purchase price and the cost of improvement will be 'nil';

(ii)

where the goodwill is self-generated, the cost of acquisition of the goodwill will be nil and the cost of improvement will also be 'nil'.

While the questions relating to 'cost of acquisition' and 'cost of improvement' have been settled by these amendments the matter relating to taxability of the amount received for the goodwill is still not free from doubt. The point to note is that, most of the High Courts as well as the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 5 Taxman 1/128 ITR 294 (SC) held that in the case of self-generated goodwill, apart from the fact that the cost of acquisition and cost of improvement cannot be determined, it is not possible to determine the date as to when the asset comes into existence. The date of acquisition of the asset is a material factor in applying the computation provisions pertaining to capital gains and, hence, the computation provisions cannot be applied as it cannot be determined whether the goodwill is a long-term or a short-term capital asset. Of course, the department is likely to take the view that the benefit of doubt may be given to the assessee and the capital gains should be brought to tax at least as long-term capital gains.

Accounting practices 12.1 General- Accounting practices are those which are followed as a matter of convention in contrast to standards which have been prescribed and are mandatory. A few of such items like treatment of deferred revenue expenditure, chit loss, and interest received during construction period are dealt with below :

12.2 Deferred revenue expenditure - Items like capital issue expenditure, preliminary expenses, technical know-how fee, etc., are treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the accounts, considering that they result in enduring benefit. However, under the Act, there is no concept of deferred revenue expenditure except when specially provided for like under sections 35A, 35AB, 35D, 35E, etc. Hence, expenditure of revenue nature, though treated as deferred revenue in accounts, should be claimed as a deduction for income-tax purposes entirely in the year in which the expenditure is actually incurred. Examples of such items are repairs and maintenance of ocean-going vessels like ships and dredgers; technical know-how fee; huge publicity campaign expenses, etc. Deductibility of know-how as a revenue expenditure and its capitalisation as plant and machinery have generated a lot of controversy. The leading authority for the proposition that technical know-how in the form of designs, drawings, etc., constitutes plant and is entitled to depreciation is the case of Scientific Engg. House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 86 . In this judgment, the Supreme Court upheld the assessee's claim for depreciation on expenditure capitalised as plant and there was no occasion to examine whether such expenditure constituted revenue or capital expenditure. The same, therefore, cannot be considered an authority for the proposition that technical know-how constitutes capital expenditure. In the following cases, lump sum/annual payments made for technical know-how even resulting in enduring benefit for periods ranging from five to ten years were held to be revenue in nature – CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 (SC), Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC), CIT v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. (P.) Ltd. [1980] 123 ITR 538 (Bom.), Praga Tools Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 123 ITR 773 (AP)(FB), Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 207 ITR 1017 (Bom.), etc. There are many cases in which this proposition was upheld and it was held that in these days of fast changing world technology, the frontiers of scientific and technical knowledge shift rapidly, the state of the art technology of modern times can neither be deemed to be permanent, nor of an enduring nature, so as to satisfy the enduring asset test. Thus, even though technical know-how acquired for improvement of technology is considered deferred revenue expenditure in accounts on the ground that the benefit accrues over a period of time, it is to be noted that under the Act, there being no provision for such concept, it has to be claimed as revenue expenditure in the year of incurring itself.

The other important issue in the context of deferred revenue expenditure is, again related to know-how, deductible under section 35AB, i.e., whether the said section applies only to capital expenditure or even to revenue expenditure. The popular opinion in this regard is that it applies to only capital expenditure, as it is an enabling section and not a disabling one and, hence, it does not cover revenue expenditure which, as it is, is allowable under section 37. Reference may be made to a recent decision in Wellman Incandescent India Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [1995] 55 ITD 338 (Cal.) upholding this contention. Yet another important issue to be considered is that technical know-how acquired for expansion of existing business by way of setting up a new project is allowable under section 35AB over a numbers of years from the income of existing business, though the new project is not commissioned and though such amount is treated as capital in the books, as discussed above. In these days of rapid and fast technology upgradation, such expenditure has to be carefully analysed and considered appropriately both in accounts and for tax purposes as between capital, revenue or combination of both. As is the case with the allowability of any expenditure under the Act, it is imperative that the deduction in this regard should also be claimed in the proper year based on express provisions and judicial precedents.

Often companies need to have their employees undergo specific trainings in order to fulfil the requirements of or in order to upskill them to fulfil a revenue contract with a customer. This may be required as a specific requirement of the customer or in order to skill the employees to execute the customer contract.

The accounting of such training costs can be debatable and often companies have treated specific training costs as a part of the contract cost.

Under Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 2015, Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers sets forth the following guidance for contract fulfilment costs:

95 If the costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer are not within the scope of another Standard (for example, Ind AS 2, Inventories, Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment or Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets), an entity shall recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract only if those costs meet all of the following criteria:

(a)

the costs relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that the entity can specifically identify (for example, costs relating to services to be provided under renewal of an existing contract or costs of designing an asset to be transferred under a specific contract that has not yet been approved);

(b)

the costs generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying (or in continuing to satisfy) performance obligations in the future;

and

(c)

the costs are expected to be recovered.

96 For costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer that are within the scope of another Standard, an entity shall account for those costs in accordance with those other Standards.

97 Costs that relate directly to a contract (or a specific anticipated contract) include any of the following:

(a)

direct labour (for example, salaries and wages of employees who provide the promised services directly to the customer);

(b)

direct materials (for example, supplies used in providing the promised services to a customer);

(c)

allocations of costs that relate directly to the contract or to contract activities (for example, costs of contract management and supervision, insurance and depreciation of tools and equipment used in fulfilling the contract);

(d)

costs that are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract; and

(e)

other costs that are incurred only because an entity entered into the contract (for example, payments to subcontractors).

98 An entity shall recognise the following costs as expenses when incurred:

(a)

general and administrative costs (unless those costs are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract, in which case an entity shall evaluate those costs in accordance with paragraph 97);

(b)

costs of wasted materials, labour or other resources to fulfil the contract that were not reflected in the price of the contract;

(c)

costs that relate to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations) in the contract (ie costs that relate to past performance);

and

(d)

costs for which an entity cannot distinguish whether the costs relate to unsatisfied performance obligations or to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations).

Therefore, based on the above guidance, if an entity incurs costs for training its staff specifically in order to execute a revenue contract with customers or as a requirement of the customer contracts, the cost may fit into a contract fulfilment cost. This is because, the training costs would relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that can be specifically identified and would generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying performance obligations towards the customers in the future.

However, the conflict arises in Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets, which states as follows:

5 This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (eg a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, ie the knowledge embodied in it.

Ind AS 38 acknowledges that an entity usually has insufficient control over the future economic benefits arising from an assembled workforce (i.e. a team of skilled workers, or specific management or technical talent) or from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset.

Therefore, this guidance would require specific training costs to be recognised as expense as incurred.

A question, therefore, arises as to whether such training costs can be capitalised under Ind AS 115 since they would fulfil the definition of fulfilment costs.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

1.1-4 Non-compete for profession - The amendment provides for taxing any sum received for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business. Does it cover any sum received for not carrying out any activity in relation to any profession? The matter is not free from doubt. The Supreme Court has held in Barendra Prasad Ray v. ITO [1981] 129 ITR 295 that the expression 'business' is one of wide import and it means an activity carried on continuously and systematically by a person by the application of his labour and skill with a view to earning an income. In that case the Supreme Court held that the expression 'business connection' used in section 9(1) of the Act includes professional connection. On the other hand, the CBDT has clarified that section 55 (which provides that the cost of acquisition of goodwill of a business shall be nil) shall not apply to professional firms (para 28.3 of Circular No. 495, dated 22-9-1987). This indicates that the Board has interpreted the term business to exclude profession.

1.1-5 Tax implication in the hands of the payer - The new provision has been introduced to override the Court judgments, which held that sum received for restrictive covenant is a capital receipt. However, there is no corresponding amendment to provide that the payee would get deduction as revenue expenditure. In many cases, Courts have held that amount paid by assessee as non-compete charges is capital expenditure and hence not allowable as deduction [Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT 27 ITR 34 (SC), CIT v. Hindustan Pilkington Glass Works 139 ITR 601 (Cal.), Chelpark Co. Ltd. v. CIT 191 ITR 249 (Mad.)]. Hence, while the recipient will get taxed under the new provisions, the payer may not get a deduction on the basis of the aforesaid judgments.

General - It is well-settled that the premium paid by the lessee for the grant of lease, whether payable in lump sum or in instalments over the whole period of the lease along with the rent, is normally capital expenditure. The periodical payment made for a lease is revenue expenditure whereas the payment made to acquire the lease would be an expenditure of capital nature [CIT v. Muhammad Hussain [2001] 114 Taxman 553 (J&K)]. Acquisition of leasehold rights - Expenditure incurred by assessee for acquisition of leasehold right for setting up of sugar factory was capital expenditure [Gobind Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1998] 232 ITR 319 (SC)]. Also see, Enterprising Enterprises v. DCIT [2007] 160 Taxman 188 (SC).

Advance lease rent - Assessee taken a land of lease on monthly rent for 15 years and was required to pay rent in advance for entire lease period in the form of guarantee deposit which was adjustable against rent of each month. Since payment was not actually a yearly payment but a capital expenditure for achieving enduring benefit over years, therefore, would not be allowable as revenue expenditure [Aditya Minerals (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 106 Taxman 337 (SC)].

Where the assessee holding leasehold for 48 years chose to pay the rent for 47 years in one lump sum with the consent of the lessor, and got no other advantage by reason of the lump sum payment except the relief of not having to make the annual payment during the period of lease, such lump sum payment is allowable as revenue expenditure. Had the assessee chosen to pay rent annually for each and every year of lease, such expenditure certainly would have to be regarded as revenue expenditure. The fact that the payment was made in lump sum for the entire duration of the lease did not alter the character of it being a revenue expenditure [CIT v. Gemini Arts (P.) Ltd. [2003] 128 Taxman 105 (Mad.)]. Also see, Coforge Ltd. v. ACIT [2021] 128 taxmann.com 99 (Delhi).

Construction on leased property - Construction made on a leased-out property cannot be treated as capital expenditure [Indus Motor Co. (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 229/[2018] 253 Taxman 97 (Ker.), SLP granted inDCIT v. Indus Motor Co. (P.) Ltd. [2018] 96 taxmann.com 220/257 Taxman 259 (SC)].

Where assessee to run its milk parlour put up structure on a leased land and in next year because of non-renewal of agreement said structure was demolished, expenditure incurred on construction of structure was allowable as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Gujarat Co-op. Milk Marketing Federation Ltd. [2014] 43 taxmann.com 398/[2015] 228 Taxman 267 (Guj.)].

Consultancy charges for renewal of lease - Where the assessee paid fees towards consultancy and assistance provided for preparation of application for renewing an existing mining lease, the fees so paid could not be said to be a capital expenditure, since the payment was made only to facilitate extension of lease and the renewal of the lease did not result in any benefit of enduring nature to the assessee [CIT v. Wolkem (P.) Ltd. [2003] 131 Taxman 84 (Raj.)].

Demolition and reconstruction - Where the assessee took premises on lease for 39 years, and then incurred expenditure on demolition and new construction to suit its business requirements, resulting in considerable savings by way of rent liability, the expenditure is allowable as revenue expenditure, since the asset created by spending the amount did not belong to the assessee but the assessee got the business advantage of using modern premises at a lower rent, thus saving considerable revenue expenditure for the next 39 years [CIT v. Madras Auto Services (P.) Ltd. [1998] 99 Taxman 575 (SC)].

Depressed rent - Where assessee made advance payment of rent in respect of leasehold premises, since advance rent was in nature of depressed rent, payment made in respect of same was rightly treated as revenue expenditure [Balmer Lawrie & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [2019] 111 taxmann.com 316 (Cal.)].

Encroachment - Where assessee had taken on lease a plot of land from Calcutta Port Trust (CPT) and it had encroached some of land belonging to CPT and on being asked paid certain amount to CPT to compensate loss suffered by CPT, payment to CPT was an expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for purposes of business and, hence, allowable [Mundial Export Import Finance (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 67 taxmann.com 31/238 Taxman 34 (Cal.)].

In that sense, it, thus, helps the dealer in carrying on or running or managing the business of share dealer/dealings or share brokerage efficiently and profitably without creating in his favour any advantage of enduring benefit on capital field. [Para 7.30] It was not in dispute that the said dealership was not transferable and neither the admission fee was refundable in any case. Even if the assessee decided or forced to terminate the dealership or if the OTCEI terminated the dealership, the admission fee was not refundable to the assessee as was clearly evident from the terms and conditions of appointment as a dealer of OTCEI. Similarly, the payment of technology cost for providing training to the assessee’s employees for the purpose of making them qualified as per OTCEI’s qualification procedure was found to be necessary or condition precedent for carrying on day-to-day business as a dealer on OTCEI and to operate the counter thereof. The aim and object of the aforesaid expenditures were, thus, for carrying on the assessee’s business and as such those were of the revenue in nature. On the facts of the case, there was no reason to hold that the assessee had derived an advantage of enduring nature on capital field or otherwise had acquired any capital asset. [Para 7.31]

The appointment as a dealer on the OTCEI could not be equated to the Stock Exchange membership of the Calcutta Stock Exchange. It is settled that if the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee’s trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of the assessee’s business to be carried on more effectively or more profitably while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on the revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future. The criteria of ‘once and for all’ payment did not render the payments in question as of capital in nature as it is settled that the expression ‘once and for all’ is used to denote an expenditure which is made once and for all for procuring an enduring benefit to business in capital filed as distinguished from a recurring expenditure in the nature of operational expenses. In the instant case, the expenditure had been incurred for running the business of share dealing and share brokerage as an integral part of the profit-earning process or operation. What was material was the nature and substance of the payment. The purport and object of becoming dealer on OTCEI was to facilitate the assessee’s trading operations or to enable the assessee to carry on its business more efficiently, extensively and profitably in the background of rapidly changing and advancing economic realities of stock business. [Para 7.32]

Therefore, the payment of admission fee to become a dealer on OTCEI and to operate the counter, and the payment for imparting training to the assessee’s employees so as to make them qualified as per guidelines laid down by OTCEI were to be held as the revenue expenditure and the orders of the authorities below were to be set aside on that issue. "What is required to be seen is the real intent and purpose of the expenditure and whether the expenditure results in creation of fixed capital for the assessee? It is important to bear in mind that what is required to be seen is not whether the advantage obtained lasts forever but whether the expense incurred does away with a recurring expenses defrayed towards running a business as against an expense undertaken for the benefit of the business as a whole?" Laying down the abovementioned test the Court held that in cases which deal with technology and software application, which do not in any manner supplant the source of income or add to the fixed capital of the assessee, test of an enduring benefit or an advantage will collapse.2 On facts, after examining the order of the Tribunal, the Court held as under :

"The fact that the application software would have to be updated from time-to-time based on the requirements of the assessee in the context of advancement of its business and its diversification, if any, the changes brought about due to statutory amendments by law or professional bodies like the ICAI, which are given the responsibility of conceiving and formulating accounting standards from time-to-time, and perhaps also, by reason of the fact that expenses may have to be incurred on account of corruption of the software due to unintended or intended ingress into the systemâ€"ought not give a colour to the expenditure incurred as one expended on capital account."

The Court also went into the question raised by the Revenue that the assessee had not written off the expense in issue; the nature of expense ought to be on capital account. This was rejected and answered by the Court stating that an assessee cannot be denied a claim for deduction which is otherwise tenable, in law, on the ground that assessee had treated it differently in its books.3

4.2 An analysis of the judgment - The Court upon analyzing the decisions of the Supreme Court and the other High Courts has rightly decided in favour of the assessee. Section 37 of the Act is a residuary section extending the allowance of items of business expenditures which are not covered by sections 30 to 36.

The Court correctly held that law pertaining to the enduring benefit concept for disallowing deduction is no longer foolproof. The test of an enduring benefit can be traced from the decision of the Supreme Court in Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT 4, wherein it was doubted and held that the test of an enduring benefit is not a certain or conclusive test and it cannot be applied blindly and mechanically without regard to the particular facts and circumstances of a given case. In the words of the Supreme Court it was held that :

"What is material to consider is the nature of the advantage in a commercial sense and it is only where the advantage is in the capital field that the expenditure would be disallowable on an application of this test. If the advantage consists merely in facilitating the assessee's trading operations or enabling the management and conduct of assessee's business to be carried on more efficiently or more profitability while leaving the fixed capital untouched, the expenditure would be on revenue account, even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future."

The case of Empire Jute Co. Ltd. ( supra) is well-settled, though the application of the same will depend on facts and circumstances of the case.

We shall now deal with the cases which pertain to expenditure incurred on computer software. Section 35A of the Act deals with capital expenditure, i.e., the price paid for the purchase of copyrights5 or patent rights, and applies only to expenditure incurred after 28 February, 1966 but before 1 April, 19986. In respect of capital expenditure on acquisition of a patent right or copyrights on or after 1 April, 1998 depreciation is allowable at 25 per cent on the written down value7. On the other hand, payments made for the right to use patents8 or a copyright is allowable under section 37 as a revenue expenditure.

In the present case, it was very well appreciated by the Court that the agreement entered into by the assessee was only a license agreement, hence, the expenditure incurred on procurement of a license of the software was held to be an expenditure deductible under section 37 of the Act.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1), read with section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Capital asset) - Assessment year 2010-11 - During relevant year, assessee, a foreign company, had acquired third party debt collection services as well as part of analytical business of its Indian counterpart as going concern on "as is where is basis" - Out of total consideration, assessee paid certain amount towards acquisition of tangible assets, and remaining amount as payment towards customer contracts, which it claimed as revenue expenditure - Being of view that such expenditure had given enduring benefits to assessee, Assessing Officer treated said expenditure as capital in nature - It was found that assessee had made payment for acquiring customer contracts and assembled workforce, which were nothing but capital assets and would give enduring benefits to assessee, and assessee was not in said business - Whether expenditure incurred for acquiring completely new business set up was income generation tool and, hence, capital in nature - Held, yes - Whether, however, when payment made by assessee was not disputed and was in terms of an agreement between two parties, Commissioner (Appeals) could not arbitrarily and unitarily reduce a part of payment made for computing depreciation - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [Partly in favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether to come to conclusion that an expenditure is capital in nature, tests to be applied are where expenditure is incurred to set up a business or for acquiring a new business or another business in same line, to commence a business, to acquire a benefit of enduring nature or for perpetuity, to acquire an asset and to acquire a source of generating income - Held, yes - Assessee purchased right, titles and ownership of two magazines/periodicals and agreement entered into between assessee and seller of two titles provided, inter alia, that seller was owner and publisher of titles, which were free from all charges, liens and encumbrances and assessee could, after purchase, use title and information in course of its

Acquisition, amalgamation, etc., of companies - Expenditure incurred towards professional charges of solicitors for effecting amalgamation was deductible as a revenue expenditure [CIT v. Bombay Dyeing & Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1996] 85 Taxman 396 (SC)].

Expenditure incurred in the nature of legal and professional fees for various services in connection with acquisition of a French company towards expansion of assessee's business in Europe held allowable [Elgi Equipments Ltd. v. JCIT [2020] 120 taxmann.com 142/[2021] 276 Taxman 141 (Mad.)].

Bonus shares - Payment made by assessee-company by way of legal and consultation fee in connection with issue of bonus shares is expenditure of revenue nature [Warner Hindustan Ltd. v. CIT [1988] 36 Taxman 106 (AP)].

Civil and criminal litigation both are includible - Section 37(1) does not make any distinction between civil litigation and criminal litigation. All that has to be seen is whether the legal expenses were incurred by the assessee in his character as a trader [CIT v. Dhanrajgirji Raja Narasingirji [1973] 91 ITR 544 (SC)]. However, it cannot be said that in every case the expenses incurred by a person exercising a trade or profession in defending a criminal prosecution, which arises out of his business or professional activities should be allowed to be deducted in the assessment of his profits or gains for income-tax purposes [CIT v. H. Hirjee [1953] 23 ITR 427 (SC)].

Legal expenses incurred by the assessee in connection with criminal litigation pertaining to criminal conspiracy for commission of offence under Essential Commodities Act, 1955 were allowable as deduction [Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 47 Taxman 244 (P&H)].
